Before he could finish his words, the captain's pistol fired. The old worker fell limply to the ground, his blood splattering on the machine. The captain waved his hand, letting two soldiers drag the body aside, and finally repeated: “Resistance will be treated as treason.”
A few minutes later, the military truck's engine roared to life and sped off into the distance. The workers glanced at each other, then numbly returned to their posts, silently reciting that supreme iron law.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.116.t: Dancers at the End of the World
strings.OMS_more_flavor.116.desc:
The television was the only source of light in Nina's living room. On the screen, a girl in traditional costume was clumsily dancing to 'Swan Lake,' her smile as stiff as a mask. This was one of the few entertainment programs approved by the League, meant to remind people of 'pure Russian traditions.' But Nina knew that behind that smile, there was nothing.

Suddenly, the picture was cut. Snow danced frantically on the screen, emitting a harsh, unsettling hiss. Then, a face filled the entire screen—it was a face without expression, belonging to some League official she had never seen before. His eyes were like two black glass beads, staring into the depths of the living room, as if they could penetrate the screen and see into Nina's soul.

“Citizens,” the voice was cold and monotonous, devoid of any emotion, “from this moment on, all television broadcast content will undergo 'purification.' Any non-Russian, decadent, or defeatist imagery will be completely erased.”

A series of unsettling images began to flash on the screen. A man being executed by firing squad, condemned as a 'cultural traitor' for possessing a novel by the Teutonic barbarians. A pit filled with books and scrolls on fire, the flames consuming those 'reactionary' ideas. A group of children, expressionless, reciting slogans of hatred for the Germans mechanically into the camera.

“Entertainment is poison, unless it serves the Great Trial!” the official's voice continued, like a cold scalpel dissecting Nina's last illusions. “We will fill every pixel with the pure Russian will. Your eyes will only see what the League wants you to see. Your minds will only contain the ideas the League instills in you.”

The program resumed. The girl began to dance again, but her smile, to Nina, had turned into a hideous grimace. The television was no longer a window to entertainment, but an eye belonging to the League, growing out of the wall, always open. It was monitoring, judging, reforming.

A bone-deep chill ran through Nina. She wanted to turn off the television, but her hand froze in mid-air. She was afraid that if she reached out, the eye on the screen would notice her, would see the fear and loathing in her heart. So she could only sit stiffly, letting the cold light dye her living room, her world, a deep black.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.116.a: Dance with the rhythm of the triple jump, until the end of the world comes.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.117.desc:
The wind howled through the passes of the Ural Mountains, like the wailing of lost souls. With fingers turned purple from the cold, Vadim secured another icy steel bar to the concrete wall. His breath condensed into white mist in the thin air, quickly dispersed by the wind. Here, he felt as small as a grain of sand.

Below him was a bottomless pit, a giant cavity being greedily hollowed out inside the mountain, ready to devour millions of Russian souls. Above him, the heavy, grey sky seemed poised to rain down the nuclear fire of the Germans at any moment.

“Hurry up, you lazy bone!” The foreman's whip cracked against the rock beside him, striking sparks. “The Commander-in-Chief has no time for you to dawdle! Every second of delay could turn a thousand Russian families into charcoal in the nuclear winter!”

Vadim didn't speak, just quickened his movements. He had once been a bridge engineer, dreaming of building magnificent structures to connect cities and people. Now, he was building a giant tomb. A tomb designed to let some live, by permanently burying others.

He looked up, into the distance. Tens of thousands of figures crawled among the mountains, like ants driven by an unseen hand. They were prisoners, dissenters, and those 'insufficiently loyal' civilians. Their flesh and blood were being used to cast the foundation of this 'national strategic fortification.' Every day, people fell from the scaffolding, their screams instantly swallowed by the roar of the wind and machinery, leaving not even a faint echo.

On the League's propaganda broadcasts, this place was depicted as Russia's last hope, a 'Noah's Ark' to withstand the apocalypse. But Vadim knew that this whole damn 'Great Trial' was nothing more than a Don Quixote-like charge by a group of self-aggrandizing old generals, and this bunker was merely to ensure that the survivors could once again judge that group of Germans after the 'Great Trial.'

As night fell, he dragged his exhausted body back to the crude barracks. Lying on the cold bunk, he closed his eyes but could not sleep. The sound of explosions from deep within the mountain, like the heartbeat of a giant beast, vibrated through his bones, and through his long-numb heart.

He thought of his wife and child. Had they secured a place in this fortress? Or would they too become dust scattered in the nuclear firestorm? This thought was more bone-chilling than the Ural wind.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.117.a: But he had no choice but to labor on mechanically.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.118.desc:
Nikita Voronov's oil-stained fingers gently caressed the old lathe his father had left him. This machine had been the pride of his family for three generations, the heart of the Voronov Machine Works. It had produced plowshares, tractor parts, and even, during the first West Russian War, secretly forged gun barrels for the resistance. It had witnessed the rise and fall of the Voronov family, a testament to their humble yet resilient survival.

Today, that heart was about to stop beating.

The factory gates were violently smashed open, and two League officials walked in. Their black uniforms were like two moving shadows, instantly draining all light from the workshop. The one in the lead, his face bearing a bureaucratic indifference, unfolded a document and read from it in a tone devoid of any emotion.

“By order of the Commander-in-Chief, Directive 734, to ensure the absolute victory of the Great Trial, the Voronov Machine Works is hereby nationalized, effective immediately. All assets, equipment, and personnel will be incorporated into the 12th Military-Industrial Production Combine.”

Nikita felt his blood run cold. He wanted to protest, to scream, to ask them by what right they were taking everything from him. But when he saw the rifles gripped tightly in the hands of the two soldiers behind the officials, all words were stuck in his throat, turning into a silent tremble.

“You can't…” were the only words he could finally squeeze out, his voice as faint as a dying sigh.

“‘Can't’?” The official let out a disdainful laugh, a sound as grating as scraping metal. “Citizen, your 'can't' is a betrayal of our great cause. Private interest is a cancer, inefficiency is collaboration with the enemy. Your factory will either spit out artillery shells for Russia, or it will be reduced to the dust of history, along with you.”

He waved his hand, and several workers were prodded with rifle butts by the soldiers, and began to affix new numbered labels to the lathes. The cold white labels, like so many tombstones, proclaimed the death of the Voronov Machine Works.

The official walked up to Nikita and slapped a new production plan against his chest. “Starting tomorrow, this place will produce only one thing—7.62mm caliber bullet casings. Your new quota is fifty thousand per day. Fail to meet it, and you'll face the consequences.”

The official turned and left, leaving Nikita alone in his 'requisitioned' factory. He looked at the cold lathe, at the faded photograph of his father on the wall, at the sky outside the window, dyed grey-black by industrial smog. He suddenly realized that he, and everything he held dear, was nothing more than a cog in the great war machine named the 'Black League'—a cog that could be replaced, be crushed, at any moment.

All of Russia had become a giant arsenal, and all of them were nameless prisoners within it.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.118.a: Every cog of the Motherland must turn for vengeance.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.119.desc:
Irina's fingertips gently traced the silk dress, the cool, smooth texture a brief respite from the lead-grey sky outside and the coal-dust-laden air. It was her wedding dress, the last bright spot in her drab life, a dangerous secret of past tenderness.

A knock like a warhammer struck the door, brutal and unanswerable. Irina's heart seized. She hastily shoved the dress into the deepest corner under her bed, covering it with a pile of grey, regulation-issue, coarse-cloth work clothes.

The door was pushed open without waiting for her reply. Two 'Economic Purification Commissars' in black uniforms entered, their eyes sweeping the humble apartment like searchlights.

“Citizen Irina Petrovna,” one said, his face expressionless, his voice like rusted iron scraping, “in accordance with the Commander-in-Chief's 'Eliminate Redundancy' decree, we will inspect your residence and remove all non-essential, luxurious, and morale-corrupting items that weaken Russia's fighting will.”

They set to work. A carved wooden jewelry box was thrown to the floor, shattering, its few cheap glass trinkets scattering, only to be crushed under merciless military boots. A fairy tale book with a faded cover was torn in two, its colored illustrations fluttering in the air like butterflies with broken wings. A small landscape painting was taken down from the wall, its frame smashed in a corner.

Irina stood frozen, ice-cold. She watched as her small home was flayed, bone by bone, all useful things defined as 'redundant' and then violently confiscated. Her home was becoming a cage as drab and grey as the world outside.

A commissar's gaze settled under the bed. He bent down, reached under, and violently pulled out the silk dress.

“What is this?” he held up the garment, a trace of cruel mockery in his tone. “Silk? On the eve of the Great Trial, does anyone still need such a thing? This is weakening our nation, this is aiding our enemies!”

“No! Please!” Irina rushed forward, trying to snatch the dress back, but the other commissar shoved her brutally to the ground with his rifle butt.

The commissar confiscated the silk and other 'redundant items,' then glanced at Irina.

“Purification complete,” the commissar said as he turned to leave. “Remember, citizen. In the new Russia, the only permitted luxury is hatred for the enemy.”

The door closed. Only Irina remained in the room. The last wisp of color in the air had dissipated, leaving only a living corpse.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.119.a: This is the most dreadful tomb of the living dead, and the worst part is, living here is no different from being dead.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.120.desc:
The recruiting officer's boots trod on the muddy path, splattering mud onto his polished leather. He paid it no mind. Lieutenant Ivan Zakharov's thoughts were already consumed by the deathly silence of the village before him.

There used to be chimney smoke here, the laughter of children, the brawls of drunkards outside the tavern. Now, there was only the wind whining through the empty houses, like a mother weeping for her dead child.

He knocked on door after door. Behind them were numb, gaunt faces. The women had no tears, for their tears had long since run dry. The old men's eyes held no light, for hope had long been extinguished.

“By order of the Commander-in-Chief, Emergency Mobilization Order 901,” Ivan's voice echoed in the empty rooms, unnaturally loud, “all able-bodied male citizens between the ages of sixteen and sixty must immediately assemble at the village square, to be conscripted to defend the Motherland from the Germanic barbarians' invasion.”

His words were like stones dropped into stagnant water, creating no ripple. The women just stared at him silently, their eyes empty. Their husbands, their brothers, their sons had all been taken away in previous drafts, disappearing somewhere west of the Urals, never to be heard from again.

“Your son is already a glorious soldier, Comrade Citizen,” Ivan said to an old woman clutching an empty cradle. He tried to make his voice sound full of strength and pride, but he himself could hear the falsehood in it.

The old woman slowly raised her head, her cloudy eyes focused for the first time. She didn't speak, just held the empty cradle tighter with her wrinkled hands. The despair and accusation contained in that gesture were more deafening than any scream.

In another house, a boy not yet a man, rail-thin, was dragged out from under the bed by his mother. The boy's face was filled with terror, his body trembling.

“He's just a child!” the mother pleaded, her voice hoarse. “He can't even hold a gun steady!”

“In the crucible of the Great Trial, he will learn,” Ivan replied expressionlessly. The soldier behind him tore the boy from his mother's embrace, dragging him out the door like a sack of grain.

When Lieutenant Ivan Zakharov left the village, a crooked, shambling line of old men and children followed him. They would become the new 'reservist soldiers,' to fill the gaps in the military's ranks. Ivan looked back at the village of only women, a sudden wave of nausea rising in his throat. He forced himself not to think about who would fill these empty cradles when these last 'men' also disappeared.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.120.a: Every inch of Russian soil will become our barracks.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.121.desc:
The harsh blare of the propaganda van's loudspeaker tore Marina from a light sleep. She lay in her cold bed, listening to the metallic voice echoing through the empty streets, repeating the same message over and over.

“...Glory to the Russian Mother! Heed the League's call, and procreate for the Motherland! Every heroic mother who bears three or more children will be awarded the 'Cradle of the Motherland' medal, double food rations, and supreme honor!”

Marina pulled the rough blanket over her head, but the voice was like a needle, piercing the fabric, piercing her eardrums, reaching straight to her weary heart.

Her husband, Alexei, had been conscripted a year ago and had not been heard from since. Her two brothers had disappeared in an earlier 'purification action.' Now, this house, once filled with laughter, was home only to her and her elderly mother, who spent her days in tears.

The door was knocked. It was the League's 'Fertility Promotion Commissar,' a young woman with a face of false enthusiasm. She held a red velvet box in her hands.

“Marina Ivanova,” the commissar said in an almost singsong tone, “according to the latest health and genetic potential assessment, you have been gloriously selected as one of the first 'National Rejuvenation Reserve Mothers.' This is your honor, and your most sacred contribution to the Great Trial.”

Marina looked at her blankly, not understanding the meaning of these words.

The commissar opened the box. Inside was a cold bronze medal, engraved with the image of a woman holding a baby. The woman's face was blurred, her expression unreadable.

“You will be transferred to the designated 'Breeding Center' next week,” the commissar continued, her tone carrying an unquestionable authority. “There, you will be paired with the League's finest, most rigorously selected warriors to bear healthy offspring for Russia's future. Your children will become the new generation of avengers. And you, you will become a hero of our nation.”

Marina's body began to tremble uncontrollably. She thought of Alexei, of his gentle embrace before he left, of the children they had dreamed of having together. And now, her womb, her body, had become the property of the League, a factory for producing future cannon fodder. She was no longer a wife, a woman, but a numbered vessel with 'natural reproductive capabilities.'

“Is this... is this my duty?” she asked in a barely audible voice.

“No, madam.” A brilliant, empty smile bloomed on the Fertility Promotion Commissar's face as she pinned the cold medal to Marina's chest, like branding a sacrificial animal.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.122.desc:
Katya's shoulders were broader than most of the men in her village. Her hands were calloused, a mark left by years of wielding an axe and repairing farm tools. The village elders always whispered behind her back, saying she was a 'man in the wrong body,' that no decent man would marry a woman who could wrestle a bull to the ground.

She had once been ashamed of this, hiding herself in silence and labor.

Until the Black League's recruiting officer came to the village.

They took away all the 'able-bodied' men, leaving behind a dead silence and despair. But the next day, the recruiting officer returned. This time, he walked straight up to Katya.

“You, what's your name?” The officer's gaze was like that assessing a warhorse, sharp and direct.

“Katya,” she answered in a low voice, instinctively trying to hunch her shoulders.

“Head up, soldier!” The recruiter's roar made her jolt. She raised her head, for the first time looking directly into those eyes, devoid of any contempt.

“They say you're not fit for marriage and childbirth,” the recruiter scanned her strong arms, a hint of approval at the corner of his mouth. “They say you're a 'masculine' waste. They're wrong. They are blind, cowards.”

He paused, his voice becoming low and seductive. “Your strength shouldn't be wasted on chopping wood and feeding pigs. Your anger shouldn't be spent on the gossip of neighbors. Russia doesn't need more weeping mothers, Russia needs warriors who can make the Teutons weep!”

He thrust a heavy AK-74 rifle into Katya's hands. The cold touch of steel was more real, more powerful than anything she had ever touched.

“Those who mocked you are now cowering in the rear. And you,” the recruiter pointed to the western horizon, stained dark red by the clouds of the First Trial, “will have the chance to win a glory they can never attain. You will wash away all the stains on your name with the blood of the enemy. You will no longer be Katya. You will be a daughter of Russia, a valkyrie of vengeance.”

Katya tightened her grip on the rifle. She looked at her rough hands, and for the first time, she felt not shame, but an unprecedented strength. The years of scars and calluses were no longer ugly marks, but medals for her new mission to come.

When she left the village with the recruiting officer, she didn't look back. She heard the shocked gasps of the elders behind her, but that sound could no longer hurt her. Ahead of her lay the fires of war, smoke, and a bloody path to 'glory' paved with the heads of the enemy.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.122.a: Let their fire burn Germania to the ground.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.123.desc:
“To be honest, I'm still not confident about the Great Trial. Those Germans have weapons far superior to ours... Did you say the above sentence to Soldier 1024561, Soldier 0600241?” In the frontline interrogation room, a Black League interrogation expert threw out a diary. It was filled with writings about wanting to live, and a pessimistic attitude towards the Great Trial.

He was clearly terrified, and quickly tried to salvage the situation. “I... I wrote this after having a bit to drink, it wasn't my original intention. I am willing to give everything for the Great Trial, even my life.” After saying this, his forehead was covered in sweat. The interrogation expert pushed up his glasses and turned to question the other person, giving him no reply.

“I, I think this is a mistake, sir. How many of us do you think can...” He was kicked to the ground before he could finish. “Nonsense! You don't even dare to try, so why are you even in the army! It's a tragedy that Mother Russia has someone as disloyal to the Great Trial as you.”

With that, he took out the pistol from his waist. Hearing the sound of the safety being released, the hearts of the two men jumped into their throats. They slowly closed their eyes, waiting for the expert to deliver their final judgment—it was the sound of the pistol being put back in its case, followed by the expert personally announcing the verdict.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.123.a: “You are both stripped of your status as Black League soldiers and transferred to the penal battalion.”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.124.desc:
“From today on, I will be your military instructor, teaching you... ordinary people how to use weapons, how to make explosives, how to disguise yourselves as much as possible when the Western Teuton invaders arrive, and how to ambush and kill them when they are off guard!”

Leonid, holding a military baton, walked past a crowd of old people, women, and children. As a warrior who had passed the Black League's test, he was initially dismissive of the task of going down to teach a group of weaklings to fight. What could a bunch of weak people accomplish? But soon, the higher-ups issued several pamphlets on so-called 'people's war,' which not only contained the content he was to teach, but also many of the crimes committed by the Nazi pigs against the Russian people. Leonid only glanced at them before cutting down the budding revisionism in his heart. Against Nazi trash, one had to use every means to make them die.

“Sir, why do we have to go to war? Aren't you supposed to protect us?” an old woman asked him.

“In your dreams!” Leonid shouted. “You don't know that those Western Teutons show no mercy just because you are women and children. On the contrary, they hate every one of us to the bone. They will do everything they can to kill every Russian they see, no matter who you are. You only want us to protect you, but you don't want to do anything for the motherland yourselves!”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.124.a: “For the Motherland, everyone should learn to sacrifice.”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.125.desc:
“I know! My father and grandfather sacrificed themselves for the Motherland, resisting those Teutons!” a child responded.
“You're right, little Nikolai.” Leonid smiled. “That's why, to defend our homes, you must learn how to deal with those Nazi invaders. Little Nikolai.” He personally took out a small pistol and placed it in Nikolai's hands. “From today, you are the squad leader of this village's Children's Army!”
“Yes, sir!” Little Nikolai imitated a salute.
“What you need to learn is simple: how to shoot and how to camouflage,” Leonid instructed the children. “If you encounter an enemy invasion in the future, what you need to do is to make them not see what you're up to, hide in places in the village where you can hide, and once you find an opportunity, use the weapons we've given you to hit these damn invaders hard!”
“As for you,” Leonid looked at the group of women and old people and sighed, “weaklings like you, the higher-ups don't expect you to have much combat capability, but fortunately, there are some things you can learn.” He brought over a basket. “Although you can't shoot, you can use bombs! From today, you must learn to throw! When you go home, you must also learn from scratch how to prepare simple firebombs. Once the enemy invades, your explosives must be able to land on their heads!”
“Now, let the training begin! Anyone who doesn't meet today's training quota will have no food today!”
...
So the day passed. Leonid waved his hand, dismissing everyone to go home. Reflecting on the morning's training, a group of frail children who could barely hold a gun with two hands, a group of old people who couldn't throw a bomb more than five steps even with all their might, only the women were reasonably adept at making Zhdanov cocktails. But during the afternoon's training, a girl nearly dropped a cocktail at her own feet. Fortunately, Leonid pushed her away. These rabble were so frightened they went into a panic, forgetting even how to run.
He sighed, lay down on his bed, and began to ponder the next day's teaching content. As he thought, a question involuntarily lingered in his mind.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.125.a: Is this really a people's war?
strings.OMS_more_flavor.126.desc:
“Everyone, drop your things and run! The air raid has started! Anyone who runs too slow and doesn't reach the air-raid shelter will get a taste of the whip!”

Jim Oleg shouted into a megaphone at the surging crowd. He was a Russian-American, his ancestors having been officers in the Tsarist army. After the October Revolution, his ancestors first joined the White Army, then came to America, becoming American citizens. His father, a 'muddle-headed fool' in the community, had been shouting about 'defending the motherland' ever since he learned of the German invasion of Russia, and had returned to the Russian land, never to be heard from again. Oleg had been following the situation in Russia from America, hoping to learn his father's whereabouts, but to no avail. His teachers told him that Russia had been in a state of anarchy for decades. Oleg was desperate to know what was happening in Russia, but had no source of information.

But soon, a group of fellow Russian immigrants came to their community. The leader, Mr. Boris, was practically omniscient. He told Oleg the reason for Russia's division: a group of national traitors and Bolsheviks were colluding, doing everything they could to undermine the unity of the Russian people, even to the point of selling out their own countrymen to the Germans. Other immigrant friends corroborated Mr. Boris's words from different perspectives. Some came from Bolshevik-controlled areas and were hunted down just for not wanting to fight their compatriots. Some came from so-called democratic governments, where people would sell out the country to the Germans for peace. Some had survived against all odds, escaping to America from so-called anarchist territories, which were in fact just bandit lairs...

In all their stories, one person was consistently mentioned: the current Commander-in-Chief of the Russian National Rejuvenation Government, Yazov. They all marveled at this commander's powerful strength and lamented that they did not live in the land of the Rejuvenation Government. From then on, Oleg became more curious about Commander Yazov. He hoped they could give him more news about Yazov. These friends also helped him in various ways: Yazov's speeches, the current situation of a unified Russia, the strong army defending the country. All this news fascinated Oleg. Finally, he made a decision.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.126.a: I will leave America and return to my homeland.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.127.desc:
When he left the Russian community, every one of his former friends saw him off warmly, and they collected a large sum of money for him, hoping he could invest it in Russia's construction upon his arrival. Oleg accepted every friend's blessing and boarded the ocean liner with his suitcase.

Poverty, but with a resurgent vitality—that was Oleg's first impression upon disembarking at the port of Magadan. Although his friends had told him that Russia was poor and backward, the reality still exceeded his imagination: many civilians were in thin clothes, yet they still made an effort to welcome the guests from thousands of miles away. Oleg tried to persuade them to rest, but they told him that Russia now needed more construction. In the west of the country, the Western Nazis were daily trying to invade Russian territory, to strip the Russian people of their hard-won freedom. They could not let the motherland fall again for their own selfish desires.

What a resilient and great nation, Oleg wrote in his diary.

Soon, he boarded a train, passed through Central Siberia, and arrived at the American embassy in Russia. Everywhere he went, he witnessed countless miracles: the Russian industry destroyed by the German Nazis was being restored at a miraculous speed; the Russian people, though working hard, always had enough to eat, and there was even no racial discrimination as he had often seen in America! All of this finally became too much for Oleg to bear. He found the local government, hoping to re-join Russian nationality and join the government. The American ambassador tried to persuade him several times, but failed.

Soon, his application was approved. He was assigned to Chelyabinsk as an administrative operative. In the accounts of the Rejuvenation Government officials, to improve administrative efficiency, they implemented an operative system, improving efficiency by assigning tasks. After participating in the work for a few days, Oleg felt from the bottom of his heart the reliability of this system: the Russian people lived in constant fear under the shadow of the Nazis, and it was only with the protection of the powerful Commander-in-Chief that every Russian could sleep peacefully. The efficient operative system could also reduce unnecessary internal friction.

Every senior treated him well. After working for a few months, he finally received his first official mission: to organize an air-raid drill and evacuation. He arrived at the designated community. It looked barren, but Oleg knew that this was a camouflage to deal with Nazi air raids. The resilient Russian people were surviving under these buildings. What he had to do was to guide them to obey the Commander-in-Chief's orders for national rejuvenation, so that they could survive better in the future decisive battle.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.127.a: National rejuvenation requires the efforts of every citizen.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.128.desc:
March 13th, Graduation Day
Heil to the Führer! Heil to Greater Germania! Heil to Moskowien!
My name is Petkov. I was born in Moskowien. When I was in school, my parents told me that we are second-class citizens of the Reichskommissariat Moskowien. The Germans came to this land to help us remove the decadent genes from our Slavic race.
Under the Führer's teachings, I understood that we must be as innately strong as the Aryans. To be as strong as the Aryans, I will first change my name, let's call me Schmidt.
...
September 16th, Night
Heil to the Führer! Heil to Greater Germania! Heil to Moskowien!
Today I met many talented young people in a famous salon in Moscow. They told me that someone like me is not qualified to change my name, I can only continue to be called Petkov. A gentleman named Shevardnadze even sternly rebuked my arrogance and ignorance. But I don't understand, why is a Caucasian like him qualified to be called Franz, while a Muscovite like me is not qualified to be called Schmidt?
...
December 25th, Christmas
Heil to the Führer! Heil to Moskowien!
Today is promotion day, but I am very unhappy. In the school's performance review, I was first, but before promotion day, my principal Wilhelm, an honorary Aryan, found me and told me that because of my Slavic blood, I can never surpass the German immigrants from Greater Germania. We Slavs are innately inferior to Aryans, so my ranking is void. But didn't the Führer teach us that the strong do not need the recognition of others?
...
April 6th, Night
Heil to the Führer!
Today is my day of shame. I joined the Moskowien Defense Force to serve those German colonists from Germania. For these past two months, my job has been to drive Muscovites out of their homes to satisfy the Germans. That old woman, even as she died, clung to her land. Did she really deserve to be executed like that?
...
August 15th
This is the last diary entry. From now on, I will get a new one. Ever since I found some pamphlets about national rejuvenation in a slave's home, those guys have been searching my house every few days, saying I harbor rebels? It seems now that those so-called Aryans and Moskowien traitors are just paper tigers. They rely on violence to maintain the lie of their so-called superiority, but in fact, my success is because I am Russian. The Germans have tried every means to trick me into being their slave. They will pay the price.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.128.a: His face darkened as he threw the diary into the fire.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.129.desc:
TOP SECRET, FOR THE COMMANDER-IN-CHIEF'S EYES ONLY
To the Commander-in-Chief:
Today, at the US Embassy, I received a letter from the American Murkoff Corporation. They expressed great interest in our Great Trial cause and wish to establish a cooperative relationship with us. According to our information, Murkoff Corporation, on the surface, is a high-tech company, but behind the scenes, it is a grey multinational corporation specializing in mind control, biochemical weapons, human experimentation, and other fields. It has absorbed a large number of scientists who participated in Operation Paperclip, the Philadelphia Experiment, and the MK-ULTRA project from our country, Germany, and Manchuria, and has achieved astonishing results in this field.
We have conducted simple negotiations with them and have reached a consensus on the following issues:
1. Murkoff Corporation promises to assist in the construction of our biochemical weapons arsenal and provide the latest research results for the Great Trial.
2. Murkoff Corporation hopes to transfer its research to our territory and requests financial and site support from our government.
Our assessment is that this cooperation is entirely beneficial and has no downsides for the cause of the Great Trial. We await your instructions for further action.
US Embassy
strings.OMS_more_flavor.130.desc:
“Ms. Valia, it has been ten months since I arrived in Russia. In these past months, your Russian Rejuvenation Government's handling of the issue of joining the Co-Prosperity Sphere market has been far too sluggish. The Empire has always maintained sufficient goodwill towards Russia, encouraging and supporting trade activities between the Manchurian and Mongolian governments and yourselves, and has even handed over a number of prisoners to you. Yet your efficiency in these months has been getting worse and worse. If this continues, the Empire will have to reconsider its economic dealings with Russia.”

Across the negotiating table, the Russian representative, Valia, spread her hands: “Mr. Kondo Isao, I must reiterate that we had numerous communications with the government of the Great Japanese Empire even before unification. Both sides have expressed a desire to deepen friendship and enhance exchanges. However, we are now the legitimate government of Russia, and large areas of the country still require construction. Furthermore, the Greater Germanic Reich government in our west has been frequently conducting military operations on the border. Our country's main focus is currently on suppressing domestic rebellion and military preparations. The approval of related procedures has been forced to be postponed. We hope for your understanding.”

“That is no excuse,” Kondo Isao waved his hand. “I, on behalf of the government of the Great Japanese Empire, hope you understand that after joining the Co-Prosperity Sphere economy, we will use the Manchurian border as a trading port. The Russian government can exchange industrial materials and oil and gas resources for development and reconstruction resources. At the same time, after joining the Co-Prosperity Sphere market, the Imperial government will support Russia more in international forums in its reasonable and lawful competition with the Greater Germanic Reich. We hope that through such sincere cooperation, both sides will receive their due profits.”

Valia paused, just as she was about to formulate her response. Suddenly, the door to the conference room was thrown open, and a squad of Black League soldiers rushed into the room, facing off with the Japanese soldiers inside at gunpoint.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.130.a: “Hey, lady, there's a limit to pressure tactics, right? What do you think you're doing?”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.131.desc:
Valia looked at the leading officer. “Hello, we are conducting Russo-Japanese trade negotiations here. Are you perhaps in the wrong place?”

“Not at all,” the leading officer replied coldly. “Just this morning, our border guards on patrol discovered the bodies of more than a dozen Russians. The patrol found that several villages had been systematically massacred. The weapons used by the perpetrators were all Japanese-made. We now have reason to suspect that the Japanese are plotting to invade our border.”

“This is slander! The Great Japanese Empire has always upheld the principles of peace and would never do such a thing!” Kondo Isao shouted.

“That's right, Mr. Kondo and his team have been in talks with us. They are certainly not conspirators!”

“But this is the truth,” the officer handed over a stack of photos, passing them around for each diplomat to see. “To ensure border security, the Commander-in-Chief has ordered that our government temporarily freeze all Russo-Japanese trade relations. All Japanese expatriates and related economic resources in Russia will be under our temporary custody. As for you, you will be repatriated to Japan in a few days.”

Valia raised her hand. “Whatever the case, I hope that Mr. Kondo can return to Japan safely. As a diplomat for Russo-Japanese friendship, a friend of the Russian people, he should not be treated this way.”

“Thank you, madam.” Kondo Isao nodded to Valia, then looked angrily at the officer and packed up his briefcase. “We're leaving!”

Watching the Japanese walk away, Valia and the leading officer exchanged a look and a high-five.

“Valia, how long do you estimate it will take for the Japanese to figure out the situation here?”

“At least three months. The people in intelligence have made arrangements. Our men have already tampered with a few things. On their way back, their vehicle will have a 'minor malfunction.'”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.131.a: By the time the Japanese react, we'll be ready.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.132.desc:
Old Emil placed his sleigh by the tree and, leaning on his staff, started down the mountain with his catch. Today was another bountiful day. He moved freely in the great forest with a hunting rifle, silently approaching his prey before firing. Though he was nearly sixty, the skills he had learned in the defense force as a young man had not faded. He alone had taken two snow weasels and a deer. He had already planned it out: once in the village, he would have the Mäkki family help him skin the animals, so he could sell them in the nearby town. The kind Germanics in town were always buying these things, and he wanted to trade for something he could use.

As he walked, he suddenly felt a profound sense of wrongness. Dusk was falling, and usually at this time, every household in the village would have lit their stoves, and the streetlights at the village entrance would be on, illuminating the path ahead. But he was almost in the middle of the village, and where were the people?

His nose twitched. The sense of unease rose to a fever pitch. He immediately dropped his catch and ran towards the outskirts of the village, but it was too late. A crossbow bolt struck his thigh, followed by two gunshots. He could tell they were silenced. But he had no time to think; excruciating pain instantly felled the old man. He fell to the ground, and a group of black-clothed soldiers swarmed out from all directions, surrounding him.

“Waiting a bit longer was the right call. Almost let someone slip away and leak the news.” A black-masked man walked up to him. “Speak, old man! Are there any Germans here? Where do they live?”

“You! You are Russians! You dare set foot on Finnish soil again!” Old Emil recognized the language, and a profound rage welled up from his heart. More than 30 years ago, Emil had been a young lad. Hearing that his motherland had been invaded by the evil Bolshevik Russia, he joined the army and underwent snow training. He and his comrades-in-arms roamed the snow-covered lands, beating the Russians black and blue, sending those scoundrels scurrying back to their own country. Later, they followed their Germanic friends east, giving the damn Russians a sound lesson. But now, they were still not giving up, they wanted to invade Finland!

A military boot kicked him in the face, nearly making Emil vomit blood. “I asked you a question, did you hear me! Where are the Nazi scum?”

“In, in the nearby town, they're just ordinary people, I don't know anything else.” Old Emil said brokenly, but his mind was made up. As soon as these invaders left, he would find his sleigh as quickly as possible and rush to the city to notify the defense force and his Germanic friends. Against the Russian enemy, the only friends the Finns could rely on were the Germanics.

A military knife slit Emil's throat, severing his thoughts. “We never said we'd let you go, garbage.”

The leading officer stood up. “Clean up the scene, leave no traces.”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.132.a: No one can escape the shadow of death.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.133.desc:
The air in the recruiting office was stagnant and cold, a mixture of cheap tobacco's acrid spice and a vague sense of despair. Major Vorontsov's office was a machine of judgment, shockingly efficient, ruthlessly impartial. Each time the stamp on his desk fell, it was like a hammer striking down on a personal fate, and he had long grown numb to it.

A young man was pushed in by two guards. He staggered, a final, unrealistic hope of a student still lingering in his eyes.

“Name, age.” Vorontsov didn't look up, his gaze fixed on the files.

“Konstantin Ilyich Rokov, twenty-four, a student.” The young man puffed out his chest, trying to keep his voice steady. “Fourth year, Department of History, Tomsk State University—”

“History,” the Major finally looked up, his grey eyes empty, “history has ended, student. The future has only one direction.” He picked up the stamp, dipped it in the scarlet ink, but did not bring it down.

The guards understood, seizing the ashen-faced Konstantin. The young man's final struggles and incoherent pleas were cut off by the heavy iron door. Moments later, a dull, short gunshot echoed from the end of the corridor. Vorontsov's eyebrow didn't even twitch.

“Next.”

Finally, a small figure appeared. He looked even younger than his age, the old coat clearly his brother's, hanging loosely on him. He stood before the desk, his hands nervously wringing the hem of his clothes. His eyes, wide with fear, nevertheless forced out a sliver of the obsequious sycophancy Vorontsov had seen on countless faces.

“Dmitry Mikhailovich Fyodorov. Fifteen.” The boy's voice was as faint as a mosquito's buzz, yet it carried the desperation of someone cornered.

For the first time, Vorontsov put down his pen. He regarded the child with interest. Fifteen. Not yet polluted by useless knowledge, not yet corrupted by a life of ease. There was no question in his eyes, only the pure, animal instinct for survival. This look, the Major was familiar with it. It was the look of the League.

“Why have you come, Dmitry?”

“To… to serve the League, Comrade Major!” The boy stood straighter. “To contribute my strength to the Great Trial! To avenge Russia!” He recited the words from the propaganda pamphlets, stammering slightly from nervousness, but every word was firm.

“And your family?” Vorontsov's voice softened for the first time.

“Father is at Factory No. 3, Mother in the textile workshop. They both say, this is our family's honor.” A fleeting flicker of pain crossed the boy's eyes, but he immediately masked it with fanaticism. “I… I want to be an honor too.”

Vorontsov looked at him, as if examining a perfect, uncut jade. This was what the League needed. Not the erudite students, not the self-righteous peasants. It was these children, shaped by hatred and hunger, polished by propaganda and fear. They were blank canvases, to be freely painted with the will of the Black League. They were the newest, sharpest blades, yet untarnished by a speck of rust.

The Major picked up another stamp and pressed it heavily onto a new file. The stamp's design was not a skull, but a gear.

“Approved. Assign to the 7th Ordnance Factory, apprentice worker.” He pushed the document to a guard, then said to the boy: “Your family will be proud of you. Your labor will be forged into bullets for the Teutonic bastards. Go, Dmitry. Go and forge vengeance.”

The boy, as if granted amnesty, bowed deeply and almost ran out of the office. As the door closed behind him, Vorontsov gazed at the lead-grey sky outside the window. For the first time, a smile of satisfaction appeared on his mask-like face.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.134.desc:
This cell was pure white, a kind of unadulterated white that could drive a man mad. The walls, the ceiling, the floor, even the eternally lit, constantly humming fluorescent tube, all emanated a cold, white glow. Professor Nikolai Andreyevich Chernov had no idea how long he had been here. The concept of time, along with everything he had once cherished—logic, reason, and the dignity of science—had been dissolved and shattered in this endless white light.

He had once been the most distinguished chemist at Novosibirsk University, a humanitarian who firmly believed that knowledge should serve the welfare of mankind. When the iron hooves of the Black League crushed the fragile peace of Novosibirsk, he naively thought that with his talent, he could secure a place in the new order and continue his research.

He was wrong. So very wrong.

When they found him, there was no trial, no accusation, only the butt of a rifle and an endless darkness. When he awoke, he was here. The interrogators came day after day. They didn't ask for secrets; they didn't need him to confess anything. Their purpose was more direct, and more terrifying.

“Professor,” a voice, always that inhumanly calm voice, whispered in his ear, “we know of your talent. Your brain is a treasure trove, a treasure trove that can forge the strongest sword of vengeance for Mother Russia. All you need to do is agree. Agree to serve the League.”

“I will never allow my knowledge to become a tool of slaughter!” Initially, he could still roar back like this, resisting with his last ounce of dignity.

The response was silence. Then pain. Their methods were highly 'scientific.' No brutal beatings, only precise torture. They kept him from sleeping for days and nights until hallucinations danced before his eyes; they submerged him in ice water until he could no longer feel his limbs; when he was at his most hungry, they brought a steaming plate of food, only to take it away the moment he reached for it.

They stripped him of his humanity, bit by bit, reducing him to a beast with only the instinct to survive. But even so, the stubborn rock of the scientist deep within him had not been completely shattered. He used logic as a shield, ethics as a wall, holding his final ground.

Until today. The door opened, and the same calm-voiced interrogator entered. But this time, he held something new—a photograph.

“Look at her, Professor,” the interrogator placed the photo before his eyes, “your daughter, Anna. Such a beautiful child. She is also under our 'jurisdiction.' She is in a good school, well-fed and housed. But you know, our resources are tight… The Great Trial demands sacrifice.”

Chernov's pupils contracted violently. The Anna in the photograph was smiling at the camera, the way she had looked the last time he saw her before he was taken.

“The ration for one girl, versus a shell filled with chemical agents… which is more valuable to Russia's future?” The interrogator knelt down, his voice as soft as a serpent's hiss. “It's a simple logic problem, Professor. Use your scientific brain. On one side, your daughter, a fragile, emotional individual of almost no use to the League's great cause. On the other, the hope of ending the Teutonic threat and saving millions of Russian compatriots. Which choice is more 'humane'? Which better reflects what you call 'serving the welfare of mankind'?”

Logic… they were using his most proud weapon against him.

Chernov stared blankly at the photograph, the interrogator's words corroding his intellectual defenses like acid. His persistence, his ethics, his beliefs… they all seemed so pale, so selfish, so laughable in the face of his daughter's innocent smile. His body began to tremble uncontrollably, a bestial whimper escaping his throat. That long-held rock of conviction finally cracked, then crumbled completely.
He had lost. Utterly. His science, his logic, his everything, had been twisted into a dagger pointed at himself.

“I… I…” he struggled to open his cracked lips, the sound that came out was foreign even to himself. “I… agree.”

A triumphant smile appeared on the interrogator's face. He put away the photograph, helped the almost-collapsed Chernov to his feet, and unlocked his shackles.

“A wise choice, Professor. Your talent will be unleashed as never before. Come, a brand new laboratory awaits you. Science, in the end, will find a way for the nation.”

As Chernov was helped out of that pure white hell that had tormented him for so long, and into another, equally pure white 'new world' filled with beakers and instruments, his eyes had lost all their light. He was no longer Professor Nikolai Andreyevich Chernov.

He was just a tool.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.135.desc:
In the university's lecture hall, the air was as cold as a morgue. The heating had been cut off early in the unification wars, every joule of saved heat to be converted into bullets. The citizens forced to attend this 're-education' sat on hard wooden chairs, wrapped in thin coats, more defendants on trial than an audience.

On the podium, Professor Anatoly Andreyevich Volgin adjusted his old-fashioned glasses. He was once Tomsk's most respected historian, a man lost in the glorious epic of Kievan Rus' and the Romanov dynasty. Now, he was just a tool, a tool to reshape history.

“Good afternoon, citizens,” his voice came through the loudspeaker, dry and emotionless. “Today, we will discuss a fundamental question: where are Russia's borders?”

He did not wait for an answer, but turned to the huge, 'uncorrected' map of Eurasia behind him.

“The traditional view, and… ah, the weak view, is that borders are defined by mountains, rivers, and those fragile treaties signed with ink and lies. They will tell you, this is Russia. A vast, passive land, waiting to be shaped. This is a fundamental error.”

He picked up a pointer and struck it heavily on the location of the Ural Mountains. “They say, this is the dividing line between Europe and Asia. A geographical… fantasy. The true Russia never acknowledges the tyranny of geography. I ask you all to recall the time of Ivan the Terrible. When he shattered the shackles of the Khanate of Kazan, was he following the instructions on a map? No. He was fulfilling the sacred mission to 'gather the lands of Rus'.”

“Look again at Peter the Great. Did he find a natural harbor on the Baltic coast? No. He carved a window to Europe out of a swamp with the bones of Swedes and the blood and sweat of Russians! With his axe and his will, he redefined Russia's western border. He understood a truth—borders are not discovered, they are created.”

Professor Volgin's pace quickened, his old academic passion seemingly ignited by a darker energy.

“For centuries, our thinkers, those… ah, writers, lost in repentance and redemption, taught us to look inward. They taught us to examine the abyss of the soul, but forgot to examine the fragility of our frontiers. While we lamented the tears of a sinner in Dostoevsky's writings, the Teutons were sharpening their blades in the lands of Prussia. While we sighed at the tragedy of the little man in Chekhov's plays, they were drawing up a 'Generalplan Ost' aimed at the complete eradication of our nation.”

He jabbed the pointer fiercely at Berlin on the map, almost piercing the thin paper.

“And so, the 'First Trial' came. It was not just a war; it was a final geopolitical verdict. It mercilessly proved: a nation that only knows introspection and not expansion, a nation content with its existing borders and without thought for advancement, its ultimate fate is to be re-divided on someone else's map, or even completely erased.”

“What did we learn from the Mongol hooves? Not peaceful coexistence, but the law of survival—either you become a wolf, or you become a sheep. What did we learn from Napoleon's cannons? Not national reconciliation, but that only a completely destroyed enemy will not return. These bloody lessons, the weak tsars and the corrupt communists all forgot! They foolishly tried to guarantee security with diplomatic rhetoric, with ideological empty talk. And the result? The result is that Germania, this huge, festering sore, still sits on our mother's chest!”

Volgin's gaze swept over every terrified or numb face in the audience.

“So, comrades, where are Russia's borders really? They are not in the Urals, not on the Dnieper, and not on that ridiculous A-A line. Our security border, our cultural border, the survival border of our nation, it is where the last potential threat is completely eradicated.”

He put down the pointer and calmly concluded.

“The Great Trial, in essence, is the largest, most ultimate 'gathering of the lands of Rus'. This is not aggression; this is surgery. We are not expanding; we are excising the cancerous tissue that threatens our survival. Therefore, Russia's border will end where the last Teuton takes his final breath.”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.136.desc:
“Open the door! Open the door! We are the League police, we suspect there are anti-government elements hiding here! Open the door immediately for a search! Otherwise, we will use force immediately!”

“Imam, we can't open the door. When have these guys ever used peaceful means? They are just a bunch of butchers, demons, destined for Hell!”

Ahmed sighed, glanced at the panicked people in the main hall. Some were hiding in their robes, shivering, others clung to their scriptures, refusing to let go. They tried to appear brave, but fear was already on their faces.

“I'll go open the door. I'll try to reason with them,” Ahmed sighed, walked to the main entrance, and opened it.

The black-clothed policemen poured in, rushing into the mosque. The stout leading officer smiled at Ahmed: “Taking so long to open the door? I thought you people couldn't understand human speech.”

“I did it to protect our people, sir. I am a Muslim. Allah teaches us to care for our Muslim brothers and help the poor. These people have been desperate these past few days, so I have temporarily sheltered them.”

“Desperate? Do you know why they're desperate?” While the two were talking, the Black League police had already arrested every person in the mosque. Their belongings were piled up in the empty space between the two men.

“Look at this, a Quran, written in Kazakh?” The officer casually flipped through a few pages and threw it on the ground. “The concept of 'Kazakh' has never existed in this world, never! This has always been a part of the great Russia, it's written in the history books!”

“But, but the Kazakh people have lived on this land since ancient times, they have their own national culture…”

“Then I ask you, who led them into civilization?” the officer roared loudly. “Over 50 years ago, Kazakhstan was a land of savages. It was the great Russian nation that led them out of a nomadic life, taught them to read, and showed them how to build an industry! But what did they do? During the First Trial, they hid in the rear, unwilling to come forward, watching as Central Asia was invaded by the Nazi pigs without trying to stop them. They even use the ridiculous so-called Kazakh national identity to expel the Russians from this region? What a load of crap, these Kazakhs are nothing but a bunch of thieves who stole Russia's achievements!”

He looked at Ahmed, his tone relaxing slightly. “For your cooperation, get out! This place will be converted into a school. The children here must receive the correct education, so they are not continually deceived by these thieves.”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.136.a: We will eradicate the heresy at its roots.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.137.desc:
The smell of blood and burnt wool mixed together, sickening. The resistance in this village was more intense than the last, and more… foolish. They had no weapons, just linked arms, blocking the soldiers' path, singing their ancient songs, refusing to leave the land they had lived on for generations.

The commissar's order was simple and direct: “Any object obstructing the League's advance will be removed.”

Now, the 'removal' work was over. Pasha, along with other soldiers, was piling the bodies onto a truck. His movements were much more practiced than a few weeks ago; he no longer vomited, no longer trembled. He just mechanically grabbed the still-warm limbs and threw them into the truck bed.

“I still don't get it, Sergei.” After throwing the bodies of a mother and child onto the truck, Pasha leaned against it, panting, and said to Sergei, who was smoking nearby. “Why wouldn't they just leave? If they leave, they live. It's that simple. For a few broken-down yurts, a few skinny sheep, is it worth it?”

Sergei took a deep drag on his cigarette, blowing the smoke towards the blood-red sky. “To you, they're broken-down yurts, Pasha. To them, they're home. Tradition. Their nation. These things are harder than life itself.”

He ground the cigarette butt under his boot. “That's why they must be cleared away. You can't reason with a stone, tell it it's in the way, and ask it to move. You can only smash it.” Sergei pointed to the bodies on the ground. “This was their own choice. We gave them a choice: obey, or perish. They chose the latter. So, this isn't our violence, Pasha. It's their stubbornness that brought about this inevitable result.”

Sergei remembered his experience in the West Russian War. A Red Army commander, because a platoon under his command refused to carry out a suicide charge, personally shot the platoon leader and then forced the rest to charge. At the time, Sergei thought the commander was a madman. Now, he understood.

“Our leaders are surgeons, Pasha,” Sergei said in an almost preachy tone, “and Russia is a gravely ill patient. Sometimes, to save a life, you have to amputate a gangrenous leg. No matter whether that leg is willing or not.”

Pasha looked at his hands, covered in the blood and brains of others. He was silent for a long time, so long that Sergei thought he would not speak again.

“So…” Pasha's voice was hollow and weary, “we… are just the scalpels.”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.137.a: The wind that night could not blow away the smell of blood in the air.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.138.desc:
The wind on the Amur River, like it was laced with broken glass, cut Kenji's cheeks raw. For over a decade, this frozen river had been his lifeline. He knew every ice crack here, every snowdrift that could hide him from the patrol boats. He knew the old Russians—those drunken warlord soldiers—their loyalty could be measured in a bottle of fine sake, their vigilance would drop with their body temperature after midnight.

But today, the wind carried only the smell of rust and death.

The crossing on the other side, a place he could navigate with his eyes closed, had changed. The crooked wooden watchtower of his memory had been replaced by a stark, angular concrete bunker, as black as eternal night. Barbed wire fences cast狰狞 (zhengrong - savage/ferocious, let's use a more fitting word) shadows like spiderwebs on the pale snow. And the sentinels… they were no longer living people, just silent specters wrapped in black uniforms.

Kenji's heart pounded heavily in his chest, but his decades of speculation had taught him to trust his luck. Perhaps it was just a more intimidating outfit. He poked half his body out from behind a snowdrift, clutching a small gold bar tightly in his hand—the 'key' he had prepared for this deal.

Just as he was about to make his usual, water-bird-like whistle, a black shadow on the bunker moved. No warning, no shout. Only a faint, metallic sound, almost lost in the wind, as light as the cracking of distant ice.

It was the sound of a rifle safety being released. Crisp, decisive, without a hint of hesitation.

All the blood in Kenji's body seemed to freeze in an instant. The instinct that had sustained him for decades now sounded a belated, heart-wrenching alarm. He was wrong. The rules had completely changed. There were no more deals here, only judgment.

He wanted to turn, to shrink back into the snow, to turn back time even for a second. But it was too late.

The second sound cut through the dead silence of Siberia. Not thunder, just a short, dry crack. The bullet entered precisely through his slightly open mouth, carrying a stream of hot, viscous fluid out the back of his head.
Kenji's body fell backward, slamming heavily onto the snow. The last thing he saw was the vast, grey, merciless Russian sky. The gold bar slipped from his loosening hand, rolled a few times on the snow, and lay dull.

A pool of crimson rapidly spread in the snow beneath him, like a grotesque, beautiful flower blooming upon death.

The black shadow on the bunker watched this red flower bloom until it stopped spreading. Then, he lowered his rifle.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.139.desc:
This cell in Vorkuta was pure grey. The walls, the iron table, the eternally lit lamp above, all were steeped in this color-stripping, industrialized despair.

Marshal Vasily Ivanovich Chuikov sat quietly. He had once forged a city's name with steel and unyielding will. Now, he was just a prisoner forgotten by history. He was not defeated by the Germans, but betrayed by the very ideal he had sworn to protect, and by the successors who trampled that ideal.

The door opened. A captain in black entered, his young face burning with the calm fire only a fanatic could possess. He placed a file on the table.

“Marshal Chuikov,” the captain's voice was devoid of emotion, “your legacy is built upon the corpses of countless Germans. It is a precious legacy, one the Motherland needs.”

Chuikov sneered, his voice hoarse. “My Motherland is the Soviet Union.”

“The Soviet Union is dead, Marshal,” the captain's voice remained unmoved. “It died of incompetence and betrayal. Now, only Russia lives—a Russia covered in scars, craving only one thing.”

The captain turned the file towards Chuikov. It was a letter of appointment.

“You have two paths before you. One is to be a monument to an era, here, forgotten by the world. The other, is to become a sword once more. We will give you an army. An army quenched in your hatred, driven by our will. Your objective is one, the place you failed to personally level in 1957—Germania.”

Silence. A long silence. Chuikov stared at the document. Everything he had believed in for his entire life had already collapsed. But the hardest, heaviest foundation within him—that hatred for the Nazis, a hatred hot enough to burn through the permafrost—remained intact.

To dance with a new devil, to complete a vengeance two decades overdue. Or to cling to the ashes of a ghost and turn to dust here?

This was not a choice about honor. It was a choice about an end.

He slowly reached out, his gaunt knuckles touching the cold paper.

“My staff,” he said in a low voice.

A faint, almost imperceptible arc appeared on the captain's lips for the first time.

“They are assembling as we speak, Comrade Marshal.”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.139.a: He prepared to die once more.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.140.desc:
Michael had lived on this land once known as Moskowien since the day he was born, just like his German immigrant father and mother. He was honest, trustworthy, and capable—just like the pure-blooded Germans described in the textbooks. The only thing that didn't fit the textbook was his kindness towards the 'inferior races.' He had even, within his means, helped some locals in distress on multiple occasions. However, the unchanging life of over 20 years was destined to end the day the Black League set foot on this land. He was captured by the Black League.



“What will happen to me? The neighbors say these Russians kill any German on sight... Will I be another soul for their blades? Or will they torture me first? …Oh God…” Michael's mind raced, his heart filled with extreme fear as he was herded by the German-speaking Black League officers. He walked for an unknown length of time, until his shoeless feet were blistered. They finally arrived at their destination: a concentration camp.

Their entire group was gathered in a square. The 200-odd Germans were so terrified by the horror stories of the League that not a single one dared to whisper.

The officer walked up to the podium and, with the help of a translator, began to shout: “Teutons, you may think we will slaughter you all immediately, but you are wrong. Commander-in-Chief Yazov has devised a more efficient, and more useful, method. You will be organized into labor camps. Anything of value you possess will be taken, extracted. Everything you are will become fuel for the Great Trial. However, those with special skills can earn preferential treatment—of course, don't think about resisting, and don't even think about slacking off or sabotage. We have the complete records of all your families, your loved ones. Our agents and collaborators are all over Germany. If you make any move, I can guarantee, your families will suffer a torment you cannot imagine. Your future will be miserable, and I won't comfort you with lies.”

He coughed, then continued: “First, you will be sterilized, just as you beasts once did to every Slav. Alright, take them away.” He even deliberately paused for a few seconds between sentences, enjoying their expressions of disbelief, observing the unrest in the crowd. He clearly enjoyed the process. Michael broke down, almost crying out loud: “Sir, I beg you, spare my life, my neighbors and the Slavs nearby can all testify, I have never abused Slavs, I…” Before the next word could come out, a bullet was already embedded in his skull. The officer impatiently wiped the muzzle of his gun with a handkerchief: “Everyone says that, so none of you are guilty? I'm talking to you nicely because most of you are skilled workers, or have some expertise in a technical field, which makes you more useful. Anyone who dares to talk back again will be shot!”

With that, he turned and walked away, leaving the guards to drag the Germans one by one into the operating rooms, only turning back suddenly to add: “This time, cuff their hands and feet tightly. Same as before, five-man joint responsibility, the punishment will be a little less severe.”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.140.a: “After all, they can't do any delicate work if they're broken.”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.141.desc:
Belle Grade hurriedly walked to the factory entrance and showed his press pass to the two guards at the gate. He strode into the factory and headed for the workers' rest area. This collection of human rights conditions under Russian rule still needed the testimony of a few last people. Yesterday, he had been busy organizing the collected materials and documents, and hadn't come to the factory all day. Just as he reached the workers' rest area, he heard a guard behind him salute: “Hello, Comrade Operative!”

Belle turned around. A soldier in a Black League uniform was already standing behind him, smiling. “Hello, Mr. Belle Grade, I am the industrial operative in charge of this sector, number 435612. You can call me Ivanov.”

“Mr. Ivanov, I am an American journalist. This is my press pass. I am here to interview your country's workers to help you obtain international aid.”

“Oh, it's you. It seems we found the right person.” Ivanov was still smiling, but his words made Belle Grade increasingly uneasy. “Let me think, according to the confession of that female worker, Vasya, she has already confirmed to us. You, Belle Grade, have attempted to spy on our country's core industrial production secrets, while at the same time, using exaggeration and fabrication to endanger the social stability of our country.”

“That's not true. I was only interviewing ordinary workers about their living conditions and did not ask any industrial questions.”

“Is that so?” Ivanov beckoned, and a guard handed him a document. It was filled with descriptions of the terrible living conditions of the factory workers and their families. “This is the draft report the League police found in your home. During your reporting, you have been widely publicizing the low level of human rights in our Russia, greatly slandering our government. What is this if not a threat?”

“Also, looking at your surname, you're British, aren't you? Looks like a hidden fascist. Damn it, take him away!”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.141.a: Announcement from the US Embassy: One of our citizens has gone missing in Russia. We request the Russian government's assistance in locating him.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.142.desc:
Vasily was from Omsk. Out of love for his Russian motherland, he had aspired to be a soldier since childhood. In 1971, at the age of 18, he fulfilled his wish and became a Russian soldier, serving the Black League.

Vasily witnessed the rise of the Black League and the unification of the Russian wasteland. Living in Omsk for so long, he often received reports of victory from the front. The newspapers, almost without exception, published stories of Commander-in-Chief Yazov's wise leadership, the enemy's constant retreat, and the great victories of the Black League. This made Vasily always believe that the Black League would lead Russia to crush its enemies and achieve rejuvenation.

The Russian Rejuvenation Government was now established. Under the leadership of Comrade Yazov, the Black League had unified the wasteland. The next step was to launch the great Great Trial against the Nazi bastards to reclaim everything that belonged to the Russian people. Vasily was assigned to work in the conscription department, in the countryside of his hometown, Omsk. Although the higher-ups had instructed that all eligible men must be conscripted, when Vasily arrived in the village, he found that there were almost no strong young men left to be seen. Vasily's work became a sinecure, and the organization gave him and his colleague Alexander a day off.

On the ridge of the field, Vasily felt a bit dazed. He remembered when he was a child, handsome young men labored in the fields, shy girls wove at home, and the fields were a picture of prosperity during the harvest. Now, the war was over, but the village was desolate. The young men had disappeared, leaving only the sick and disabled old people and women to watch over their homes. The fields were overgrown with weeds, a scene of desolation as far as the eye could see... The unification by the Black League had not brought happiness to the people, had it?

“Operative 736585, it's time to leave. Comrade Vasily, you seem to have something on your mind,” his colleague Alexander asked him.

Vasily returned to reality from his thoughts. A dangerous thought seemed to have just flashed through his mind. He collected his thoughts and replied:
strings.OMS_more_flavor.142.a: “Operative 657605, it's time for us to get to work.”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.143.desc:
“Russian compatriots! Citizens of Kazan! Please wait a moment, listen to me! Please?”

The people of Kazan's October Street came out wearily from their various workplaces, in a hurry to get home and rest. But as they turned a corner, they saw a large truck. A few people were squatting on the truck, handing out bread to the crowd that had gathered below. One person stood on the truck, holding a propaganda leaflet and a megaphone, shouting loudly to the assembled citizens.

“Compatriots, I have always believed that we Russians are inherently entitled to enjoy freedom and democracy, we have the right to strive for a life with dignity! Stable jobs, sufficient food, full human rights! We Russians must live with dignity in this chaotic era. No matter how the Nazis destroy our homes, we must still maintain hope for life!”

“My political view is simple: what our people have always wanted is stability! No matter the era, or who the ruler is, they should not destroy the hard-won stability. The people of Russia have endured the destruction and oppression of numerous divisive elements, they should not have their stable lives destroyed again because of a dictatorship!”

“Recently, I heard that the government has issued a forced relocation decree, claiming it is to protect our people from Nazi invasion, requiring our people to move to the eastern regions. Please, everyone, think carefully, isn't this a destruction of our stable lives? What our people hope for is a stable life, stable emotions. With them, we Russian people can regain our dignity. With dignity, our people will not fear the oppression of power, and will dare to fight against external invading enemies…”

“The police are here!”

Someone in the crowd suddenly shouted. The onlookers scattered in all directions, some even dropping their bread. A few policemen turned the corner, took out their guns, and first shot out the tires, deflating them.

“Good luck today, caught a few revisionist elements who aren't afraid of death.” The policemen jumped onto the truck and handcuffed the few people. The intellectual in the lead was still shouting at the leading policeman: “Sir! Please listen to me, the government, for its so-called Great Trial theory, is even ignoring the will of the people, forcing the people of this turbulent region to move to unfamiliar places. This…”

“Shut up, garbage,” the leading policeman punched him. “Dignity, is dignity bigger than a German bomb? The Nazis are about to invade Russia, and you garbage with cars are letting the people block your way to oppose the League's policies, and then shouting about some crap stability, dignity, to get the people to oppose the government? Search him, see if he's a Nazi spy!”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.143.a: Whether it's confirmed or not, today's execution quota is filled by them.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.144.desc:
To: Commander-in-Chief Yazov

From: Aleksandr Sakharovsky, Yevgeny Savintsev

The second round of nuclear counter-strike strategy discussions has concluded and is available for review.

The primary nuclear counter-strike facilities in the western part of the Motherland have been completed, with the remaining parts still under construction. The nuclear missiles for deployment are being assembled and loaded in designated factories. The Main Directorate for the Protection of State Secrets, Vympel special forces, the Ministry of National Development, and other departments have fully intervened for monitoring. During this period, the Nazis have conducted multiple rounds of infiltration into our western bases, attempting to locate our nuclear weapon bases. Thanks to the timely discovery and action by our various departments, possible intelligence leaks have been prevented.

Intelligence networks indicate that the scale and quantity of nuclear weapons held by the Nazis far exceed previous estimates. In recent years, the Nazi militarists have been widely publicizing the threat from our country, increasing the size of their nuclear arsenal, and adding a greater number of more powerful nuclear devices. We have reason to believe that the Nazi high command is determined to fight a nuclear war. Once the Great Trial begins, they will inevitably launch a full-scale nuclear surprise attack on our various cities, destroying our army and our major cities. Our western nuclear facilities will be destroyed in the first round of counter-attacks under high-intensity Nazi nuclear strikes.

All departments have reached a unanimous opinion. The League must retain a final nuclear exchange force to break the balance of nuclear power around the world and promote the realization of the final Great Trial. After discussions by multiple departments, we need a data collection system. This system needs to continuously monitor the radiation levels, seismic activity, and nuclear explosions within our country. After a nuclear strike on the Motherland, this system will check the communication network with the League's military. If communication is normal and commands are received, this system will remain silent. Once communication is lost, this system will grant final launch authority to the duty officers in the missile silos.

To ensure the effectiveness of the counter-strike and to prevent potential degenerate elements from gaining control of the strike force, all departments believe it is necessary to design a fully automated 'Perimeter System.' It will be our last hope to complete the Great Trial.
...
The Great Trial is supreme.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.145.desc:
Timoshenko stood before the launch pad, gazing at the brand-new, iron behemoth forged by Russia's finest masters. The hopes and fears for the future nearly burst from his chest. Behind him, a group of technicians and engineers in washed-out work clothes, along with operatives and soldiers with awe and bewilderment in their eyes, held their breath, awaiting the final test—a test of whether the Russian nation could reforge its own backbone.

To complete this test, over the past few months, this team had overcome, even leaped over, countless difficulties and obstacles: the missiles obtained through the life-and-death struggle of intelligence operatives were not intact, and the design blueprints were incomplete. To crack the missile's secrets, the engineering team worked day and night, disassembling and reverse-engineering. Technicians crawled over the missile's surface again and again, testing and drawing. Countless questions almost immediately filled the draft papers. They also had to repair the damaged parts. The entire team was exhausted in the process, but everyone gritted their teeth, unwilling to give up hope.

After the reverse-engineering was complete, the materials used for the missile body became a new problem. Special alloy steel, special rubber, and all kinds of unknown materials nearly drove the research team to despair. To complete this task, a secret nationwide resource allocation and research effort was launched. Domestic and foreign intelligence agencies were fully mobilized for their needs. Countless outstanding achievements from home and abroad were sent to them for use. Timoshenko still remembered when they conducted the first large-scale test firing of the cobbled-together replica engine. The roaring flames illuminated Timoshenko's sunken eye sockets, and also the tear-streaked faces of everyone present.

Finally, the assembly was complete, and it was time to launch. A huge countdown was ticking on the command center's screen. Timoshenko sat at the main console, his eyes glued to the screen. The officer beside him, though expressionless, had his hands tightly gripping the armrests of his chair.

“Ignition!”

A dazzling fireball erupted from the missile's tail, followed by a huge roar. Russia's first intercontinental ballistic missile, the 'Satan,' began to slowly rise. Everyone looked up, watching with awe and hope as this crude iron beast continued to soar into space. And the beast did not disappoint.
