“Children,” Major Saken's voice was hoarse but firm, “the beasts of the Black League are twenty kilometers away.”

The crowd fell silent. Abay saw Mainur tie the white cloth strip around her forehead; it was clearly the material for a shroud.

“We have no tanks, no planes,” the major raised his remaining right arm, “but we have every brick, every drop of blood in Shymkent!”

Someone started singing 'Wake up, Kazakhs,' and gradually, everyone joined in. Abay remembered his father's words before he died: “For decades, our nation has been fighting for its own destiny... Whether it was the Tsar or the Soviets, we never surrendered... Abay, you must remember: the Kazakh people can be defeated, but they will never surrender.”

At noon, dust rose on the horizon.

“They're here!” the boy in the watchtower shouted.

Abay lay behind the sandbags, for the first time seeing the Black League's army clearly—dozens of tanks in a wedge formation, followed by an endless line of infantry. The sunlight reflected coldly off their gas masks.

When the first shell landed on the city gate, Abay was thrown to the ground by the blast wave. He got up and saw that half of Major Saken's body was gone, but the old man was still pointing forward with his remaining arm.

“For Kazakhstan!”

Someone shouted this slogan, and then, a miracle happened. The ragged crowd surged towards the iron tide like a wave. Abay saw Mainur charging at the front with a kitchen knife; the naan seller holding a homemade firebomb; even the university student who had fled from Almaty was waving an iron bar...

The second wave of artillery covered the charging crowd. A sharp pain shot through Abay's left leg, but he still struggled to crawl forward. Through the smoke, he saw the Black League soldiers reloading, their cold barrels aimed at the last batch of charging old people and children.

Abay stood up with all his might, holding up the national flag he had taken from someone's hand. In the instant the rain of bullets pierced his body, he seemed to see his father's smiling face… 

Then, he let out one last cry:
strings.OMS_more_flavor.176.desc:
As Colonel Ivan Kozlov's leather boots stepped over the broken glass of Frunze's central square, the setting sun was bathing the 'Victory Monument' in a blood-like light. He reached out and touched the not-yet-dry blood on the monument's base. The sticky sensation at his fingertips was like caressing a piece of rotten flesh.

“Is this what victors look like?” he asked the empty square, his voice echoing among the bullet-riddled buildings. Three days ago, the Kyrgyz were fighting the Black League army here. Now, only a few uncollected bodies remained, one of which still clutched a Kyrgyz flag, burned down to half its size.

Kozlov slowly walked towards the city hall, the hem of his greatcoat sweeping over the scattered leaflets on the road—these were self-printed by the resisters, their content quite chaotic. The city hall's bronze doors were twisted from an explosion, a severed hand stuck in the crack, a wedding ring on its ring finger reflecting a faint light.

“Colonel, you should see this,” a lieutenant lifted the curtain to the basement, a hot, putrid stench rushing out. More than thirty 'resistance army' officials were crammed into this room, once used for storing archives, all executed in a kneeling position, the bullet holes in the back of their heads neatly aligned.

“They call this a strategic reserve,” he kicked a moldy flour sack in the corner. “With this stuff, they thought they could compete with the Black League's army. What a pipe dream.” Kozlov couldn't help but let out a cold laugh.

As night fell, Kozlov stood on the reviewing stand of the former Victory Square. Searchlights cast his shadow onto the walls of the opposite building, as huge as a demon. Sappers were placing explosives at the base of the monument, while his aide held a captured antique pocket watch and began the countdown.

“Ten, nine, eight…”

He thought of those scoundrels in the so-called 'camps' in the city's outskirts. They must be being covered by the Black League's artillery fire at this very moment. These mongrels must still think they can snatch back what they consider to be their Kyrgyz motherland's 'territory' from the enemy, just like a dozen years ago.

“...three, two, one!”

Amidst the deafening explosion, the thirty-meter-high monument slowly tilted. Kozlov watched as the inscriptions celebrating victory shattered in the firelight. Marble fragments crashed onto the square, crushing the unclaimed bodies once more.

“Report, Colonel, Frunze radio station is operational,” the communications officer handed him a microphone.

Kozlov cleared his throat, his voice broadcasting from the city's remaining loudspeakers: “All Kyrgyz people in the city, whether you have surrendered or are still resisting…” he crushed a rotten head that had rolled to his feet, “...please abandon your foolishness. You have only one true motherland, and that is the Black League...”

After the smoke cleared, the newly erected Black League flag fluttered in the square. Kozlov took the vodka from his aide and raised a toast to this dead city: “To a double victory—we have destroyed your army, and you… have long since destroyed your own souls.”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.176.a: To celebrate this victory, the Colonel specially ordered the dead city to be sacked once more.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.177.desc:
The sound of gunfire was already approaching the columns of the Navoi Opera Theater. Fragments of musical scores were scattered on the marble steps, and a broken tanbur string trembled slightly in the wind. The refugees crowded into the boxes and corridors fell silent, until the white-haired old conductor climbed onto the stage, his trembling fingers brushing over the dust-covered piano keys.

“Sing,” the old man's voice echoed under the dome, “for the last journey of our motherland.”

As the first note sounded, the soldiers of the Black League kicked open the gilded doors. The eyes behind the gas masks swept over the full audience—women holding babies, old soldiers leaning on crutches, students in tattered clothes—all with their backs straight. The piano music grew louder, the old conductor's withered fingers suddenly became strong. Everything seemed to return to twenty years ago, to the golden age that once belonged to Tashkent.

“The wheat of the Altai is full and plump...”

Singing rose from every corner. The melon seller sang in a hoarse voice, the textile worker beside him had a clear voice, and between them lay a young man with a bullet in his stomach, his harmony gradually turning into a gurgle of blood. In a box on the second floor, a professor from Tashkent University held his wife, singing the chorus with perfect diction.

When the Black League officer raised his pistol, a little girl in the front row suddenly stood up. She wore traditional Uzbek seven-colored braids, her coal-stained skirt swaying to the rhythm: “The cotton of Mirzachul is as white as snow...” The bullet pierced her small chest, but the song poured from more throats.

Gunfire and singing intertwined under the baroque dome. The old conductor's white suit was stained red with blood splattered from the piano, but he stubbornly struck the keys. An old woman with glasses, leaning on a silver-headed cane, walked onto the stage. She had once been a minor actress, and now she sang with a toothless mouth: “The land of prosperity blooms with joy...” Three bullets made her fall back as if in a curtain call.

In the symphony of gunfire, the lyrics became clearer and clearer: “Friendship forges your strength!”—a bullet shattered the crystal chandelier; “Labor achieves your glory!”—a soldier in body armor kicked over a music stand; “May peace forever reside in this land!”—the final chorus mixed with the sound of shattering glass.

When the officer stepped over the bodies onto the stage, the old conductor was playing the finale with blood-stained fingers. A gas mask was pressed to his ear: “Old man, your Uzbekistan is dead.”

The piano music stopped abruptly. The old man smiled and turned his head, his cloudy eyes reflecting the stacked bodies in the audience—some still in an embrace, some with their fingers clasped together, a mother had used her body to create a final shelter between the seats.

“No,” the old conductor said softly, his fingers suddenly crashing down on the keys, “she will live forever in the hearts of everyone who knows this song. You beasts will never conquer this land…”

After the final gunshot, the theater fell silent. Only the wind, passing through the bullet holes, made a whining sound in the metal pipes of the organ.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.177.a: The song is gone with the dust.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.178.desc:
Day 23: Namangan

In Namangan's central square, new bullet holes were added to the base of the bombed-out monument. In the morning, Black League soldiers marched local residents in columns past it. I noticed an Uzbek old man being pushed down in front of the monument, and a Kyrgyz merchant, usually indifferent, suddenly stepped forward to intervene. After two gunshots, the blood of both men soaked into the shell-shattered ground. The shops and windows around the square remained tightly shut, with only the wind carrying ash through the empty streets…

Day 46: Andijan

To my surprise, Andijan at night showed a strange vitality. A surviving woman told me about what was happening in an abandoned textile factory: residents oppressed by the Black League gathered there secretly. They passed around underground publications, scrounged for military equipment, and spoke in low voices. An old man who had lost his right hand once cursed to her how the soldiers of the Black League had brutally murdered his family… In the early hours of the morning, gunshots broke the silence. Facing the Black League's armored vehicles, three youths of different ethnicities linked arms and charged forward without regard for their own safety… The moonlight shone on their mangled limbs, the combination of coagulated blood and the shadow of their bodies like a grotesque modern sculpture…

Day 61: Leninabad

Leninabad's streets were terrifyingly quiet, like walking into a huge tomb. In my memory, Leninabad had been a city full of rebellious spirit, but now the people were left with only numb faces. When a Black League soldier dragged a young girl past, a resident finally stood up. When the gunshot rang out, I saw people of different ethnicities spontaneously standing together. Their blood flowed down the gutters into the Syr Darya…

In the Western media, the Black League is portrayed as the 'maintainer of order in Central Asia,' their atrocities beautified as 'necessary stabilization measures.' These people claim this is a 'necessary sacrifice,' but what I see is a naked crime against humanity!

The people of Fergana do not need your pity, they need the truth. Those Uzbeks you call 'extremists,' those Tajiks you label as 'separatists,' those Kyrgyz you slander as 'thugs'—they just want to live peacefully on their own land. When the blood of three feuding nations finally flows together, is that not enough to show who the real devil is?

The Western world can continue to play deaf and dumb, pretending to know nothing about all this, but history will ultimately remember: in Fergana's darkest hour, it was these 'barbarians' who taught us what humanity is, what dignity is.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.178.a: And they were merely fighting for the most legitimate rights for their country…
strings.OMS_more_flavor.179.desc:
To my dearest Abdul:

By the time you read this letter, I will have already set out on the arduous journey to Afghanistan with our children. The saffron pot we planted together on the windowsill, I have entrusted to our old neighbor Nasir's care—it is blooming beautifully, just like the sea of flowers bathed in the spring sun in front of the Dushanbe University library where we first met twenty years ago. Do you remember? The Vakhsh River was so clear then, and we always loved to dream about the future by the fountain in the central square. You said you would take me to see every beautiful inch of our motherland.

Our motherland was once so proud, my dear. The snow-capped peaks of the Gissar Range shone in the morning light, and the rubies of Badakhshan glittered in the museum. Do you remember our wedding day? You pinned a bright red poppy in my hair, saying it was like the undying flame of Tajikistan. We were so naive then, thinking that this beauty would last forever.

The fires of war have destroyed everything. I will never forget that day, when our motherland's heart was torn out, Badakhshan and Fergana—our poor children never even got to see these two beautiful lands. But even so, we still had hope, hoping for a good life, and for a prosperous motherland. We believed then that as long as we had faith in our hearts, no matter how great the difficulties, the motherland would never truly perish.

But now, my dear husband, I must tell you a cruel truth: the Tajikistan we so deeply loved is dead. Yesterday, as I was taking the children through the square, it was already piled with bodies. The Black League has turned our home into a living hell, with only the harsh whistles of those terrifying soldiers echoing in the streets.

I must leave, Abdul. Little Ali has not had a drop of milk in three days, and Marhabo has started talking to an empty can. At dawn tomorrow, we will take the cart arranged by old Nasir and cross the border into Afghanistan. I dare not tell the children that they may never see their beloved father again.

If you can read this letter, if you are still alive, I beg you to come and find us in Mazar-i-Sharif. But please do not blame yourself, my warrior. You chose to fight for our motherland to the last moment, and I must find a sliver of hope for our children.

I must stop writing now. The situation is very bad, and I do not know if the children and I will reach Afghanistan alive. May God grant that you see this letter, and may He forgive us for the choice we had to make.

Abdul, let go of your obsession. The motherland is dead, and we will never see her again…

Forever yours,

Malika
strings.OMS_more_flavor.179.a: “If there is another life, I will still love you, for all eternity.”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.180.desc:
The setting sun dyed the marble buildings of Ashgabat blood red. Azat dragged his injured left leg, moving through the narrow alleys. His uniform was tattered, but the Turkmenistan border guard badge on his chest was still polished to a shine. A month ago, when the Black League's tanks rolled over the border, his company had scattered like a sandcastle. A bullet had grazed his temple, and he had survived by falling among the bodies of his comrades.

As he turned the last corner, Azat's fingers unconsciously touched the key in his pocket—it was on a string his six-year-old daughter, Altyn, had made for him before he left, with a blue glass bead on it. The sound of the key turning in the lock was unusually clear, followed by the screeching of the door hinge.

“Sabina? Altyn?” his call echoed in the empty apartment.

On the living room table, half a piece of moldy naan was left on a plate. Beside it was a shattered teacup, the dried tea stains looking eerily like blood. Azat's army boot stepped on something hard and crisp on the floor—it was Altyn's reading primer.

The bathroom door was ajar.

Azat's world stood still after he pushed open that door. His wife, Sabina, lay in the bathtub, her pale hands still in an embrace, her daughter Altyn in her favorite blue dress in her arms—if one ignored the black hole in her temple. On the edge of the bathtub was a bar of soap, the lemon-scented soap Azat had brought back from the military commissary on his last leave, now stained pink with blood.

Azat knelt before the bathtub, his trembling fingers brushing over his wife's cold eyelids. He suddenly remembered the night two years ago before he left, Sabina was giving Altyn a bath in this very bathtub, the little girl's laughter and splashing water soaking his military trousers. Then, this city was still called the “White Pearl,” and the nights at the border post were filled only with the whispers of the wind and stars.

Night fell completely. Azat, with his last bit of strength, placed his wife and child side by side on the bed and covered them with the blanket embroidered with traditional Turkmen patterns. He took out the treasured vodka from the back of the wardrobe—he had planned to drink it with his comrades after the war—and now drank it alone under the moonlight.

The alcohol burned his throat, but his memories grew clearer. He remembered during recruit training, the instructor pointing to the Karakum Desert and saying: “We are not just guarding the border line. Behind us are not only our homes and families, but also tens of thousands of happy families.” He remembered the beautiful Ashgabat, his beautiful wife and child, the comrades with whom he drank and talked…

As the first ray of dawn shone through the curtains, Azat had already cleaned his service pistol. He kissed his wife and child's foreheads one last time, and hung Altyn's glass bead around his neck. In front of the city hall, the Black League commander was inspecting his troops, the medals forged from the blood of the Central Asian people looking dim in the sunlight.

As Azat rushed out from the crowd, he vaguely heard his daughter Altyn calling him. The first shot shattered the commander's kneecap—a common technique used by border troops against smugglers. The second shot was aimed at his heart, but was deflected by a guard who suddenly lunged forward.

As a sharp pain spread from his back, Azat fell to the ground, and saw his blood spreading on the ground, like—a beautiful rose garden? Though Azat had never seen one in his life, it all felt so familiar. His blurry vision suddenly became clear:

On that rose garden stood his comrades, and Sabina, and Altyn, the little one with her arms outstretched, running towards her father…
strings.OMS_more_flavor.181.desc:
The world, seen through the eyes of the 20th century, seemed to hold no more secrets. All lands had been surveyed, and ships now sailed upon the most distant seas. Those misty, dream-like regions, unknown a generation ago, were now submissively serving Europe’s needs; steamers were heading directly for the long-sought, divergent sources of the Nile. The Victoria Falls, first seen by a European half a century ago, now obediently powered turbines; the last primeval forests along the Amazon’s banks grew steadily thinner under the axe; Tibet, the sole remaining virgin territory, had been unveiled. The old maps and globes, where ‘unexplored territory’ was wildly exaggerated by experts, now displayed a planet fully known to the 20th-century man. The will to explore sought new paths: downward, to the wondrous fauna of the deep sea, and upward, to the boundless firmament. For since the Earth had temporarily yielded all its secrets to human curiosity, the only untrodden routes lay in the sky, and so the steel wings of aircraft raced to attain new heights and distances.

Yet, until our very century, the naked Earth had hidden its final mystery from view. These were two minuscule, fractured fragments of its body, two spots it had saved from the rapacity of its creatures: the South Pole and the North Pole—the axis of its corporeal form. For millennia, the Earth had spun on the axis of these two virtually lifeless, abstract poles, guarding these pure places from defilement. It hid this ultimate secret beneath layers of icy barriers, sending eternal winter as its guardian against greedy men, building the most magnificent ramparts of cold and blizzards to block all passage. The terror of death and danger turned back the bravest. Only the sun itself might steal a fleeting glance into these locked-off domains; the eye of man had never seen their true visage.

In recent decades, expedition after expedition had set out, but none had reached its goal. The body of Andrée, the finest of the brave, was only now found after resting for thirty-three years in a glassy coffin of giant ice. He had attempted to fly over the Arctic in a balloon, never to return. Every assault shattered against the crystalline fortress forged of frigid temperatures. From time immemorial until today, this part of the Earth had veiled its countenance, a final victory for it over the desires of its creatures. Like a virgin, it preserved its purity against the world’s curiosity.

But the impatient young 20th century stretched forth its hands. It forged new weapons in laboratories, found new armour against danger, and all hardship only intensified its ardor. It wanted to know all truth. It desired, within its first decade, to possess all that had been unattainable for millions of years. Personal courage was now combined with competition between nations. They no longer fought merely to claim the poles, but to possess the flag that would be the first to fly upon this new land. And so, a crusade composed of various peoples and nations set out to conquer this place, sanctified by intense desire. Shock after shock was launched from all the world’s continents. Humanity could wait no longer, for this was the last secret of our living space.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.182.desc:
The nuclear winter is a scar that will never heal in the sky. Ash-grey clouds hang heavily overhead, severing all memory of sunlight. I walk stooped, a dessicated corpse, clutching the tattered scraps of cloth around me, each step sinking into the cold, viscous fallout. The biting wind is a dull blade, scraping against exposed skin, stealing the last vestiges of false warmth. Before me, only twisted rebar spears the black dust, like the rotting ribs of a giant beast pointing towards the sky, silently proclaiming the utter death of an age. In this silence, my goal is pathetically humble: a piece of putrefaction barely fit for my mouth to ease the burning in my stomach, or a scrap of decaying wood still capable of igniting, bringing a brief, false warmth.

A half-collapsed ruin of a colossal structure blocks my path, like a toy carelessly discarded by a god. I fumble my way into a dark fissure, and a heart-stopping crunch echoes beneath my feet—glass or dried bone, I can’t tell. By the murky light, like foul water, leaking from a high crack, I can barely discern the outlines of countless vast metal frames—**bookshelves**, the skeletons of knowledge, now violently broken, leaning and piled against each other, forming tombs of despair. The air is thick with the damp, mortal decay of utterly rotten paper, mixed with the omnipresent dust; every breath is like swallowing ash. My numb, frozen fingers rake blindly through the thick, black dust mixed with paper scraps. Most of the pages dissolve at a touch, turning into grimy mud at my fingertips. Knowledge? That fertile old world? It has long since silently weathered into the dust beneath my feet.

Just as the cold tide of despair was about to drown me, my fingers brushed against a hard, angular anomaly deep within a dark crack formed by a fallen shelf. This abrupt, unyielding touch was like a faint thorn, piercing the callus of my numbness. I held my breath, using both hands to scrape away the heavy dust and debris, and finally dragged out a heavy object.

It was encased in a dark cover with a fine, textured grain. It felt cold and resilient in my hand, like treated hide, yet abnormally stiff. I vigorously brushed away the heavy layer of dust, revealing a profound, night-like base color. In the center of the cover, several raised symbols were fluid and elegant, faintly shimmering with a dull, gold sheen—almost entirely obscured by dust in the gloom—the final trace left by an ancient, long-broken craft. I did not recognize these symbols; they were the strange incantations of a lost civilization. My fingertip trembled with an almost religious reverence as I cautiously turned the resilient cover. The pages inside were yellowed, carrying the subtle fragrance of time, yet miraculously intact, their edges even lined with soft gold. What shook me to my core were the illustrations tucked between the pages: people in strange metal armor, mounted on magnificent steeds, set against a background of billowing smoke and raging fire. One image, in particular, instantly seized all my attention: a man with a trimmed beard, draped in a dark, swirling cloak, riding a warhorse white as silver. He lifted his chin slightly, his gaze piercing the mist like a sharp sword. In those eyes burned a will that I could no longer comprehend, one bordering on arrogance, a strength that mastered the storm rather than being torn apart by it—a contrast to this dead wasteland that was both sharp and suffocating.

I slowly bent down, the dust covering my ankles. The weight in my hands was real and alien, as if I held a splintered bone of civilization. The strange golden symbols remained silent, yet they held more power than any words I knew. They spoke of binding, gold leaf, and an almost sacred respect for the text—all of which had been lost in my world.

 The wind still wailed through the ruins, but now it no longer sounded only like lamentation. It became background noise, setting off the absolute silence of this miraculous book. I stood there, holding a messenger from a forgotten age. At the very end of meaning, what I found was not food or fuel, but a monument—or perhaps a memorial—erected by a man named Stefan Zweig to the brilliant moments of mankind.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.182.a: And so, he took the book back and read it carefully.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.183.t: Robert Falcon Scott, The Man Who Advanced on the South Pole
strings.OMS_more_flavor.183.desc:
Scott, a Captain in the British Royal Navy, a perfectly ordinary naval captain. His service record was practically identical to the rank register. His time in the navy had earned him great satisfaction from his superiors, and later he had organized an expedition with Shackleton. There were no special signs to hint at the hero within him. In photographs, his face, like that of thousands of Englishmen, was stern, resolute, and devoid of expression, as if his muscles were held rigid by an inner force. Grey-blue eyes, a tightly closed mouth. His countenance bore no hint of romantic line or cheerful color, only the suggestion of a powerful will and a mind that considered the world's realities. His handwriting was a certain type of English script, clear and without ornate flourishes, written quickly and neatly. His style was lucid and precise, moving in its veracity like a report, untainted by any fantasy. Scott wrote English as simply and vigorously as Tacitus wrote Latin. One might assume he was a man of practical concerns, entirely without dreams. In England, even the most specially gifted geniuses were often rigidly crystalline, elevating everything to the level of duty. Scott was precisely such an Englishman, having connected with British history hundreds of times. He had campaigned in India, conquered countless scattered islands, accompanied colonists to Africa, and participated in innumerable global conflicts. But wherever he went, he presented the same cold, reserved face, bearing the same staunch resolve and collective spirit.

Yet, his steely will was already manifest in his actions. Scott was determined to complete the work Shackleton had begun. He organized an expedition, though funds were scarce. This did not deter him. He sacrificed his own property and incurred debts, confident in his success. His young wife had just given birth to a son, yet he did not hesitate, leaving his Andromache like a modern-day Hector. Friends and comrades were soon found. Nothing in the world could shake his resolve. A peculiar ship named the *Terra Nova* carried them to the edge of the ice sea. Peculiar because it was dually equipped: half like Noah's Ark, laden with live animals, and half a modern laboratory with thousands of instruments and a vast library. For everything necessary to sustain life and the nourishment of the spirit had to be brought to that desolate world. Strangely, the most complex and refined technology of the new age was combined with the most primitive defenses of early man—skins, furs, and live animals. And the entire expedition, like the ship, had a dual and curious nature: it was an act of adventure, yet meticulously calculated like a business transaction; it was a daring endeavor, yet one of the utmost caution—every detail was precisely accounted for, yet the possibility of unforeseen accidents remained ever-present.

They left England on June 1, 1910. It was a day of brilliant sunshine on the Anglo-Saxon island kingdom. The grass was green, flowers bloomed. The gentle sun hung high in a cloudless sky, radiating light. As the coastline gradually vanished, they were immensely moved, for everyone knew that this farewell to the warm sun would last for years, perhaps forever for some. But the British flag flew from the masthead, and they were satisfied, knowing that this flag, a symbol of the world, would accompany them to claim the only part of the Earth yet without a master.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.183.a: And so, the struggle to claim the South Pole began.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.184.desc:
After a brief rest, they landed in January 1911 at Cape Evans in McMurdo Sound, the perpetually frozen edge of the pole. Here, they built a wooden hut to prepare for the winter. December and January counted as summer, for only during this period did the daytime sun hang for a few hours in the white, metallic sky. The walls of the house were made of planks, much like the base camps used by earlier expeditions. But within this hut, one could feel the progress of the age. Their predecessors had used foul-smelling whale-oil lamps, sitting in dark cells, weary of their limited vision. A monotonous series of sunless days had exhausted them. Now, these 20th-century men could see a microcosm of the entire world and all of science within the four walls. An acetylene lamp shone with a bright white light. A film projector magically displayed images of distant lands, scenes from the temperate zones brought back from afar. An automatic piano played music. A gramophone played songs. Books disseminated the knowledge of the age. A typewriter clattered in one room. Another room was a small darkroom, where films and color slides were developed. A geologist examined rocks with a radiological instrument. A zoologist searched captured penguins for new parasites. Meteorological observations and physics experiments exchanged results. During the dim, sunless months, each of the thirty men had their own expertly interconnected work, turning isolated research into shared knowledge. Every evening, they delivered specialized reports, attending university-level lectures amid the jagged ice mountains and the polar cold. Each sought to impart their knowledge to others, perfecting their understanding of the world through fervent mutual discussion. Specialization of research precluded any arrogance; they simply wished to mutually benefit in a collective environment. In this prehistoric world, in this solitude without the concept of time, these thirty men exchanged the latest achievements of the 20th century, and it was through these achievements that they could feel not only every hour but every second of the world's clock. It is moving to read in their records how these serious men celebrated with gusto around a Christmas tree, and how they published a humorous small newspaper, whimsically named *The South Polar Times*, in which they exchanged cheerful jokes. There, a small event—a whale breaching, a Siberian pony stumbling—would become headline news, while the extraordinary—the shimmering aurora, the terrible cold, the extreme solitude—became commonplace and routine. During this period, they only dared to undertake small excursions, testing the motor sledges, practicing skiing and dog-sledging, while simultaneously building depots for the subsequent great journey. Yet, the calendar pages tore away very slowly until the warm season (December). The ship carrying mail from home sailed through the sea of floating giant ice to reach them. They now dared to venture out in groups, training for daytime marches during the frigid season, testing various tents, and mastering all necessary experience. Of course, not everything they attempted was successful, but the countless difficulties only imbued them with new courage. When they returned from their excursions, frozen and exhausted, they were greeted by cheers and a warm stove. After days of hunger and cold, they felt that this comfortable little wooden hut, established at 77° South Latitude, was the most peaceful place in the world.

But one time, an exploration team returned from the west, bringing news that silenced the entire hut. The returnees reported that they had discovered **Amundsen’s** winter camp en route. Scott immediately understood: besides the cold and danger, another man was now challenging him for the honor of being the first to discover the Earth's final secret. This man was the Norwegian, Amundsen. Scott measured repeatedly on the map. When he discovered that Amundsen's winter camp was situated 110 kilometers closer to the South Pole than his own, he was utterly stunned, yet not disheartened. 'For the honor of our country, brace up!'—he wrote proudly in his diary.

Amundsen's name appeared only this once in his diary and never again. But one can sense that from that day on, Amundsen's name became a shadow that perpetually hung over the isolated hut in the icy wilderness, disturbing him every moment.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.184.a: The silence of the Antarctic was broken by the sound of the marching columns.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.185.t: The March to the South Pole
strings.OMS_more_flavor.185.desc:
Watchmen rotated constantly on the observation hill a mile from the hut. A lone instrument mounted on the slope, like a cannon aimed at an invisible enemy, tested the heat of the approaching first sun. For days, they waited for the sun's appearance. The dawn sky was already transforming with colorful auroras, but the orb of the sun remained perpetually below the horizon. However, this sky, radiant with wondrous colors—this harbinger of the sun's reflection—already filled the impatient men with joy. The telephone finally rang, bringing the news from the top of the observation hill to the cheering men: the sun had come out, revealing itself for an hour for the first time during the winter's darkness. The sun’s rays were so weak and faint they could barely bring life to the frozen air, and the solar waves hardly registered a deflection on the instrument. Yet, the mere sight of the sun was enough to elicit laughter. To take full advantage of this brief period of light—though, by our usual concept of life, it remained a terrifyingly cold winter, there it signified the arrival of spring, summer, and autumn all at once—the expedition prepared intensely. The motor sledges rattled ahead, followed by sledges pulled by Siberian ponies and Eskimo dogs. The entire journey was meticulously divided into stages. Storage depots were established every two days' march, stocking new clothing, food, and, most crucially, kerosene—liquified heat against the infinite cold—for the return journey. Because the entire team would set out initially, then gradually return in batches, the final group—those chosen to conquer the Pole—had to be left with the most ample supplies, the strongest traction animals, and the best sledges.

Despite the meticulously crafted plan, which even accounted for the details of various possible misfortunes, it did not work. After two days of travel, all the motor sledges broke down, collapsing into useless burdens. The Siberian ponies were not in as good a condition as anticipated. However, the organic tools proved slightly superior to the mechanical ones here, for even if the sick horses had to be killed midway, they could still leave a few hot meals for the dogs, augmenting their strength.

On November 1, 1911, they set off in groups. From the film footage, this peculiar expedition began with thirty people, then twenty, then ten, until only five men walked alone across the white wilderness of the lifeless, prehistoric world. The man at the front was always tightly wrapped in furs and cloth, revealing only his beard and a pair of eyes, looking like a savage. A fur-covered hand held the reins of a Siberian pony, which dragged his heavily loaded sledge. Behind him was a man similarly dressed and postured, and behind him, another such man… Twenty black dots formed a line on the boundless, glaring white of the ice and snow. At night, they crawled into their tents, building snow walls against the wind to protect the Siberian ponies. The next morning, they set off again, walking through the freezing air—breathed by humans for the first time in millions of years—with monotonous, desolate hearts.

But worries accumulated. The weather remained terrible, and sometimes they could only cover 30 kilometers instead of the planned 40. Every day became precious to them, for they knew that in this solitude, another invisible man was advancing on the same goal from the other side. Here, every minor event could escalate into danger. An Eskimo dog ran away; a Siberian pony refused to eat—all this caused anxiety, for in this desolate snowfield, everything useful became incredibly precious, and living things were priceless because they were irreplaceable. The fame that would be etched in history might depend on the four hooves of a pony, and a sky filled with wind and snow could hinder the completion of an immortal achievement. Simultaneously, the health of the team became an issue. Some suffered from snow blindness, others from frostbite. The Siberian ponies grew increasingly exhausted as their feed diminished. Finally, the ponies all died just at the foot of the Beardmore Glacier. These horses, their friends, had lived in this solitude with the explorers for two years. Everyone knew their names. They had been gently stroked countless times, yet now the heartbreaking task had to be done—to slaughter these loyal animals here. They called this sad place 'The Slaughter Camp.' It was from this blood-soaked spot that a part of the expedition turned back, while the remaining members prepared for the final effort to cross the perilous expanse of the Beardmore Glacier. This was the steep, icy fortress built by the South Pole to protect itself, which only the fervent flame of human will could breach.

They covered less and less ground each day, for the snow here had turned into hard, frozen shards. They could no longer glide on skis but had to drag the sledges. The hard ice shards gouged the sledge runners, and their feet were worn raw walking on snow as hard as sand, yet they did not yield. On December 30th, they reached 87° South Latitude, Shackleton’s furthest point. The last supporting party had to turn back here, leaving only five selected men to continue to the Pole. Scott chose those he deemed unsuitable. These men did not dare to disobey, but their hearts were heavy. The goal was within reach, yet they had to return, conceding the honor of being the first to see the Pole to their comrades. However, the selection had been made. They shook hands again, concealing their emotional intensity with masculine fortitude. This small party finally split into two smaller groups, one heading south towards the utterly unknown South Pole, and the other north, returning to their camp. They turned back from both directions occasionally, to take a final look at their living friends. Soon, the last silhouette disappeared. They—the five selected men: Scott, Bowers, Oates, Wilson, and Evans—continued their lonely march toward the utterly unknown South Pole.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.185.a: The will of man is always strong.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.186.desc: The diaries from those last days reveal an increasing sense of unease. They began to tremble, like the blue needle of a compass near the pole. 'The shadow moves forward on our right, then sweeps around in front to the left, slowly circling our bodies, but this period is endlessly long!' Yet, sparks of hope shone brighter through the lines of the diary. Scott recorded the distance covered with increasing fervor: 'Only 150 kilometers to the Pole, but if we continue like this, we really can't hold on.'—The diary thus recorded their utter exhaustion. Two days later: '137 kilometers to the Pole, but this distance will become very, very difficult for us.' But then, a new voice, filled with confidence in victory, suddenly appeared: 'Only 94 kilometers to the Pole! Even if we can't reach it, we're very, very close!' On January 14th, hope turned into certainty: 'Only 70 kilometers left, and our objective will be reached!' And the next day's diary revealed their joy and almost cheerful mood: 'Only 50 kilometers left to the Pole! We will reach our goal no matter what!' These exhilarating lines make one acutely feel how tautly their hope was stretched, as if their entire nervous system was trembling with anticipation and anxiety. Victory was at hand; they had stretched out their hands to this last secret of the Earth, and with one final effort, the goal would be reached.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.186.a: Another testament to the powerful will of Old World mankind.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.187.desc:
'Spirits are high,' the diary recorded. On January 16th, they set off earlier than usual in the morning, hoping to see the magnificent secret sooner. Anxiety had dragged them out of their sleeping bags early. By noon, the five determined men had covered 14 kilometers. They marched with high spirits across the desolate white snowfield, for it was no longer possible to fail now; the decisive deed for mankind was virtually complete. But suddenly, one of the companions, Bowers, grew uneasy. His eyes were fixed on a small black spot on the boundless snow. He dared not voice his suspicion: that someone might have already planted a marker there. But now, the others, too, were horribly thinking the same thing. Their hearts trembled, though they tried to reassure themselves—much like Robinson Crusoe desperately tried to mistake the strange footprints he found on the deserted island for his own, in vain—they told themselves it must be a crack in the ice, or perhaps a shadow cast by some object. They approached nervously, all the while deceiving themselves, though they knew in their hearts: the Norwegians led by Amundsen had been there before them.

Before long, they found a ski pole stuck in the snow, tied with a black flag, surrounded by the remains of a campsite—ski tracks and many dog prints. In the face of this harsh reality, there was no longer any doubt: Amundsen had camped here. The Earth's South Pole, which had been untouched for millennia, or rather, unseen by the world since ancient times, had been discovered twice within a molecular span of time—fifteen days—a phenomenon unheard of and unbelievable in human history. And they were precisely the second group to arrive; they were only one month late. Though millions of months had passed since antiquity, this one month's delay now seemed far, far too late—for humanity, the first arrival possesses everything, the second is nothing. And they were the second group of humans to reach the Pole. All their effort was in vain, their hardships appeared ludicrous, and the hope of weeks, months, and years felt like madness. 'All the toil and hardships, the exposure, the endless troubles—all for what? Only for these dreams, and now they are all gone.'—Scott wrote in his diary. Tears welled up in their eyes. Despite their exhaustion, they were sleepless that night. Like men condemned, they continued their final march to the Pole cheerlessly and hopelessly, a route they had originally intended to charge toward with shouts of triumph. No one offered comfort; they merely dragged their feet forward in silence. On January 18th, Captain Scott and his four companions reached the Pole. Since he was no longer the first to arrive, nothing here struck him as particularly brilliant. He merely glanced at the heartbreaking spot with cold eyes. 'There is nothing to see here, no difference from the horrible monotony of the previous days.'—This was the entirety of Robert Falcon Scott's description of the Pole. The only unusual thing they found there was not created by nature but by their rival: Amundsen's tent, flying the Norwegian flag. The Norwegian flag fluttered aggressively and triumphantly over this fortress breached by man. Its occupier had even left a letter waiting for the arrival of this unknown second place, confident that he would follow, and asked him to deliver the letter to King Haakon of Norway. Scott accepted the task, faithfully undertaking this most merciless duty: to testify before the world to the achievement of another man, a feat he himself had so ardently pursued.

They forlornly planted the British flag—the belated 'Union Jack'—next to Amundsen's flag of victory, and then departed from this place 'that had betrayed their great ambition.' A bitter cold wind swept over them from behind. Scott, with a sense of foreboding, wrote in his diary: 'The return journey makes me dreadfully afraid.'
strings.OMS_more_flavor.187.a: The crusaders reached the end. Was it what they truly wanted?
strings.OMS_more_flavor.188.desc:
The return journey increased the danger tenfold. On the way to the South Pole, the compass guided them, but now, besides the compass, they also had to follow their original footprints back. For weeks of travel, they had to meticulously avoid straying from their previous steps, lest they miss the pre-established depots, where food, clothing, and, most crucially, gallons of kerosene—condensed heat—were stored for them. But the swirling snow blinded their eyes, making every step fraught with anxiety, for straying off course and missing a depot meant walking directly toward death. Moreover, they now lacked the boundless energy of their initial journey, the thermal energy provided by the rich nutrition and the warm barracks of the Antarctic home.

Furthermore, the steel-like will in their hearts had now slackened. On the outward journey, they were filled with infinite hope, a hope that embodied the curiosity and yearning of all mankind, which granted them boundless strength. They possessed superhuman power when they considered that their endeavor was an immortal feat for humanity. Now, they fought merely to save their own skins, for the survival of their ultimately mortal flesh, for a return home without glory. Perhaps, deep down, they feared going home more than they yearned for it.

Reading the diaries from those days is terrifying. The weather grew worse and worse; the cold season arrived earlier than usual. The white snow beneath their soles hardened, forming thick, icy shards that felt like walking on cleats, sticking to their shoes with every step. The bone-chilling cold consumed their already exhausted bodies. Thus, when they finally reached a depot after days of timid progress and misdirection, they briefly rejoiced, and a flame of confidence flickered back through the lines of the diary. Throughout the grim solitude, only these few men continued to walk. Their heroism is admirable, best proven by Dr. Wilson, the scientist, who continued his scientific observations even when death was steps away, dragging 16 kilograms of precious rock samples on his sledge in addition to all the necessary supplies.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.188.a: At least, they should still be able to return.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.189.desc:
Yet, human courage was gradually eroded by the immense power of nature. The nature here was ruthless, its accumulated power of millennia allowing it to summon cold, ice, snow, and storms like a spirit—using all these destructive arts against the five reckless brave men. Their feet were long frostbitten, and their food rations grew scant, allowing only one hot meal per day. Due to the lack of heat, their bodies had become extremely weak. One day, the companions horribly discovered that **Evans**, the strongest among them, had suddenly lost his mind. He stood aside and stopped walking, muttering ceaselessly, complaining about all the hardships they had endured—some real, some illusory. From his incoherent words, they finally understood that the unfortunate man had gone mad due to a fall or immense suffering. What to do with him? Abandon him on this lifeless ice plain? No. But on the other hand, they had to rush to the next depot without delay, or else… The diary does not clearly state what Scott intended to do. At one o'clock in the morning on February 17th, the unfortunate British Naval Petty Officer died. That day, they had just reached 'The Slaughter Camp,' where they rediscovered the ponies butchered the previous month and ate their first substantial meal in a long time.

Now only four men continued the journey, but disaster struck again. The next depot brought new, agonizing disappointment. The kerosene stored there was far too little, meaning they had to ration this most essential supply—fuel—the only defense against the extreme cold. In the icy darkness, surrounded by howling blizzards, they opened their eyes fearfully, unable to sleep. They barely had the strength left to turn over the soles of their felt boots. But they dragged themselves onward, Oates among them walking on feet whose toes were already gone to frostbite. The wind blew harder than ever. On March 2nd, they reached the next depot, only to be met again with terrible despair: the fuel stored there was once more frighteningly scarce.

They were now panic-stricken. One can sense how Scott struggled to conceal his fear in the diary, yet cries of desperation repeatedly burst through his enforced calm. 'This cannot go on' or 'God help us! We cannot endure this toil much longer,' or 'Our play is drawing to a tragic close,' until finally the terrible confession: 'We are in a very critical position. I doubt if we can get through. God help us, we are in a dreadful plight, chiefly due to the fuel.' Nevertheless, they dragged their weary bodies forward, gritting their teeth, desperately pressing on and on. Oates grew steadily weaker, becoming a burden rather than a help to his friends. One midday, the temperature reached -40°C, forcing them to slow their pace. The unfortunate Oates not only felt but understood that continuing would bring ruin upon his friends, so he made his final preparations. He asked Wilson, the scientist, for ten morphine tablets, to hasten the end when necessary. They struggled on for another day with the sick man. Then, the unfortunate man asked them to leave him in his sleeping bag and separate his fate from theirs. But they firmly rejected the idea, even though they knew it would undoubtedly lighten their burden. The patient then stumbled for a few more kilometers on his frostbitten feet, all the way to the campsite for the night. He slept with them until the next morning. When they woke up, they looked outside, where a raging blizzard howled.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.189.a: Oates suddenly stood up and said to his friends: 'I am just going outside and may be some time.'
strings.OMS_more_flavor.190.desc:
The remaining men shivered. Everyone knew what a walk outside in this weather meant. But no one dared to utter a word to stop him, nor did anyone dare to reach out for a final handshake. They all simply felt with awe that Lawrence Oates—Captain in the British Royal Dragoons—was walking towards death like a hero.

Now, only three tired, weakened men dragged their feet across the boundless, iron-hard ice and snow wilderness. They were utterly exhausted, devoid of all hope, sustained only by hazy instinct, staggering with every step. The weather became increasingly terrifying. At every depot, they were greeted by new despair, as if deliberately tormented, with only minimal kerosene, meaning heat, left. On March 21st, they were only 20 kilometers from the next depot, but the blizzard raged with murderous intensity, making it impossible for them to leave the tent. Every night they hoped to reach their destination the next day, but by the next day, having only consumed one day's ration, they could only pin their hope on the day after. Their fuel ran out, and the thermometer pointed to -40°C. All hope was extinguished. They now had to choose between two deaths: starvation or freezing. For eight days, the three men fought against their inevitable fate in the tiny tent, surrounded by the white, primeval world. On March 29th, knowing that no miracle could save them, they decided not to walk further toward their doom, but to wait proudly for death to arrive in the tent, regardless of the suffering that awaited. They crawled into their sleeping bags, never once letting out a cry of distress to the world about their final tribulations.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.190.a: Did the struggle for the South Pole end here?
strings.OMS_more_flavor.191.desc:
The fierce blizzard struck the thin tent like a madman, and as Death silently approached, Captain Scott recalled everything connected to him. For only in this extreme silence, unbroken by human voice, did he become tragically conscious of his intimate affection for his country and for all mankind. But in this snowy wilderness, only an inner mirage called forth the images of all those connected to him through love, loyalty, and friendship. In his final moments, Captain Scott wrote letters to all those living people he loved with his frozen fingers.

The letters were deeply moving. With death imminent, there was not a trace of sentimentality, as if the air of the lifeless sky had permeated the writing. The letters were addressed to those he knew, but spoken to all mankind; written for his time, but meant to endure forever.

He wrote to his wife. He reminded her to look after his most precious legacy—his son—and primarily cautioned her not to let him be lazy. In the final act of one of the world's most sublime historical deeds, he made this confession: 'You know I have had to force myself to pursue—for I was always a lazy fellow.' Even in his dying moment, he remained proud, not regretful, of his decision. 'What I can tell you about this expedition is that it has been far better than sitting comfortably at home!'

With the utmost sincerity, he wrote to the wives and mothers of the companions who shared his tragic fate, testifying to their heroism. Despite his own impending death, he comforted the bereaved with a strong, sublime emotion—for he felt such a death was worthy of memory, and such a moment was great.

He wrote to his friends. He spoke of himself with great modesty but of his nation with immense pride, saying that at such a moment, he was overjoyed to be a son—a worthy son—of this people. He wrote: 'I do not think I have any cause to regret this journey, which has shown that our race has not lost its hardihood and power of endurance.' In his dying moment, he offered a friendly expression to a friend, a word he had never spoken in his life due to masculine stubbornness and the chastity of his soul. In his letter to his best friend, he wrote: 'I have never met a man in my life whom I admired and loved more than you, but I have never told you what your friendship meant to me, for you had so much to give and I so little to offer.'

His final and most poignant letter was to his country. He felt compelled to explain that his failure in this struggle for British honor was through no fault of his own. He listed all the accidents that had led to his failure, and with the immense sorrow unique to the dying, he earnestly appealed to all Britons not to abandon the families of the fallen. His final thoughts were still not of his own destiny. His last written words were not about his death, but about the living: 'For God's sake look after our people.' Below this were several blank pages.

Captain Scott's diary was kept until his last breath, until his fingers were completely frozen and the pen slipped from his stiff hand. It was the hope that someone would find these diaries beside his body—testaments to his and the British nation's courage—that gave him the superhuman will to write until the final moment. His last entry was a wish scrawled with his frostbitten fingers: 'Send this diary to my wife!' But then, sadly and decisively, he crossed out the words 'my wife' and scrawled the terrible correction: 'my widow.'
strings.OMS_more_flavor.191.a: We praise the fervent spirit of the heroes!
strings.OMS_more_flavor.192.desc:
The comrades residing in the base hut waited for weeks, initially with confidence, then with slight worry, and finally with increasing unease. They dispatched rescue teams twice, but the terrible weather drove them back. These men, having lost their captain, waited uselessly in the hut through the entire long, dark winter, their hearts shadowed by disaster. For months, the fate and deeds of Captain Robert Scott were sealed in snow and silence; surely the white ice had encased them in crystal coffins. It was not until the Antarctic spring arrived, on October 29th, that an expedition finally set out, at least to find the heroes' bodies and their news. On November 12th, they reached the tent, finding the heroes frozen in their sleeping bags, with the deceased Scott embracing Wilson like a brother. They found the letters and documents, and built a stone cairn for the tragically fallen heroes. A simple black cross stood atop the snow-covered cairn. It stands alone to this day in the silver-white world, as if this world will forever conceal the evidence of that heroic human feat.

But no! Their story was unexpectedly, miraculously resurrected. This was the brilliant miracle created by the technological world of our new age. Friends brought the negatives and film reels home and developed the images in chemical solutions. People once again saw Scott and his companions on their march, and discovered that besides himself, only one other man—Amundsen—had seen the Antarctic landscape. Scott's last words and letters were swiftly transmitted via wire to an admiring and astonished world. In the British National Cathedral, the King knelt to mourn the heroes. Thus, what seemed to be fruitless labor bore fruit again; what was a missed opportunity became a great cry to humanity, demanding that it concentrate its strength on goals yet unattained; magnificent destruction, surviving in death, from failure arose the will to climb infinite peaks. For only great ambition will ignite the fervent heart to attempt deeds where achievement and easy success are highly improbable. A man who destroys himself in a battle against overwhelming and unconquerable fate is ennobled in spirit. All these are the greatest tragedies of all ages, which a writer only occasionally creates, but life creates a thousandfold more.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.192.a: However, the technological world of the new age was consumed by a nuclear conflagration.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.194.desc:
Sorrow, a trembling sorrow!
This is a song of farewell.
Even weary bones are burnt out, and moist skin returns to the earth.
Gods of Death race across the wilderness, hazy, twisted smoke, and blazing flames!

Sorrow, the sorrow of life!
The color of blood stains the earth,
But can it usher in a new age?
Oh, surviving Soldiers of Sorrow!

Men who court death without fear,
For the ladies they wish to protect.
Ladies who court death without fear,
Towards the gentlemen they hold dear.
What have we gambled? What will remain?
I pray, I pray for a new age to come!

Sorrow, a painful sorrow!
All I know now is this: I kill a warrior whose name I do not know.
Clinging to life, spitting up blood!
The ranks of Death, swift as a gale,
I have no way to resist!

Men fighting in blood,
For the wives and children waiting in their hometowns!
Ladies fighting in blood,
For the men they put their faith in!
What have we gambled! What will remain!
strings.OMS_more_flavor.194.a: I pray, I pray for a new age to come!
strings.OMS_more_flavor.195.desc:
Sadness like fragments,
In closed-off streets, glass-like snow falls.
Even the eyes searching for tomorrow gradually dim beyond the darkness.
Caught in the torrent of a time driven by unknown forces, my heart does not know where to go,
Deep inside my nearly shattered core, only my heartbeat remains.

In the shining wind, I can hear your voice.
'Praying that peace will never be broken,'
This dazzling light makes me believe without doubt.

That blue haze on the blue horizon is still vividly etched in my eyes.
Whenever I close them, what seems to appear before me
Are those warm times... and those unforgettable memories...
Constantly repeating mistakes, I had become numb like a mere organism.
But even if I must live on, covered in scars, I will never let anyone see my tears.

In the light of the wind, I see your smile.
'Praying that peace will never be broken,'
I gaze at that light—
For whom is this unyielding pain? I finally feel it clearly!
Meeting you was a miracle in the universe of billions of stars.

It was only at farewell that I understood the kindness within you.
I can proudly say every day that you are the most important person to me.

Someday, I can say with certainty,
In the shining wind, right there, I saw your smile.
'Praying that peace will never be broken,'
I gaze at that light...
strings.OMS_more_flavor.196.desc:
Believe...
Man matures through layers of sorrow.
Now, my love, trembling in loneliness,
Let me tightly embrace your sorrow.

Believe...
Tears, return to the sea!
The longing grows more intense,
The cosmos slowly turns dark red.

Yes, my dear, yes, my beloved!
The one I love deeply, must once again...
Yes, my dear, yes, my beloved...
I want to return to your side,
No one can survive alone.

Shadows cloud my heart when I think of those who will not return.
Now, if you can sail from beyond the sorrow,
I believe we can reunite one day.

Believe...
Tears, return to the sea!
Tortured by love,
Endless longing permeates the cosmos!
Yes, my dear, yes, my beloved!
strings.OMS_more_flavor.196.a: I want to return to your side, no one can survive alone.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.197.desc:
On a rooftop where stars continually drift down,
I listen alone to the music box of the sky.
Covering my eyes, I walk across a glass tightrope.
We are all children of the lonely circus.
The sadness of being alone,
The squeaking rope, and the trembling heart...

The Sound of Silence, this Sound of Silence!
'I want to meet someone with gentle eyes,
Whisper into my ear, I am right by your side...' so it says.

Lightly falling tears form the Chinese character for 'person' in my palm,
Sending a warm current through my heart.
Every time I give up, I still don't lose heart.
The cowardly clown at the end of the road!

In the starless sky without applause,
The performers of the giant ball lift their hands!
The Sound of Silence, this Sound of Silence!
The darkness accumulating in the gentle street is...
strings.OMS_more_flavor.198.desc:
Can you hear it? You can hear it, the roar from afar!
The soul trembling in the darkness, the beginning of awakening.
Is that towering form, tearing out of the earth, proof of justice?

The power of the legendary Giant God, tears the galaxy apart.

The roaring Titan summons a lightning-fast strike.
Do not tremble, fix your gaze, the moment of resurrection.

Should we fight, can we still fight? Oh, timid soul!
Show courage to the pressing evil force!
Is that shining form flying into the cosmos the cry of life?

The power of the legendary Giant God, will tear the galaxy apart!
This final strike, shatters everything to protect itself!
No need to fear, open your mind, the moment of resurrection.
O people! O life! Behold this power!
strings.OMS_more_flavor.199.desc:
Who ordained that time must move forward?

Erasing the brand of life, overwriting history.

A beautiful sword connects people,

Driving away the ceaseless cycle of sorrow and grief!

The shape of life between you and me,

Dedicated to this planet, a symbol of the <UNKNOWN>.

Everyone once believed that time could flow backward.

That new marks could be inscribed on the pitch-black calendar.

Stars twinkle, smiling upon living beings.

Sun and Moon warm the Earth.

The joy of breaking free from the shell, cultivating a benevolent heart,

Slowly healing the wounds of the past.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.199.a: Arbitrary x belong to C, human(x).
strings.OMS_more_flavor.200.desc:
Despair is a sweet trap, the door is tightly closed.

The heart is a battlefield, no one can be saved.

A tiny heart, manipulated by fate,

Soldiers resorting to force begin the slaughter.

In this crumbling fairy tale world, is even life treated as a game?

The pain in my heart can never be forgotten,

Desire is a poisoned apple, what is gained worth anything?

What can be left for the children of the future?

The joy of living together vanishes in the distance.
\A lullaby like a prayer comes from afar,

Believing in the true, the good, and the beautiful, forgiving all.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.200.a: Like compassion, all that's needed is to share and understand each other.

strings.OMS_2WRWCE_PostApoc_category_desc:
£GFX_OMS_great_trial_top 



Life beneath the surface is worse than ever before. Every scrap of resource must be carefully accounted for and treasured.
Our resources are abstracted into Supplies £Antarctica_texticon_SUP, Militarization £Antarctica_texticon_MIL, and Legitimacy £Antarctica_texticon_LEG. These three values reflect our current **surplus**, not our total stockpiles. Thus, even if our stockpile drops to zero, we will not be completely destroyed.
Additionally, we can see how many Task Forces we have. Task Forces can be deployed into the nuclear wasteland. Once they complete their current assignment, they can be deployed for other missions.

The Crusade Operations begin...
We still cannot train armies as we have not completed unification!
strings.OMS_stunning_silance_tt: The Economic System will be re-enabled!
strings.OMS_propaganda_to_people: Propaganda to the People on the Necessity of the Operation
strings.OMS_search_supply_in_wasteland: Deploy Task Forces to Search for Available Resources
strings.OMS_rading_wasteland: Scavenge Available Equipment from the Wasteland
strings.OMS_game_begins_desc:
A struggle to decide our fate has begun. We have emerged from the bunkers, attempting to rebuild our home, but the rebels from the 'Anti-Omsk Coalition' are all that await us. Or perhaps, the Third Era of £smuta Great Turmoil has begun. Our mission, and the fate of the world, depend on this.

However, this time is different from any before. This 'Era of Great Turmoil' has only two sides: the Black League and the rebels. Rather than a 'Great Turmoil,' this is more akin to a Second Russian Civil War. But what sets it apart is that this war will be unprecedentedly brutal, and we are ready. When the time is right, we shall retake the irradiated lands and exterminate the rebels.
strings.OMS_a_letter_from_omsk_desc: After assessing the balance of power and the remaining strength of the League, the League's Central Command has reached a conclusion: as long as we can consolidate the League's scattered forces, we can undoubtedly eliminate all enemies. Be they reactionaries or the Teutonic barbarians from Germany, they will be crushed beneath our feet. Therefore, communicating quickly with all military districts to unify local resources is the League's most urgent task. This will also be the main directive of the Great Trial before we eliminate all bandits and turn the Teutonic concept into history.
strings.OMS_machine_in_kazak_desc:
Andrey Matviyenko, our man. He has held the line in Kazakhstan for years, having truly cast aside all that is useless and enforced efficiency across the entire Kazakh region.

However, under the continuous nuclear strikes, the cities of Central Asia have been almost completely destroyed, and we have been forced to lose control of the region due to the circumstances. Fortunately, the core loyalist forces of the League still remain, and the reactionaries are insignificant, but the troops under Andrey Matviyenko's command still obey us. With a single order from the Central Command, we can try to consolidate local resources and use Central Asia's geopolitical advantage to further expand our influence throughout all of Russia.
strings.OMS_mid_asia_reconstruction_desc:
According to reconnaissance reports, there are still relatively large remnants of industrial equipment in the southern Kazakh region. Although the industrial system established in Kazakhstan before the war was not completely destroyed, it still requires a significant amount of time to repair due to years of disrepair and other factors. This is an opportunity, not a misfortune.

We shall mobilize supplies and direct our soldiers to the southern Kazakh region to investigate, recover usable industrial resources, and secure our rule there—if rule is still needed.
strings.OMS_train_their_army_desc: The central Kazakh forces seem to be in worse shape than ours. Their 'troops' cannot possibly be combat-effective—if they can even be called troops. Our soldiers maintained their readiness after the reforms, but clearly theirs did not. The Kazakh soldiers are nothing but a bunch of degenerates; corruption runs rampant with no oversight, factory production vanishes without a trace, and the black market thrives... Clearly, we need to drastically reform the Kazakh forces, and as a prerequisite and a test for them, they will carry out training in Central Asia.
strings.OMS_kras_machine_desc:
Alexander Sakharovsky, a leading figure of the League's Reformist Faction, once worked closely with the Commander-in-Chief during the Great Trial to achieve our great cause—it's fair to say that without him, the Black League would not be here today. He was once tasked with commanding the garrison of Krasnoyarsk, a major resource and railway hub. When the Great Trial arrived, the local bunker system served its purpose perfectly, securing vast amounts of precious industry, manpower, and supplies for us.

However, the ruined surface world inevitably hindered our communication with the local League forces. Fortunately, after a long period of regrouping, we are now able to re-establish effective governance over the area and use it as a base to eliminate the surrounding reactionaries.
strings.OMS_go_west_desc:
Kansk, a treasure trove with abundant natural resources, especially coal, was a key industrial center for us before the Great Trial. Even when the nuclear strikes hit, a portion of our forces remaining there firmly defended it. Now, with a little consolidation, we can contact the old guard there and re-establish control over Kansk.

Furthermore, Kyzyl is a vital passage connecting Russia and Mongolia and possesses large developed agricultural areas. Its strategic significance is self-evident; holding it means we can advance or retreat. The threat from potential enemies in northwestern China will be greatly reduced. This region has long been, is now, and will continue to be the frontline in the fight against the Co-Prosperity Sphere. Therefore, we must secure Tuva.
strings.OMS_eternal_factory_desc:
Since the beginning of Fimbulwinter (Nuclear Winter), Midgard (Earth) has been submerged, and the surface is no longer suitable for Níðhöggr (Human) life. Thus, in Krasnoyarsk, a group of people who lost their directives have gradually descended into madness. They have cast aside emotion—because it is useless for work; they have cast aside socialization—because it is unnecessary activity; and they have cast aside life—because they are nothing more than machines with a lifespan.

The only thing they do is work on the production line,
for they have already cast aside everything else.
strings.OMS_rekindle_revolutionary_enthusiasm_de:
After a long wait, the revolutionary fervor that once burned in the heart of every citizen has been extinguished. Now, at this moment of revolutionary crisis, they have forgotten what we are fighting for.

We do not fight for wealth, nor for official titles or emoluments,
We fight for the Black League, for the Great Trial.

The fire of revolution shall be lit again. Bind it, torment it, burn it to ashes, scatter it into the sea! But it shall return, and it shall burn with an unparalleled intensity.
strings.OMS_ural_devil_desc:
Many affluent regions around the Ural Mountains were once among the most desirable places in Russia, especially the South Urals. When Mother Russia was still being carved up and consumed by wicked warlords, this land suffered greatly—but thankfully, the League saved her. We freed the people from the hands of Lysenko and Dirlewanger and transformed the South Urals into a vital stronghold for the Great Trial.

The Commander-in-Chief once envisioned this area as a hiding place, and as a result, the League stationed heavy troops and a vast amount of supplies here. This gives us an enormous advantage in regaining control of the Urals; at a single command, the war machine will be reactivated.
strings.OMS_calling_to_lazarenko_desc:
Lazarenko once commanded the Ural Military District, responsible for the entire Ural Mountains region. However, after the thermonuclear war, a large part of the region fell into the hands of the reactionaries for various reasons. Yet, the Ural Military District still maintains absolute control over the South Urals, and their strength, controlling the Treasure Mountain, cannot be underestimated. We can use this as a base to further advance the Great Trial.

The Central Command will reassign this close confidant of the Commander-in-Chief and key League figure back to Omsk, with another person taking over the work in the Ural region, as his function in a central position is undoubtedly far greater than in a provincial one.
strings.OMS_sneak_attack_ural: ...and a Swift Attack on the Urals
strings.OMS_sneak_attack_ural_desc:
The Urals will be directly governed by the Black League's Central Administration. Lazarenko harbors a certain... 'unstable ideology.' Giving him control over the South Urals could lead to unforeseen consequences. Should he raise the banner of rebellion, the League would instantly crumble. He himself will be made the commander of the Redemption Brigades. We would rather kill a thousand innocents than let one guilty man go.

We have lost once; we cannot afford to lose a second time.
strings.OMS_peace_annex_ural_desc:
The command staff's opinion is too extreme. Lazarenko is a loyal soldier of the League; he would never raise the banner of rebellion. Even if he has some rebellious tendencies, they are irrelevant. At this point, we must pool all our strength to overcome the present crisis. Not only will I not directly attack the Urals, but I will also send reinforcements to the region. With a great enemy at our gates, weakening our own strength is suicidal!

When brothers quarrel at home, they must unite against the insult from abroad.
strings.OMS_remember_the_moscowien_desc:
In the plans for the Great Trial, Moscow is a city the League must retake. It is the heart of Russia, one of its symbols, and the critical operational base for pushing into Germany after the Great Trial and utterly slaughtering the Teutons. To this end, Yazov sent his confidant, Yevgeny Savintsev, as Army Group Commander to retake Moscow from the Germans and ensure its safety. The last message the League received before the successful Great Trial was that Savintsev had successfully recaptured Moscow and issued an order to the Russian forces in the region to staunchly defend the city. However, after the worldwide wave of death descended, we completely lost contact with Moscow.

After countless years and immense sacrifices, our forces have finally traversed the death zone along the line and reached Moscow. We have been able to establish contact with the few remaining Russian remnants there. Here, we witnessed the ultimate loyalty to Russia: Yevgeny Savintsev was valiantly killed defending the Russian people when the Trial arrived. The Commander-in-Chief has ordered: while accepting all remaining Russian forces in the Moscow region, we shall also conduct memorial ceremonies across the entire territory, honoring the martyrs who sacrificed themselves for the great cause of Russia.
strings.OMS_war_in_the_pocket_desc:
Since its occupation by the £GFX_OMS_teutons_texticon Teutonic bandit gangs, Moscow has been their domestic 'place of exile.' They have exploited it too deeply, too profoundly. The red star atop the Kremlin was replaced with their evil Nazi symbol, and the people were enslaved by the hateful Teutons, living lives worse than dogs.

After the Great Trial, there were no glorious troops in Moscow's bunkers, nor did the 'Great Trial' bring a 'Golden Age.' All it brought were war-torn soldiers, a desolate ruin, an irradiated land, and a shattered home.

What sin did I commit!?

Is it the 'Great Trial's' fault? No, absolutely not. The 'Great Trial' can never be wrong. This is all the fault of those goddamn Teutons, all because of those goddamn Teutons.

But what if it truly is the Great Trial's fault? No, that can't be.
strings.OMS_road_to_stalingrad_desc:
We still do not have a direct supply line to the remnants in Moscow. To reinforce the front, we will formulate a plan aimed at striking the former Volgograd region, allowing the Moscow remnants to establish land communication directly with the Kazakh region, thereby laying the foundation for future large-scale military aid.

Simultaneously, this will become a critical point for us to encircle the rebels. War is imminent.
strings.OMS_soldiers_in_leningrad_desc:
Citizens, hear me! Despite countless losses, despite the terrible defeat in the war, the Teutons have no soldiers left! They have no warships, no weapons, and no ammunition! Knowing this, why must we surrender to them!

Fellow countrymen! We must never trust those weak rebels. They only know how to hide and cling to life under the banner of pacifism, ignorant of courage and sacrifice. We absolutely cannot entrust the fate of our Motherland to them!

Remember the arrogant declaration made by that bug named Hitler when he seized power! He said that the Teutons are God's chosen race, and the people of Russia are an ancient, obtuse people lacking self-awareness, and therefore the ancient Russians must obey the Teutonic leadership. True, some Russian capitulationists and opportunistic politicians may fit his description, but this does not mean that what they said is the whole truth!

......
strings.OMS_the_great_stall_had_end_desc:
......

Think about it: Germany is so far from us. Hiding in their bunkers, how can they possibly understand our current situation!

The decadence and corruption of the Soviet Union are absolutely not a justification for German tyranny. The Teutons want to establish a fascist regime over the entire planet; we must never submit to them! The Black League is a government that truly values human rights, and the survival of humanity in the nuclear war is owed to the ingenuity of the Black League's citizens.

Hitler also claimed to be fighting Soviet weakness and corruption. Is that a reason to massacre hundreds of millions of innocent civilians? What right does that demon have to say such a thing!
