\“There is nothing out there! No children's laughter, no golden waves of wheat, not even a single damned Teuton left for me to judge! Only hunger! Only sickness! They see me as a devil! Comrade Karbyshev, is this the end point of your theory? To turn everyone into devils, and then let the devils devour each other in this hell?\”

His fist smashes against the bulletproof glass with a dull, heavy thud; his knuckles instantly split and bleed, the blood slowly running down the glass, like a line of desperate, bloody tears.

\“You lied to me! All of you lied to me! You used a vague, illusory 'Great Ideal' to turn me into a beast... that only knows vengeance! You made me personally destroy everything I swore to save! Now, you hide in your grave, enjoying the honors of a hero, while I, Dmitry Yazov, must bear the sin of this entire world, living in this hell I personally created! Answer me! Karbyshev! Answer me!\”

His roar echoes repeatedly in the confined bunker, slamming against the cold walls, only to return to his own ears. The old man in the photo continues to smile gently.
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.22.a: If I cannot sway the gods of heaven...
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.21.desc:
Following the roar, there is a deathly silence.

Yazov slumps down in front of the observation window, his body sliding to the floor along the cold wall. He gulps for air, each breath feeling like he is swallowing broken glass, searing his lungs. In the bunker, only his heavy, rasping breaths remain, along with the constant, low hum from the ventilation system. That sound is like the pulse of this dying world.

He lifts his head, his gaze vacant, staring at the gray-white, eternally unchanging scene outside the window. The wind and snow persist; the world is like a faded, static portrait of the deceased. The questions, anger, and curses he had just screamed with all his strength seem to have been instantly absorbed by the dead silent earth, leaving not a single echo. Karbyshev did not answer him. The earth did not answer him. The millions of restless souls of the dead who haunted his mind day and night have also fallen into an eerie silence.

This silence is more terrifying than any frantic accusation.

He slowly crawls back to the table and picks up the old photo, which is now stained with his blood. He uses the cuff of his military uniform to carefully wipe the bloodstain off the photo paper, gazing at Karbyshev's gentle yet profound eyes looking back at him through the spectacle lenses. In the years past, filled with fire and ideals, he regarded those eyes as the lighthouse guiding him through the darkness. Now, behind that gentle smile, he reads something he never perceived before—is it weariness? Pity? Or a... sorrow that had already foreseen the ending?

Perhaps Karbyshev never intended to deceive him. Perhaps the great mentor himself was a believer captured by a grander theory named \“Hatred.\” He constructed a perfect, pure utopia forged by the fire of vengeance, but he never truly calculated that the fuel required to light that fire was, precisely, humanity itself.

Yazov suddenly feels an immense fatigue, a bone-deep weariness that makes his soul tremble. He is no longer angry, no longer sad. The roar that exhausted all his emotions seems to have also carried away the last part of his \“humanity.\” What remains is only a hollowed-out shell named \“Dmitry Yazov.\”

He understands now. Karbyshev's silence is the final answer. There is no divine oracle, no judgment, and no salvation. The moment he pressed the button that determined the fate of the world, he personally strangled all possible responses. He所追求的那个绝对正义的、纯净无暇的理想乡，其最终形态，就是这片绝对的、纯净无暇的、永恒的死寂。

He places the photograph back on the table, setting it squarely. Then, he sits back in the chair that symbolizes supreme power, his body straight and rigid, as if he has returned to the unsmiling, steel-willed Marshal. But he knows that something has been shattered forever. He is no longer the angel of vengeance, nor the master of salvation. He is merely a slightly higher-ranking gravedigger in this massive cemetery.

From this moment on, he will no longer roar. He will spend the rest of his life listening to this symphony of \“Silence,\” which he personally composed. Until this boundless silence completely consumes him as well.
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.20.desc:
An encrypted report from the Frontline Political Department was delivered to Yazov's desk. The cover was marked \“Top Emergency\” in red, but the content was not about enemy movements; it was an \“Analysis of the Spread of Negative and Nihilistic Thought\” within the League. The report, in cold, unemotional language, documented an increasing number of frontline soldiers privately questioning the ultimate goal of the \“Great Trial.\” They defeated the Teutonic bandits and achieved ultimate revenge, only to find themselves in a hell worse than before the war. Radiation sickness, starvation, and severe cold circled above everyone's heads like vultures, mercilessly pecking at their remaining lives.

\“We liberated Russia, and then what?\” a veteran who participated in the Battle of Moscow was recorded saying in an unofficial conversation. \“We drove the Teutons into hell, and we moved in with them. My son... he died in the ruins of Penza, not from a Teuton bullet, but from a plague we couldn't see. He died without knowing why we had to pay all this. For this scorched earth? Or for the stomachs that will never be full?\” The report also included other unsettling records: a young replacement soldier suffering a mental breakdown while on guard duty, repeatedly muttering, \“We are all dead, we just haven't realized it\”; an artillery squad openly mocking a political commissar's speech while drunk, calling it \“the biggest joke in the world.\”

The report's conclusion was that the army's morale was destabilizing at an unprecedented rate. The long period of arduous combat and the horrors of the post-nuclear war had completely eroded the soldiers' will. They no longer believed in the grand narratives, no longer fought for a vague \“future.\” They only cared about where the next meal would come from, whether the bunker was warm enough, and if they would survive until tomorrow. The commissars suggested in the report that stricter discipline and more frequent ideological education be employed to suppress these \“dissonant voices.\” Yazov slammed the report onto the desk with a dull thud. He felt a helpless rage. These commissars fundamentally misunderstood; the problem was not discipline, but hope. When a person's hope is utterly crushed, any sermon becomes pale, and any threat becomes irrelevant. The soul of this army is dying.
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.19.desc:
A greater crisis stems from internal corruption; it is more fatal than any external enemy. War destroyed the old order and also gave birth to a new privileged class. While ordinary soldiers fight over half a piece of moldy bread and risk their lives for a few bullets, some officers and logistics bureaucrats holding power exploit their authority to hoard goods and enrich themselves. Medicine, food, clean water, fuel—things on the wasteland equivalent to life itself—have become their bargaining chips, the cornerstones for building their underground kingdoms. A military organization once renowned for its strict discipline, firm will, and absolute integrity is now beginning to rot from within, emitting an unpleasant stench.

Marshal Yazov personally handled a particularly egregious case. A major responsible for frontline food distribution was discovered to have secretly hoarded enough refined food and medicine for a company for a month, while the troops under his command suffered mass non-combat losses due to starvation and disease. During the interrogation, the major showed no remorse and even seemed somewhat self-justified. He was once a war hero, with two medals pinned to his chest. \“Marshal Commander,\” he sneered, \“The times have changed. Loyalty and ideals cannot fill an empty stomach, nor can they ward off radiation sickness. We won the war; now it's time to enjoy the fruits of victory. I merely took what I deserved. What do the lives and deaths of those fools waiting to die in the mud have to do with me?\”

Yazov said nothing more. He drew his pistol and shot the major through the forehead. Warm blood splattered onto his cold cheek. But in his heart, he knew he could execute one corrupt officer, but he could not eradicate corruption itself. When the sole goal that held the entire League together—the \“Great Trial\”—has been achieved, and the promised future is nowhere to be seen, human greed and selfishness spread like a virus on the breeding ground of power. The Black League, this giant born for war, is being crushed by its own weight. He killed a symptom but was helpless against the underlying disease. He looked around, as if he could see countless pairs of greedy eyes glistening in the darkness, waiting to feast on the decaying corpse.
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.18.desc:
The inspection convoy stops in front of a village that has been leveled to the ground. The armored personnel carrier's tracks grind over the scorched earth, making a grating sound that sets teeth on edge. This was once a dot on the map, a home, a place that held laughter and cheer, now only unrecognizable wreckage and radioactive dust drifting in the cold wind remain. Yazov silently dismounts the armored vehicle, his heavy military boots crunching on the rubble, a piercing sound as if treading on countless shattered memories. The soldiers mechanically fan out, searching the ruins for anything of value—unopened cans, sealed medicine, or even half a bottle of uncontaminated water. But mostly what they find are shattered family photos, the happy faces on them blackened by fire; charred books, knowledge and culture turned to ash in the flames; and deformed kitchen utensils, silently recounting the domestic life that once existed here.

A young soldier, his face as pale as the black snow falling from the sky, comes forward, holding something in his trembling hands, as if carrying an immensely heavy sacred object. \“Marshal Commander... look.\” His voice is hoarse, filled with uncertain fear.

It is a children's book, badly burned and incomplete. The colorful illustration on the cover is blurred, but one can faintly make out a story about a little rabbit, a story about innocence and beauty. The soldier carefully opens the pages, afraid that this fragile relic might turn to dust in his hands. Tucked between the pages is a childish drawing: a crooked stick-figure family, holding hands, standing in front of a simple house colored with crayons, with a massive, brilliant sun above their heads. In the corner of the drawing, a line is written in a shaky pencil script: \“Papa, Mama, and me.\”

Yazov reaches out, removes his heavy glove, and gently strokes the rough paper with his calloused fingertip. In that instant, he remembers something, yet seems to remember nothing at all. Perhaps his own distant, already blurred childhood, perhaps the timid look of a child hiding behind his mother, seen in a village early in the war. The small, complete world contained within this drawing, all the child's hopes for the future, has now, along with the child who drew it, become fuel for the \“Great Trial,\” a negligible cost in his grand blueprint. He waves his hand, signaling the bewildered soldier to step back. He独自站在这片废墟之中，寒风吹动他大衣的下摆。他第一次感到，他所带来的这场“胜利”，或许比任何一场惨烈的失败，都更加沉重，更加无法饶恕。
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.18.a: They made a desolation and called it peace...
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.17.desc:
The convoy drives along the former front line, once the main route for the Black League's armored torrent pushing westward. Now, scattered along both sides of the road are endless steel wrecks, forming a surreal tableau of the apocalypse. Destroyed tanks lie like the skeletons of dead behemoths, their cannons drooping weakly, pointing toward the polluted sky; burnt-out armored vehicles, their blackened hatches like mouths agape in despair; shattered trucks, their beds strewn with unrecognizable military supplies... They stand like silent gravestones, wordlessly recounting the war's savagery. These machines, once the League's pride, the steel fortresses the soldiers trusted, the iron fist of the \“Great Trial,\” are now cold coffins burying them, slowly rusting and decaying alongside their flesh and blood on this cursed land.

Yazov orders the convoy to stop. He walks up to the wreckage of a tank. A large-caliber armor-piercing round has torn a massive hole in its side armor, revealing a scene of melting and scorching inside. He remembers this unit, remembers its commander, a young man named Pavel, who always had a shy smile but fought with the ferocity of a bear. He had personally presented the flag to Pavel's unit, and he remembers the fanatical light in his eyes as he shouted, \“For Mother Russia, for Comrade Karbyshev.\” Yazov watched them rush to the battlefield, towards the \“glory\” he promised. But now, Pavel and his crew, along with their steel mount, are rotting here, without even a complete corpse to piece together.

A political commissar accompanying them, a middle-aged man who always tried to find positivity in despair, clears his throat, attempting to say something. Maybe he wanted to say, \“Their sacrifice was glorious,\” or quote some line about heroism. But when he sees Yazov's eyes, he cannot utter a single word. It is a look mixed with exhaustion, regret, and bewilderment, like burnt-out ashes where not a single spark remains. Yazov does not look at him; he speaks in a low voice, as if whispering to himself: \“Glory? No... there is no glory here, only death. We bought an endless graveyard of steel with countless young lives like Pavel's.\” He pauses, his voice trembling uncontrollably, \“We told them it was for the future. But look here—is there a future left?\” He does not wait for an answer, turns, and walks back to the vehicle, leaving behind a figure of utter desolation.
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.16.desc:
Volodya lets out a long breath; the white fog from his mouth fogs his glasses, making him almost unable to see the surroundings. He lifts the hand clutching the reins and wipes the lenses with his sleeve, then lowers his head to look at the grey horse's head. The mane on its neck droops over its eyes. He pulls hard on the bridle and calls out; the old horse turns its head and follows him southward.

The horse's hooves are long worn smooth; every step on the frozen ground makes a crisp, faint sound. Since his unit was scattered last week, he has wandered here with the grey horse for seven days. The ration biscuits are gone, and the ice shards in his canteen are rock hard, clutched in Volodya's palm. Last night, he slept in the ruins of a bombed-out flour mill. Volodya pulled out the cloth packet from his chest pocket. Inside are three wrinkled potato seeds, taken from his hometown's vegetable patch last autumn. His mother had laughed then, scolding him, \“You're going to war, and you're still worried about planting vegetables.\” Now the seeds are warm against his chest, having melted some of the ice frozen on them.

\“If you don't keep moving, I'll butcher you and eat you,\” Volodya mutters into the grey horse's ear, his voice hoarse. No sooner had he spoken than the horse suddenly pricks up its ears, violently pulls the reins loose, and charges toward the shadow behind a broken wall. Volodya is yanked off balance, nearly falling headfirst to the ground. He scrambles up, about to curse, but is frozen by the sight before his eyes.

The grey horse is pawing at the rubble in the corner of the wall. In its hoof prints, a green sprout has pushed through the broken soil. The tender yellow tip of the sprout is wrapped in mud, yet it shines glaringly in the grey ruins. Volodya crouches down, his fingertip gently touching the tiny leaves.

The wind blows from the east, carrying the scent of melting snow. The horse lowers its head and nudges the sprout with its nose, then turns back to Volodya, its eyes shining as if quenched with light. Volodya carefully rewraps the potato seeds, tucks them into his inner pocket, and when he looks up again, he sees the eastern sky has turned a pale blue-green. It is not the red of artillery fire; it is the color of dawn. He climbs onto the broken wall and sees the horse's shadow stretched long in the morning light. The green sprout is slowly unfolding its leaves, reaching towards the light in the east.
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.16.a: The endless grass on the plains...
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.15.desc:
Dawn came exceptionally early. Just as the eastern horizon cracked open with a golden seam, Volodya was startled awake by the horse's neighing. He rubs his frozen face and climbs up, seeing the horse pawing at the fog; the old cloth strip on its mane flutters straight. A white figure emerges from the mist, like a moving ball of light.

It is a white horse, its mane gilded in the morning light. Where its hooves tread, even the ashes turn a bluish-gray, like dead wood about to sprout. The grey horse breaks its reins and charges forward; the two shadows leap and gallop among the ruins, one covered in mud, the other shining brightly, smashing a translucent hole through the thick fog. Volodya chases, stumbling into a shell crater, where he sees his own face reflected in the pooled water. His gas mask has cracked open at some point, and the light from the east is now penetrating the fissure, washing the muddy gray from his eyes into a clear amber.

The white horse stops in front of the ruins of a church and gently nudges the old cloth strip on the grey horse's neck with its nose. With a pull, the strip transforms into countless white butterflies, circling Volodya in a halo. He instinctively touches the cloth packet on his chest. Opening it, he is stunned. All three potato seeds have sprouted; tender stems penetrate the cloth, pushing out tiny blue flowers. The patterns on the petals perfectly resemble the \“Promise\” symbol his mother used to draw in the vegetable patch.

\“This way.\” A woman's voice emerges from the mist. Volodya looks up and sees a girl in a blue cloth dress leading the white horse, followed by over a dozen people. They are holding clay pots filled with seeds. The girl smiles and says, \“We found a plot of land to the east where we can plant once the snow melts.\” They scatter the seeds from their hands onto the ground, and tiny green shoots instantly emerge.

Volodya follows them eastward. His horse and the white horse walk side by side in the lead, their hooves treading a path of light green through the ruins. He suddenly understands: his horse is not just an ordinary mount; it is hope, digging a path in the abyss. The white horse is not an accidental light; it is the promise matured by hope. The sun in the east rises higher and higher, shrinking the shadows of the ruins. He touches the blue flower on his chest; the light on its petals is warm to the touch. It turns out that hope is never waited for; it is like a seed, gritting its teeth to drill through the darkness, like light, daring to force its way through even the densest fog.
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.14.desc:
Pavel bid his mother farewell. It was an extremely brief, yet infinitely long goodbye; there was no hug, no instruction, only a few glances across the yard, and a stiff hand gesture in the air, neither a plea to stay nor an urge to hurry. This was followed by a silence that lasted for dozens of seconds, broken by the driver.
\“Are you getting in or not?\”
His mother quickly handed him a package, then stood silently, like a statue, meeting Pavel's gaze. Pavel clearly remembers that day: he was wearing the newly issued, dye-smelling dark green greatcoat and a steel helmet. He cast a final glance at his mother, then resolutely got onto the vehicle and never looked back.
...
Night falls, and stifled, intermittent sobs begin to emerge from every corner of the trench. Suddenly, a messenger shouts, \“Where is Pavel Petrov? There's a letter for you.\” Pavel walks forward, trembling, and shakily tears open the envelope. In the letter, his mother asks if he is still cold, if the new greatcoat fits. But his hands now are filled with the blood and filth that can never be washed away. Whenever the cold trench water washes over his ankles, his soul begins to tremble in its depths, as if he sees the eyes of his fallen comrades watching him from afar.

He recalls his mother's gaze before he left—a gaze that held no glory, no expectation, only an empty sorrow he couldn't comprehend at the time. Perhaps she already knew that her son, dressed in his brand-new greatcoat, had died the moment he embarked on his journey. What lives now is merely a corpse burdened by a mountain of blood debt. His comrade Grigori carries the weight of a letter and a few rifles, for he has seen death too often. Pavel, however, carries the weight of the dead souls' gaze, watching him from heaven or hell; the physical weight seems trivial. On this land, whose debt is lighter?
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.13.desc:
Grigori spits a mouthful of bloody phlegm onto the ground; it quickly freezes into a dark red chunk of ice on the surface. Tucked away in the pocket of his greatcoat is a piece of paper carelessly wrapped in cloth, its edges slightly yellowed and permeated by sweat and body heat. It is a letter written by his hometown comrade just before he died, asking him to personally deliver it to his distant wife and aged mother.

In the past twenty-four hours, the order to break out was given three times. Each time, the charge bugle turned into the funeral song of the unit. Soldiers rushed out like a tide, only to retreat like a tide, but those who returned were no longer living men, but a dam of bodies, shattered by subsequent artillery fire, piled up at the front line. This defense line, made of corpses, blocked the only path to survival.

The political commissar crouches behind a pile of slightly drier soil, which is mixed with flecks of crimson and not yet fully dry. \“Brothers, comrades! Don't panic! Keep charging!\” But in the next moment, a stray bullet rips through the air, and the commissar falls straight to the ground, a hole shot through his brow, the ground behind him stained crimson. Silence descends, so quiet one could hear a pin drop, only the reverberation of the projectile's passage lingers.

Order, in that moment, completely evaporated.

Chaos spreads like a virus among the survivors. Some old soldiers, driven mad by endless despair, begin turning their guns, shooting at the backs of their own men.

\“Rather than being caught and skinned alive by the bastards across the way, it's better to die by your own kind, a quicker end.\”

Grigori points the cold muzzle at the center of Pavel's back; the madness in his eyes burns fiercely like ignited gasoline, reflecting a scene from hell. Pavel in those bloodshot eyes, saw the shrapnel piece on his own greatcoat's chest bleeding outwards—a wound he sustained while covering Grigori. That was his hometown comrade's blood, and now, this friendship, bought with fresh blood, must be repaid with his own.

Just then, a heavy artillery shell tears through the air, exploding precisely in a gap in the barbed wire not far away, instantly throwing Grigori to the ground. At that very moment, the pursuers outside let out an animalistic howl, speaking a dialect no one could understand, closing in on them from all sides. The blood drops on their bayonets gleam in the dim twilight, falling onto the snow and blooming into a field of seductive, crimson flowers.

The instinct for survival overwhelms everything else. Pavel violently shoves Grigori away, stepping over his still-warm comrade, charging desperately toward that gap. The feeling beneath his feet is sticky and soft; he dares not look down. Suddenly, a cold hand grips his ankle like an iron vice. Pavel turns back in terror, meeting a pair of eyes he will never be able to forget...
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.12.t: At fifteen, I joined the army...
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.12.desc:
When the stamp on the conscription roster heavily pressed down on the three characters \“Alexei,\” his worn-out straw sandals were still stained with the moist, warm soil of his hometown's wheat fields. His mother said nothing, merely tucking a repeatedly laundered linen handkerchief embroidered with wild roses into his feverish chest pocket. The stitching was dense and tight. Her calloused fingers lingered on his chest for a long time before she finally said just one thing: \“My child, don't lose it.\” A snow of white blossoms was falling from the old locust tree by the village entrance, scattering and sticking to the conscription team's black cart, like someone scattering paper money made of crushed silver for this long journey.

\“When I drive out the Teuton devils, I'll come back and marry you!\” He clung to the railing at the back of the bumpy cart, shouting hoarsely at the increasingly small figure running after him, his voice distorted by the swirling dust and the bitter wind. Anya's red headscarf flashed in the grey-yellow dust, like a poppy flower. He reached into his inner pocket and took out a long-cherished marble, which he had traded from his younger brother in childhood—it was as blue as the clear lake at the east end of the village. He carefully tucked the marble into the inner fold of the handkerchief his mother gave him. He wanted his mother to see, and Anya to know, that he still carried a piece of home, carrying their memory.

As the convoy crossed the first river, he saw a bloated floating corpse among the reeds in the river bend. The tears in its grey-green uniform were in the same pattern as the brand-new uniform he had just been issued. An old veteran with a cigarette dangling from his lip patted his stiff shoulder and said nonchalantly, \“Don't be scared. When you get to the Western Front, you'll see more of these than fish in the river. You'll get used to it.\”

That night, they slept in a drafty church; half the face of the icon was collapsed, staring at them with a single vacant eye in pity. He dared not sleep, spreading the handkerchief on the cold stone floor as a pillow. The embroidered wild roses on the cloth were slightly swollen with his silent tears. In a blurred dream, he saw Anya squatting by the river at home, washing clothes, the heavy wooden mallet repeatedly beating against the bluestone, thump, thump, thump... The sound was like the rhythmic counting of the days since he left home.

When the bugle call to march tore through the morning fog, he looked toward the eastern horizon one last time—the last time in his life. A red sun struggled to climb from beneath the horizon, coating the distant grassland with a thin, warm layer of gold, that was the color of his hometown's wheat fields at harvest, as he remembered. He did not know that this single glance was his eternal farewell to his hometown. He subconsciously tightened his grip on the handkerchief in his chest pocket. On the fabric, warmed by his body temperature, one thread of the wild rose his mother had stitched with all her heart finally broke with a series of unseen, minute cracking sounds. The feeling was as if a fundamental connection between him and his hometown had also been severed forever.
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.12.a: River city songs and flutes flow; rain has passed over the level mountain, and the moon is full over the west tower.
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.11.desc:
When the messenger's horse hooves shattered the last thin layer of ice in the puddle by the village entrance, Alexei's mother, Yekaterina, was squatting in front of her chipped clay pot, turning over dried wild vegetables she had gathered last autumn, which were now completely moistureless. The snow from last winter had not fully melted, and the icicles under the eaves hung long, refracting a chilling light in the pale sun. A deathly silence blanketed the village, broken only by the whimpering sound of the wind sweeping through the dilapidated fence.
\“Excuse me, is this Mrs. Yekaterina?\”
A young man in a gray standard-issue greatcoat slides off his exhausted horse. His military boots are caked with congealed mud, and embedded in the mud is a small, charred piece of fabric—a material only found on Western Front uniforms. The young man looks no older than twenty, but his face carries a weariness that does not belong to his age, etched by gunpowder smoke and death. From a severely worn canvas bag, he carefully produces a flat, rusted tin box. The lid is not tightly closed, and a corner of a wild rose-embroidered handkerchief, whose original color is long gone, peeks out from the gap. The stitches on that handkerchief were once so fine, but now it is soaked with dried, black bloodstains.
\“Alexei... my... what happened to my son?\” The old woman's hand suddenly stills at the edge of the clay pot; the dried wild vegetables on her fingertip fall rustling into the pot's bottom, making a tiny, unnerving sound. Her eyes are fixed on the tin box.
The messenger says nothing. He simply hands over the cold tin box in silence, almost ritualistically. Yekaterina takes it; the box is much lighter than she expected. She opens the lid. Inside, besides the blood-soaked handkerchief she had personally sewn, there is a smooth, blue marble, which Alexei had won from his younger brother in childhood—it was as blue as the clear lake at the east end of the village. Next to the marble is a folded, official notice, its writing blurred by rain: \“On March 17th, Comrade Soldier Alexei Ivanovich died heroically in the outer Berlin campaign. Remains unrecovered. You are hereby notified.\” The last four characters, \“Remains unrecovered,\” are obscured by a large patch of deep purple liquid.
The messenger silently mounts his horse. Before leaving, he takes one last look. The old woman is clutching the empty tin box tightly to her chest, like an infant, trudging toward the old locust tree at the village entrance. He knows that in the tree hollow, she had hidden a hard, stone-like wheat cake she saved for Alexei. The bite marks on the cake were from last year, when Anya from the neighboring village, too hungry to bear it, had gnawed on it while borrowing food. The girl who always waited at the village entrance for Alexei's letter later went to the Western Front with a stretcher team and never returned.
Later, the surviving villagers would say that that night, the old locust tree, which had long been dead, blossomed with white flowers that fell all over the ground like snow. The petals gently covered the tin box the old woman had placed beneath the tree, as if laying a thin, white shroud over it. And on Yekaterina's pillow, the color of the wild rose finally faded completely, leaving only the empty outline of the stitching—like a lie that could not be finished, slowly and utterly cooling down in this endless, cold night.
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.11.a: A few years of youth, three lives' drunken dreams, a cool autumn in June.
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.10.desc:
Internal Affairs Commissioner Sergey's fingers, clutching the report binder, turned corpse-like pale from the excessive force. His polished boot heels clicked a sharp, nervous rhythm on the cold concrete floor of the command post. \“Reporting, Comrade Marshal Commander,\” his Adam's apple bobbed violently, but his voice, though artificially trained, was loud to the point of being strained, \“According to the latest statistics, food reserves in all districts are ample, the average daily ration standard has stabilized at eight hundred grams of potatoes, no civilians are starving, and morale is stable.\”

\“When I inspected the frontline model community last week, I even saw children happily flying kites in the square.\” Sergey seemed eager to add vivid proof to his report, using his slightly trembling fingertip to point at a brightly colored illustration on the page. The picture indeed showed a little girl in a red dress, holding high a pigeon-shaped kite, its invisible string floating toward a corner of the sky that was incredibly blue and cloudless.

Yazov suddenly stood up without warning, his military boot grinding a few pieces of crushed coal on the floor, making a grating sound that set teeth on edge. \“Now, let's go see it for ourselves.\” His voice was terribly calm as he walked straight toward the door. Sergey's face instantly turned bloodless, like the gray mud in the corner of the wall, as if an invisible cold wind had stripped away all his pretenses.

As the convoy drove out of the city, grey-black snow began to fall. The birch trees along the road were bare; under their branches hung dark, humanoid... \“things,\” whose faces were half-eaten and blurred by hungry crows. They hung from the trees like strings of dried, gruesome fruit. \“It's... it's just the few we didn't have time to deal with earlier... they'll be... they'll be cleaned up soon,\” Sergey mumbled incoherently, turning his face away, afraid to look out the window.

The massive iron gate of Granary No. 3 was ajar. The moment the guard pushed the door open, a mix of moldy and sour stench hit them full force. Inside the warehouse, empty sacks were piled high like mountains. A rat in the corner was brazenly gnawing on a piece of bread that had grown green mold, not even scurrying away as a live person approached. Yazov bent down and picked up a ration card trampled into the mud. The date on it was a fortnight ago, and the ink of the signature had long dried into a gray smear.

\“And the children in the picture?\” he suddenly asks. His voice is soft, but it pierces Sergey's eardrums like an ice pick. Sergey's lips tremble violently, unable to utter a single word. Yazov does not press him further. Instead, he turns and walks toward the so-called \“Model Square\” not far away. The girl in the red dress from the illustration is gone. The wreckage of the pigeon kite is in pieces, its string tangled on a bare utility pole. In the corner of the square, a girl so thin she is nearly skeletal squats, laboriously gnawing on a frozen piece of tree bark with her teeth; the blood seeping from the corners of her mouth is stark against her pale face.

\“Uncle,\” the girl looks up, her eyes utterly devoid of the brightness a child should have, shining like two pieces of broken glass, \“My kite... was torn apart by wild dogs.\”

On the return drive, Sergey finally breaks down, covering his face, letting out stifled sobs like a wounded beast. Yazov merely watches him silently, his face devoid of any expression. He picks up the beautifully made report binder that has fallen onto the floor mat. He flips through the pages, which are already yellowed and creased, with an air of detachment. The snow outside the car window falls heavier and heavier, quickly covering the things along the road, turning them into one single white mound.
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.10.a: The sky is gradually stained with darkness, an ebony-like darkness.
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.9.desc:
“We'll go here.” Yazov's finger pressed heavily on a nearly forgotten corner of the command map. The village's name was blackened by years of ink bleed, like an old stain that couldn't be completely scrubbed away.

The adjutant's face instantly turned ashen, his lips twitching a few times before he finally didn't dare raise any objections, forcing himself to arrange the itinerary. As the motorcade rattled to a halt at the village entrance, Yazov narrowed his eyes: the scene before him was **unsettlingly clean**. The adobe walls had clearly just been whitewashed, and the still-damp coating emitted a pungent odor in the cold wind; strings of corn hanging under the eaves were red like burning flames, painful to look at; a few women in brand new floral padded jackets were sitting around the stone mill at the village entrance, chatting and laughing, the dough they were kneading as white as fresh fallen snow.

“Commander! The Commander is here!” A man with a face full of smiles rubbed his hands together and approached from the village. The wrinkles on his face were crammed with deliberate, almost **fawning cheer**, and he introduced himself as the village elder. Yazov ignored his outstretched hand and walked straight toward the stone mill. Seeing him approach, the chattering women instantly fell silent, like chickens choked by the neck, and frantically hid the dough in the bamboo baskets beside them, white flour clinging to their fingertips dusting down. From the corner of his eye, Yazov noticed something dark brown peeking out from the bottom of one woman's basket—the color that only comes from being heavily mixed with **bran and straw chaff**.

“The harvest this year, it looks good?” He squatted beside an old woman who was stitching a shoe sole. The backs of the old woman's hands were covered in cracks deep enough to see bone, and the coarse hemp thread left deep marks on the calloused fabric. “G-good... very good...” The old woman's voice trembled slightly with nervousness, but her gaze involuntarily darted toward the low adobe house behind her. The window of the house was covered with tattered newspaper, and a child was peering out through a gap in the paper, his stomach concave like a shriveled sack, starved so much his chest was pressed to his back.

The women's chatter never resumed. Following their fearful gaze, Yazov saw a man in a gray overcoat standing beneath the brand new white wall at the village entrance. He stood with his hands behind his back, his hip holster gleaming with cold metallic light in the overcast sky. The village elder's smile froze completely on his face. He lowered his voice and stammered, “T-that's... a comrade sent by the superiors... to protect our safety.”

With a *snap*, the hemp thread in the old woman's hand suddenly broke. Taking advantage of everyone's attention being on the man in gray, she quickly shoved a half-piece of hard, dry food into Yazov's palm. It was a *wotou* (steamed corn bread) mixed with grass seeds and wood shavings, the coarse grains painfully pressing into his hand. “D-don't let them see.”

Yazov, clutching the *wotou* that was harder than a stone, slowly stood up. On the brand new white wall behind him, a patch of whitewash, unable to withstand the cold wind, flaked and crumbled down, revealing the damp, black, **rotten mud** beneath. The man in the gray coat stared at him motionlessly, his gaze sharp enough to count every secret in Yazov's pockets. In the distance, a burst of children's “laughter” suddenly rang out, clear as a handful of glass beads clattering together, but it could not, by any means, cover up a single, utterly suppressed **cough** coming from that low adobe house.

That cough, faint as a sigh, was like a red-hot steel needle, gently, yet mercilessly, piercing through the illusion of a so-called “Peaceful and Prosperous Age” meticulously papered over with lies, whitewash, and **fear**.
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.9.a: Since all things are void, where can the dust fall?
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.8.t: A Walk in the Woods: Part One
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.8.desc:
The celebratory fireworks burst open in the twilight with a false gold and red, and deafening cheers battered the windows of the command post like a tide. Yazov tossed the medal-studded uniform, heavy as a chainmail, onto the command desk, the metal badges colliding with the mahogany in a harsh clamor. He did not look back, his military boots crunching over the scattered dead leaves and gravel as he trudged step by step toward the depths of the dead, silent forest behind the command post. The German swastika had just been consumed by fire on the Red Square, trampled into the mire by millions of feet, but the scorched earth beneath his feet stung his soul more than the frozen soil of Leningrad. This land was the great scar of “victory,” and fresh, warm blood was still constantly seeping from beneath that scar.

He touched a segment of a dead tree trunk, scorched by flash and heatwave. The bark was cracked, and the intersecting lines on it looked like a map of war. The wind and snow of 1941 howled without warning from the depths of his memory: a seventeen-year-old him, clutching a bundle of cold explosives, charging towards a German tank in knee-deep snow. The sparks from the detonator briefly illuminated the cyanotic faces of his comrades, in whose eyes burned a flame almost innocent in its intensity. But now, from within the shattered, mountainous piles of steel wreckage, emerged a **desolation** more hideous and intangible than Fascism or Nazism. The distant river bend was shrouded in a layer of black mist, so dense that not a single ray of light could penetrate it. A fisherman's net hung on a dead branch by the shore, containing a few half-dead fish, their scales still embedded with tiny shrapnel marks. This was the **tumor left by victory**, which had spread deep into the very bloodstream of this land.

The greatcoat contained the night's cold wind, and the wind carried a faint smell of blood from an unknown source. Yazov suddenly chuckled softly, the sound starkly abrupt in the empty woods, startling a few cold crows dozing on the dead branches. He finally realized that he was the most ridiculous and pathetic buffoon in this grand tragedy: raising the banner of “Revenge” and “Liberation,” dragging the whole world into a sea of fire; he thought he had completely smashed the Teuton's iron hooves with nuclear bombs, but he failed to guard against the desire of human nature and the **arrogance of power**, which, in this so-called “peace,” gnawed at the land and rivers more efficiently than war.

He knelt on the freezing permafrost, watching the moonlight stretch his shadow into a hunched, distorted question mark. What more did the war destroy than the Reichstag in Berlin? Than the Fascist regime? This forest before him was quietly dissolving in the breeze, the river foamed with the scum of dead fish and rotten shrimp, and displaced compatriots foraged like wild dogs in the city ruins... All of this was merely the funeral objects of his “Great Victory.” When he charged toward the Tiger tank with an explosive pack all those years ago, the only thought in his heart was to “ensure our descendants do not suffer this hardship,” but **his descendants were quietly dying in an unknown corner**.

The thick fog in the woods rose, gently, yet mercilessly, enveloping this medal-bedecked, utter failure. He knew he could not save all the suffering on this land, but he thought, at least, he should plant a seed in this endless reflection and pain. Just as beneath the heavy snows of Leningrad all those years ago, there were always some frozen soils stubbornly, despairingly, nurturing the bud of the next spring...
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.7.desc:
Yazov's consciousness was trapped in a cotton-like darkness, the aftershocks of artillery fire still tap-dancing in his skull. When he opened his eyes, he saw fig trees all over the mountainside drooping with honey-colored fruit, streams floating with water lilies, and dewdrops shattering into stars on the grass blades—this was neither a bombed-out command post nor a temporary hospital on scorched earth.

“Dmitry Timofeyevich.” A familiar voice came from the creekside.

Yazov turned. His military boots left no trace of mud on the moss. **Karbyshev** was sitting on a smooth stone, his uniform crisply ironed, chalk dust on his cuffs, drawing something in the stream with a branch. The water flowed through his fingers, producing silver-fish-like flecks of light.

“Mentor?” His throat tightened. The person he longed for, the one who was worlds away, had appeared right before him. He tried to raise his hand, but found his arm as heavy as if filled with lead...

“Look at this garden,” Karbyshev said without turning around. Where the branch traced a line, seedlings emerged, instantly turning into heavy wheat heads. “There's no barbed wire, no watchtowers, even the shovels are rusted with verdigris... This is how men should live, isn't it?”

Yazov felt his uniform; the medals and bullet holes were gone. On his chest was only a warm pocket watch, which, when opened, contained a willow leaf. He saw his reflection in the mud by the stream: his seventeen-year-old self, clutching a freshly issued textbook, following Karbyshev through the birch forests of Leningrad.

“They said you died. Died in the forest.” He squatted down, and the stream water flowed over his ankles, blossoming into a string of lilies of the valley. “I went there later, it was a good place...”

Karbyshev planted the branch into the soil, and it instantly grew into a towering oak tree...

The wind stirred up petals across the sky. On the distant field path, people in work clothes were harvesting, and children were chasing butterflies. The sight stung him with a bitter ache.

This was what they swore to protect: not medals, but the peace that allowed lilies of the valley to bloom by the stream.

A tremor suddenly tore the dream apart. The oak leaves rustled down, bearing scorched holes. Karbyshev's figure turned transparent, and the chalk dust drifted into ashes...

Yazov reached out to grab, only to hold a handful of **scalding broken glass**.

The world outside the dream was collapsing. The rebar of the bunker let out a sharp, mournful cry... He snapped his eyes open. Before him were Ustinov and a group of doctors watching complex instruments. Without knowing when, he was clutching a scorched leaf in his hand. It looked exactly like the first leaf that had fallen from the oak tree in the Garden of Eden.
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.7.a: Fate guides the obedient, and drags the resistant.
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.4.desc:
The dark day was nearing dusk, the sky colored black by clouds drifting from afar, and the shunting locomotive let out a grating, ugly howl. As the train slowly stopped, the entire regiment began to disembark. As usual, Kalmykov arranged the whole regiment into formation, preparing to march to the barracks and await inspection by the superiors.

To be honest, he felt a little fortunate in his heart that he had actually survived this Great Crusade. Among the old comrades who set out with him, Panteley died from drinking unclean water, Manzhulov stepped on a mine while covering him to clear a Teutonic stronghold, and even the most respected Petro jumped into a river after a mental breakdown the day before they were announced to be returning home. He had lost too many old friends like this, and to be back alive, he sincerely felt God's blessing.

Everyone knew the war was over; the Teutons had been thoroughly exterminated. The superiors had specifically notified Kalmykov of this great victory, and he, in turn, passed the good news to the soldiers of the entire regiment. The soldiers ate their last rations, walking out of the train station joyfully, but the sight that greeted them was a different picture: still-uncleaned ruins and broken walls, rats running rampant in the streets, and corpses that had already turned into skeletons. By the time they reached the barracks, everyone had fallen into an eerie silence.

At the barracks, the Division Commander stood before a hastily constructed platform, flanked by a committee of military officers. The soldiers looked up, watching him puff out his somewhat portly belly, adjust his belt, and begin to speak in a hoarse, unpleasant tone.

“Soldiers, as great Slavs, we have finally completed the Great Trial, eliminating the wicked... the... Teutonic bandit gangs. But now, within our nation, there is still a group of **revisionists**, who, under the banner of peace, want the... want the army to relax its control, to relinquish authority to a so-called democratic government! This is intolerable! On this day of victory, our army must be very strong! Like... like the Commander-in-Chief, obey your superiors and bravely kill the enemy!” The stammering officer, who was clearly not used to giving long speeches, pointed behind him: “Now, you have ten minutes to eat. After that, we will immediately head to the designated location and eliminate the traitors!”

The soldiers watched as the cooks wheeled in a large pot. The moment the lid was opened, a stench rushed straight to their noses. The soldiers' anger instantly erupted.
“What the hell? What stinks so bad?”
“Dammit! This is **rotten vegetable slop**!”
“We lived hard lives before, and now it's even worse!”
“I don't want to live with a rifle anymore! I want to go home!”
...
Kalmykov realized things were going south. He strained his voice, hoping to calm the soldiers, but their shouts rose and fell, impossible to suppress. At that moment, a gunshot rang out behind him. The Division Commander had fired a round into the air.
“Are you... trying to revolt?”
After a brief silence, a soldier suddenly raised his weapon and fired at the Division Commander on the platform. One after another, soldiers picked up their weapons and opened fire on the other officers in front of them. The military police in the barracks rushed in, and the two groups instantly clashed.
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.3.desc:
The unease of the past few days had prevented Yazov from getting a good night's sleep for a week straight. The packed itinerary across West Russia, combined with his tense mental state, had nearly suffocated him. Finally, after accidentally being caught and drenched by a sudden downpour, Yazov fell ill.
······
The things in the dream were bizarre and motley, yet the Old General's curse was forever the main theme of this nightmare. That passage seemed etched into Yazov's mind, impossible to shake off: “The people of the future, standing at the other end of time, will scrutinize everything we did at every turning point of destiny, and then, **we will be eternally infamous**.”
······
He abruptly sat up, feeling his consciousness return to his body. Then, looking at the pale ceiling and the surrounding mass of complex medical instruments, the sense of suffocation rushed in like a tide. Yazov breathed heavily, filled with shock and doubt, as if something had been drawn out of his body. The doctor nearby immediately stepped forward, concerned: “Comrade Commander-in-Chief, your body has not fully recovered yet. It is best not to engage in strenuous activity for the time being.”

Yazov lay back down: “Thank you, Comrade Doctor. How long was I unconscious?”

“Eight hours, Comrade Commander-in-Chief.” Hearing this, Yazov let out a breath, relieved that he hadn't wasted too much time. As for the illness, it was probably caused by being overworked, being restless, and catching a cold at the wrong time... Regardless, Yazov felt he desperately needed a change of thought. It was time to escape the bad memories of the past. After all, the League must be on the right path, and we are doing the right thing, aren't we...?

A flaw suddenly appeared in the chain called Logic: “**What exactly is the right thing?**” Undoubtedly, the Great Trial was meant to save the Russian people—he had always believed this, and all League supporters believed it too. So, now, have the people truly been saved? This sacrilegious thought had never been seriously entertained by him before, but now, he had to admit, he hesitated. However, the problem wasn't severe. As long as Yazov could prove that what he was doing was the path to salvation, he could discard these damnable, soul-shaking ideas...
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.3.a: He can only pray that the outcome will be as he desires.
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.2.desc:
Yazov suppressed the unease in his heart and continued his stroll through Samara, but when he looked down at the city and saw only ruins, rubble, and lifeless earth, the memory he wished to forget resurfaced in his mind like a curse. He knew the bulk of the city was now beneath the bunker, but the more he tried to reassure himself, the more the curse plagued his mind.

······

His journey concluded, Yazov tossed and turned on his bed, the Old General's words constantly washing over his reason and memory. The passage was like a tiny pebble caught in a precision gear—not earth-shattering, yet it nearly brought Yazov's thought process to a halt: “I had a dream. In that dream, the people of the future looked down upon a desolate, ruined Russia. And they judged us—they judged the League—because it was destined to lead Russia to ruin.” In this deliberately forgotten memory, the Old General's figure was so clear, his voice so earnest and vivid, but the content he spoke was like a fatal bullet that, after a long flight, struck Yazov right between the eyes.

\“Haven't the Old General's words come true? Does that mean I am wrong? In that case, is the Fourth Theory merely my delusion, or the Old General's revelation? Is this what the League was supposed to be in the Old General's vision?\” Yazov shuddered. He could not think any further; he had to stop himself. Even though he knew very well that procrastination would not solve the problem, only let it worsen.

So he switched the light back on, put on his greatcoat, and attended to his official duties. **Dmitry Timofeyevich Yazov** bypassed the thought, shrinking back once more, turning into a small cog silently working within a machine.
strings.OMS_yazov_GG.1.desc:
Facing the biting cold wind, Yazov stepped out of the bunker. This time, he planned to tour the major towns of all West Russia, not only to ensure control but also to take a good look at the people on the Russian land. Soon, the special train traveled from Omsk to the Urals, and then continued its transfer, until...
······
Samara City
······
What met Yazov's eyes was a tomb cast in reinforced concrete—though that description was inelegant, it was the most fitting. Above the ruins, a few dozen sparse black dots moved back and forth among the gravel and rubble—they were agents executing their duties. Yazov recalled an investigation report he had read: the permanent surface population of the entire city of Samara was **less than ten thousand**, and most of them suffered from radiation-induced illnesses. Although a considerable number of people had been moved into the bunker, nearly a third were still lost during the nuclear strike. This number filled him with extreme heartache; these were the precious lives of the Slavic nation!

Yazov then walked toward the outskirts of the city. The first thing he saw was a dilapidated wooden hut that had lost its original color due to massive electromagnetic radiation and the passage of time, surrounded by a dead, silent environment. As he looked at the scene, as if by some strange twist of fate, a fragmented memory abruptly floated into his mind. He tried hard to recall who had said those words and what the full context was, but to no avail. He could only continue looking, filled with doubt.

Inside the house, Yazov saw a skeleton. The walls around the skeleton were covered with tools that had lost their color due to erosion by time: a saw, a knife, a dog chain, a bow and arrows... An old-fashioned hunting rifle lay on the ground. The skeleton was dressed in leather clothes, its hand resting on a dog-like skeleton. It looked like the skeleton of an experienced old hunter. It was sitting peacefully in a chair, and both the dog's and the hunter's skulls had a large hole—evidently, a long time ago, perhaps even before the nuclear war, the hunter first shot the dog and then **himself**. Yazov could almost picture the scene of this hunter's life, battling wits with wild beasts and contending with nature in the mountains. This reminded him of the Old General. In the final months of his life, did he also fight bravely but fruitlessly, like this hunter, and finally, like this hunter, willingly embrace death?

......No, it was different. He had inherited the Old General's legacy. It should be this way, and it could only be this way...

But he looked out the shattered window, and the place that was once a forest was now only a patch of charcoal. Vaguely, only the roots of some charred tree stumps remained to remind people: this used to be a woodland... Suddenly, he remembered. That passage came from **Old General Karbyshev**.

And the full scope of the memory terrified him; his previous self-assurances now appeared so ridiculous in this context:
strings.OMS_GT_GUI_DESC_TT:
“A colossal war will ultimately destroy human civilization, and no one can be pulled from this Möbius loop.”

Here, you will receive the latest war reports and take action to purge the £GFX_OMS_teutons_texticon Teutons.

The light to ultimate victory has been lit, and we shall eliminate the threat of the £GFX_OMS_teutons_texticon Teutons,

Forever.
strings.OMS_despotism_BRY_LONG: Fatherland, Unity, Independence, Freedom, and Liberation - For the Russian Alliance

Note from the developer:
Note: After this, a thermonuclear war will be triggered, causing significant lag. Post-nuclear war content will not load until the lag ends.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.200.desc:
“Decay does not exist merely on the level of thought; it also manifests as the filthy form of greed and laziness, entrenched deep within the very strongholds upon which we depend for survival.\“
Generalissimo Yazov's voice echoed in every corner of the bunker. Following the previous purge of ideological disloyalty, he turned his attention to another equally fatal enemy: bureaucratic corruption. In this crisis of life and death, the officials responsible for allocating supplies and managing industry had turned their power into a tool for self-enrichment. Food rations were withheld, weapon parts were sold on the black market, and crucial industrial plans stalled. These actions were like a fatal tumor, eroding the very foundations of the Black League's survival.
The purge immediately commenced. This time, the executioners' targets were not only ideologically impure intellectuals or wavering officers but also those glamorous officials with hands stained by ill-gotten gains.
A logistics official named Grigory was arrested publicly. He was accused of hoarding vast quantities of scarce canned food and medicine and trading them privately on the black market. Crates of contraband were discovered in his home—supplies that could have saved the lives of countless soldiers and workers. In the tribunal, he attempted to defend his actions, but his voice was quickly drowned out by the roar of angry citizens and officers.
Another engineer, responsible for weapons production, was arrested for inflating production data and profiting from it. His reports listed countless guns and shells that should have been produced, but in reality, these items did not exist. In his factory, many workers were idle due to a lack of essential tools and raw materials, and production had ground to a halt. His execution order was delivered within a day, making him the first typical case of a corrupt official within the bunker.
\”These vermin are more terrifying than German bombs,\“ Yazov said in a subsequent broadcast. \”They corrupt our souls. They steal the soldier's rations, they delay the production of weapons, and they defile the great cause we fight for with their self-interest.\“
The purge's effect was immediate. After a brief period of chaos, order in the bunker became more stable. Generalissimo Yazov looked at the submitted trial reports, his face expressionless. He believed that, for the sake of a pure and powerful Russia, any obstacle must be ruthlessly swept aside.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.200.a: The Great Trial requires everyone to fulfill their duties.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.201.desc:
The bunker's gigantic blast doors slowly opened with a heavy mechanical groan. A long-lost beam of light, carrying a faint trace of fallout dust, fell upon the bunker's cold entrance. Since the endless inferno drove humanity underground, this door had been sealed for an untold number of years. Now, the surface radiation levels had finally dropped to an acceptable range. Under Generalissimo Yazov's command, the first teams to return to the surface, composed of the most elite reclaimers, were preparing to step onto this unfamiliar homeland.

Each of them was equipped with simple anti-radiation suits and tools, but their hearts were filled with complex emotions. Most of them had only ever seen blue skies, white clouds, and vast plains in textbooks and the memories of the older generation. Now, what lay before them was a desolate and lifeless wasteland. The once-prosperous city of Omsk was reduced to ruins; twisted steel skeletons and charred rubble were the only urban relics. There was no sound of wind, no birdsong, only the crunch of gravel beneath their feet. This shocking silence was more penetrating than the most terrifying nuclear blast—it spoke volumes of the end of an era.

A young reclaimer named Ivan Petrov discovered a rusted children's toy car among the ruins. He gently picked it up and wiped the dust off with his sleeve, as if he could see the past world full of laughter through it. A flash of sorrow crossed his eyes, but it was quickly replaced by a resolute determination. This destroyed world was precisely the vision of what 'The Great Trial' they fought for was meant to prevent. They had to act to make the Motherland rise from the ashes.

As planned, they established the first checkpoint within Omsk city, not only to monitor radiation levels but also to declare the Black League's absolute sovereignty over this land. The work of rebuilding houses proceeded simultaneously. Using salvaged industrial equipment and reclaimed metal, they began repairing residences. All work was unfolding in an orderly fashion so that more people could resume normal production and life.

\“We shall re-tame this wasteland,\” the commander of the operation wrote in his report to the Generalissimo. \“We will rebuild the Russian homeland with our sweat and will. We will establish a state composed entirely of strength, industry, and martial spirit. Russia shall become a beacon of justice and civilization, illuminating this world polluted by corrupted Nazi ideology.\”

That night, Ivan Petrov wrote in his diary: \“Today, I touched the wreckage of the old world. It was not as vibrant as in the textbooks; it is merely a ruin now. I wonder if our 'Great Trial' is precisely to ensure that this silence never falls upon the Motherland's soil again.\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.201.a: The Old World is gone; a new world shall be reborn.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.202.desc:
Looking at the distorted images on the screen, an unprecedented sense of emptiness and unease filled his heart. He had envisioned that civilizations in other regions had long been destroyed, but the reports from the front lines were vastly different from his expectations.

\“Comrade Generalissimo,\” a signaler reported, \“we detected Teutonic signals at Observation Point 7... not old ones, but currently in use.\”

This news was like a sharp dagger thrust into Yazov's beliefs. He had thought that all Teutonic remnants had been reduced to ashes in the nuclear baptism. But intelligence showed that Teutonic forces had survived. They were not consumed by the hell he himself had unleashed; instead, they had established a new order. On their homeland, like stubborn weeds, they were still fighting for survival. This was undoubtedly a mockery of Yazov's conviction and a merciless negation of the Great Trial's perfect conclusion. Everything he had planned day and night, the result for which countless Russians had sacrificed, turned out to be merely a fantasy.

Even more shocking was the second report from the reconnaissance team. Near the Ural Mountains, radio signals from multiple armed factions were detected. According to intelligence analysis, these forces were not the unified 'Black League' but various rebel factions. The Bolsheviks and liberal remnants he had purged and eliminated had actually survived; they had seized the strongholds established by the League and formed new organizations. Their flags bore no League symbol, only the negation of 'The Great Trial.' They had once been an internal problem for the League, but now they had become a massive external threat.

Yazov felt an emptiness he had never known. He had thought he was the architect of the final revenge, only to discover he was merely the originator of chaos. He had personally brought forth Hell, but this Hell was more complex and tumultuous than he had imagined. His 'Great Trial' had not ended everything; it had created a new world that was more bloody and cruel. This sense of nihilism was slowly devouring him. His faith, his goal, his entire life, all seemed to have lost its meaning.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.202.a: For Russia, I must defeat them a second time!
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.203.desc:
In the bunker's communications room, the ticking of the telegraph machine became the sole main theme. Yazov stood before a massive operational map, his eyes fixed on the markers representing troops and strongholds. He had pulled himself out of the previous nihilism, pouring all his energy into a new 'Great Trial' strategy. The remnants of the old world sought a resurgence, but he would destroy them once again.

According to the Central League's assessment, despite the League's heavy losses, as long as they could reconsolidate the scattered League units, they still possessed enough power to crush everything. Whether it was the struggling Teutonic barbarians or the reactionary forces and bandits on Russian soil, all would be trampled underfoot.

Yazov issued the most urgent order: send telegrams to all known military districts and partisan groups, demanding their return to the fold. The wording of the telegram was filled with Yazov's characteristic coldness and resolve: 'Annihilate all banditry, and utterly reduce the Teutonic concept to history.'

One telegram was sent to the Far Eastern Military District, addressed to Colonel Pikalov. His troops were near Lake Baikal. Yazov believed Pikalov's loyalty and tenacity were sufficient to overcome all difficulties. The telegram promised that once he integrated the Far Eastern resources, the League would dispatch elite forces to support him.

Another telegram was sent to Alexander Lazarenko, the commander in the Ural Mountains. He had once been considered a 'waverer' for questioning the ideology of 'The Great Trial,' but he and his troops remained the elite core of the League. Yazov's telegram did not mention past grievances, simply stating the facts: only by uniting could they completely eliminate the enemy.

However, the telegraph responses were not all positive. Some telegrams vanished without a trace, indicating that some units might have been annihilated in the chaos or chosen to become independent. Other replies were full of doubt and distrust. They questioned whether Yazov's 'Great Trial' had truly brought victory, or merely more confusion.

Despite this, Yazov did not waver. He knew that the path to unifying Russia would always be accompanied by suspicion and betrayal. But as long as he could regroup those genuinely loyal to the cause of vengeance, his 'Great Trial' still had a chance of completion.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.203.a: Issue a call to all regions, regardless of their past loyalty.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.204.desc:
\“To the Generalissimo, my unit has completed control of Krasnoyarsk and is ready to sweep the surrounding areas at any time...\”

On the screen of the communications room, a long-awaited response finally appeared. The telegram came from **Krasnoyarsk**, a strategic location that had been isolated by the surface chaos. The dispatch was signed by **Alexander Sakharovsky**, the reformist leader who had been wholeheartedly aligned with the Generalissimo and had made great contributions to the Black League during the Great Trial. His troops had been garrisoned in this metallurgical and railway hub. When the Great Trial arrived, the local bunker system functioned excellently, preserving a large amount of precious industry, manpower, and supplies for the League.

Yazov's face showed no emotion, but a ripple flashed in his eyes. In the face of the fractured reality, this reply from an old comrade was undoubtedly a light in the darkness. Sakharovsky's telegram was concise and powerful. He reported the situation in Krasnoyarsk: the bunker system had survived the nuclear war, industrial facilities were preserved, and the local League forces had stabilized their position under his command. However, he did not mention external exploration, only emphasizing that after a long period of recuperation, they were now re-equipped with the capacity for effective local governance.

This telegram was of great significance. Strategically, it meant the Black League had gained massive support from the rear. Krasnoyarsk, as a vital industrial and resource center with abundant manpower and coal resources, would provide crucial support for the second phase of 'The Great Trial.'

But on a personal level, this telegram also brought complex emotions to Yazov. He had personally brought Hell to Russia, witnessing too many people degenerate and go mad in the silent solitude, yet there were still people like Sakharovsky upholding the League's original ideals. They had not been misled by the surface chaos and still adhered to the ideal of the Great Trial. Their existence was a silent affirmation of Yazov's path of vengeance.

However, Yazov also knew that consolidating Sakharovsky's forces would not be simple. This telegram was the beginning of cooperation, but it would also bring a lot of trouble to his old friend. He needed to unite all those loyal to the Great Trial, not create more problems for them. How to best utilize the strength of the various bunkers would be a challenge Yazov must face in the journey ahead.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.204.a: Contact Sakharovsky again to discuss the rebuilding of the Eastern Front.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.205.desc:
It was the sixth day since the troops departed. Yazov tossed and turned in the officers' command post and began reviewing the dispatch reports of the various external liaison teams. He meticulously read the movement requests and reports from teams sent in all directions, wrote down his instructions, opened a drawer, and placed them in pre-prepared folders, from which the staff would forward them for execution. The folder for exploration instructions around Omsk was already full, and the folder for the westward teams also contained many documents. Only the folder for the teams sent to the East remained empty.

He sighed, about to return to the general command to continue the meeting, when the signaler next to him suddenly gasped and began operating the black-and-white typewriter in front of him. Yazov quietly watched the young soldier gradually translate the telegram. Soon, the clacking of the typewriter stopped, and a complete survey report was handed to Yazov.

**To the Generalissimo: Regarding the Status and Challenges of Our 'Westward' Movement**

Since our unit departed eastward, aside from encountering numerous destroyed facilities along the way, multiple factions have launched attacks against us. According to our reconnaissance, these factions are mostly bandits who emerged in various settlements after the Great Trial, but there are also small loyal League units fighting them, to whom we have provided sufficient weapons, ammunition, and communication facilities for contact.

Our vanguard has reached **Kyzyl**. According to reconnaissance, there are temporarily no signs of other factions' survival in the surrounding area. Due to the mountain's influence, large tracts of land remain relatively intact. During our arrival in this area, some League garrison forces have already completed the survey and leveling of the land. The League can deploy personnel to resume production activities at any time.

Our main force has reached **Kansk**. According to the survey, the infrastructure in this area is severely damaged, and a large number of factory facilities are completely ruined due to a lack of timely maintenance. Coal mining facilities, being buried deeper, are relatively well-preserved, and we have promptly begun resuming production. Please provide instructions, Generalissimo.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.205.a: Prioritize the resumption of industrial production in Kansk to restore the League's energy supply.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.205.b: Prioritize controlling Kyzyl to ensure the safety of agricultural production.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.205.c: Kansk and Kyzyl are both crucial; both must proceed simultaneously!
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.206.desc:
Crickets began chirping under the night sky. Moonlight pierced the darkness, casting a glow on Sokolov and the members of his Brotherhood. They had built a bonfire in a square and were sharing the spoils they had plundered that day. It was another fruitful day; they had unexpectedly found some arms and eliminated a few small, uncooperative gangs. The new recruits were a bit reserved; some fiddled with their fingers, others quietly kicked at the dirt underfoot. The gang leaders in the middle of the fire were enjoying themselves. Sokolov grinned, pulled out a rolled cigarette, and lit it up. He tilted his head and shouted.

\“Misha! Is the meat ready?\”

\“Almost, Boss! Bringing it right over!\”

He turned and looked at the distant ruins: \“How wonderful. How did this small place manage to store so much stuff?\”

Suddenly, a few bursts of thunder echoed from the distant night. Sokolov quickly scrambled up as a series of explosions immediately followed the line of the bonfire. The Brotherhood's newcomers started to panic. A cadre, yelling for them to stop, was instantly gunned down. Immediately after, lights from all directions tore through the darkness. A stream of figures in black passed through the night, firing accurately at the disorganized gang members. Sokolov was quickly handcuffed by a man in black. His remaining few subordinates were also captured.

\“I knew it. You guys didn't all die off,\” he said, looking at the familiar Black League soldiers, a bitter smile on his face. \“So, the supplies we got were all League caches?\”

\“Of course. These are all the Generalissimo's orders,\” the leader in black nodded. \“Including the small gangs you eliminated, they were all guided by us. For that, we actually have to thank you for wiping out the minor forces we couldn't locate. Alright, any last words?\”

\“Can't we join the League's Penance Brigades?\” Sokolov held his breath and posed his final question.

\“No. We are restoring order in the Urals.\”

\“Then, give me one more cigarette. Let me have one last puff.\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.207.desc:
The telegraph machine was silent for a long time until the reply from the Urals arrived, bringing a moment of calm to the bustling communications center. The telegram was signed by **Lazarenko**, a core figure of the League who had been stationed in the Ural Military District, responsible for the administration of the entire mountain range. After the thermonuclear war, most of the Ural region had been temporarily lost to reactionary forces due to the surface chaos. However, under Lazarenko's iron fist, the Ural Military District still firmly controlled the Southern Urals, guarding this 'treasure mountain,' and their strength was not to be underestimated.

The message was concise, reporting the current situation in the Urals and confirming their loyalty to Omsk. This undoubtedly provided Yazov with a measure of comfort. Lazarenko was not only a close friend of the Generalissimo but also a key figure in the League; his very presence was a symbol of formidable strength. Yazov immediately decided to transfer Lazarenko back to Omsk to take on a more important central role.

A few hours later, a dilapidated transport plane landed on the Omsk bunker's makeshift runway. Lazarenko stepped out of the cabin; his military uniform was covered in surface dust, but his eyes were still firm. He and Yazov were reunited in the deep operations room of the bunker. There were no lengthy pleasantries, just a firm handshake before they began discussing the current situation.

Lazarenko described his experiences in the Southern Urals in detail. He spoke of the process and difficulties of underground life and the obstinacy of the opposition remnants, but his tone was mainly one of confidence. He believed the forces under his command were capable of eliminating any threat and laying a solid foundation for the final victory of 'The Great Trial.'

\“Comrade Generalissimo,\” he stated solemnly, \“the Urals are our cornerstone. With it, we can further advance the Great Trial. The troops and commanders I leave behind there are absolutely capable of completing the tasks you assign. And I am ready to serve you at the center, dedicating my full strength to the League's great cause of vengeance.\”

Yazov nodded. He knew that transferring Lazarenko back to the center was the correct decision. His presence would greatly enhance the cohesion of the League's central command, and his military talent and profound understanding of the surface world would provide strong support for Yazov's strategic planning. The Ural Military District would be handed over to a new commander, who would utilize Lazarenko's influence to develop the Urals' potential as much as possible, radiating across the entire Russian land.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.207.a: \“Very good, Lazarenko. How are the troops' rations?\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.208.desc:
\“According to the covert investigation by the team members, the local garrison in Kazakhstan exhibits extensive malpractice and corruption. Large quantities of factory war materiel are missing, the morale of the recruited troops is low, they severely lack proper training, and they are even openly plundering civilians... There are severe shortages in supplies; except for high-ranking officials, resource scarcity affects everyone from grassroots civilians to soldiers. The investigation indicates that large amounts of supplies are being funneled into the black market for sale...\”

Watching the secretary read the document before him, Yazov felt a deep anger. In the order he envisioned, there was no place for such ideological decline and moral corruption. Had he and like-minded people such as Karbyshev and Matveenko shed their blood so that these scums could live in luxury? Seeing his worsening state, the secretary paused the report. Yazov blinked, temporarily suppressing his rage: \“Continue.\”

The secretary pulled out a second report and continued: \“Generalissimo, according to the report from the investigation team, the League Security Headquarters has been monitoring the Kazakh garrison. The summary is that almost the entire Kazakh garrison is involved in corruption cases. It could be said that some officials even actively use corruption to facilitate their work. The headquarters is concerned that if we take rash action against them, the Kazakh high command might actively participate in a rebellion.\”

*It's truly rotten*, Yazov thought. The silent Chief of Staff suddenly interjected: \“Your Excellency Generalissimo, I have an idea. The current Kazakh high command is still somewhat friendly to us. We can use the pretext of troop training to conduct a sudden inspection and then liquidate them one by one under the guise of resuming training. As long as we stabilize order, we can gradually replace the personnel in Kazakhstan.\”

\“But this way, they will conceal themselves! They will destroy evidence and eliminate witnesses! If we don't eliminate all of them, our order will be destroyed by these corrupt elements!\”
