\“But we need to ensure the security of Kazakhstan, Generalissimo. We are currently short on manpower. If the Kazakh forces rebel against us again, we cannot spare enough people to suppress the rebellion right now.\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.208.a: Send a crack team of officers to supervise their training.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.209.desc:
The cold wind howled relentlessly. Over the ruins of Petrograd, the Black League's dispatched forces had established settlements one by one. After the endless dust of destruction had settled, the League's forces immediately began their westward march, arriving at this great city marked on the map as the former capital of Russia. Though it was no longer great: endless ruins, scattered bones everywhere, even the Winter Palace, once a great cultural symbol of the Russians, was now just a pile of rubble. Deep into the night, specific personnel in the troops turned on the pre-set radio and tuned to the designated channel. Yazov's voice quickly traveled across thousands of miles, reaching the ears of every listener.

\“Compatriots! My brothers and sisters!\” Yazov's voice was like a clap of thunder, breaking the winter silence. \“I see your fatigue, and I feel your pain! We have paid too much, lost too much! But please, stand tall, raise your chests, because I am here to tell you the truth!\”

His voice was full of power, every word piercing straight to the heart: \“Now, on our soil, a group of cowards hiding in the gutters has emerged! They fly the flag of pacifism and spread the vilest lies! They tell you we have lost! That the war is over, and we should lay down our arms and grovel before the Teutons! They are wrong! They are terribly wrong! I stand here today to tell you: **The Teutons have no soldiers left!**\”

Everyone looked at each other in astonishment, silently turning up the volume on their radios. \“Those rats in the gutters—they have no supplies, no weapons, and certainly no ammunition! They deceive us with lies and fear; they only know how to cling to existence and beg for mercy from the enemy. They hand over the Motherland's fate to the arrogant Teutons, thinking that by hiding under the enemy's protection, they can barely survive! Just like the Russian traitors of the past, who established some nonsensical democracy! They are unworthy! They are unworthy of being a Russian!\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.209.a: No Russian will ever grovel before the Motherland's traitors!
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.210.desc:
As the series of roars ended, Yazov shifted his focus. He began to trace back history in a subtle tone, directing his spearhead at the Teutonic ideology.

\“Do you remember **Adolf Hitler**, that most malicious, most disgusting, and arrogant pest among all Teutons? Half a century ago, he declared us Russians as savage, ignorant people lacking conscious awakening, saying we must forever submit to them! Perhaps those capitulationists fit his description, but that is certainly not us! **We survived the nuclear fire!** We are the ones who dared to face Hell! We are the ones who have inscribed the fire of vengeance into our bones! We are the true backbone of Russia!\”

\“In the war for national vengeance that we started, they cried out in the name of justice, threatening to drop nuclear bombs on Earth, using fear to force us into submission and realize their autocratic ambitions! But we did not yield! Under the League's powerful preparations, we Russians escaped destruction and live on this land today! Those surrenderists shouted that the League was fighting an unjust war, but we stand here today not because of the enemy's so-called justice! But because of the sweat and struggle of every citizen of the Black League!

\”They thought they had won! They thought their atrocities had been forgotten by everyone!\“ His voice was full of scorn. \”Those Teutons hiding in distant bunkers—they don't even know how we rebuilt our homeland from the rubble in this wasteland! Their most basic order has collapsed. How can they compare to the great Russians!\“

His tone suddenly became heavy and sorrowful, as if speaking for all the departed souls: \”Tell me, can a nation that has slaughtered billions of lives be called just? Is this not the vilest, most evil nation?!\“ His words awakened the terrible sights people had witnessed, and many soldiers in the settlements silently bowed their heads.

\”But true justice has not vanished! We Russians are the last hope for humanity! We every one of our citizens and soldiers will forever remember the accumulated crimes of the Teutons. We will not allow the Teutons' 'justice' to destroy our homeland again!\“

Yazov's speech burned like a fire, pushing the listeners' emotions to a climax. He successfully pulled people out of the abyss of despair, forging a new faith for them with hatred and hope. He knew it was time to tell them the final answer.

\”The wicked Teutons still exist in the West,\“ his voice echoed over the ruins.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.210.a: \“The Great Trial is not over! Our vengeance is not over!\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.211.desc:
When Yazov uttered, \“The Great Trial is not over,\” the crowd fell into a sudden silence. In years of propaganda, the Teutons had been portrayed as the League's most heinous enemy, but when the news came that this enemy was not utterly annihilated, many soldiers began to waver, and murmurs immediately arose. Just then, Yazov's confident and steady voice came through again.

\“After failing to force us into submission with military might, they dropped nuclear bombs, destroying the world's civilization with the deaths of billions, trying to destroy us! But they were wrong! They underestimated us!\” Yazov's voice was filled with the attitude of a victor. \“Look at their so-called Greater Germanic Reich! Their civilization has declined; they cannot even reply to us because their manpower has been slaughtered by their own nuclear bombs! The so-called powerful Teutons in the surrenderists' mouths are now merely walking corpses!\”

\“In the past, the Teutons used countless despicable surrenderers and morally degenerate slaves to weave a so-called unified lie, an Iron Curtain that shrouded the old world. It was we Russians, with our own courage, who shattered the Teutons' myth of invincibility and crossed this Iron Curtain created by the Teutons! Our sacrifices were not meaningless! We live here today to complete the final reckoning of the old world!\”

Yazov's voice became solemn and majestic. He issued a final call to everyone: \“After crossing countless deaths, all Russians must stand up and unite under the League's banner! We must not give the Teutons any chance to rise again! Destroy the Teutons, end this damned history, and upon the corpses of the Teutons, we shall rebuild a world that truly belongs to Russia!\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.211.a: \“Long Live the Black League! Long Live the Great Trial!\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.212.desc:
Astakhov lay on what was called a bed—in reality, just a bundle of straw stuffed into rags—gazing longingly at the window, which still showed a hint of sunlight outside. Since he opposed the League's conscription for the so-called Great Trial months ago, he had been imprisoned here. He couldn't recall how long he had been locked up now—three months? Or longer? He had thought he had adapted to the solitude underground, but now that he was back on the surface, he still craved the sunlight outside.

He turned over, trying to close his eyes. Suddenly, the sound of the cell door and keys clanking rang out. Just as he tried to get up, two soldiers burst into the cell and immediately punched him twice. As he curled up in pain, the soldier in front of him placed a hood over his head and roughly dragged him out.

In Astakhov's perception, he was quickly brought from the damp cell to an open space outside. The feeling of sunlight on his body even made him feel a little warm. Then he was loaded into a car. Even through the hood, he could hear the solemn military music outside and the dictator Yazov's speech.

\“Citizens! Soldiers! My compatriots! The final war has begun! Yes, we have once again embarked on a campaign! This is not an ordinary war; it is a total war, a Third Great Trial that will determine the survival of our nation and the future of humanity!\”

*Here we go again*, the dictator was weaving a bunch of lies to trick innocent Russians into their deaths, he thought. After driving for an unknown duration, the car stopped at a location. Several soldiers dragged Astakhov out and removed his hood. Astakhov stared, and before him was a silent crowd.

\“Criminal Astakhov, you resisted the state's conscription system and advocated surrender to the Teutons! The government has now sentenced you to death, to be carried out today!\”

Before he could retort, a soldier shoved him to the ground. \“Damn you, dead traitor.\” The sound of a bullet being chambered was suddenly slow and clear. Immediately following, a crisp boom rang out.
\“The traitor is dead! Long live Russia!\”
The thunderous cheers became the last sound he ever heard.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.213.desc:
Colonel Naidyonov looked at the relevant supply list handed to him, then at the schedule on the wall, and couldn't help but rub his forehead, starting to worry. Following the order to continue the Great Trial, the League Security Department and Logistics immediately began requisitioning supplies within the bunker perimeter and searching several military bases. When they returned, their vehicles were loaded with all sorts of supplies: large quantities of barely edible canned goods, various rifles, automatic rifles, and some explosives—enough to arm hundreds of soldiers. The headache was that many of the weapons and ammunition were poorly maintained, and by the time the League soldiers discovered them, many had already rusted.

He continued his rounds in the warehouse, and another dispatch team returned from outside. He walked up to the stopped vehicle and asked the man in uniform with the agent's insignia: \“Brother, did you find anything usable?\”

\“We found a pile of weapons, but the problem is that many of them need to be reconditioned.\” The agent pulled out a magazine, inserted it into a submachine gun, and fired a few rounds into the air, only for it to jam. \“As you can see, the weapon failure rate is terrifyingly high. These things need to be reprocessed to be used normally.\”

Naidyonov looked at the pile of unopened crates on the truck; they were stacked as high as a small mountain.

\“Immediately send a telegram to the League's Civil Affairs Department to conscript skilled workers from the entire society. The military will cover the costs of requisition and transport. We need to redouble our efforts.\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.213.a: At least there's no hope of sleeping for the next few days.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.214.desc:
The howling cold wind swept across the night plain, directly striking the paper window. Farmer Ivan stood on one leg, listening to the roaring wind outside, then looked at the red-hot stove in the distance. A wave of warmth filled his heart. He was finally back on the surface.

He turned around. In the kitchen across the room, his wife was cleaning up the dishes. The smell of black bread, recently put into the stove, was beginning to permeate the air. This peaceful life made him recall the dull and mechanical days underground: facing gray walls, wearing thick clothes, planting so-called anti-radiation crops in tasteless soil. That tedious life was over; he was ready to embrace a new one.

Suddenly, there was an urgent knocking at the door. The familiar rhythm sent a chill down Ivan's spine. Before his wife could open it, the door was smashed open. Three soldiers in black uniforms, enveloped in wind and snow, barged in. The leader wore the conscription officer's insignia. \“Ivan Fyodorov?\”

\“Sir, wasn't the war over? The Security Department said I could go home when we came back up!\”

The conscription officer unfolded a document: \“The Generalissimo has issued an order. To complete the Great Trial against the Teutons, the reserve scale is to be reinstated and expanded starting today. The army requires the participation of every citizen. Come along now.\”

His wife looked at the men before her, suddenly falling to her knees, tears streaming down her face: \“I beg you! He just returned! He only has one leg! He has proof of serious injury!\”

\“That doesn't matter!\” The conscription officer snapped back impatiently while ordering Ivan to be dragged away. \“What the state needs now is obedience, not freedom. If we don't defeat the Teutons, do you expect to hide in the rear like cowards?\”

Ivan was roughly hauled out of the house. He looked back at the home they had barely settled into. The smell of black bread was scattered by the cold wind. His wife's face, distorted under the wooden window, gradually blurred and vanished in the howling wind. He murmured in his heart: \“I'm sorry.\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.214.a: His figure was pushed into the line of newly conscripted farmers, disappearing beyond the distant horizon.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.215.desc:
Lavr Shtyemenko and Kirill Morozov were deep in a tunnel, digging dirt with picks and shovels alongside their fellow workers. A worker ran over from afar, shouting that the whistle had blown and it was time to eat. The two stopped their work and headed to the kitchen for a meal.

For workers like them, uneducated and without families, mealtime was often the happiest—at least they could chat and reminisce about the past, provided they didn't say anything anti-League. The two talked about everything in their accented Russian, and soon the conversation turned to their current home.

Shtyemenko vividly described his past misfortunes: when they were underground, the League promised him a wife, but the woman was frail and died during childbirth. The promised, larger dwelling was also lost. Morozov chimed in; he had also tried to find a wife underground, but there were hardly any women where he was. Even after they reached the surface, he was beaten by the League police for getting too excited upon seeing a woman.

After finishing their meal, they lay down on their temporary bunks. Looking up at the faint yellow light, and seeing no foreman patrolling, they began talking about the recently resumed Great Trial and the engineering work they were doing.

Shtyemenko was still very worried. He remembered that when the Great Trial was first underway, the League front lines constantly proclaimed invincibility, claiming they had reclaimed the Motherland's territories like Moscow. He was even planning to rush west to live a good life, only to be suddenly relocated underground while the surface was bombed for an unknown period. He worried that if war were to start again, he would need to find a better shelter.

Morozov smiled at this. He reminded Lavr that the Generalissimo had said the great enemy, the Teutons, had no counter-attack capability left. Once the Great Trial was over and all the Teutons were dead, they would surely live a good life.

The whistle blew. The two climbed out of bed and continued their day's digging work as instructed by the foreman.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.215.a: One can only hope it'll be quick.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.216.desc:
Vasily's leather boot stepped over a shell crater, grinding the dud shell casing under his foot into the dirt. He walked up to the recruits, who were all flustered like startled geese, and roared in his hoarse voice.

\“Tell me, have you all been underground for too long? Have your bodies rusted, and do you no longer know how to fight a war!\” His raspy voice was grating, like a knife scraping a whetstone. \“Start with you—answer me one by one!\”
\“Yes, Sir! My military education taught that when the enemy is rapidly advancing, we need to provide stable suppressive fire to overwhelm the enemy's attack!\”
Vasily slapped the squad leader across the face, leaving him stunned. \“You idiot! Don't think I didn't see how you fought! For five consecutive minutes, you were firing non-stop at a so-called target in the same spot, wasting how much ammunition, and even reloading in the open! If I were your enemy, one grenade would take out the only fire support in our squad!\”

\“You!\” His finger pointed at the chest of the deputy squad leader next to him. \“Tell me, why did you run to a shell crater outside instead of taking cover in the trench after the shelling started?\”

The deputy squad leader's Adam's apple bobbed, and he finally spoke: \“Sir, the knowledge I learned in the bunker was that after a barrage begins, the enemy's shells generally don't continuously bomb the same spot. Hiding in a shell crater gives a high probability of dodging the shelling.\”

Vasily's face moved closer. The deputy squad leader could even see the beads of sweat hidden in his wrinkles.

\“Very good.\” Vasily suddenly flared up, delivering another slap to the back of the deputy squad leader's neck, pressing the man into the trench and forcing him to look intently at the fortifications below: \“Tell me, what did you dig here?\”

\“A... a trench?\”

\“You think you can just run out!\” Vasily's voice and grip pressed down from above. \“Modern artillery can control their shelling accuracy to a very small area! You think a shell won't hit a crater, but you only weren't killed by chance! What you need to avoid shelling are **trenches**! And you all run out in a rush to dodge shells. If the enemy artillery fires intermittently, all of you will die!\”

Sergey sighed, suddenly feeling his workload had increased.
\“From now on, forget everything you learned underground!\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.216.a: \“I'll personally teach you raw recruits how to fight.\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.217.desc:
Private Ilya Grishaga nervously glanced at the ceiling above and then at the officer checking documents in front of him, instinctively swallowing hard. He and the rest of the 78th Infantry Battalion stood in neat rows outside the newly constructed barracks, waiting for the Commissar and officer to decide their performance in the great Western Campaign. Ilya remembered that before the war started, his platoon was found to have many members who could not recite the Generalissimo's quotes during a loyalty inspection and was specially designated as a disloyal collective, with some members immediately taken out and shot. Just in the recent skirmish, some soldiers were caught by the guard troops for being terrified on the battlefield and dropping their weapons to flee.

Ten minutes later, Commissar Voronkov strode out of the barracks, accompanied by two fully armed guards, looking at the recruits who were visibly uncomfortable but still gritting their teeth, with a forced smile. Ilya closed his eyes, thinking, *This is it, I'm finished*. Unexpectedly, Voronkov's next words were beyond everyone's imagination.

\“Congratulations! You have passed the loyalty test! You have proven your loyalty to the League!\”

Most of the soldiers immediately looked at him in disbelief, including Ilya, who had his eyes closed. He spoke up: \“Sir, we passed the loyalty test?\”

\“Of course. I and the members of the guard troops conducted a repeated verification and confirmed that you performed admirably in the campaign to eliminate the Teutons. To commend your loyalty, headquarters has issued a new batch of supplies for you and will award you a new battle flag.\”

Then his tone abruptly shifted: \“However, military regulations also clearly state that a soldier must not interrupt or disrupt military order without reason while an officer is addressing the troops! So, who was the one who just spoke? Step out and receive two lashes as punishment!\”

Ilya sighed, stepped out, stripped off his shirt, and lay down on the ground.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.217.a: Survival of a great disaster is surely followed by good fortune.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.218.desc:
Lazarenko sat in his office chair. The work this month was endless. After the order to continue the Great Trial was issued, all military organs were operating at full capacity, overcoming all difficulties, even at the cost of hindering the normal progress of reconstruction. But the task had to be completed. Just as he was thinking this, the phone rang, and he skillfully picked it up.

\“Lazarenko, it's Yazov. I... I'm a little tired.\” Lazarenko heard Yazov exhale a long sigh before finishing his sentence, and his heart sank.

\“Generalissimo, you must take care of your health. Russia and the Great Trial still need you. You should rest immediately; we still have a lot of work to complete.\” He chose his words carefully, trying to avoid provoking Yazov.

\“No... Lazarenko. I'm calling to tell you that to meet the economic needs of the Great Trial, I have ordered a reduction in the benefits of most grassroots officials to ensure the supply of materiel for the Great Trial. Now, many people are starting to oppose me. Therefore, I plan to launch another wave of purges...\”

\“You cannot do this, Generalissimo!\” Lazarenko interrupted him, saying earnestly, \“Generalissimo, the foundation for our front-line advance right now is a stable rear. This is not part of the plan!\”

\“You think I don't f***ing know that!\” Yazov suddenly roared. \“For the cause of the Great Trial, you, I, every Russian has made too many sacrifices, and now you tell me the Teutons are not completely dead! I know those people have objections. When have they *not* had objections? I've been arguing with them all day, and they still disagree! You're the only one I can trust! I'm handing this task over to you now. You must curb the ambitions of these bastards!\”

\“Generalissimo—\” Before Lazarenko could respond, Yazov had hung up the phone. All that was left on the other end was the buzzing dial tone. He let out a long sigh and slowly put down the receiver.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.219.desc:
\“Agent 1156487, we need to ask you some questions regarding your recent work.\” Security Department official Dolgov sat at the table, looking at the young agent across from him. Two guards stood outside the door to prevent the accused from attempting to escape. Recently, a new head of the Security Department was suddenly appointed from above, and a notice was issued requiring a large-scale ideological inspection within the League. Personnel in every department had to be subjected to very specific questioning. The effect was obvious; in yesterday's inquiry, someone was discovered neglecting his duties and uttering illegal statements slandering the Generalissimo and the Great Trial.

\“Regarding the recent underground statements slandering the Generalissimo and the Great Trial, as a production inspection official, how much information do you have?\”

\“None. I've been monitoring the underground production lines recently. The workers aren't saying anything.\”

Dolgov glanced at the personnel behind him, then turned back. \“Then, during your recent work on the surface, did you encounter any specific statements from these anti-League elements?\”

\“I told you, no. I have nothing to do with those lunatics. My home is in the concentrated residential area arranged for League agents. How could there be anti-League elements there?\”

\“One last question. After we suspended your duties, did you utter any complaints about the Generalissimo or your superiors?\”

\“N-no.\”

\“Unfortunately, Agent, you have failed the lie detector test,\” Dolgov delivered the verdict. \“Your mouth is certainly tough, but unfortunately, it's not tougher than the lie detector. We will terminate all your duties. You're going to prison.\”

\“Please, sir! I have a family! I want to work! I worked for the League for a long time to get this position! If I confess everything, can I get a reduced sentence?\”

Dolgov pushed a small notebook toward him. \“Write down all your crimes here.\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.219.a: \“And finally, remember to swear your loyalty.\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.220.desc:
Rusted, cold wind poured into the airbase, or strictly speaking, the aircraft graveyard, sweeping across the faces of every League soldier and officer present. For the Great Trial, an order was issued from above: all League reconnaissance teams, while exploring, must also search for potential airbases and transport any potentially usable aircraft back to the League for test flights. Thus, this relatively less-damaged airbase quickly became an aircraft graveyard.

Officer Benchuk and a group of mechanics walked the runway, checking the condition of these past 'Iron Birds' in various locations, just like the other teams. The results were simply appalling: most of the transported aircraft were heavily rusted, and even the internal components were severely damaged. What was worse, the League currently could not produce the most critical modern electronic equipment for aircraft, such as avionics and electronic control systems, rendering these advanced planes useless.

Since the newer planes were a bust, they had to look for older ones. Soon, an **Ilyushin Il-2** attack aircraft from the old Soviet era came into view. Although the wooden structure of this aircraft was badly damaged, its structure was simple, and League mechanics quickly suggested reverse-engineering its repair after inspection. Other external parts, though severely damaged, were not difficult to restore. Even better news was that after applying to the League for documentation, personnel at the base quickly located the relevant production data. They were part of countless modified aircraft designs the League had obtained when they took over Surgut in the past, and they were now proving useful.

He gestured to a pilot nearby. The pilot opened the cockpit, entered the plane, and the control system had been restored to normal after refurbishment. Drawing on the flight experience he had simulated underground, he quickly began flying. After circling a few times at low altitude, he landed the plane in an open field. The technicians swarmed the aircraft to perform another inspection.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.220.a: A good start is half the battle won.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.221.desc:
\“The supply needs for the front have not been fully met! Why aren't you guys going down to continue ramping up production instead of admiring the view!\” Captain Kalmykov yelled, banging the blackboard covered in data at the officers below.

\“It's not admiration, we are powerless!\”

\“Nonsense! We were just careless!\”

\“If you think you can do it, why don't you try? How many people are willing to go back down for hard labor?\”

\“Stop arguing, stop arguing... this won't do!\”

The noisy arguments finally ceased. A respected Company Commander stood up and bowed to everyone. Then he turned around: \“I request you listen to my report.\”

\“Please sit and speak!\”

The Company Commander placed his hands on his knees and continued:

\“I've been involved in the underground work for a while now. Honestly, if we hadn't gone outside at all, the production underground wouldn't be hard to manage. But the problem is, we now have to manage both the surface and the underground. As you know, resource surveying and agricultural recovery on the surface haven't really gotten off the ground, and now suddenly there's a demand for a massive collection of resources to continue the Great Trial. Many farmers have gone to the front. The people who came up are also unwilling to go back underground. You have to understand, at the slightest sign of trouble, these people immediately drop everything and run into the ravines. By the time we find them, they are mostly either dead or crippled.\”

Captain Kalmykov was silent for a moment, then spoke: \“But we also need to know that as officers, we must obey orders. Especially at our level—which of us hasn't been bullied? The fact that I'm a Captain is already the peak for me. Furthermore, Russia needs a savior like the Generalissimo. Without his leadership, we would have been blown to the sky by the German bombs long ago...\” He paused for a few more seconds, then said, \“I think the Generalissimo is clever. Once the Teutons are all killed and the Great Trial is over, he'll definitely reduce the workload. We can't be in the Great Trial forever, can we?\”

The officers talked until midnight. They finally settled on the next course of action: to moderately reduce the people's fear through material rewards, then get them back underground to continue production. They would also conduct appropriate daily oath-taking activities and paramilitary training to prevent people from thinking about anti-government ideas in their spare time.

When the night was quiet, and most of the officers were asleep, the Company Commander suddenly sat on Kalmykov's bedside and whispered:

\“You have to understand, Alexey... I love our army, I love our Russia. When I came back to the surface and smelled the wild grass, I wanted to cry... And when I helped the common people build houses and farm on the surface, I loved it even more... But now I'm thinking: what are we doing? Can this really bring a good life to the Russians?\”

\“What are you trying to say?\” Kalmykov asked alertly.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.222.desc:
Engineer Tomilin stood among this pile of steel giants, or rather, the graveyard of these steel giants. Since the external exploration team discovered these iron beasts, an immediate order came from above: they must find a way to start these vehicles at once and train a batch of tankers to head to the Western Front to eliminate the Teutons. He checked the military manuals sent to the base: the League's self-produced **T-72B**, Teutonic armored vehicles, and transported **Leopards**... It was a real mess, he thought.

After clearing the dust, he began working with a group of apprentices and mechanics to determine which could still be used. The Teutonic armor was immediately ruled out. Although they looked finely crafted, they were severely damaged. All the glass was either shattered or ruined, turning to dust with a light touch. Even some instruments the League could manufacture now could not be installed in them. In contrast, the League's tanks, despite being heavily damaged and dusty, had rough and simple construction that ensured extreme ease in component replacement. Many of them were not completely destroyed, only externally rusted from long storage. After Tomilin and his apprentices figured out the structure of the tanks from the wreckage of a dozen or so vehicles, a functioning tank, assembled from parts cannibalized from countless others, soon rolled out onto the testing ground. Listening to the massive clanging noise of the tank, he thought, *In the future, we will have to figure out a way to build a better one*.

War was cruel; he had witnessed it firsthand. But to win this brutal war, the League needed everyone to utilize all available resources. These thousands of fragments needed to be put together one by one to become truly usable weapons. He only hoped that with these things, the League's soldiers could eliminate the Teutons, this mortal enemy of Russia, with the minimal number of casualties and complete the Great Trial as the Generalissimo had said. On the day the war ended, he would definitely open a bottle of vodka to celebrate.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.222.a: \“Drive slower! This thing won't take much punishment!\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.223.desc:
Nick watched with interest the changes in his teammates. Since coming to the surface, several young men had transformed from dull training fanatics. Pyotr's bovine eyes now blinked incessantly, afraid of missing anything. Alexander, who rarely spoke, would now say a word or two every so often, sometimes even babbling incoherently, with one sentence unconnected to the next. Nikolayevich would occasionally chuckle to himself, though Nick could tell it wasn't genuine, but sad. Everyone had changed since they came to the surface, adapting to surface life in their own ways.

\“Are the higher-ups sure there's a huge armory here?\” Pyotr pulled a map out of his backpack, which had a big circle drawn over the area they were in. \“They can't even find the basic location?\”

Nick squinted, carefully scanning the ground for any trace. \“Didn't you read the briefing? These places were specially given anti-nuclear camouflage to prevent the Teutons' planes from finding them. Especially after the Great Trial, the ground has been covered by a mess of ash for an unknown period, but the general location shouldn't have changed, which is why they sent us to look.\”

\“What's a plane, Boss?\” Alexander interjected. \“We're tens of thousands of kilometers from the Teuton border, right? They supposedly didn't reach this far, so how could they find our armory?\”

\“I know. A plane is something that can fly in the sky above us. They say it flies higher than our guns can shoot, can fly all the way from the bunker to the west of the Motherland, and can drop big hand grenades to blow up the enemy...\”

The group searched for a long time, soon becoming breathless and exhausted. They found a concrete building to rest. After resting for a while, they resumed the search. As Nick was searching the east wall, he suddenly saw Nikolayevich pulling at a wooden board in the northwest corner. \“Are you crazy! You're going to make the load-bearing wall collapse!\”

\“Hey, what if it's hidden right here!\” Nikolayevich yanked hard, and the wooden board, along with half the wall, collapsed, nearly burying him. Nick was about to curse at him when he suddenly saw a flash of silver light peeking through. When the dust settled, he shone his flashlight on it and tapped it with his gun. \“Holy shit, no way!\”

The group immediately began frantically searching along the wall. They quickly found a door. After unlocking it with the key provided by headquarters, the soldiers stood there stunned, unable to believe what they saw.

Dozens of neatly organized shelves were filled with automatic rifles, magazines, and support guns. The boxes below had glaring biohazard symbols on them. Behind the door next to them, there were countless artillery shells.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.223.a: \“God, we've really earned a merit now.\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.224.desc:
The quiet **Volga River** has witnessed endless history. The people who traversed the land of the Volga gave birth to countless stories of courage and suffering, stories that are sung by later generations, becoming footnotes in history.

This land witnessed the unfailing Red Banner; red and white flags clashed fiercely over this Russian stronghold. The courage of the man of steel overcame all difficulties, writing his own legend.

This land also witnessed the demise of a great nation. The criminal named **Bukharin** carried out endless construction here but failed to preserve the rising Red Banner. Teutonic legions from the West carried their swastika banners across the Caucasus mountains and arrived on this land. In a brutal war, the Volga witnessed the children of Russia fall tearfully on the Motherland's front lines, and the Soviet Union, like the Volga, flowed away.

After the Teutons occupied **Volgograd**, endless atrocities unfolded on this land. The symbols of Russia's past existence were ruthlessly destroyed. Russian resistance was crushed under the Teutons' iron heel, and the Russian people were mercilessly slaughtered. A large number of Caucasians served as German collaborators, and countless Teutonic immigrants settled in this famous Russian city, now **Paulusburg**. The remaining Russians either fled their hometowns or became the most miserable slaves, tools of Teutonic rule.

The Great Trial arrived, and the evil was finally reckoned with and ended. Led by Generalissimo Yazov, the Russians crushed the once-invincible Teutons with blood and steel. Countless Russian soldiers crossed the Volga with fury, driving the Teutons out of this land and slaying the Caucasian collaborators. They began attempting to rebuild this famous Russian city. But their story was abruptly cut short. The nuclear fire raining from the sky burned their dreams to ashes. Countless Russian soldiers died brutally in the scorching flames and the endless nuclear fallout, and years of radiation had all but killed all life. This land ultimately became a dead zone.

But the story is not over. When the trumpet of the Great Trial sounds again, Russians, filled with the will for vengeance, cross mountains and rivers to finally return to this land. They are determined to rebuild this city and step over death.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.224.a: Until the final vengeance is complete.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.225.desc:
Since the fires of Fimbulwinter burned down the old world, Midgard has become a scorched earth, no longer suitable for human habitation. However, deep in Siberia, beneath the forgotten industrial ruins of **Krasnoyarsk**, a stranger and more terrifying civilization has been born. Here, there is no Yazovian fury for revenge, no fanaticism for unification, only a cold and pure, almost manic, production.

The air underground is thick with the mixed scent of oil, rust, and sweat, yet no one complains. The workers move like ghosts on the production line in the dim light. They were once humans of flesh and blood, but now they have discarded emotion—emotion is a useless burden in never-ending work. They have discarded socializing—communication is a non-essential activity in the face of ruthless production efficiency. They have even discarded life—they are no longer living souls, but a group of machines with life.

Their eyes are hollow and dull, like white slates from which all memory has been erased. Their movements are precise and repetitive, without a single superfluous pause. Fingers skillfully operate long-rusted mechanical arms, accurately tightening, welding, and assembling metal parts. There is no conversation, no song, and even their breathing is barely perceptible. The only sounds are the monotonous and rhythmic roar of the running machines and the crisp clang of metal impact.

Here, there are no Marshals' speeches, no flags flying, and no promises of the future. The only thing they have to do is work on the production line. What are they producing? No one knows; perhaps they no longer care themselves. The only thing they remember is the work itself. They have discarded everything else, including the yearning for freedom, love, and hope. They have given themselves over to this factory, becoming its perpetual prisoners and most loyal slaves.

This is a terrifying state. They have no resistance, no pain, no resentment. They are satisfied with this way of survival without thought or emotion, as if, after the nuclear baptism, this is humanity's only way out. They are no longer human; in the most primitive way, they have become a part of the factory.

This Perpetual Factory is like a cold and precise heart, beating tirelessly beneath the dead wasteland of Krasnoyarsk. What it produces may not be weapons or tools, but the most profound mockery of the old world and the final judgment on human fragility and madness.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.238.desc:
21:47
\“Didi-didi-di... Didi-di... Didi-di...\” As the red, top-secret radio successfully transmitted the last piece of critical intelligence, Kuznetsov immediately leaned back in his chair. The high-intensity work of a month—treading on thin ice, cautiously searching and investigating, and transmitting intelligence like a spy on their own soil—had left him exhausted. However, a small sense of elation filled his heart. He understood that after this experience, he would no longer be a mere Lieutenant Colonel in the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Thinking this, he sighed softly and closed his eyes to rest.

21:49

Relieved of his worries, Kuznetsov opened his eyes, tuned the radio, and, according to plan, successively transmitted the code to the special forces troops lying in ambush everywhere. Electronic noise echoed in the small room, and these signals were about to unleash a storm across the entire province.

21:50

\“Whoosh—\” This was the sound of the bodyguard of **Shelokov**, the Krasnoyarsk City Minister of Agriculture, collapsing after being hit by a tranquilizer dart.

\“Bang!!\” This was the sound of the gate of Shelokov's detached villa being violently breached.

\“Who are you? Are you rebelling?!\” This was the sound of Shelokov's terrified scream after two soldiers restrained his limbs.

\“We are **Alpha Squad**, special forces directly under Generalissimo Yazov. We have now secured all evidence of your involvement in the systemic corruption network of the Krasnoyarsk region. You will be charged with treason, misappropriation of resources, corruption and bribery, and twenty other crimes. If you wish to avoid the death penalty, expose a few more people or provide key evidence. If you do so, you and your family will have a chance to enter the Penance Brigades.\” This was the deep voice of the soldier wearing a black beret.

\“Okay, I... I promise I will cooperate! Don't kill me! Don't kill me!!!\” This was the sound of Shelokov's despair.

······

21:51

Yakov, Deputy Mayor of Krasnoyarsk City, was arrested and confessed to his crimes.

Pavlov, Deputy Director of the Krasnoyarsk Police Department, was arrested.

······

This storm swept across the entire Krasnoyarsk Province, resulting in the arrest of 5 city-level officials and 30 bureau-level officials. Although this operation yielded great results, Kuznetsov understood that Sakharovsky, who was most likely at the top of the corruption network, was no easy opponent. Next, he rushed non-stop to the Krasnoyarsk Provincial Governor's Office.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.239.desc:
Shelokov sat in the interrogation room chair, trembling as he wrote his confession. Kuznetsov pushed the door open and entered. Shelokov grabbed Kuznetsov's sleeve like a drowning man grasping a straw, pressing his hand onto the notebook, and pleaded: \“Comrade, this is part of the intelligence. It's too important; I need you to confirm its basic content before making a decision...\”

Kuznetsov was visibly impatient: \“You bastard, what the hell is this? Are you going to talk or not? If you don't say it now, I'll send you to rot in the mines immediately!\” Shelokov was on the verge of a breakdown. He almost whispered with a sob: \“Evidence concerning Governor Sakharovsky!\”

Kuznetsov's heart first skipped a beat. Then, a wave of excitement mixed with dread washed over him. He felt himself swaying. After taking a few deep breaths, he forced himself to calm down and ordered Shelokov: \“Let me see it first.\”

Picking up the notebook, after only a quick glance, Kuznetsov was certain that the information was highly likely to be authentic! He pondered for a moment, then asked: \“Where is the original?\”

\“In... in Central Area A, the third maintenance tunnel, under the seventh movable floor tile on the left... wrapped in a waterproof cloth... it's a chip... it has everything you need...\” he sobbed. \“Take it... please... take it away! I can't take it anymore... I have nightmares every night because of this blasted thing...\” It had been intercepted by one of his subordinates—an idiot who thought this could be a stepping stone to promotion and wealth—when he was accidentally maintaining a circuit on the Governor's office's independent communication line. The fool then actually handed over the chip, which contained data on huge illegal resource trades, black market transactions, and secret instructions for intended corruption and embezzlement! Undeniably, the contents were enough to cost hundreds of people their heads, and its value was incalculable... But this hot potato was not a ladder to promotion for him; it was a death warrant. He had neither the courage to use it to blackmail anyone nor the ability to handle it. He could only live in fear day and night, like a fool holding a bomb.

For a moment, Kuznetsov felt a strange sense of detachment. He recalled that Shelokov's personal file stated that before the war, he was merely a professor of electronic industry at Omsk State University, and now, this hellish underground world had turned him into this...

However, none of that mattered to him now. Kuznetsov signaled a soldier, who immediately turned and left. The special commissioner looked at the Shelokov, who was limp as mud and on the verge of a nervous breakdown. He struggled to tell himself to calm down, to be calm. But when the long 40 minutes passed, and the soldier confirmed the findings, he burst out laughing.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.239.a: \“That old bastard definitely didn't see himself being exposed here!\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.175.desc:
Military training used to be a rather easy task for Sokolov. It didn't matter to him how strict the standards were or how many died during the training; what did a few deaths of unfit men matter in the vastness of Russia? There would always be patriotic men to fill the ranks.

However, this simple job is now starting to give Sokolov a headache. The environment underground is far inferior to the surface. Even with the League constructing massive ventilation systems, the amount of air a person can breathe each day is limited. He had a platoon of soldiers exercise for a morning according to the old standards, but the Security Department informed him to stop the training—their breathing capacity was already nearing the daily waste-air processing limit.

Then there are the training standards. The old army would default to sending soldiers to the harshest environments, giving them minimal gear, forcing them to return to the camp on their own, and then subjecting them to 'pain education' during their reception, to teach them discipline and forge the strongest-willed and most capable soldiers. But last week, a fool in the forces did just that. He ended up killing more than a dozen men, and the rest lost their combat effectiveness due to starvation. The superiors immediately sent him to a penal battalion.

The old standards won't work, but the job still needs to be done. Sokolov paced back and forth in his office for a long time before finally devising a solution. He cut the original long-distance cross-country into short-duration bursts, eliminated all explosive exercises, and increased the training volume for basic movements like standing at attention and crawling. For the remaining time, thankfully, there were plenty of books and video materials in the training hall; he'd just have them catch up on their reading and viewing.

He nervously submitted this heavily revised training regimen. A short while later, the directive from above arrived: Approved.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.176.desc:
\“Hello everyone, and welcome to 'The Principles of Rebirth,' sponsored by the Russian National Revival Group. We will personally teach you how to survive and become an outstanding citizen of the Motherland once we return to the surface!\”

Igor stared intently at the television. In the sunless environment of the bunker, opportunities for dozens of people to gather and watch even a short, simple broadcast were exceedingly rare. Igor had long since lost track of how long he had been underground. Since the cataclysmic Great Trial began, Igor, like most citizens, had been brought to this perpetually unchanging subterranean world. Here, the familiar sunlight was gone, the chirping of crickets was absent, leaving only the sight of other helpless people brought underground with him. The smile that once graced Igor's face was gone, replaced by an endless void.

\“Hello, I am Grigori, a League Agricultural Professor. Today, I will lecture on how to carry out agricultural cultivation after we return to the surface. You must all know that the air on the surface is now filled with nuclear radiation.\” He pointed to the sky displayed on a nearby screen: \“If our people go out unprotected, they will die quickly...\”

Die? The word turned over in Igor's mind, stirring a memory. After arriving underground, continuous earthquakes had terrified everyone. But once the tremors stopped, some people stood up and protested, claiming the war was over and demanding the League let them go home. In response, the League had them all shot.

\“...After the air settles, we will need to decontaminate the surface soil. Remember, do not plant seeds on the surface; the radiation will kill all unadapted seeds. To counter this, we have already cultivated some radiation-adapted seeds, and we will overcome the disaster as quickly as possible so you can all return to your work...\”

Igor didn't clearly hear what was said next. He was fixated on the seeds, and memories surged from the depths of his mind. He used to be a farmer, working daily on the state farm. Harvest time was his happiest moment—the golden wheat, the corn, the cattle, and the dogs were his daily companions, an essential part of his past life.

When he finally snapped out of it, the broadcast had ended. Igor returned to his cramped dormitory, lay on his bed, and before closing his eyes, he made a note of the program's airtime.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.177.desc:
Underground, there is no concept of time like on the surface. As a result, most citizens and officials often collapse into bed after completing their mandated workload, conserving precious electricity for the League's continued existence. Today, however, a new meeting was underway in the Cultural Department's conference room.

\“Take a look,\” Commissioner Sergei said with a smile, seated in the center of the Cultural Department's seats. On the table were several open books; some contained romantic tales, while others described a doctor's observations within the League. \“Your work has been somewhat negligent. The Marshal Commander has issued an order to promote the excellent spiritual culture of the Russian people, and omissions like these can easily lead to complacency among our citizens.\”

\“It is our oversight. Please forgive us,\” the Cultural Department officials bowed their heads. After a moment, Minister Fyodorov looked up, admitting the error in their work. \“I will promptly correct these mistakes and confess my faults to the Marshal Commander.\”

\“More than correcting mistakes, he desires a new standard,\” Sergei glanced at Fyodorov, then pulled a slip of paper from his pocket. \“Your test has been passed. I hope you will correct these errors through your work and fulfill your duty to the revival of Russia.\”

After Fyodorov took the note and discussed it with the officials, a new prioritized cultural publication list was swiftly produced:

(1) Frontline Experiences: Focused descriptions of Russian soldiers' heroic deeds on the battlefield, their camaraderie, and war experiences of national pride and dying for the Motherland.
(2) Spiritual Interpretation: Propaganda for the heroic acts of Karbyshev and Marshal Commander Yazov, emphasizing loyalty to and support for the Great Trial.
(3) Local Customs: Archival and promotional records of Russian regional cultures and customs, ensuring the preservation of Russian national characteristics and traditional practices, and emphasizing the unity and coexistence of the Russian people.
(4) Anti-German Propaganda: Full-force reinforcement of hatred education against the dark history of Nazism, exposing and deepening a systematic explanation of the Teutonic people's national inferiority, and destroying the entire foundation of Nazi culture from scientific, racial, and various other perspectives.

After careful deliberation, Fyodorov added a final revision.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.177.a: Aside from these standards, all other works will not be granted publication permits. Illegal printing will be immediately suppressed.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.178.desc:
Belyakov never liked dealing with common folk, neither at work nor outside of it. Over the years, he had one impression of them: ungrateful wretches. When it came to work, these people would bow lower than anyone and speak with the softest tones, but as soon as they left the job, they immediately forgot Belyakov's goodwill. Although Belyakov considered his temper to be quite good, encountering so many ungrateful wretches, he could only accept his bad luck.

The superiors recently issued another order: \“Increase work efficiency, avoid spiritual corruption.\” To this end, they held meetings for three consecutive days, where the leaders prattled on about ensuring work quality, reading the works of the Marshal Commander and Commander Yevgeny, and so on. This talk might fool the young newcomers, but Belyakov summarized it in one sentence: overtime, and unpaid overtime at that.

Sure enough, something recently happened in Sector D of the bunker. A family had a death but didn't report it to the government, resulting in the air purification system for the entire residential area becoming overloaded. By the time the police kicked down the door, the system was already at its limit. For this, the superiors swiftly issued an order: all government personnel would be divided into teams and sent down to designated civilian communities to go door-to-door, standing guard, immediately cleaning up and reporting any issues that arise.

As for Belyakov, since he was older, the leaders, after a unanimous discussion, gave him a very easy job.

\“How is the situation with the Sector D duty staff?\”

\“Reporting, Commander. All Sector D staff are present and accounted for, and firefighting work is proceeding in an orderly manner. Please rest assured!\”

Waking up every day, sitting down, and reporting to his superiors every ten minutes on a work situation he knew nothing about—this was Belyakov's new job.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.179.desc:
Galansha carried his tray and sat down in a corner. Just as he was about to eat, someone sat down across from him with a tray. He looked up and saw his old acquaintance, Burkin, a scout also in the Vympel unit. They exchanged a smile. As Galansha cut his bread, Burkin lowered his voice, \“Brother, what have you guys been up to the past couple of days?\”

Galansha's hand slowed. He quickly scanned the surroundings and replied quietly, \“Engineering work. The superiors said we'd eventually return to the surface, so we need to prepare. What about you, brother? What's your unit been doing recently?\”

\“Ha, little brother, let me tell you. Five days ago, the brass sent me to a factory, saying there were rebels lurking, and I was supposed to catch them. I spent a whole day watching those mannequins on the assembly line and didn't find anyone who looked like they wanted to rebel. I wasted a day there and didn't even get a proper meal. When I went to find the factory director, guess what the guy was doing? Drinking cheap vodka!\”

He shoved a small piece of synthetic meat into his mouth, chewing vigorously as he spoke: \“Yesterday, the superiors ordered us to clear out a rebel stronghold. They said these guys were opposing the Marshal Commander and trying to sabotage the Russian revival, so I went. You won't believe it, when I got there, the whole unit consisted of several old men and two teenagers. *These* are the current Vympel forces?\”

Galansha frowned. Burkin continued rambling: \“It was a disaster. A few of us were assigned to a minefield at the front. Allegedly, the rebels had mined it in advance, and we were told to clear them. What the hell? Didn't the sappers or those Teuton trash used to do this kind of thing? The most damn annoying thing was that the guys in the squad acted like they hadn't had any training. One kid just walked straight onto a mine! Thankfully, I was quick enough to stop him from moving and then defused it, or else we'd all be feeding the lice.\” Galansha looked at his comrade, trying to find words to argue, but couldn't speak. He suddenly felt a genuine exhaustion, a profound emptiness creeping into his heart. Russia wasn't like this before, so why now...? Marshal Commander Yazov couldn't have made this mistake... but was this truly unrelated to the Marshal Commander? He shivered, casting these thoughts out of his mind.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.179.a: \“Brother, I'm a bit tired. I need to hurry back, have a couple of drinks, and go to bed.\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.180.desc:
A group of new recruits stood in a bare square, facing a line of prisoners in uniform. Since the emergence of resistance against the League, the Black League had been systematically sweeping previous underground hideouts, bringing out the rebels and executing them. An officer quietly approached the recruits, his eyes narrowed, staring into the multitude of eyes fixed on him. His gaze was sharp and profound. Whenever a recruit met his eyes for a few seconds, they would immediately look away, afraid to meet his stare.

\“It is a great pleasure to see you here, defenders of the League!\” the officer announced loudly, his voice echoing in the soldiers' ears. \“I am Aleksandr Semyonov. I have reviewed your files. Before enlisting, you held various identities: farmers, workers, scum of the Motherland. By rights, you should all be at your posts, or shot.\”

\“But!\” his tone suddenly intensified, \“Traitors have emerged in the Motherland! They attempt to overthrow the government, rambling about freedom and revolution! In reality, they are trying to stop the Russian people from completing the final Great Trial! They are the most hateful of all—Spiritual Teutons!\”

\“Therefore, to test your loyalty, I sincerely invite you to participate in the execution of these traitors.\” Semyonov ripped the hood off one of the prisoners. \“Sir, do you still insist on opposing the Great Russian Revival Government?\”

\“You bastard! Just kill me! I will never serve this reactionary government...\”

Semyonov ruthlessly covered the man's mouth, then raised a hand: \“Execute.\” 'Bang, bang, bang,' a series of gunshots rang out, and the prisoners fell to the ground. Semyonov issued a second order: \“Now, stab these wretches in the heart again, just in case they're faking death.\”

\“Commander, is it not wrong to insult the dead? The Bishop taught us we should have some compassion..\”

Semyonov drew his pistol and fired at the source of the voice, leaving a bloody mark on the recruits' memory: \“The Marshal Commander taught me that loyalty to the Motherland is paramount. If someone obstructs the Motherland's revival for the sake of some so-called belief, then their existence is meaningless.\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.181.desc:
The sun rose and set as usual, its light filtering through the scattered radiation-filled air and onto a patch of shade. Lister sat beneath a tree, squinting, enjoying this hard-won warmth. For him, no past ambition, however grand, was as valuable as simply living another day. Since the bombs fell, Lister's life had changed. His former German Fatherland had been incinerated in endless flames. Superiors, family, duty—everything had departed from him. As a survivor, all Lister could do was maintain the most basic existence with the few others who remained.

As the sun set, Lister stood up, slowly unbuttoned his coat, shook the dust from his clothes, and walked towards the distant estate. There, a few former Wehrmacht members had cleared and cultivated a small manor using found farming tools. Children studied and played in the yard, and the old comrades talked and reminisced about the good old days while tending to the fields.

He walked back into the courtyard and embraced his wife, Valentina. Memories had tormented him throughout countless days of hiding until he met her, Valentina, his beloved. She gave him a new, beautiful life: building their residence bit by bit on the ruins, sewing his clothes when he was injured, and the joy of finding food. He suddenly felt that the past didn't matter anymore; living out his life like this after despair and death was good enough.

\“Boom!\” A familiar sound reached Lister's ears. He struggled to recall what it was: a mortar. He instinctively wanted to run out of the estate, but the shells had already landed, and yellow smoke began to spread through the courtyard. All of Lister's emotions coalesced into a single, helpless sigh—what was meant to come, had come. He took Valentina's hand and quickly hid inside a room.

The sounds from the manor gradually faded. Smoke seeped through the door. Lister and Valentina exchanged a look, then embraced. These Germans had walked through darkness and death with resolve and determination, yet they did not receive heaven's favor. Destiny showed its immense ruthlessness at this moment. The German song of rebirth came to an abrupt end here.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.181.a: Night fell, swallowing all life with it.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE_181_tt:
They paid the price of extinction for their people's wicked past.

For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope.
—Jeremiah 29:11
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.182.desc:
Yazov sat upright in the center of the command post, maintaining his usual rigid posture, awaiting the final response. There were always people who resisted stubbornly, but the Black League would always be the ultimate winner. He thought this to himself, but he no longer yelled or became furious as he once did. As the savior of all Russia, he had the duty to lead Russia and her people through the Great Trial. Although the reports suggested the resistance was gaining momentum, Russia had already sacrificed too much for the final victory—this was nothing.

\“Ring-a-ling-a-ling...\” The telephone finally rang. Yazov picked it up.

\“Marshal Commander, I have reached the designated negotiation site and conducted talks with the so-called resistance forces. I have important news to relay. The resistance forces propose that if we can meet the following conditions, they will agree to lay down their arms: end Russia's military administration, elect a civilian government, ease regulations, and cease military dictatorship...\” The seated officers' brows furrowed the more they listened, but Yazov suddenly chuckled: \“These conditions are quite incredible. Did you inform them of Russia's current situation?\”

\“I did, Marshal Commander, but the leaders of the resistance said some nonsense, something about: 'Although life in Russia is difficult now, the current military administration has caused too many Russians who shouldn't have died to perish due to unjust distribution. What Russia needs now is fairness and development, and the so-called Great Trial should end. Furthermore...'\” He swallowed hard. \“Speak.\” \“They said: 'If the Germans have truly been completely annihilated as the Marshal Commander claims, then what is our next step?'\”

Yazov's smile vanished. He suddenly felt a wave of malevolence rush from his toes to the top of his head. He yelled into the mouthpiece: \“Your mission is complete. Now we know: these people are beyond saving.\” He nearly smashed the receiver back onto the hook, then turned to the officers present: \“Are our men in position?\”

\“Supplies for some regions are still en route. The main troop deployments are in place and ready to launch an attack at any moment.\” After a brief silence, an officer stood up and replied.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.182.a: \“Launch the attack immediately. Kill all these traitors.\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.183.desc:
Grigori called out and lit a kerosene lamp. Immediately, a large group of shadows walked out of the darkness and joined his ranks. The clothes they wore were disparate, and their identities were each more complex than the last: there were soldiers with Soviet Union revolutionary medals, a worker missing an arm, and even a few holding a black, white, and yellow flag who stood at the tail end of the column. They marched noisily towards the designated location in the west. In a few minutes, they were to attack a Black League military camp.

A few minutes later, they arrived at the site. Grigori raised his binoculars for a look. Fortunately, the Black League soldiers were still sleeping. He gave the signal, and the attack immediately began. Several elite soldiers sneaked up on the camp guards. After a few slight sounds, two guards fell to the ground. 'Bang,' a gunshot sounded in the distance, and the camp began to stir.

\“Shit, charge!\” Grigori didn't hesitate, immediately yelling. A group of people grabbed their rifles and began firing, while others pulled out prepared Molotov cocktails and threw them into the camp. The Black League soldiers, after an initial panic, began to fight back. Some, under the command of their officers, quickly sought cover, and the seasoned soldiers also tried to illuminate the area and counterattack. But with the night growing darker and the surprise attack, the soldiers were still at a disadvantage.

Suddenly, dozens of bright lights tore through the pitch-black night. Grigori fixed his gaze on them; the lights came from glowing military caps, beneath which were the familiar gas masks—the main Black League force had arrived! Before the insurgents could react, a few muffled sounds came from the distance, followed by a series of explosions. Most of the insurgents panicked under this barrage. Some tried to drop their weapons and flee, but they quickly fell under the guns of the surrounding Black League soldiers.

Without a second thought, Grigori grabbed his gun and led the charge. He knew that the whole group had fallen into chaos, and if he didn't quickly organize an offensive, the Black League dogs would once again dominate them. After he led a fierce charge with a group of soldiers, the leading officer was killed, and the Black League garrison began to retreat. He raised his gun and shouted, \“For Russia!\”

Unfortunately, his opponent was thinking the same thing. A distant sentry pulled the bolt on his rifle, fired at the weapon-wielding Grigori, and hit him squarely in the chest.

The Cossack warrior suddenly lost all his strength. His body began to slide helplessly to one side. The shouts and cries of his comrades gradually faded from his sight, but in the last moment before death, he suddenly and truly felt what it meant to be alive.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.183.a: Freedom is worth the sacrifice of every person.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.184.desc:
Since the nuclear war began, 250541 has been confined to this facility. They call it a bunker, saying it is the seed of Russia's revival, the ultimate bulwark against the Germans. However, 250541 only feels it's a huge, stuffy cage. Still, if it really can be used to defeat those Germans, then staying here and enduring it is fine; after all, he's been in tougher places.

The facility trembles occasionally, and if you listen closely, you can hear muffled booming sounds. Days passed by with these sounds as their soundtrack. Frankly, 250541 didn't know how many days had passed. There was no calendar in the facility, and while the work here was somewhat easier than on the surface, it was enough to make one lose track of time and stop thinking too much. Maybe it was just a different place for work.

Every Sunday, 250541 had to go to the center to listen to the 'Black Hat' give a speech. They said it was to maintain the Russians' willpower and faith, but the Black Hat always talked about the same things—either how much damage their efforts were inflicting on the Germans, or how the facility would restore Russia's greatness in the future. 250541 was thoroughly bored of it.

This Sunday was different. The Black Hat didn't stand on the podium and rattle off the ear-callousing speeches of the past. He sat slumped in a corner chair, arms crossed, staring at a nervous-looking man in a white coat, as if trying to drill a hole through his chest with his gaze. The White Coat slowly walked onto the stage from the side, cleared his throat with his back to the audience, then took out a piece of paper, alternately looking at it and nervously glancing at the audience. Then he began: \“Comrades, we are at the most glorious moment of the League! The revenge bombs we have forged are relentlessly blasting those German devils every single day. We will level their cities, and they, in turn, want to strike back at us. This is why we must stay here. And what bomb has such massive power? The bombs we and they possess are called nuclear bombs, and this kind of bomb...\”

250541 didn't understand a single word of what the White Coat said next. But he did understand *that* was where the booming noises came from! The enemy was dropping bombs on them, and look, they had no idea they had already hidden in this huge hole!

Perhaps those booming sounds would stop tomorrow. Would that mean they had won? If that truly happened, he would definitely run back to the surface, hide in his old house in the woods, and drink all the liquor he had secretly stashed in one go. By then, since the Germans would have been taught their lesson, maybe the Black Hat would be happy and just leave him alone? Maybe they'd even have a celebration themselves? Maybe......
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.184.a: Thinking these thoughts, 250541 smiled and fell asleep.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.185.desc:
Three days, 250541 counted, and he hadn't heard the booming sounds for three days. Since the White Coat's speech a few days ago, 250541 felt almost resurrected, constantly anticipating the moment the bombs outside would stop. Even his steps, as he daily moved things back and forth at Gate 6, became swifter.

'If I move a few more, will the day we return to the surface come a few days sooner?' Thinking this, the heavy boxes that made him sweat profusely every day seemed more agreeable, as if they contained some kind of treasure. But what was inside them? Why was there so much to move every day? 250541 hadn't considered this question, and he had long known that it was best not to overthink the League's affairs; just follow orders, why bother with the rest?

Four days passed, 250541 counted, and there was still no sound of bombs. Had the German bastards run out of bombs? Or had they already pulverized all their cities? Was the 'Great Trial' the Black Hat spoke of finally over? Were they going to let them go home? My old...

\“Hey!\” A yell snapped 250541 back to reality. \“Stop daydreaming! Do you want to eat tonight?\” 250541 again lifted the heavy box he had put down just a few seconds ago.

Today was the ninth day, tomorrow would be the tenth.

'Are they still not going to let us go back?' 250541 found it increasingly difficult to stop thinking about this. 'What exactly are these boxes for?'

\“Hey, Aleksei, do you know what these boxes are for?\” After moving a box to its destination again, 250541 asked his co-worker 250423. \“I don't know. They just told me to drive all these to Gate 7.\” After speaking, 250423 glanced around, leaned in, and cautiously asked, \“Don't overthink these things, you know that, right?\” Whether he heard him or not, 250541 looked towards Gate 7, nodding vaguely.

On the tenth day, in front of Gate 7, 250541's heart pounded. He hid among the stack of boxes, watching the workers at Gate 7 come and go. The ceiling lights shone brightly, casting pitch-black shadows. 250541 regretted what he was doing. 'Bribing the foreman is a capital offense!' 250541 wiped the sweat from his brow. 'And the patrol could find him missing at any moment.' 'But, but, I've already come this far...'

250541 hastily tried to tear open a nearby box, but his hands were trembling uncontrollably. Then he heard someone nearby saying something: \“These, you'll drive them directly to Gate 1 this time. 250876 can't drive, so you'll take the truck. Understand?\” After hearing this, 250541 thought for a moment, startled, his eyes widened. He steeled his resolve and forcefully ripped open the box.

What was inside the box? Square, quite rough, and a little abrasive to the touch? 250541 was stunned.

It was a box of bricks.

The very bricks they had always been told were for rebuilding Russia on the surface.

250541 finally understood. There were seven gates. After Gate 7, the load naturally returned to Gate 1, then passed through the hands of a dozen people, and returned to Gate 6. This way, the work would never run out, and their 'willpower and faith' would never erode during their time underground.

Even after taking care of the Germans, the League would still be the League.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.185.a: 250541 fell asleep. Tonight, he didn't overthink anything anymore.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.186.desc:
Quiet, leisurely, comfortable. These words seemed irrelevant to the Black League, but since the nuclear war began, the bunker's radio had grown quieter day by day. Now, if you wanted to get any sound out of it, you'd probably have to kick it.

Thus, the radio operator, Rodion, found himself with rare free time. He forced himself not to think about the Black League and began reading a few books he had hastily brought down from the surface. Rodion didn't know what was in all of them, but one science fiction novel called 'The Heat Death' particularly captivated him.

In this book, humanity in the 2100s approached a unified communist society closer than ever before. Just as the prophesied utopia was about to be realized, it ultimately failed for various reasons, causing people to gradually doubt human nature. Amidst this doubt, a school of thought arose, claiming that Marx, centuries earlier, had not only constructed that future utopian society but had also inadvertently pointed out another possibility for the future: the complete collapse of human society.

The school claimed that the contradictions of human nature were unsolvable, and all social development merely used more complex social systems to temporarily mask these contradictions. When the complexity of society reached its limit, the previously concealed contradictions would erupt in a blowout, leading human society towards an inevitable and complete collapse, which they called the 'Heat Death of Civilization.'

To people who had just experienced a Great Collapse, this all seemed incredibly plausible. Nations across the world accepted this theory, and humanity's goal shifted from social development to preventing the total collapse of human society.

In the wreckage left by the Great Collapse, one could see various fantastic attempts to prevent the Heat Death of Civilization: there were anti-utopian societies practicing the annihilation of human emotion, transhumanists attempting to modify human nature, groups who outright abandoned modern society for primitive worship, and idealists who still believed in a unified communal society.

The one that caught Rodion's attention the most was an extremist organization. They claimed that human society was beyond saving, and they must destroy the current human society to rebuild a brand new one through their own hands. This extremist organization called itself the 'Cure for Humanity,' yet it practiced every form of terrorism and totalitarian rule imaginable, still justifying it as a necessary cleansing of humanity.

At the end of the novel, this extremist organization launched nuclear weapons globally. After the nuclear apocalypse, the survivors not only failed to follow the extremist organization's command to rebuild a new civilization but instead formed a united resistance army against them. Ultimately, human society met the 'Heat Death of Civilization' in an endless civil war.

Rodion closed the book and threw it into the trash.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.187.desc:
On the grayish-hued grassland, artillery boomed, and smoke and ash billowed. Inside a trench, a few people were huddled together, discussing something. \“7524,\” the lieutenant called out, addressing the new recruits in front of him: \“Agent 7524!\” Yet, no one responded.

\“Hey, Dmitry, he's calling you.\” Reznov nudged the distracted Dmitry next to him. \“Oh, what is it? No, yes!\” Dmitry startled, stammering his reply. The lieutenant frowned but let it go. All the newly conscripted soldiers were like this.

\“We need to sneak over, blow up that machine gun bunker with explosives, and make no sound on the way.\” So, a few people stood up, hunched their backs, and slowly crept along the trench toward the machine gun bunker.

An unpleasant odor of unknown origin wafted through the trench. As Dmitry walked, he took out his canteen and gulped down the water. Ever since receiving his conscription notice, he had been depressed, and it wasn't entirely because he didn't want to go to the front. When Dmitry was 12, his mother was killed by a German bomber. Since then, he had worked tirelessly in the factory for the Great Trial. But now, they weren't fighting Germans at all. Dmitry was conscripted to kill his own countrymen. Looking at the people in the distant machine gun bunker, their relatives were probably killed by the Germans too, right? Thinking this, Dmitry sighed inwardly and twisted the cap back on.

Just then, a 'bang' came from a distance. A black speck dropped from the pale sky and landed abruptly next to Reznov. Flames instantly engulfed, consumed, and then spat him out. The half-charred Reznov heavily slammed down next to Dmitry. *Thud*. Dmitry looked down; Reznov's black, scorched corpse lay quietly by his feet, accompanied only by a faint sizzling sound. The canteen in his hand slipped, hitting the ground with another *thud*. Dmitry was stunned for a few seconds, his vision blurred, his legs went weak, and then he screamed in terror.

\“7524, shut up! You're going to expose us!\” the lieutenant said impatiently. But Dmitry didn't respond, continuing to scream. Reznov was the only friend he had known at the factory. How could this have happened?

\“7524!\” The lieutenant leaned in and shoved Dmitry hard, but he was still engulfed in his emotions, continuing to yell. \“The new recruits are all like this.\” The lieutenant habitually drew his small knife and, without hesitation, sliced across Dmitry's neck as cleanly as cutting pork. Blood instantly spurted out, splashing onto the empty canteen. Dmitry gurgled, falling next to Reznov. A few seconds later, he made no further sound.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.188.desc:
*buzz buzz buzz...*

The alarm dragged A out of his deep sleep. A rubbed his tired eyelids, slowly sat up, leaning on the bed, staring blankly at the foot of the bed for a few seconds. Then, he got off barefoot and walked a few steps towards the locker. Opening the locker, A realized he was already wearing his work uniform. He hurriedly put on his shoes, grabbed yesterday's leftover dry bread, and quickly walked out of the dormitory.

*Bang, bang, bang, bang*. Four sounds; one workpiece was finished. 'During training, the instructor always said to be extremely careful when machining this part, but after getting used to it, it's the same routine over and over.' Thinking this, A wiped a large bead of sweat from his forehead with his hand, flicked it to the side, and finally wiped his hand on the blackened thigh side of his pants. Just then, the next workpiece arrived, followed by another *bang, bang, bang, bang*.

*Ding ding ding ding...*

Not long after the last workpiece was finished, the meal bell rang. A unhurriedly put down his tools, stretched his exhausted arms a few times, and walked toward the mess hall. Today's meal was the same indescribable food. He swallowed it with the semi-stale bread; it still didn't taste very good. Bite after bite, accompanied by the factory's rumbling roar, A finished the last piece of bread.

*Ding ding ding ding...* Right on cue, the work-call bell rang. A stood up and walked back to the factory.

*Bang, bang, bang, bang...* A smoothly finished several more workpieces. 'It's all the same routine. It's not as careful as the instructor said it needed to be.'
