A thought, casually wiped the sweat from his forehead, flicked it hard to the side, and finally wiped it on the blackened patch on his pants' thigh. Just then, the next workpiece arrived.

*Ding ding ding ding...* It was time for dinner. A rushed to the mess hall as usual, eating dinner quickly, leaving only one piece of bread for the next day's breakfast. He then rushed back to the factory. The evening shift always felt so rushed.

*Bang, bang, bang, bang...*

Workpiece after workpiece went by. Staring at the next one, A began to think again: 'The instructor said to be very careful when machining these parts, but after getting used to it, it's essentially the same routine.' After thinking this, A wiped the sweat from his forehead, flicked it to the side, and finally wiped it on the thigh of his pants—*rip*, the pants tore.

\“Ah!\”

A's hand froze. He glanced at his pants, then sharply looked up, suddenly seeing all the workers around him performing the exact same motions. Their faces were all washed out by the harsh white light, blending into a single mass. In their hands, the loud *bang, bang, bang, bang* sounds continued. Identical workpieces moved past, one after another. Looking around, the massive factory was unnaturally spacious, yet he felt a suffocating crowd. The continuous *bang* and *rumble* sounds from all directions immediately pressed down on him, as if four gigantic walls were pushing, about to crush him to death. But in just two or three seconds, the workpiece he had been staring at passed by. Snapping out of it, A frantically grabbed his tools and turned back to work.

*Ring ring ring...* The quitting time bell rang.

A shuffled his feet toward the employee dormitory, pushed open the door, tossed the dry bread onto the table, and, as if drained, fell straight onto the bed.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.188.a: He forgot to take off his work uniform again.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.189.desc:
Under the cloud-covered sky was a boundless snowscape, with a distant horizon separating gray and white, like two strokes of paint on an oil canvas. In the center of the snowfield, a few twisted wooden huts emerged sparsely from the ground—this was where the nuclear-radiation-fleeing vagrants had sought refuge.

The village had no name. The vagrants built shelters, forged tools, and cultivated fields, but they never named the village.

The sun had just risen in the murky sky, and a grayish haze lingered in the air beneath the clouds. The hunter who lived at the edge of the village grabbed his bow, took a swig from his canteen of liquor, pushed open his door, and went out hunting. Before long, the children in the village ran to the hunter's doorstep to play. The largest, darkest, and thinnest child chased the others, but stopped after a few steps, squatting listlessly and staring blankly at the distant trees. The other children, seeing he was no longer chasing them, played with snow piles where they stood, but soon grew bored and dispersed.

Just after noon, the farmers set up their stalls in the center of the village. Under a makeshift canopy made of rags, a farmer with cracked skin sat in front of his stall, idly looking at the few potatoes spread on the table. \“How much for this?\”

Hearing the visitor, the farmer slowly looked up, opened his dry mouth, and spoke in a hoarse voice: \“One bullet for five.\”

\“I'll buy five.\”

Taking the bullets and placing them in a rusty can, the farmer lowered his head and continued looking at the potatoes.

In the afternoon, the village's only doctor sat at a table with a pen, the tip pressed against his notebook, but unmoving. These were his last few pages. Since the flight, patients came daily, and the pages of his notebook were quickly used up, yet he remained stubborn about recording their symptoms. Gazing at the few pages remaining, the doctor wanted to write something—he wanted to record everything that had happened in the land once called 'Russia' over the past forty years, or perhaps the various city ruins along the migration route, or even just jot down an interesting anecdote from last month... \“Doctor, I don't feel well.\”

The doctor dismissed his wandering thoughts, looked at the incoming patient, asked about the symptoms in detail, and recorded them on the few remaining pages.

Soon after, the sun was about to set, and the hunter arrived home with his catch. Opening the wooden door, his wife's cooked meal was on the table, emitting a fragrant aroma. The hunter, who had been hungry for half a day, placed the wild boar he was carrying by the wall and sat at the table to feast.

\“You're back?\”

\“Mhm.\”

\“Good that you're back.\”

\“Mhm. Caught a boar.\”

\“Dinner's ready.\”

\“Mhm.\”

After dinner, the hunter lay on the bed, looking at the night view outside the window, thinking about tomorrow's matters. Thinking and thinking, he fell asleep.

Finally, the sun fully set. The last ray of sunlight vanished, and the dark clouds covered the sky, blending into the night. On one side, the moon slowly rose. A faint moonlight shone through the clouds onto the snowfield, like a streak of blue on a black canvas.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.189.a: Perhaps one day, the dark cloud will finally disperse.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.190.desc:
Agent 181410 was driving through the mountains and forests when the Great Trial began. It wasn't until countless nuclear weapons streaked across the sky, flying west, that he realized the Great Trial had started. He immediately had to take refuge in an abandoned bunker by the roadside. After hiding for a day and a night, 181410 felt no activity, so he left the bunker. The sky was pitch black, but the carnage 181410 had envisioned—like a German counterattack or bombing—had not occurred. 'Perhaps it's because our Great Trial was well-prepared and completely vanquished the Teutonic barbarians, giving them no chance to strike back,' he thought to himself. Then, 181410 found the car he had hastily parked on the side of the road earlier. It still ran, so 181410 drove away.

The sky remained murky. Beneath it, the ecstatic 181410 drove on. He drove crookedly, like a drunkard behind the wheel. \“We did it, yes, we did it! The Marshal Commander must have succeeded. Mother Russia has finally defeated the Teutonic barbarians, and the Motherland will prosper!\” He shouted deliriously. \“I told you, Commander Yazov's Three Great Theories are the absolute truth! Long live the Marshal Commander! The Great Trial has finally arrived, and the humiliation and suffering our Mother Russia endured are finally over! We have truly avenged the Motherland; the inferior Teutonic barbarians are all dead! Hahahahaha!\” The more 181410 thought about it, the more excited he became, even starting to laugh hysterically. \“What should I do next? After completing the Great Trial, after achieving vengeance against the Teutons, what is my purpose?\”

Suddenly, a series of questions filled 181410's mind. It was true: after planning the Great Trial for so many years, 181410 had never considered what he would do once it was over. With the completion of this goal, 181410's heart was seized by an unprecedented emptiness. Just then, he saw a glimmer of light on the horizon, pointing east, the direction of his hometown. No doubt, that light must be the rising sun. He immediately turned the car around, racing towards the newborn sun, towards his hometown, to tell the folks in his town that the Great Trial was successful and the Russian nation had risen!
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.190.a: \“Glory to you, my Russia. Glory to you, my Marshal Commander!\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.191.desc:
Then, he had a thought. \“Oh, right, I should devote myself to building Mother Russia. Yes, yes! After such a brutal war, the Motherland must begin reconstruction, and I will be the builder who rebuilds the Motherland and makes it prosperous and strong!\” Thinking this, 181410 felt completely satisfied. \“So, how should the reborn Russia be built? What was that city the Teutons were most proud of called? Let me think. Oh right, Germania. Yes, that's what it was called. From now on, even the most remote small town in Russia must be better, bigger, and more luxurious than Germania! Yes, that's how it must be! And our capital should be more magnificent and spectacular than Tokyo and Washington combined! I must build the Motherland to be like this!\” 181410 chirped happily, driving toward the light in the east that represented his hometown. \“Wait, could Commander Yazov have died in the nuclear blast? If he died, who will lead us? No, absolutely not! Omsk has the strongest bunker. The Marshal Commander will definitely survive... *click... click... click...*\” As he drove toward the light, 181410 suddenly heard a strange series of clicking sounds. He stopped and rummaged through the clutter in the car to find the source of the noise.

Suddenly, he froze, his hand trembling as it gripped the source of the clicking—a Geiger counter. \“Wait, why is there still nuclear radiation here?\” Just as he was puzzled, a purplish-red sunset appeared in the western sky, piercing through the black smoke and revealing the azure sky. Illuminated by the sun's light, 181410 finally saw clearly: his former hometown had become a ruin engulfed in a sea of fire. Its desolation was far more severe than any German atrocity 181410 had ever heard of. A strong gust of wind blew, extinguishing the sparks in the sea of fire and blowing out 181410's sanity.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.191.a: Why is this happening? The Great Trial was successful...
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.192.desc: *Click... click... click...* The Geiger counter continued its liberal clicking. 181410 painfully pressed his head against the steering wheel, trying not to look at the misery before him. \“Why, why is this happening! The first trial didn't destroy my hometown, the second one didn't, and even the Great Trial didn't. But now, it's completely a ruin! Wasn't the Great Trial over? Wasn't the Russian nation supposed to be revived? What the hell kind of revival is this?!\” 181410's eyes were red, and a few drops of murky tears fell. Thinking of how he had just been planning how to build a better Russia, he suddenly felt ridiculous. \“What the hell is the Great Trial, and the Marshal Commander? It's all nonsense! Yes, that's right. Yazov is a beast in human form, a grand deceiver who fooled the Russian people, binding them to his perverse hatred for the Germans, ultimately causing our Mother Russia to suffer such great hardship! Furthermore, if even a town like my hometown has been destroyed, what about all of Mother Russia...?\” Thinking this, 181410 felt a chill that erupted from his very bones. \“No Russian demanded vengeance against Germany. No one wanted to fight anymore. Yet, that animal Yazov used the so-called Three Great Theories to constantly deceive Russians into going to the battlefield to slaughter and realize his own ambitions, his own delusions! Yazov is the true traitor to Mother Russia!\” Thinking this, the fury in 181410's eyes matched the sea of fire before him.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.192.a: \“To hell with the number 181410! My real name is...\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.193.desc:
Mikhail drove fast and aimlessly across the endless Russian steppe. He had once been drawn in by the Three Great Theories, believing the Great Trial was everything in his life.

But now, everything had changed. However, Mikhail had invested so much into the Great Trial that he only remembered himself as Agent 181410 and had forgotten his own name.

Mikhail drove to a high vantage point. He looked up, gazing into the distance. The cities in the distance were all shrouded in thick smoke and filled with wailing, yet Mikhail's memory told him these were places that had escaped the ravages of the war decades ago and had developed peacefully. But now, under the rule of that vengeance-crazed lunatic Yazov, they had also been reduced to this state. Thinking this, Mikhail clenched his jaw, his fingernails digging into his palm.

He hated. He hated Yazov, that grand deceiver who had plunged Russia into suffering once again. He hated himself for so easily believing Yazov's lies and felt ashamed of his earlier fantasies about a bright future... He turned his head and saw the boundless steppe. The azure sky pierced through the rolling black smoke. The grass and trees on the ground swayed gently with the breeze. With things as they were, Mikhail could only stand on these ruins, bathed in the solitary evening wind.

Suddenly, he felt that the endless steppe before him was incredibly beautiful. He finally remembered his name. He was Mikhail Yuryevich, named after a jewel in the crown of Russian culture. He realized that for so many years, he had been obsessed with the ridiculous Great Trial, and this was the first time he had wholeheartedly gazed upon the magnificent steppe of Russia. Amidst the vast and distant sky and earth, Mikhail was finally free from years of fanaticism and felt an inner peace. He walked on the Russian steppe, feeling the fragrance of the soil and its wondrous texture. 'I love this land,' he thought joyfully. All the fervor, all the anger, all the resentment, and regret disappeared, leaving only love for this steppe. Gradually, Mikhail walked further away, his sturdy figure slowly becoming a blurred black speck, disappearing into the vast land.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.193.a: “It is not seeking happiness, nor fleeing it in haste!”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.194.desc:
A young agent stood holding his breath in front of a broken wooden door. He knocked first, but there was no sound from inside, no sign of life. So, he took out the file given to him by the Reconstruction Bureau.

According to the file, this area was not a target during the nuclear war, and one of the Black League's top agents happened to be operating in the area, meaning he had a high probability of surviving the nuclear war. Furthermore, according to nearby villagers, a suspicious man was indeed lodging here.

\“From the archives, he truly is a fine comrade of mine! This comrade outstandingly completed so many missions and was extremely devoted to both the Great Trial and the Marshal Commander. This is the example we should follow; he is a model for our generation!\” he thought to himself, reviewing the archive.

The young agent's thoughts returned to the present. Facing the silent wooden door, the young agent decided to lean back, then violently kicked out one leg, driving his thick heel into the old door lock. Due to the immense impact, the wooden door finally rattled and shook open.

What met his eyes was a solemn man dressed in a black robe. He was quietly reading a book that was not particularly thick. Seeing the visitor, the man gently placed the book face-up on a nearby table, and his soft gaze fixed on the eyes of the uninvited guest.

\“You are Agent—Number 181410, right?\” the young agent asked directly.

\“I was 181410, but now, I am only Mikhail Yuryevich. The 181410 you are looking for is not here. Please leave!\”

The young agent suddenly picked up a wooden plank nearby and swung it toward Mikhail's head. Mikhail lightly raised his hand and caught the plank flying towards his head with one hand. \“Still sharp, old comrade! Come back with me. The Black League has been rebuilt under the leadership of Marshal Commander Yazov. We are short-handed now.\” Hearing the names Yazov and the Black League, a strange look flashed across Mikhail's face, but it was quickly replaced by a look of composure.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.194.a: \“Come on, come back with me and fight for the Black League, for Mother Russia, for Commander Yazov!\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.195.desc:
The young agent extended a friendly hand to Mikhail, inviting him to leave with him. Mikhail suddenly tilted his head, standing stiffly, as if contemplating some complex, unspeakable secret. Just as the young agent was puzzled, Mikhail slowly stood up, and the smile on the young agent's face grew brighter.

Mikhail followed the young agent out of the hut and into the yard. At this point, Mikhail straightened his posture and solemnly said to the young agent: \“I will no longer serve or work for the Black League or Yazov. I will only serve Mother Russia.\” Hearing this, the young agent replied with a slight chuckle, \“The Black League and Marshal Commander Yazov are the embodiment of our Mother Russia! Only the Black League and Marshal Commander Yazov can protect and nurture our Motherland! Senior, you must be confused. Have you forgotten even this?\”

\“No, you are wrong. Yazov or the Black League are not, and can never be, the representatives of Mother Russia. Yazov is a maniac, a lunatic, a grand deceiver! To achieve his so-called vengeance ideal, he would even let Russia be destroyed along with it! He fooled everyone and enslaved all the Russian people to achieve his perverse goals!\” Hearing this, the young agent's eyes darkened, and his initial enthusiasm was extinguished. \“So, that's how it is,\” he muttered to himself. \“I see! I see! I understand everything!\” Seeing the young agent's look of sudden understanding, Mikhail felt a sense of relief.

\“It's not too late for you to make a different choice,\” Mikhail said sincerely. \“I understand completely now. The reason the Great Trial was not entirely successful, why the Teutonic barbarians still exist, and why Mother Russia suffers at their hands, is because of faithless traitors like you!\” the young agent roared, then drew the pistol from his waist.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.196.desc:
Years of life on the steppe had not dulled Mikhail's skills; rather, his senses had become sharper. Just as the young agent prepared to draw and shoot, Mikhail threw the wooden plank in his hand, striking the agent's hand and knocking his pistol away. The dark iron-colored handgun fell about five meters behind the agent. Mikhail then drew his own pistol from his waist with lightning speed. Looking at the dark muzzle pointed at him, the young agent closed his eyes, but still cursed Mikhail as a traitor under his breath.

\“Let us settle this the Russian way,\” Mikhail said calmly. \“Let's end our dispute with the most traditional game.\” With that, Mikhail also threw his gun about five meters behind him. The young agent was stunned for a second by the sight, then instantly turned and sprinted forward to grab his gun. Mikhail's reflexes were still superior. Just as the agent grabbed his gun, he heard the crisp click of Mikhail engaging his gun's safety. Having no other choice, he shoved the muzzle out from under his armpit on the other side of his body and expertly blind-fired behind him. Ultimately, the young agent knew he was a step too late. Before he could pull the trigger, he had already heard the *click* of Mikhail's pistol trigger, followed by a loud bang, and then...
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.196.a: Two gunshots—one after the other—pierced the silence of the steppe.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.197.desc:
When the young agent looked back, he saw that Mikhail had raised his arm straight up and fired a shot into the sky, while his own shot had squarely hit Mikhail's heart. The young agent's marksmanship was indeed excellent. Mikhail was killed instantly.

The young agent looked at Mikhail's corpse before him and felt a sudden sadness. He couldn't understand why the Black League's once most outstanding warrior had fallen to this state. His number, 181410, had represented so much honor, so much glory, and was so admirable, yet he had met such an end. It was truly regrettable.

What puzzled the young agent even more was that Mikhail clearly had the chance to kill him, but instead fired wildly into the sky. \“What a lunatic,\” the young agent sighed with emotion. \“And those bizarre ravings—only a lunatic like that could utter them.\”

Then, the young agent moved Mikhail's body into the wooden hut and retrieved his gun. It was then that the young agent noticed the book Mikhail had been reading when he burst through the door, which was now lying open on the table. As if drawn by the book's gravity, the agent's curiosity was piqued. The young agent picked up the book and began to examine it closely.

The book was old and thin. The pages were yellowed but intact; every page was complete. Judging by the year, it must have been produced during the Tsarist era. The cover was embellished with gilded edges. The author was already blurred and illegible, but the title remained clear, printed in blood-red ink in a script font—*The Demon*.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.197.a: \“Let me see the page 181410 was just reading.\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.198.desc:
...The melancholic Demon, the banished spirit,
Hovering over the sin-steeped Earth,
The scenes of his beautiful past years,
Appeared one after another before him:
He recalled when, as a pure Seraph,
He brilliantly displayed his talents in the bright abode;
He recalled when the swift-racing comet,
Often returned his smile with an affectionate smile,
To signify a greeting;
He recalled when, with a thirst for knowledge,
He peered through the perpetual mist,
Looking down at the swarms of floating, God-abandoned stars;
He recalled when, as a favorite of creation,
He kept hope and was full of love!
He never doubted, nor felt hate,
The centuries of useless and tedious time,
Had not affected the purity of his soul...
And much, much more... but to recall all this
Was now beyond his strength!
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.198.a:
\“And it wildly prayed for the storm,
As if only in the storm lay peace!\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.199.desc:
Marshal Commander Yazov's voice was as fierce and merciless as the north wind, penetrating every crevice of the bunker. His eyes, filled with the fire of vengeance, swept across the war room, finally resting on the banners symbolizing loyalty and dedication. Yet, in his eyes, an unseen decay was breeding beneath those banners. At this moment of life and death for the Great Trial, any trace of betrayal or weakness was an unforgivable crime.

\“We will rebuild our home on the ruins of the nuclear war,\” Yazov's voice was low and powerful, \“and for that, we need to endure the trials of hunger and chaos. But now, some thieves are exploiting their official positions to steal the Federation's precious supplies. They think they've gotten away with something, but they cannot escape the eyes of the League.\”

As the order was given, the atmosphere in the bunker immediately tightened. Agents known as 'Executioners' moved like ghosts through the corridors. Their targets were comprehensive: dissenting officers, officials whose dedication to the cause of vengeance had wavered, and anyone deemed a potential destabilizing factor. Concurrently, the League issued a public notice, promising rewards for verified reports of suspected corruption.

A young officer named Sergei Ivanov was taken away for privately complaining about food rations. He insisted his remarks were not malicious, only intended to improve the soldiers' lives. However, in the eyes of the 'Executioners,' this was merely an excuse for weakness and wavering. Another elderly engineer was scrutinized for insisting that a certain biological weapon research project was too wasteful. He tried to argue with data and theories, but his words were powerless before the Great Trial. In Yazov's creed, any sacrifice was necessary for the Great Trial, even those who had contributed to the League.

As the purge deepened, the bunker became quieter, but this silence did not stem from peace; it sprang from fear. Everyone was careful about their words and actions, afraid of becoming the next target to be 'excised.' Yet, within this atmosphere of dread, Yazov saw the purity he desired: a League utterly loyal to the cause of vengeance, free of any dissonance. He firmly believed that only this could ensure Russia's victory in the final 'Great Trial'.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.199.a: This purge will ensure our will is one.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.125.t: Pulling the Radish, Bringing Out the Mud
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.125.desc:
“Knock, knock, knock”

Yazov's office received another visitor. The guards brought in Agent 350234, namely Kuznetsov.

Looking at the middle-aged man who seemed vaguely familiar, Yazov paused to recall his identity—the man had once been a district-level cadre in Omsk’s Ministry of Internal Affairs. Due to his exceptional ability and meticulous logic, Yazov had exceptionally promoted him to Lieutenant Colonel, reporting directly to him. He remembered having dispatched him to the Krasnoyarsk region for an anti-corruption investigation. Stopping his train of thought, Yazov pointed to the opposite chair, signaling for him to sit down.

“What are the results of the investigation?”

“It’s rotten, Comrade Commander-in-Chief... The situation in the Minusinsk bunker complex, where you sent me, is seriously amiss. But when I requested to look up certain data, or to investigate departments where corruption might exist, everyone—from grassroots staff to module supervisors—was stalling, misleading, and subjected us to information lockdown and comprehensive surveillance. There were even instances of data mysteriously disappearing and key witnesses dying in ‘accidents’... The resistance we faced is not isolated; this is absolutely a vast network of connections. They’ve done an excellent job of covering their tracks, and we haven't found any decisive evidence on the surface. I suspect there are monumental problems involved... but I am unable to uncover them... Marshal Comrade, I need you to send more elite, trustworthy MVD assault teams, grant me the highest authority across regions and hierarchies, and give me direct, real-time communication access to you.”

Upon hearing this, Yazov’s face turned grim, like still water. His body leaned slightly forward, fingertips constantly tapping the armrest, and he scrutinized Kuznetsov with an icy gaze. After a long silence, he finally spoke: “Agent 350234, are you sure you can be responsible for your words? You must know that if this is true, the implications are incredibly deep. Other investigators haven’t reported any problems. How am I to believe you?”

Kuznetsov took a deep breath, meeting Yazov’s eyes and sensing the brewing storm within him: “Comrade Commander-in-Chief, I am willing to bear all responsibility. As for credibility, I have some personal intelligence here. I ask you to review it.”

...As he read, the air around Yazov seemed to solidify. He frowned: “Are you certain that even parts of the MVD organs in these areas have been compromised? How did you get this information? Why is your intelligence more timely than that of my intelligence agencies?”

“Comrade Commander-in-Chief, I have some acquaintances in these places. They were personally involved in this corruption network, and I successfully turned them using your name without prior authorization, which is why you are able to see this document... Rest assured, this information is absolutely reliable.” Yazov rubbed his temples, pondering for a long time. Finally, he made a decision: “Fine, I will grant your request. But if there is no result in the end... you know what your fate will be.” Kuznetsov felt his voice was as low as thunder, but surprisingly, the voice of the man of steel even carried a hint of... trembling? He could faintly discern it.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.126.desc:
Kuznetsov stood before the door to the Marshal’s office, clutching the final investigation report, which was no thicker than his finger yet weighed a thousand pounds. The low hum of the surrounding air circulation system sounded like the dying gasp of a man. He knew this report would turn the entire Union upside down, but... there was no turning back now.

“Enter.” Yazov’s steady voice came through the communicator, and Kuznetsov pushed the door open. Perhaps it was psychosomatic, but Kuznetsov felt the walls he had seen countless times before were now about to crash down. He steadied his restless mind. Looking ahead, Marshal Yazov sat behind the massive metal desk, his back to the door, seemingly resting with his eyes closed.

Kuznetsov did not exchange pleasantries. He placed the report directly on the desktop and pushed it across. “Comrade Marshal,” his voice was dry, “Final confirmation. Your comrade-in-arms, Sakharovsky, is the core node of the entire Krasnoyarsk corruption network. The evidence chain... is complete.”

Yazov did not turn around immediately. His knuckles were white from clenching, trembling slightly and uncontrollably. Time seemed to stand still for several seconds. Finally, Yazov slowly rotated his chair. His face, which had once struck terror into his enemies and awe into his subordinates, was now ashen, like the cracked bark of a tree ravaged by radiation. It was etched with guilt, exhaustion, and the profound disorientation of utter betrayal. Yazov’s gaze fell upon Sakharovsky's name on the report’s cover, his eyes vacant and numb, as if he had aged ten years in an instant.

“Sakharovsky...” Yazov’s voice was extremely low, like a sleepwalker’s murmur or a groan squeezed from the depths of his lungs, “Aleksandr... Sakharovsky...” He repeated the name and patronymic, not the general's title, but the most intimate form of address. They were the last survivors of the old Black League to crawl out of the Siberian Warlord Era, comrades who had stood side-by-side to decide to push the nuclear button and drag the entire world into the abyss. Yazov had always secretly cherished a faded photograph deep in his office drawer, showing two energetic young men against a backdrop of Omsk’s coniferous forest before it was burned by nuclear fire—one of them was precisely the despicable traitor who had betrayed the Union's ideals.

Yazov did not open the report. He raised his head, his eyes moving with difficulty from the document to Kuznetsov. The Marshal’s lips moved, but in the end, no sound came out. In those hawkish eyes, Kuznetsov saw cracks clearly for the first time—not anger, not malice, but a shaking of belief, a shame so deep it was bottomless, and the consequent, minute yet fatal, doubt about the very structure he had built.

“He... was discussing strategic matters with me just a few days ago...” Yazov’s voice was so soft it was barely audible, carrying a weariness Kuznetsov had never heard before. The sentence seemed to drain all the strength from Yazov. He slumped back against his chair and waved his hand, signaling Kuznetsov to leave.

Kuznetsov saluted silently and turned to go. The heavy alloy door shut behind him. The only sounds left in the office were the eternal, low hum of the ventilation system and the report lying quietly on the cold desk—its words like a sharp blade, slicing through the gigantic web of corruption, and simultaneously cutting into the Marshal's heart. Walking down the frigid corridor, Kuznetsov felt for the first time that the “Great Trial” might not only be judging the Germans.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.126.a: Once cracks appear, they cannot be stopped.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.127.desc:
As the Black League army marched forward, Zoya's assault brigade was forced to halt. Their momentum was checked by a group of unwelcome “guests.”

“Did you get anything out of them?” Zoya stepped down from her vehicle, looking at the German soldiers huddled before her, terrified, hands trembling over their heads, faces streaked with snot and tears.

“No, Major. They don’t understand Russian.” The soldier responsible for the interrogation had no sooner spoken than he received a hard slap across the face.

“You couldn’t get anything out, and you’re not moving up with the unit? Notify the vanguard to speed up. We’re going to be the first unit to burn Germania to the ground.” With that order, he appointed himself judge over these German prisoners.

“It would have been better if you knew a little Russian, but alas, you know nothing, only foolishly resisting us.” The words were immediately followed by a gunshot, and one head tumbled to the ground.

“You wouldn’t even tell me where your commander or your headquarters are. Such idiotic swine.” A second roar, accompanied by a gunshot, killed another German.

“Now, there’s only you left. Are you finally willing to confess? What else do you know?” The dark muzzle of the gun pressed against his lower jaw. Finally, spurred by extreme terror and incontinence, he broke.

“I’ll talk! I’ll talk! I’ll tell you everything! I am...”

“Bang”

“Cowards, and those who speak Russian, will only become obstacles on our path of march.” He spat on the corpses, then commanded.

“Everyone must march over their bodies! Let these Teutonic savages realize that they are not invincible!”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.127.a: After the deafening crunching, silence returned.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.128.desc:
“Please, I truly don't know anything else, please...”
Before he could finish, the German man’s mouth was plugged by a cold gun barrel. “You are born guilty, and we are your judges.” With that, the gunman pulled the trigger, and the German, who had been desperately pleading moments before, went still. The shooter took out a handkerchief, meticulously wiped the pistol, then tossed the handkerchief onto the floor and walked out of the interrogation room.

This was Babrov, a seasoned interrogation expert. His job was to capture and interrogate German spies within Russia. He possessed exceptional interrogation skills and used them to acquire a wealth of useful intelligence.

One day, he was bewildered when he heard that a suspected spy was to be brought in for questioning, and that they were reportedly Russian. He couldn't understand why these Russian children would betray their own motherland to help her enemies. His hatred for these people was no less than his hatred for the Germans.

Babrov arrived at the interrogation room to wait for the prisoner. The room was small. A wooden chair for the prisoner sat in the center, and although the surrounding walls were frequently cleaned, some bloodstains inevitably remained. Various tools for his work were placed around the wooden chair. After waiting for about half an hour, the door was finally knocked. “Bring her in!” Babrov shouted. As the door opened, Babrov felt a familiar face enter. Once the person stood still, Babrov suddenly recognized who she was. “Natasha?!”

This was the first time Babrov had ever been so emotional in the interrogation room, but he quickly calmed down. The person before him was his daughter, Natasha. “Why did you betray your country, or rather, betray me!” Babrov almost roared. “The Black League cannot save Russia! It will only destroy the world!” the female prisoner shouted back. A silence followed. Babrov was the first to break it: “Speak. Save me the trouble of using those tools.

“Will you kill me, Father?”

Babrov froze. The Black League had long trained him to be the state's most loyal guard, but the things etched into human genes are always difficult to change. If it were anyone else, Babrov would have wanted to hack them into mincemeat, but the person before him was his daughter, his own flesh and blood. He simply could not bring himself to raise a butcher’s knife against his own child.

Babrov incessantly questioned himself: Where is the ruthlessness of the past? Bring it out! Where is the efficiency of the past? Reclaim it! Finally, after silently reciting the oath he had once sincerely shouted, he drew the pistol from his belt and aimed it at the despicable traitor before him. “I am so sorry, Anna.”

A gunshot. The Black League had one less traitor.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.128.a: Hesitate no more, for your Motherland!
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.129.desc:
Ivan, as usual, came to collect his allotted rations after a long day of labor. The biting wind violently whipped through his patched cloth coat, making him shiver involuntarily. His perpetually unkempt hair was blown back by the strong gust. Ivan rubbed his calloused hands—a testament to his long hours of work.

“Sigh, what can I do? Without these rations, what will happen to the children? Should I watch them starve to death?” He grumbled to himself, but dared not show it on his face. As always, he went to collect his daily portion, but unlike usual, the quantity was visibly less.

“Why is there so little today?” Ivan’s eyes widened. This much would barely feed two or three people, let alone leave anything for him and his wife. The attendant calmly and skillfully pulled out a piece of paper. “See this? The highest directive personally issued by Marshal Yazov! From now on, all resources are prioritized for the military! Black and white, clear as day!”

Ivan clenched his fist, the veins bulging like thick branches. But between starvation and punishment, he ultimately chose the former. Still, his heart felt a deep unrest. “Why should we starve and freeze just because we are unwilling to go to the front line to die? Are we born to live like this?” A raging fire ignited in his heart, one that refused to be extinguished.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.129.a: The Great Trial will achieve Russia's revenge, but what then?
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.130.desc:
Hans Berger could smell the air—it wasn't the usual coal smoke of a Moscow winter, but a more pungent, sickening smell mixed with a highly diluted poison gas. Listening to the shouts, gunshots, and the increasingly near footsteps outside the window, his sweat and tears ran together, inseparable. He prayed, tightly holding the hand of his wife, Elsa, as the two of them tried to slip out the back door of their general store.

However, they couldn't evade them. The alley was blocked by two Black League soldiers in black quilted coats, their armbands embroidered with the double-headed eagle. The two soldiers immediately saw them and aimed the dark muzzles of their rifles at them.

“Deutsche?” The middle-aged man leading them spoke in slightly awkward German. The couple couldn't speak Russian, so the two soldiers immediately understood their identity. Hans felt a cold dread in his heart. He racked his brains, but could only stutter out some meaningless sounds—his throat was temporarily paralyzed from extreme tension. The middle-aged man ignored him: “Documents?” He nudged Hans’s face with the gun, a clear threat. Hans’s mind went blank, but Elsa reacted, fumbling on her person and producing the identity documents issued by the German authorities in Moscow. The middle-aged man flipped through them, and upon seeing 'German Descendant Resident' filled in the place of origin field, a vicious smirk spread across his face. He gestured, and the younger man behind him violently smashed his rifle butt into Hans’s abdomen. Hans groaned, curling up. Elsa let out a short shriek, but was instantly and brutally muffled by the young man's hand.

“Berger... Hans Berger...” The middle-aged man read the name on the document, as if reading an entry on a death list. “Moved in from Munich in 1943. ‘Technical Specialist.’” He looked up, his icy eyes meeting Hans’s pained and terrified gaze for the first time. “Technical Specialist? For whose technology? Nazi war machine technology?” His voice suddenly rose sharply. Hans knew what he was saying, but the suffocating sensation intensified, making him wish he couldn't understand, at least then he wouldn't suffer this torture... 

“No... no!” Hans struggled to explain. He was just an ordinary electrical engineer, only wanting a safe haven in the chaotic post-war world. But the leader stomped a foot onto his shoulder, pinning him firmly to the cold, filthy snow. 

“Shut up! German pig!” the leader spat. “You enjoyed twenty years! Living in our houses, eating our food, breathing our air! Now, the ‘Great Trial’ has come!” He violently raised the document, and before the eyes of Hans and the terrified Elsa, brought the sharp edge of his logging axe down hard! 

The sound of the paper tearing was piercing. The document was cleaved in two, the photo registered with the Commissariat sliced right down the middle by the axe blade. The leader tossed the two broken halves of the document onto Hans’s face like discarded garbage. 

“Take them!” the leader ordered. The young man roughly yanked the nearly paralyzed Elsa up, then kicked Hans, motioning for him to stand. Hans struggled to his feet, his vision blurring from the sharp pain in his abdomen and shoulder. He saw a dilapidated military truck parked at the alley entrance. Its rear was open, and in the shadows, it seemed already packed with people. Despair sank into his heart like a lump of lead. Was this the “Great Trial”? Where would they be taken? Concentration camps? Mines? Or executed directly in some abandoned factory?
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.131.desc:
“Hey! You Slav over there! Get over here!” Karl glared, his eyes wide, at the surrounding prisoners of war. He had been doing this job for quite a while. With Omsk’s brutal campaign against German civilians in the east, he had completely lost any sympathy for the POWs. All that remained in his heart was love for his Fatherland and hatred for foreigners.

As one prisoner after another walked toward the wall, the gunshots continued in succession, even growing louder. Clearly, the soldiers executing the prisoners were also full of rage...

“Wait, why are the gunshots getting closer?”

Suddenly, the main gate was violently pushed open by several Black League soldiers. Upon seeing Karl’s German uniform, the leading soldier, without a word, unleashed a torrent of bullets onto him.

In his final moments, Karl’s vision began to blur and his surroundings darkened. Warm, wet blood soaked through his clothes from behind. His arms slumped weakly to the ground, denying him the chance to raise his right arm. As the Russian soldiers burst deeper into the concentration camp, firing at the executioners, Karl completely lost consciousness. Snowflake after snowflake covered his corpse.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.131.a: Even the hateful have their own pitiable suffering.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.132.t: The Bumpy Road Nears its End
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.132.desc:
The Omsk Grand Square was once again filled with people—it had not hosted such a crowd since Yazov swore his oath here to march west. The black mass of soldier formations stretched out as far as the eye could see, filling every gap in the square. The scene could no longer be described merely with the term 'killing intent.' This was the Abyss, an Abyss formed by the hatred and fury suppressed over a half-century of Russian suffering.

Into this Abyss, Yazov ascended the stage.

“Warriors!” Two piercing gleams shot out from Yazov’s normally placid eyes. Every ravine on his face was etched with the hatred forged by long hardship and the deep underground. After a brief silence, he slammed his fist onto the cold metal podium with a dull 'thud': “We know that those Teutonic beasts in the West still survive! These maggots, who have defiled our holy land, still hide in the dark bunkers! They think the Great Trial is over! They think they can escape God’s wrath!” Yazov’s voice suddenly rose: “But we all know, the Revenge is not finished! As long as one single Teuton still lives, the Great Trial will not end! We, the Black League, resurrected from the ruins, we have swept away the Nazi remnants in Eastern Europe, and purged the filth and traitors from within! Now, only one goal remains: Germania! The source of this Teutonic plague of sin!”

He paused, then continued to roar: “This time, there is no retreat! We will exterminate every last cell carrying the poisonous Teutonic blood! We will turn the entire Germanic nation, the entire German state, all the Teutons, into corpses, into ashes! We will erase the very words ‘Germany’ from history, from this planet, from the entire universe!”

“Warriors! It’s not over! The Union has a great gift for you!” Saying this, he unveiled the black cloth beside him, revealing rows of barrels marked with biohazard symbols, and stacks of ammunition boxes painted with black skulls. His voice was slightly distorted by emotion: “Do you see? Improved plagues, more efficient poison gas, powerful corrosives, and chemicals that make life a living hell! Open your valves! Blood-wash every ruin, every bunker, every swamp! Drag them out, crush them like cockroaches! Burn all the Teutons into charcoal, melt them all into putrid water, hack them all into meat paste!”

“Warriors!” Yazov took a deep breath. He felt like he was in a dream, and despite a slight dizziness, he roared out with all his might: “Ignite the fire of purification! For our hatred! For Mother Russia! Advance! For decades of blood debt! Advance! For the final, the last, the Holy War! ADVANCE!!!”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.133.desc:
In the lead-gray conference room, smoke lingered heavily, refusing to disperse. Yazov was reviewing reports submitted by various military districts. Sakharovsky handed him a document: “Commander-in-Chief, this is the execution plan and current progress for the second phase of the Western General Plan. Our chemical and biological weapon stockpiles are sufficient, and conventional weapon production is enough to sustain us through the Great Trial. However, the Army Groups are facing a shortage of reserve manpower. The Union may need to further expand conscription.”

Yazov sighed: “Front line status?”

“The situation in East Prussia and West Poland is favorable. The German resistance is weaker than we anticipated. Many of their areas have not even rebuilt modern social order yet. The current balance of power is completely the opposite of what it was during the first phase of the Great Trial. Our intelligence even suggests that Germany’s remaining industrial capacity is only half of ours. Therefore, our war capability is unquestionably superior to Germany’s.” Sakharovsky then handed over another document: “And, there is more good news, Commander-in-Chief. The survivors in Britain have rebuilt their regime, but they currently lack the capability to aid Germany. There is no central government with ruling power in the French region. However, Switzerland preserved a significant amount of strength during the nuclear strikes, and we may need to note their threat. Overall, Germany’s Western European allies have been greatly weakened. Report complete.”

Yazov nodded. He then motioned for the next speaker. Drozdov chose his words carefully, trying to make his points less abrasive: “Commander-in-Chief, this is an inspection report on the environment of the lost territories in Eastern Europe. Because we were unable to construct adequate fortifications there during the first phase of the Great Trial, the local environment is causing much greater attrition to our personnel and supplies than in Russia proper. Our logistics are under extreme pressure. If this situation continues, I fear our supply lines may collapse before Germany is completely exterminated. Therefore, I propose... to temporarily pause the offensive...” As he spoke, his voice grew less assured, and Yazov merely cast a cold glance at him, as if looking at a dead object. Feeling the chill, Drozdov quickly tried to cover himself, his voice even stammering due to nervousness: “Com-Com-Commander-in-Chief, I am absolutely not a defeatist. It’s just that, given the current situation, a high-intensity offensive could be counterproduc—”

“Enough! Shut your mouth! If you utter such treasonous words again, I will have you stripped of your post!” Yazov was clearly enraged. Drozdov fell silent, terrified. He saluted, concluding his report.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.133.a: The other generals who attempted to advise Yazov silently closed their mouths upon seeing this.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.134.desc:
The “Ekaterina” Bunker Complex, Tyumen Region

Anastasia broke the last piece of moldy dry bread crust in half, stuffing one half into her daughter Masha’s mouth and clutching the other in her sweaty palm. They were huddled in the corner of a cold concrete staircase at the rationing station. In front of them was a seemingly endless line reeking of sweat. Masha's small body was bundled in her mother's worn, shiny old coat, looking hollow. She wasn't crying, but simply looked at the tiny bit of food in her mother's hand with her excessively large, unusually clear blue eyes: “Mama, the bread is so small.” Masha’s voice was light as a feather, carrying the confusion unique to a child. “It used to be this big.” She gestured with her little, frostbred red hand; the size she indicated would have lasted them two days.

Anastasia’s throat tightened. She couldn’t explain to this child, less than ten years old, the new Black League notice, the ink still wet, posted on the wall: “Everything for the Final Revenge! The Rear is the Front! Reduce rations for non-combat personnel to support the ‘Great Trial’ Front!” She couldn’t explain the word ‘Inapplicable’ written across her benefit card, earned by her husband’s death, nor the portion on her ration card that had been violently crossed out repeatedly and stamped with a smaller number in red. Her husband had died in an exploration mission ten years ago, and now, the Black League’s ‘Order’ was trying to choke his widow and surviving child.

The queue moved at a snail's pace. Finally, it was their turn. The soldier's face behind the window was hidden by his greasy winter hat, only his emotionless eyes were visible. He glanced at Anastasia’s crumpled ration card, then at Masha behind her.

“Widow? With a burden?” The soldier’s voice was devoid of warmth. “New rule this month: non-core labor force, a twenty percent cut in rations. Take it.” He tossed out two dry bread biscuits, each only the size of her fist and hard as stone. Anastasia’s heart sank immediately: “Officer! Please... the child... this isn't enough...”

“Next!” The soldier ignored her, continuing his mechanical movements. Anastasia and Masha were quickly pushed aside by the crowd. She desperately clutched the two small, rock-like biscuits, pulling Masha as she stumbled backward, only to bump into an officer wearing a brand-new military greatcoat. The officer disgustedly brushed the corner of his coat where Anastasia's ragged sleeve had touched it, as if swatting a fly. He was carrying a bulging military mess tin; the lid wasn’t shut properly, and the tempting aroma of real dark rye bread and sausage wafted out.

Masha’s little nose twitched, and her eyes instantly lit up. She tugged at Anastasia’s coat, her voice filled with innocent wonder: “Mama, it smells so good! That Uncle’s bread is so big!”

The officer paused, his cold gaze sweeping over Masha’s sallow little face. A slight smirk touched his lips, as if mocking the child’s naïve comparison. Anastasia violently tightened her grip on her daughter’s cold hand, pressing her head into her own thin chest, preventing her from looking again.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.135.desc:
Since Karbyshev’s death, Yazov's mental state has been deteriorating. Now, he has clearly developed severe paranoia, and has turned his suspicion towards the Black League’s officers and soldiers. To ensure there are no ‘Teutonic agents’ in the military, Yazov personally appointed several confidantes to investigate the army. Now, the results have finally come out—

“No spies found? What do you mean ‘not found’?” Yazov challenged the members of the investigation team before him, the hair on his head standing up. The team members dared not breathe, terrified of becoming Yazov’s next target of suspicion.

After a long silence, one of them finally dared to answer: “Report, Commander-in-Chief, we have vetted every registered Union soldier except for you. We even vetted each other, but we did not find any correspondence with the Teutons...” Yazov stood up and slammed his fist onto the desk. The team members knew they were in deep trouble.

“Get out! All of you, get out! Keep searching! Or I’ll have you shot too!” Yazov dismissed them. The team members naturally didn't dare to linger and immediately rushed out of the office.

After the office was empty again, Yazov violently pounded the desk. Looking up at the ceiling, tears welled up in his eyes. He felt immense self-contempt and remorse.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.135.a: “Am I truly unable to inherit his legacy...”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.136.desc:
Agent No. *5**3*9* was nervously rushing towards Warehouse No. *27**. The respirator hose on his protective suit swayed with his violent heartbeat and hurried pace. His pupils behind the mask were violently dilated, and his lungs contracted with increasing force. The veteran agent once again commanded his body—which belonged to him, but even more so to the Union—to use all its strength for the Great Trial. Even though time had left its mark on his body, his loyalty to the Great Trial remained as fresh as ever.

Although his mind had made countless predictions and imaginings about the situation inside the warehouse, he was now as agitated and apprehensive as he had been decades ago, the first time he held a gun on the battlefield. The difference was that this time, the weather-beaten warrior was finding an ‘old partner’ again to crush the traitors of Russia and the Teutonic filth, rather than a green recruit choosing a ‘new weapon’ to face the revisionists and the military districts.

Agent No. *5**3*9* watched the old door grow larger and clearer. He couldn't help but recall being a logistics officer during the first Great Trial in 1976, working sixteen-hour days, shuttling exhaustedly between West Siberia and the Moscow front. He was tired then, and he was tired now, but as long as the Great Trial was unfinished, he would not stop. This was the command Marshal Yazov had impressed upon him, and one he had always firmly remembered and executed. The mark branded by the Judge must never be forgotten.

His thoughts ended. Agent No. *5**3*9* stood before the warehouse door. The quantity of resources inside would determine how many agents could better dedicate themselves to the great mission. Excitedly, he pulled out an extremely old key, scarred and heavily worn, yet it still worked for the scarred agent and this thick, old, rusty door.

The key turned with a groaning crack, like a breaking bone.

The old door dragged open with a whimpering moan, like a broken leg.

Agent No. *5**3*9* stepped into the depot from which he had collected goods countless times long ago.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.136.a: A bitter, yet genuine, laugh escaped him.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.137.desc:
After the nuclear war, warlords sprung up like mushrooms across the Russian land. These warlords held varied ideologies, but without exception, they were the local ‘petty emperors.’ To prevent them from rebelling or causing trouble in the rear, Yazov decided to deploy these idle figures to the front line, to serve the Union. Of course, not everyone supported this decision...

“Hey! Mikhail! You Red scum, get over here!” “You running dog of the bourgeoisie are no better! Aleksandr!” With that, Mikhail and Aleksandr started another brawl. Mikhail tackled Aleksandr to the ground, slamming his elbow into his teeth. Aleksandr desperately punched Mikhail’s abdomen. The two remained deadlocked until the political officer arrived. They were just two sacrifices of this policy. Their constant feuding over political differences gave their squad leader a massive headache. Their comrades were used to it and even found entertainment in it.

Of course, these two were just two examples among countless in the Black League, but undoubtedly, this measure did not necessarily guarantee the Union’s stability.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.137.a: At least the rear doesn't have a headache anymore, right?
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.138.desc:
“Dmitry Alexeyevich Petrov?” A Black League police officer shone a bright light onto Petrov. Petrov squinted, instinctively shielding his eyes with his arm.

“Y-yes...” He was still in a state of extreme terror. He remembered he was just walking down a street that had been repaired a few days ago when someone suddenly clamped a rag over his mouth from behind, and he passed out. The next thing he knew, he was in the interrogation room.

“Speak! Have you had any contact with the Teutons!” The police officer roared at Petrov, saliva spraying onto his face. But Petrov was momentarily stunned by the question.

“Contact? This is a miscarriage of justice, Officer! I’ve always worked in Russia; I’ve never even seen a Ger— I mean, Teuton!” The police officer listened, then impassively clapped his hands.

“Ivan! Turn off the camera!”

Another officer named Ivan pushed open the door and skillfully twisted the surveillance camera from the ceiling. Then, the two officers pulled out pre-prepared batons and swung them at Petrov.

“Speak! Where are your Teuton accomplices! Tell us now!” The two took turns hitting Petrov with their batons. Petrov couldn't endure three rounds before he confessed. “I’ll talk! I’ll talk! I’ll tell you everything! I met that Teuton on Yazov Street, number 123, in Omsk! Don’t kill me! Don’t kill me!” Petrov, desperate to save his life, fabricated a location. His face was covered in bruises and contusions, blood constantly streamed from his nose, and a freshly knocked-out tooth lay on the floor, its root stained red with blood.

Upon hearing this information, the two officers finally stopped and took Petrov to the prison. But when they searched all over Omsk, they discovered there was no such thing as “Yazov Street, number 123.” And Petrov was just an ordinary citizen.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.139.desc:
Pantelei led several children into the conscription office. Quite a few people were already inside. As the Union’s external expansion deepened, they found more underground caches. Following this, a new round of conscription began. Initially, they could find capable young men and some middle-aged men. But soon, all they could find were women and children. Consequently, the Union formally lowered the conscription age to single digits, and the children they could find began to participate in military administration affairs.

As new recruits, these young children were sequentially told to strip in the cold room of the underground conscription office. Several military clerks were recording their details one by one. An agent in patent leather short boots walked back and forth nearby. Upon seeing Pantelei enter, his eyes instantly brightened.

“Pantelei, assign these ones to me. Several capable workers have died from exhaustion recently, and we simply don't have enough people to supervise production. We need more people to watch over the laborers to prevent them from rebelling.”

“Can you cut down on the abuse, Ivanovich? Everyone knows you beat your subordinates at the slightest provocation, killing a few every so often and leaving their bodies mutilated. How many people will be left to work after this?”

While the two men were talking, the white-haired military doctor inside the room had already begun conducting physical examinations on the children with the clerks.

“Chest size... height...”

“This is clearly a sickness caused by radiation exposure. Note it down...”

“Stop moving, now I need to check your eyelids.”

“Take off your pants, what are you trying to hide!”

Soon, the results of the children’s physical examinations were out. The officers in the room each picked up a copy to read. Pantelei had just scanned the reports of a few of the older children in the front row when a dark-haired inspector leaned in close to his ear.

“Brother, assign these older kids to my deployment unit. We’re seriously short of new hands to do work lately. Don’t forget, we still rely on our unit to procure supplies outside.”

“Hey, what are you two doing? These people rightfully belong to my Industrial Production Department. Many workers are slacking off during work hours, forgetting their national duty. If there aren’t enough qualified soldiers to guard them, how can work proceed?” Ivanovich impatiently tapped his finger on the desk and yelled.

Pantelei ignored the men’s argument. He scanned the physical examination reports of several children. The oldest child was 8 years old, less than 1.2 meters tall, and weighed only 15 kilograms. The youngest was only 6 years old. Looking at these skeletal children, Pantelei suddenly shivered involuntarily. A wave of nausea washed over his entire body.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.139.a: I am a murderer, an absolute villain.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.140.desc:
Yevgeny Nikolaevich walked into the distance, carrying a flamethrower. The thick radiation suit blocked the continuous flow of poison gas outside, and it also isolated the raging fire of anger that was now erupting from him. Since the Great Trial began, his daily life consisted of training and labor in the bunker. He also had to listen to the daily broadcast detailing the atrocities of the Teutons. From that day forward, he felt a constant need to do something; this sacred revenge was not over. Finally, he earned the qualification to march west as part of the first clearance unit.

The mission brief from headquarters indicated that although the Teutons had suffered heavy losses under the Great Trial, settlements might still exist on the road to the Teuton capital, Germania. They had to ensure that not a single Teutonic force or Teuton person survived in these places. Only then could the Teutons be denied any chance of ever reviving.

Soon, instructions came over the radio, indicating suspicious personnel activity at the designated coordinates. Yevgeny and his squad boarded the armored vehicle. In the silent roar of the engine, he slowly breathed the air that had been filtered countless times by his gas mask, an air permeated with the smell of metal and burnt charcoal, trying to suppress the unease in his heart.

The destination quickly appeared before them. Yevgeny led the squad in a search. Soon, they found the door to a half-buried fallout shelter. After a quick survey, they confirmed traces of human activity. After confirming there was no defense, the squad breached the door and poured in. The light of their flashlights instantly cut through the shelter's pitch blackness, illuminating the faces of the people inside.

After their eyes adjusted to the dark, Yevgeny looked around. A group of Teuton trash was huddled in the corner. One section of the wall was covered in colors and scribbled with various phrases. Yevgeny understood a little German. He scanned the wall; the largest line read: “Do not forget the blood debt of the Slavic inferior race!”

“So, you haven’t forgotten. Good. We haven’t forgotten either.” Yevgeny grinned, then raised the flamethrower in his hands.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.140.a: The gushing flames, along with his rage, instantly set the Teutonic scum alight.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.141.desc:
“Thank our Commander-in-Chief, citizens! With the establishment of contact with the Union High Command, we have received personally-issued food and material support from the Commander-in-Chief as a reward for our loyalty!” The radio broadcast sounded again. This time, it was no longer hollow revenge propaganda, but truly brought good news to this nuclear war shelter in Nizhny Tagil.

Upon hearing these words, many residents of the bunker were at their designated workplaces. Some were in the workshop, some in the underground tunnels, and some were idle in their rooms. When they heard the news, many raised their heads, nearly numb, unable to believe the news was true.

“To ensure that the use of food and supplies can continue to support the complete fulfillment of the Great Trial, loyal citizens, we will further implement a rationing system. However, unlike before, we now have more materials. Therefore, we now announce that from now on, we will adopt a **labor-based rationing system**. If our citizens undertake more labor for the Union, they will be eligible to receive more food and materials!”

Soon, a long line formed to receive rations. People continuously came to the designated mess hall to collect the increased supplies—although they were not much different from what they usually managed to forage, consisting mostly of potatoes, turnip soup, and so on. But the preparation and flavor did show a difference, and many people’s expressions visibly changed after tasting them. Black League agents also began distributing more materials based on the level of labor contribution in the shelter. Soon, the line reached a shifty-eyed man.

“Officer, I am from the propaganda department. I have conducted multiple propaganda sessions for our Union, helping to stabilize morale and allow everyone to better endure these days. I believe I have the right to claim more bread.”

“Oh, is that so?” The Captain on the side looked at the agent distributing the supplies, who shook their head, then looked at the civilians behind the man: “I think our clever Russians should be able to distinguish who has contributed labor, yes?”

The man looked at the soldiers surrounding him, his courage instantly failing, and he fell to his knees: “What are you saying?! Absolutely not... I was truly confused, I don't know what got into me... Please forgive me... Please believe me, I would be ashamed if anyone else did such a thing...”

The Captain looked at the man, who was full of shame and utterly disgraced, and suddenly laughed. He immediately kicked the man and said calmly: “Some people always make mistakes, forgetting that Russians are a nation that firmly remembers history. Of course, we can temporarily forgive this kind of mistake. But we don’t like everyone making this mistake. After all, our bullets still need to be shot at the Teutons.”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.141.a: “As for you, take your meager share and get back to work.”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.142.t: The Investigation and Statistics Bureau in Action
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.142.desc:
“File No. 000041. Rank: Lieutenant General. Charge: Treason, espionage. Execution by firing squad carried out.”
······
“File No. 000579. Rank: Colonel. Charge: Corruption, dereliction of duty. Indefinite penal servitude.”
······
“File No. 006439. Rank: Sergeant. Charge: Assault, disturbing military order. Transferred to the biological laboratory.”
······
“File No. 012980. Rank: Clerk. Charge: Leaking state secrets. Used to test the potency of new poison gas.”
······
······
Yazov flipped through the documents from the Investigation and Statistics Bureau one by one, feeling as if the lives of enemies were slipping through his fingers, which put him in a good mood. There were still many spies, and counter-revolutionaries could never be fully eliminated. Yes, as long as the Teutons existed, the danger to the Motherland would never disappear. Eliminating all Teutons and traitors to achieve the Motherland’s revival—wasn't this the legacy of Karbyshev?

Yazov laughed maniacally. Those who obstruct the Great Trial need no trial; they must be executed immediately. He picked up the phone for the Investigation and Statistics Bureau and gave yet another order:
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.142.a: “Increase the intensity of the investigation. The power of execution is yours.”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.143.desc:
Dmitry Yazov stood before the massive operational map table in the General Staff Headquarters. His withered finger slowly traced the battle line pointing towards Germany’s remaining territory, a line that was nearly stagnant due to the overly slow pace of advance. “Another great stagnation,” Yazov’s voice was hoarse, jarringly loud in the silent command post. “But the final chapter of the ‘Great Trial’ will not tolerate this!” He violently slammed his fist onto the tabletop, making the marker pieces rattle. “The Teutons hide in the ruins, thinking this will delay their demise? Do they think our resolve will be eroded by distance and attrition?” He sneered, his voice devoid of warmth. “Tear off their façade. Let them and the compromising, defeatist traitors among us see that all resistance is futile against the power of the Union!”

He turned to the Chief of the General Staff, who was frozen in fear: “Notify all Army Groups on the front line. Effective immediately, implement ‘Protocol Zero.’”

The command was then concretized, becoming a series of cold instructions transmitted through encrypted lines to the distance:

“First: All Infantry Divisions, cancel rotation and rest. Reserves are to fill the line and commit to non-stop attacks. Casualties are not a priority consideration. Goal: Exhaust the German Army’s last bullet and break their last soldier.”

“Second: Artillery units are to fully employ the ‘Koschei’ series of chemical incendiary shells and persistent suffocating munitions. Priority targets include enemy logistics nodes, suspected command posts, and densely populated areas. Tactical and strategic targets are no longer to be distinguished. Create continuous kill zones, stripping them of their mobility and supply space. Remember to tell them, production is not an issue, the Union will find a way.”

“Third: Engineer units are to execute a ‘Total Scorched Earth’ policy along the line of advance. Destroy all facilities and resources that cannot be immediately utilized. Contamination agents are to be poured into water sources.”

“Fourth: Further expand the conscription scope. The number of female soldiers needs to be increased. Food rationing will prioritize combat troops. The home front... will tighten their belts themselves.”

A weary-looking logistics general’s lips moved, seemingly wanting to say something. But Yazov gave him no chance: “We climbed out of nuclear ruins and civil war not to be trapped in this damned stagnation again! The ‘Final Revenge’ has no end. Either Germany disappears from the map entirely, or we shed our last drop of blood. There is no third way.”

He turned, staring at the map again, his withered hand pressing down hard on the location representing Berlin, as if he meant to gouge it out of the paper.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.144.desc:
Pavel’s memory was a frozen field repeatedly ploughed by artillery fire. He couldn't remember the last time he saw a whole roof, nor what air without the smell of gunpowder tasted like. He only remembered hatred. That hatred was not the grand oath Yazov screamed over the radio, nor the bright red slogans printed in the pamphlets distributed by the political officer. It was more like the mud clogging his sidearm, the perpetual taste of rust in his canteen, the dust—tens of years’ worth—that he couldn’t cough out of his lungs—a physiological existence, requiring no thought.

The German village they were in didn't even have a name on the map. It was like a festering wound on the face of the earth, oozing pus made of rubble and ruins beneath the leaden-grey sky. The Geiger counter was the only living thing in this dead silence, tolling their funeral with its monotonous ‘click-click.’

Pavel kicked open a farmhouse door. It was empty, but the traces of life had not yet been completely erased by the cold. A family photo hung on the wall; the man in the picture held his wife, and two blonde children smiled innocently in front of them, the background a green field and a cow. Pavel stared at the photo, his face expressionless. He didn't wonder where the people in the photo were now. He only saw, in the photo’s background, the shadow of his own village, long since reduced to charcoal.

He remembered having a wife, her hair the color of wheat. He remembered having a daughter, who always liked to tuck wildflowers into his cap brim. These memories flashed like faded ghosts, bringing no sorrow, only making the cold hatred that had settled in his bones grow heavier and colder.

“Sector sweep, execute purification protocol.” The squad leader's monotone voice came through the earpiece, melding with the beat of the Geiger counter. Purification, what a clean word.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.144.a: He pulled the bolt, the motion as natural as eating or drinking.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.145.desc:
The cellar door was propped shut by a sack of sprouting potatoes. When Pavel broke it open with his rifle butt, a smell of earth, rotting vegetables, and human fear surged out. There were living people inside.

He slid down the ladder, his boot landing on the slippery mud floor. In the dim light, several pairs of eyes stared at him like frightened mice. An elderly man with white hair, clutching a rusty pitchfork—his last weapon. A middle-aged woman was desperately shielding two children behind her. The children’s eyes were wide with terror, but they didn’t even have the strength to cry. Their faces were smeared with mud, presumably for camouflage, but they were not invisible to Pavel’s eyes, which had long grown accustomed to the darkness.

The old man shouted something in German. Pavel didn't understand, and didn't want to. In his eyes, this was no longer a family, nor even a group of people. They were **weeds**. Poisonous weeds growing all over the body of Mother Russia, sucking her blood, gnawing at her flesh and bone. His mission was not murder, but **weeding**. A necessary piece of farm work, delayed for too long.

His finger did not tremble in the slightest. The muzzle flash briefly illuminated the cellar, and also illuminated the light that instantly went out in the woman's eyes. The children didn't even have time to scream before the momentum of the bullets threw them against the wall. Finally, the old man. Before he could even raise the pitchfork, a neat hole appeared in his brow, and his body slowly fell backward, knocking over the sack of sprouting potatoes.

It was over. Only Pavel’s breathing and the heavy smell of blood remained in the cellar. He stepped forward and crushed a child’s toy wooden horse under the heel of his military boot. The sound of splintering wood was sharp, like ice cracking. He did not feel satisfaction, nor guilt, only the emptiness of a job completed. No different from a farmer finishing the last row of a field at dusk.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.145.a: He stamped out the kerosene lamp that was still flickering.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.146.desc:
Night fell. Ash-black snow began to drift down, covering the bloodstains and spent casings. Pavel sat on the burnt farmhouse threshold, cleaning his rifle. The residual heat of the barrel provided a faint warmth through his glove.

The mission was complete. This village... was “purified.” Every cellar, every corner, had been checked. There were no living Teutons left. His lifelong hatred, his sole reason for existence, seemed to have been exhausted in this short day. Now, the cold hatred that had sustained him was gone, leaving a black hole in his chest, more desolate than the radiated wasteland.

He looked up at the night sky, stained a morbid purple by the radiation clouds. He tried to remember what the Volga River looked like. He remembered the water, the fishing boats, the bonfires on the riverbank on summer evenings. But those images were now blurred, like a distant dream. He strained to remember, trying to recall his wife's face, the tone of her voice.

The fragments of memory were like ashes scattered by the wind; no matter how hard he tried, he couldn't piece them together. Had he won? He had avenged his hometown, his wife, and his daughter. But his hometown was long gone, and his wife and daughter... their faces and names were now just as vague, distant, and insignificant as the faces and names of the Germans who had died by his gun today.

War had taken everything from him—his home, his family, his future. And today, when he finally exacted his revenge, he was horrified to find that the war had also stolen his last possession—that pure, driving hatred. Now, he had nothing.

The rifle was polished to a shine, reflecting the cold light of the snow. It was more real than him, more alive. Pavel sat there blankly, letting the snowflakes fall onto his shoulders, slowly turning him into a cold statue without a tombstone.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.146.a: He couldn't remember his daughter's name.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.147.t: Dust in the Motes of Light
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.147.desc:
In Germany. In a bombed-out church.
Fragments of stained glass lay scattered like cheap candy on the floor. The midday sun streamed through a hole in the dome, casting a straight column of light, like a late, meaningless judgment from God. Countless specks of dust rose, spun, and fell within the column of light. You watch them for hours.
Your rifle rests beside you. It is cold, quiet. Like a loyal, sleeping dog.
Someone calls you Pavel.
That name feels like an ill-fitting old coat on you. You try to say it in your mind: *Pavel*. Your tongue feels a strange stiffness. The man named Pavel had a village, a wife, a daughter. The man named Pavel had magma made of hatred, suffering, and vodka rushing through his veins. He injected this magma into the barrel of this gun, firing it at every living thing on this land.

You remember pulling the trigger. You remember the recoil hitting your shoulder. You remember blood splattering on the wall, like a clumsy abstract painting. You remember warm organs steaming in the winter air.

You remember all of this.

But you don't remember the hatred.

Yesterday, the hatred was still there. It was a hot stone lodged in your chest, preventing you from breathing, but also allowing you to stand. It showed you the direction and gave meaning to your actions.

Today, the stone is cold. It has crumbled into dust, mixing with the church’s debris, floating aimlessly in the light column.

You look down at your hands. A pair of hands covered in calluses and scars. Dried blood and black gunpowder residue are embedded in the fingernails.

These hands. They have killed. They once held a child. They once stroked a woman’s hair.

Now, they are just hands. Two tools made of bone and flesh, attached to the end of your arms.

You are an icon, moving on a map. A unit. With health points, with organization. You move from one province to another. You execute directives.

Attack.

Defend.

Purge.

These directives come from a place you cannot see, transmitted through the static in your headphones or the political officer’s purple, frostbitten lips.

You never questioned.

You once believed that when the last Teuton fell, there would be a sense of relief, a triumphant satisfaction. You would hear the Volga singing, you would see your fallen comrades smiling in heaven.

But you hear nothing, see nothing.

You only see more dust.

You stand up and walk to the altar. The statue of Christ on the altar has had its head blown off, only one outstretched arm remains in the pose of embracing the world, looking ridiculous and pitiful. You are like him, an emptied vessel. You were once filled with hatred, and he was once filled with faith.

Now, both of you are empty.

What was the meaning of this Trial, this great, holy Revenge?

Was it for a better world? You look around, and this wasteland, saturated with toxins and shrouded in death, is the world you helped create.

Was it to console the departed souls? But you can no longer remember their faces.

You are no longer Pavel.

You are not a revenger.

You are just the last superfluous part left behind by this Trial. A rusted ghost that has stopped working.

You reach out and wave your hand in the light column, disturbing the dancing dust motes.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE_147_tt: In those days men will seek death and will not find it; they will desire to die, and death will flee from them.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.148.desc:
Your name is Dmitry, and you are eighteen years old. Your Motherland is not a specific piece of land, but an underground ark cast from concrete, steel, and hatred. Your creation myth began the moment General Karbyshev was martyred in the ice, and your hymn is the combat slogan distributed daily.
