For you, ‘Germany’ is not a geographical term, but a symbol of Original Sin carved into the soul—it is the serpent, the apple, everything unholy that must be purified by fire.

Today, you finally step onto that promised land, the land that must be destroyed. The abandoned highway stretches like a massive gray scar to the horizon. The hissing of your gas mask’s breathing valve is your sacred song. Your rifle is cold and heavy, your cross. When the squad leader points to the silhouette of broken buildings ahead, your heart pounds, not from fear, but from a holy ecstasy that has been eighteen years coming. You are about to fulfill your destiny.

The battle is simpler, and more... pure than you imagined. A Teuton veteran hiding behind a broken wall, his Iron Cross reflecting the dim light. As he raises his rifle, you pull the trigger. No hesitation. The dull sound of the bullet hitting him is the most pleasant music you have ever heard. As he falls, you feel an invisible shackles being removed from the body of Mother Russia. You step over his corpse. The blood sticking to the sole of your boot makes you feel as though you have crossed the threshold to heaven.

At night, by the faint light of the armored car, you write everything down in your diary. The ink bleeds on the poor-quality paper, but the handwriting is firm with excitement. “Today, I have washed the road for my unborn descendants with the blood of the Teutons. Fire and steel shall be our baptism, ruins and ashes our altar. Marshal Yazov guides us, and the spirit of Karbyshev protects us. This Holy War is glorious.”

You close the diary, listening to the sporadic gunshots in the distance. That is your comrades continuing the great purification. You close your eyes, and in your dream, you see a sea of fire, and at the end of the fire, are the golden wheat waves and the clear blue sky of Russia.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.148.a: I am standing at the gates of Hell, and I shall be the one to knock.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE_148_tt: I am full of the fury of the Lord; I am weary with holding it in.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.149.desc:
The sense of the sacred has an expiry date. One month later, you realize that the great work of purifying the world is essentially no different from assembling magazines on the bunker assembly line—repetitive, precise, and a growing, suffocating numbness. The ecstasy has long faded. What drives you now is an efficient, Spartan-like professionalism. Break the door, search for the enemy, shoot, confirm the kill, move to the next coordinates. Your actions are as regular as a pendulum, your heart as calm as an ice surface.

Yet, your senses are betraying you. They begin to capture insignificant details, uncontrollably falling out of focus like a damaged camera lens. You remember how the cornflower pattern on the wallpaper in a room set ablaze by a flamethrower curled, blackened, and finally turned to ash. You remember a sack of apples scattered next to the corpse of a German woman; one rolled to your boot, still bearing a small, unburnt blush of red. You remember seeing a crooked sun drawn in colored chalk on the blackboard when clearing a kindergarten; a stray bullet had pierced the exact center of the sun, leaving a black hole.

These images themselves do not evoke your sympathy—'sympathy' is an emotion that was genetically removed before you were born. But they make you irritable. A kind of inexplicable annoyance that disrupts the purity. The Holy War should be an epic, a symphony; the background should be Wagner’s *Ride of the Valkyries* and the burning Reichstag. It shouldn't be these... trivial fragments that belong in a family photo album. The wreckage of an accordion, a dropped doll, a smashed dinner plate... Their existence contaminates the absolute nature of this Trial, making the sacred ritual of revenge look like a hysterical, smash-and-grab street fight.

The content of your diary begins to change. No longer are there passionate hymns, replaced instead by cold work logs: “Target Area D7 purged. Ammunition expended: 112 rounds. Civilians found: 17, handled. Confiscated: three boxes of canned food, half a sack of moldy bread.” The handwriting is neat, like filling out an expense report. You no longer record your feelings, because you have nothing left to feel. You are merely recording facts. An apple, a pierced sun. These are also facts. You write them in too, without comment, just like logging the consumption of ammunition.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE_149_tt: I looked, and behold, there was no man; I gazed, and there was no light.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.150.desc:
Intelligence reported that the town's library was the regional commander’s last stronghold. It cost you three soldiers to breach the main door. The library was filled with the smell of rotting paper and old wood; sunlight streamed through the bullet-riddled windows, casting mottled shadows on the piles of books, like a desecrated temple.

The demon's lair you expected, the ultimate embodiment of evil you had fought all your life, was finally found in a small, windowless storage room. There were no maps, no radio, no final fanatic guard detail. Only an old man in a wheelchair, covered by a dirty blanket. The air was thick with the stench of urine and the sour smell of death. He was the legendary commander, the ‘Butcher of Cologne.’

He was already blind. His cloudy eyes stared blankly ahead, drooling from the corner of his mouth, uttering meaningless, rattling sounds. He didn't even realize you had arrived. He was already a living corpse, a breathing lump of flesh that had been judged ahead of time by time and disease. The Iron Cross medal on his wall was covered in dust, and the uniform symbolizing his sin smelled of mold.

The squad leader looked at you, signaling with his eyes. It was your turn. This was your trophy, your glory. Go, finish this Teutonic demon, offer this final, most precious sacrifice to your faith. You raised your rifle, the muzzle aimed at that aging, unconscious head. You imagined Marshal Yazov's resolute gaze, and you tried to summon the holy fury that had sustained you for eighteen years.

But there was nothing.

You were facing not a demon, but a pathetic, putrefying creature. Killing him would bring no glory, only the tedious feeling of cleaning up a janitor’s mess. Not killing him, however, would mean that everything in your past, the sacrifice of your comrades, had been a total black comedy revolving around an empty shell.

Your faith, at this moment, in this cramped storage room filled with the smell of decay, flickered like a candle in the wind, and then went out completely. You fired one shot. The sound was muffled amidst the piles of books. You had completed the mission.

On the last page of your diary, with a trembling hand, you wrote only one word. After writing it, you threw the diary into the pile of burning books.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE_150_tt: For the same fate awaits all, both the righteous and the wicked, the good and the bad... later, all go to the dead.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.151.desc:
Many years have passed since the world-destroying war, and as time flows on, the wounds of the past are gradually being smoothed over. The survivors raise their heads and continue advancing toward the next day.

On the silent Russian lands, rumors persist that Bukharin still lives—the man widely considered inseparable from the Soviet defeat. It is said he is now hiding in a deep, remote forest. Some seek to find and judge him, while others hope to use him to understand the pre-cataclysm past, the history that many have forgotten, as if it never happened. Other rumors claim that the Teutons, with whom the Russians share a blood feud, also survive in the distant West, but that is too far to verify easily.

A faction is fanatically propagating the belief that all humanity has endured is the will of God. They label the time before and after the cataclysm the Old World and the New World, proclaiming that God allowed the Old World to perish, and they, the humans born in the New World, are His messengers. Their mission is to lead the people of the New World forward, to avoid repeating the Old World's mistakes, and allow the New World to flourish upon the corpse of the Old. Naturally, some oppose them, arguing that the Old World has not entirely vanished, that many things prove its continued existence, and that they are not messengers of God but utter frauds.

Yet another group consists of the remnants of the Old World, their memories filled with the sealed, kaleidoscopic histories of the past. They cannot accept the fact that they have lost most of what they held dear. They have become either frenzied or depressed, asserting that everything in the present is fake, a void. They are unwilling to emerge from the illusion of the past; they cannot break free. The past tightly coils around them like chains. They are all people living in the past—people who should have died in the cataclysm.

However, every person on the wasteland, every person in the New World, is, without exception, desperately searching for stories of the cataclysm or the time before it. Be it oral accounts or documented records, they greedily absorb everything related to the past. They may have smoothed over the wounds of yesteryear, or perhaps they have not. Everything of that past has seemingly been torn into a thousand pieces and scattered across the world—some thrown into the ocean, never to see the light of day, some hurled into magma, turning to dust to be scattered to the boundless distance by the wind, and some landing in human hands, coming to be known.

The past has become a void, and humanity is responsible for filling it, fragmented and messy though it may be.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.151.a: Men continue to search for the stories of the past, piecing together the broken tiles of history.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.152.desc:
Yazov stood on a height, using his central argument to introduce the reason for his speech: \“Comrades! I know that all of you feel stifled living in the bunker, but the bandits who once ravaged Mother Russia are still standing in their Germanian lair! And what we must do is embark once more on the path of vengeance against our Western enemies!\”

After he finished speaking, the numerous Black League soldiers below applauded. Although they still possessed some enthusiasm, Yazov clearly sensed that a great portion of them were spent, with perhaps half only managing a bitter smile.

Inevitably, Yazov felt rage. He had done so much for them, leading them to avenge themselves against Germany, and in the end, they were not truly worshipping him but starting to complain? 

Traitors. Yes, even after the nuclear bombardment, the Teutons must have dispatched spies to closely monitor their every move on the Russian land! Traitors must have infiltrated this place! Yazov reconsidered. With current conditions alone, they could not defeat the Teutons. They must locate the supply caches stored across Russia before the nuclear war, and simultaneously, he must ensure the army remains as valiant as it once was.

But what exactly caused this low morale and empty stomachs?
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.152.a: There is a traitor, a seller of his kin.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.153.desc:
\“Once, the great founder of the League, the statesman, the military strategist... our Father of the Nation, Comrade Karbyshev, always placed his hope in us, entrusting the League to me, hoping that one day we could complete the Great Vengeance against the Teutons,\” Yazov shouted to the crowd, his words laced with sorrow and tragedy to incite the emotions of the army's soldiers.
 
\“······But sadly, the Great Teacher Karbyshev could not live to see the Russian Motherland break free from the Teuton's clutches and complete the Great Trial against them. He left us prematurely, lost in the vast forest······\” At this, many soldiers below consciously or unconsciously wept, grieving for the creator of the Black League.

\“But now, we are absolutely determined to achieve vengeance against the Teutons! We will slaughter the Teutons, leaving not a single piece of armor and making rivers of blood, fulfilling Comrade Karbyshev's dying wish!\” With that, the numerous Black League soldiers below erupted in cheers, applauding their leader—Dmitry Yazov.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.153.a: But is this truly what Karbyshev would have wanted?
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.154.desc:
\“Comrades of the League! Soldiers of the Army! Russians!\” Yazov began his address with an invigorating shout.

\“Since we first defeated the Teutonic Devils, the entire nation has held immense enthusiasm for their utter eradication—this, I believe, you know well.\” Snowflakes were blown by the fierce wind onto Yazov's hat and greatcoat, covering his insignia and medals, seemingly refuting Yazov's insane idea on behalf of the audience below.

Yazov cleared his throat: \“I know that many do not agree with my view, believing that after a world-destroying nuclear war, we are completely incapable of confronting the Teutons again. But I must declare—these people are despicable defeatists!\”

The statement stunned the audience. Many bodies jerked, but then, perhaps realizing their 'improper' behavior, they quickly relieved the awkwardness with applause and cheers. Yazov had anticipated this reaction, but he hadn't expected so many people to be so-called 'defeatists.'

What to do? Leave everyone present here, then send a few men over to mow them down with submachine guns? Yazov didn't have the confidence to do it, or rather, he had lost his former 'madness' since the nuclear war. If he killed so many people, who would defeat the Teutons? And how would future generations view him? A bloodthirsty killer? Yazov thought for a moment, and finally made his decision—
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.154.a: Make an example of one, and the others will understand.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.155.desc:
\“Oh, what the hell is this shit?\”

Vladimir stared, shocked and incredulous, at the letter mailed to the entrance of their company building. It 'righteously and sternly' claimed, with absurd and idiotic reasoning, that their company had violated the so-called 'DMCA Copyright Law,' infringing upon another entity's industrial copyright. Vladimir angrily slammed the letter onto his desk. \“What utter nonsense! I haven't seen anything on the market that looks remotely similar to the shovel we designed. Why the hell do they say I'm infringing? And what the fuck is a DMCA?\” Vladimir's thoughts were manifold, but he finally made a decision. \“Hand this letter to Marshal Yazov to look at, maybe he'll have some idea?\”

Yazov was sitting in his office. After unifying all of Russia, he finally had some rare downtime. He slumped in his chair, sipping coffee, reminiscing about the good old days with Karbyshev······

\“Commander-in-Chief! Our military shovel supplier has an urgent matter!\” Yazov's secretary burst open the office door with a loud bang. Startled, Yazov spat out the coffee in his mouth, splashing the papers on his desk.

\“Can't they handle it themselves? Why bother me?\” Yazov's eyes were wide with anger, annoyed at Vladimir and his secretary for interrupting his much-needed rest. \“Apologies, Commander-in-Chief Yazov, but you must see this!\” Yazov took the letter from his secretary's hand, read a few lines, and then asked in confusion:
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.156.desc:
My name is Pyotr. I’ve been a line worker on the assembly line at the Black League’s military shovel factory for less than a month. My days are usually ordinary, but this morning a letter filled with incomprehensible rhetoric arrived in the factory mailbox. It said: \“Attention, a dmca copyright infringement notice has been issued for this product. This complaint will be reviewed, communication will be made with the company producing this product, and details and information regarding subsequent matters will be provided.\” We were instantly in an uproar. The boss, Vladimir, was shocked when he heard about it, as he knew absolutely nothing about this 'Dmca.' So he quickly used his channels to contact Comrade Yazov, but even Comrade Yazov was completely bewildered. Then, something more serious happened: the clothes on our backs, the reinforced concrete in our factory walls, our machine tools, the iron blocks stored in our warehouse, and even the socks in Vladimir’s office all began receiving these 'dmca notices.' It’s said that even Marshal Yazov's hat and tea mug were not spared. And no one knows where these things came from, only that they were sent by someone named 'Script.' Heaven knows why he would do this? And why is his name so strange?

Eventually, our factory learned that \“A successful Black League DMCA takedown will enter a 10-day to 1-month removal period. During this time, if the complaining party does not send an email to 'Steam' requesting the removal of the DMCA, the reported party will most likely be ordered to cease production/have its business license revoked.\” Although we never figured out what organization instructed that strange person to send this file, when we sent an appeal letter to the email address mentioned in the notice, the letters we received mysteriously vanished! How amazing!

The League was in chaos for a while because everything was being sent these threatening letters! The worst thing is that the identity of the person who was sending 'dmca' notices everywhere was never disclosed, but I learned from my cousin in the Ministry of Justice that a private company with a name starting with 'V' eventually arrested him. They supposedly used the method of \“banning the Script account?\” Unfortunately, the organization behind that person remains at large······ it's truly hateful!
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.156.a: What the hell is all this?
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.157.desc:
Father was right.

Today, I saw the sun. The elders in the bunker always described it as a giant ball of eye-stinging fire, but in my logbook, I must honestly write that it is more like a warm, orange badge suspended in the firmament. Its light is not searing; filtered by a thin, never-dissipating gray veil of cloud, it gently spills over this vast··· endless land. For the first time in my life, I felt small, not the smallness squeezed out by the concrete walls in the bunker, but the willing surrender to something truly great, called 'the world.' The loud clang of the steel elevator door closing behind me sounded like a ceremonial cannonade for me, for us, ushering in the new age!

The air, yes, the air! The Commissar ordered us to keep our gas masks on, saying the air was poisoned by the Teutons. But I secretly lifted a corner of my mask and took a small breath. The smell··· was completely different from what my father described. It lacked the scent of pine or the smell of earth after rain. It was complex, carrying rust, burnt wood, and a kind of··· dry dust. Yet, this is still the smell of 'freedom'! The real scent that the circulation system can never fully filter out! I love this smell; it makes me feel alive, no longer an existence maintained by nutrient paste and a number in the bunker.

We are advancing west. The armored personnel carrier is bumpy, but I insisted on opening a narrow slit in the observation window. Everything I see is both exactly like the propaganda posters and completely different. Destroyed houses are like the skeletons of giants, and twisted rail tracks point toward the void of the sky. This is scorched earth, this is hell, this is a monument to Teutonic sin. But there is no fear in my heart, only a sacred sense of mission burning. I, Pavel, an ordinary soldier of the Black League, will personally cleanse this land and water the peaceful wheat field of my father's stories with the blood of the enemy. The company's song is already ringing in my ears; though muffled through the gas mask, every note strikes my heart.

Father always told me before sleep that before the nuclear blast, the world was a song. Now, it is only noise and silence. But we will become the new singers! We will compose the overture with gunfire and play the magnificent movement with artillery fire until the Final Judgment is complete, and the world will once again hear the Russian Mother's lullaby. I wipe my sidearm over and over. Its gun body is more real, more trustworthy than anything I ever saw in the bunker. I can't wait. I can't wait to see the first enemy, the first symbol of sin that needs to be 'deleted.' This will be my first, and purest, gift to the New World.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.157.a: He wrote the final sentence with force. \“Let the Trial begin! For the League!\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE_157_tt:
Then the Lord said to Moses, ‘Stretch out your hand toward heaven, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, a darkness to be felt.’
—Exodus 10:21
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.158.desc:
I killed a man today.

I wrote this sentence, crossed it out, and wrote it again. The ink bled on the paper, like an indelible stain. I do not know how to record this. This was not the battle I expected. No charge, no shouting, not even decent resistance. The ruins of Danzig were like a giant, silent cemetery. We were merely passing between the gravestones, searching for ghosts that had not yet completely decomposed.

He was hiding in a half-collapsed cellar. The squad leader kicked open the rotten wooden board and shone his flashlight inside. What we saw was not a weapon-wielding Teutonic soldier, but an··· old man. His body was withered like a dry branch, clothed in rags, holding a gray, mold-spotted hard stone in his hand—we later learned it was a solidified block of concrete. He saw the barrels of our guns, but showed no panic, no anger. He merely raised the stone tremblingly and repeated one word in a language I couldn't understand. His eyes, those murky, almost lusterless eyes, were pleading.

The squad leader nudged my lower back with his gun barrel. 'Rookie, your turn.' His voice held a hint of impatience, almost boredom. My heart instantly froze. This was my first time, my 'baptism.' I had trained countless times, punching holes in thousands of targets on the shooting range. But the targets were made of paper; they wouldn't look at you with that kind of gaze.

I raised my gun. My hand was shaking. I tried to summon the slogans I had memorized by heart, the bloody history of Karbyshev and the millions of massacred compatriots. But now, they all turned into hollow noise. In my sight, there were only those eyes. They held no hatred, no fear, only a kind of··· pure confusion that I couldn't understand. As if asking: Why?

I closed my eyes and pulled the trigger.

The gunshot echoed loudly in the ruins. I opened my eyes. He didn't drop instantly like a target. The bullet made a small hole in his chest, and dark blood slowly seeped out, staining his ragged coat. He looked down at his chest, then back up at me, and that confused look deepened. Then, he simply crumpled, like a statue molded from poor-quality clay, all support suddenly removed, quietly collapsing into a heap. The block of concrete in his hand rolled to my feet. It was all over.

In my diary, I should have written, 'I eliminated an enemy for the League.' But now, all I want to know is, what did that last word of his mean? And those eyes··· why is it that all I see when I close my eyes are those eyes? They stare at me, like a question that will never be answered.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE_158_tt:
then the Lord God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature.
—Genesis 2:7
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.159.t: Day Forty-Five: The Bitter Honey of Canaan
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.159.desc:
Another cleansing operation.

That word, the Commissar likes to use it. \“Cleansing,\” as if we are clearing away trash, not extinguishing one life after another. On the barren grasslands of Walterland, we are like a group of tireless farmers, harvesting the remaining lives. The order said these villages sheltered partisans. But all we found were silent old men and women with vacant eyes.

Killing has begun to feel as natural as breathing, and just as tedious. Resting the butt of the gun on my shoulder, feeling the recoil, and watching a body fall. My movements are becoming more practiced, but my heart is becoming emptier. The pin-prick of pain I felt in the ruins of Danzig has become dull. In its place is a deeper, pervasive numbness.

Today, we surrounded a farmhouse. Inside, we heard a woman crying and children screaming. When I kicked open the door, I saw a woman shielding two children with her body. Her blonde hair was messy, her face smudged with stove ash, but her eyes···

Those eyes were like two blue shards of ice, piercing deep into my memory.

Father once showed me an old photo from before the nuclear blast. It was my mother. I don't remember her; there were no records of her in the bunker. But in the photo, she had those very eyes. Father said Mother died in a Teutonic air raid, and at the time, she was also shielding··· shielding a sister I never had.

I fired the gun.

My body moved on its own, as if it wasn't mine. The bullet tore through the air, and the woman's cries ceased abruptly. The children watched in horror as their mother fell, then looked at the barrel of my gun.

In that instant, my mind was blank. I felt as if I saw my father standing before me. He was not wearing the Black League uniform, but the patched-up old work clothes issued in the bunker. On his face was the same··· incomprehensible confusion mixed with sadness that I saw when I killed the old man in Danzig.

Was I, too, once shielded like this? Was I, too, once the protected child in another story?

And what am I··· doing now?

Later, I sat by the fire, flipping through my diary. I saw the fervent words I wrote on the seventh day and felt like I was reading a stranger's story. Is the Pavel who longed to 'cleanse the world' the same Pavel who shot a mother's likeness today?

I thought of the bunker, of my small 'home' with just a bed and a storage box. There were no windows, no real sunlight, but at least··· there were no cries there.

My memories began to blur. Father's face and the face of the old man in Danzig overlapped in the firelight. The eyes in Mother's photo and the eyes of the woman who fell today became the same pair.
I suddenly had an absurd and terrifying thought.

Could every old man I kill here be my father?

Could every woman I kill be my mother?

In the Final Judgment, am I judging··· myself?
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE_159_tt:
I said in my heart with regard to the children of man that God is testing them that they may see that they themselves are but beasts.
—Ecclesiastes 3:18
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.160.t: Day Sixty-One: The Blood of the Lamb
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.160.desc:
Moist air blows in from the Baltic Sea, carrying a salty, tear-like smell. We are camped in a marsh. The cold, damp weather and ceaseless fighting have stretched the company's mood thin, like a bowstring pulled to its limit. Last night, a comrade named Sergey broke down. He threw his gun into the mud, knelt there, repeatedly slamming his head against a dead tree, shouting his wife's name.

Today, the Commissar gathered the entire company.

Sergey was dragged, bound hand and foot, to the front of the formation. His eyes were vacant, and he was still muttering something. The Commissar stood on a stone, his voice like tempered steel, cold, hard, and devoid of warmth.

\“A soldier of the Black League has no family, no past, no weakness!\” His gaze swept over every one of us. \“Your merciful Mother is Russia, and your Father is Marshal Yazov! Your faith is the spirit of Comrade Karbyshev! Any form of pity is a betrayal of the League! A betrayal of our fallen compatriots! A profanity against the sacred cause of the Final Judgment!\”

He pulled out his pistol.

\“Think of Marshal Yazov! Think of Comrade Karbyshev! Did they waver for a moment while enduring their hardships? What does your suffering count for compared to theirs? Compared to what our entire nation has endured?!\”

A gunshot.

Sergey's body recoiled and fell into the mud and water. No more prayers, no more calls. Everything fell silent. Only the rustling of the wind through the reeds remained.

I stood in the formation, watching the scene. My body did not shake, and my heart did not even register a major ripple. It was a numbness that transcended fear, a feeling of being completely emptied. The Commissar's words were like a surgeon's knife, precisely excising the last remnant of the tumor in my heart named 'humanity.'

Yes, he is right.

To survive, one must abandon feeling.
To win, one must become a tool.

Home, father, mother··· these are all illusions. They are decaying flesh that must be cut out to prevent infection. The only truth is the order. The only meaning is pulling the trigger.

That night, I burned the copy of my mother's old photograph. The flame licked the photo paper; those blue eyes looked at me one last time, then turned to ash. I also tore out the diary pages from the past few days and threw them into the fire. Those questions, that confusion, that raving about 'father' and 'mother,' were all proof of weakness.

From today, Pavel is dead. What lives on is a soldier. An executor··· with no past and no need for a future.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.160.a: \“I volunteer to be the blade of the Trial.\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE_160_tt:
Command Aaron and his sons, saying, This is the law of the burnt offering... The fire on the altar shall be kept burning; it shall not go out.
—Leviticus 6:9
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.161.t: Day Ninety-Eight: Babel on the Earth
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.161.desc:
Log Entry. Date: Trial Day +98. Location: Sector G-4, Former Silesian Industrial Complex. Weather: Continuous acid rain. Visibility: Poor.

Today's Mission: Clear Furnace #3 and surrounding ancillary buildings. Alpha Team handles the east wing, Bravo Team (our team) handles the west wing. Resistance Encountered: Moderate. Enemy units consist mainly of local militias and retired veterans, armed with light weapons and a small number of explosives.

10:00 - Operation commences.

10:17 - First contact at the entrance to Warehouse C. Enemy 2 personnel, MP40, cleared. No casualties on our side.

10:45 - Advance along the pipeline corridor. Narrow passage, tripwire explosive x1 discovered and disarmed.

11:23 - Entered the main furnace building. Enemy strongpoint located on the second-floor platform. After suppressing fire, cleared using hand grenade x2. Confirmed enemy units x4 KIA. Our soldier Ivan sustained a graze wound to his left arm from shrapnel, bandaged.

12:30 - Midday break. Ration: Type B nutrient bar x1, purified water 500ml. Ammunition check: 7.62mm x 94, hand grenade x2. Equipment status good.

13:10 - Continue advance. Search of ground-level worker's lounge. Discovered hidden civilians x7 (male 2, female 3, child 2). Processed according to Regulation L-7.

Did I··· forget something.

14:05 - Alpha Team reports the east wing is cleared. Bravo Team begins final sweep of the underground pump room.

14:28 - Remaining enemy unit x1 in the pump room, armed with a hunting rifle, resisting stubbornly. Cleared.

15:00 - Mission complete. Entire area controlled. Today's Combat Results:

Team Confirmed Kills: 7 combat units, 7 non-combat units.

Team Ammunition Expenditure: 7.62mm x 88 rounds, hand grenade x2.

Team Personnel Loss: 1 light injury.

Captured Supplies: Rifles x3 (damaged), canned food x12 cans (label corroded, pending inspection), miscellaneous medical supplies.
Mission Efficiency Assessment: Excellent.

Temperature: 6 degrees Celsius. Humidity: 92%. Wind Direction: Northwest.

It rained today.

I feel··· good. High efficiency. Smooth operation. Physical functions normal. Pulse steady.

Hope tomorrow will be better.

For the cause of the Great Trial.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.161.a: \“What are the coordinates for the next objective?\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE_161_tt:
I have seen everything that is done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and a striving after wind.
—Ecclesiastes 1:14
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.162.t: Day One Hundred and Thirty-Four: The Sweat of Gethsemane
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.162.desc:
It's raining. Raining again. Black forest, black rain. The trees here are all dead, like burnt fingers reaching for the sky. They call the resistors 'Werewolves.' A bunch of children. Hiding in the woods, shooting at us with homemade bombs and rusty hunting rifles. Laughable.

The fight was short. They didn't even know how to properly set up crossfire. We lost an APC and two men were injured. Then, it was over. We swept them out of the woods like raking autumn leaves.

I killed a... a boy.

He was about my age. Maybe younger. I came around a tree, and he was fumbling to load an old rifle. When he saw me, there was no fear on his face, only a beast-like astonishment. I fired. Instinct. Training. Like breathing. When he fell, something slipped out of his tattered jacket pocket. It was a piece of paper. A piece of paper, wet with rain and folded neatly.

It was a drawing. Crayon. Childishly drawn, with crooked lines. A yellow, smiling sun. Below the sun were three small stick figures holding hands. A man, a woman, and a smaller child. In the corner of the drawing, a name was scrawled crookedly in pencil: Klaus.

The Sun.

That's right··· how long has it been since I saw the real sun? Not in the bunker. On the surface, it is only a dim orange disc. Did I··· ever draw the sun? In the bunker's nursery, with the rationed, never-enough crayon stubs? I can't remember. Father······ Father's face, I can't recall it. The harder I try to think, the more blurred it becomes, until only a pair of······ a pair of sorrowful eyes remains.

I stood by the boy's corpse, looking at the drawing. The rain washed the colors across the paper, and the yellow sun wept colored tears.

Then, I heard laughter.

Not my comrades. It was a kind of······ children's laughter. Very clear, right in my ear. I spun around; there was only the sound of rain and wind in the forest. I heard it again. This time, clearer. They were calling my name. Pavel.

\“Pavel, come play.\”
\“Pavel, the sun is out.\”

I started to tremble. Not from the cold. I raised my gun, aiming at the dark woods.

\“Who's there?!\” I roared.

No one answered. Only the lingering, children's laughter. It came from all directions, burrowing into my ears, into my mind. They were laughing at me. Laughing at me, the··· monster who killed the boy who drew the sun. I began to shoot wildly, emptying an entire magazine. Bullets tore the bark and splashed water in the mud.

But the laughter didn't stop. They were still laughing.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.162.a: Silence! All of you, shut up!
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE_162_tt:
Should women eat their offspring, the children of their tender care? . . . Look, O Lord, and see!
—Lamentations 2:20
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.163.t: Day One Hundred and Fifty-One: The Rain of Gomorrah
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.163.desc:
Blood. It's red. Warm.

The city is burning. No, the world is burning. I feel like I am standing by the huge furnace that is incinerating the world, and every breath inhales hot ash. Steel melts, stone weeps, and the air is filled with screaming and the smell of roasted meat. It's magnificent. This is a symphony, a requiem for the dead personally conducted by Marshal Yazov. Shells are the timpani, machine guns the violins, and my rifle··· is the principal flute, playing the most gorgeous, sharpest movement of death.

Yes, yes, they are singing in my ear. The children who never existed in the bunker, the children I personally sent to see the sun. Their voices are no longer distant; they have sprouted directly from my spinal cord, resonating through my teeth. They swing on the trapeze in my mind, knocking on my skull with their bones, singing hymns to me. \“Pavel,\” they giggle, \“this is Babylon, the lair of the Great Harlot. Tear down her walls, smash her children against the stones!\”

I know, I know! This is the source of sin. Every brick is soaked with Russian tears, every inch of the sewer flows with Slav blood. Every living thing is a poisonous snake and deserves to die.

Purification. That word, I remember it. What a beautiful word. Like the first dewdrop of morning, falling on a red-hot iron plate, instantly evaporating, taking all the filth away. I am executing a sacred baptism, with fire and steel.

The Commissar is dead. I watched him die. Yesterday afternoon, three seventeen. A 152-millimeter shell, precise, elegant, like God's scalpel. His upper body flew onto the roof over there; his lower body remained where it was, twitching, like a crushed beetle. I watched his intestines hang from the utility pole, fluttering like holiday streamers in the wind. So beautiful. He was always roaring in our ears that we were the blade of the Trial. Well, the blade dulls with use, but the offering is eternal. He became the plumpest piece of meat in our grand sacrifice. Good. That's fair.

I see them. Those crawling out of the basement, hands raised, clutching wrinkled white cloth. They are begging for mercy. Begging mercy from whom? From the dead Commissar? Or from me?
HAHAHAHAHAHAHAHAHAHA!

I am not Pavel anymore. Who is Pavel? An idiot who would write \“I do not understand\” in his diary? A coward who would tremble because of a naive children's drawing? No. He is dead. Killed thoroughly by the children's laughter, by the sun that wept colored tears for the blonde boy.

I am the firestorm. I am the acid rain. I am the sulfur and wrath descending from heaven. I am the extension of Marshal Yazov's steel will, the incarnation of Comrade Karbyshev's avenging spirit! I am the prophet of the New World, the gravedigger of the Old World!

The children are clapping their small hands in my ear; their voices drown out the artillery fire. \“Kill, Pavel, kill them all,\” they sing. \“The sun is coming out soon, red, beautiful sun!\”

Of course, I must kill. This is my sacred duty. This is my communion. That young soldier holding a family photo, his golden hair covered in brain matter and dust, so beautiful. He wanted me to see his wife and baby. I glanced at them. Very lovely offerings. Then I shoved the gun barrel into his mouth. Bang. The world instantly became quiet. So good.

My comrades······ Sergey, Ivan······ the way they look at me is strange. Like they are looking at a wild beast, a monster. They don't even dare to approach me. How ridiculous. They are the blind ones, their eyes covered by the mere appearance of flesh and blood. They cannot see the avenging Seraphim circling above this city of sin. They cannot hear the sacred songs urging me on. They are lost lambs, yet they presume to judge the one wielding the shepherd's crook with their pathetic morality······ No, I am not a shepherd. I am the wolf, commanded by God to kill all the diseased sheep.

Today, I drew another sun. With a German officer's blood. On the wall of his office. It's a good drawing. Very round. Very red. Like Father's··· No, do not think of Father. Father is dead. I am too. We are all dead. Everyone is dead.

We are merely corpses wearing human skin, dancing tirelessly at this grand funeral dedicated to the Void.

So much fun.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.163.a: This page of the diary is illegible.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE_163_tt:
Then I saw an angel standing in the sun, and with a loud voice he called to all the birds that fly directly overhead, “Come, gather for the great supper of God.”
—Revelation 19:17
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.164.t: Day One Hundred and Seventy-Two: \“It is Finished\” on Golgotha
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.164.desc:
It is finished.

Smoke still rises from the charred skeleton of the dome, like gray, weary, never-dissipating sighs floating toward the leaden sky. I stand alone on top of this massive tomb called the 'Reichstag,' my feet resting on shattered stone carvings, melted metal, countless twisted shell casings, and a thick layer of white powder that puffs up with the wind. I grab a handful and rub it between my fingers. The texture is fine, the sensation cold. I don't know if this is the century-old archive burned to ash, or the cremated remains of a parliamentarian. Perhaps there is no difference. Everything eventually returns to dust.

This is the end. The final coordinates pointed to by every map in the bunker, the sacred climax of every Commissar's speech, the sole navigation point of my one hundred and seventy-two days of hellish journey. This is the sanctuary of all my zealotry, all my killing, all my dreams and ravings. I have imagined this moment countless times. I thought that when I stood here, the sky would descend with fiery revelation, the earth would tremble with my victory, I would hear the souls of millions of fallen compatriots singing hymns of praise, and I would feel a god-like ecstasy of incinerating the Old World and creating a new epoch.

But I feel nothing.

The children's laughter in my ears is gone. As if they were just mischievous kids leading the way for me, and now that the destination has been reached, they have scattered, returning to their non-existent homes.

The burning heat in my blood that urged me to kill and made me tremble has also cooled. Like an overheated engine that has finally run out of its last drop of fuel, now only cold, dead steel remains.

The grand visions of 'Angel of Destruction' and 'Sacred Purification' in my mind have silently faded away, like the hot flush after a high fever.

What remains··· is nothing.

A vast, dead, chilling void, emptier than the deepest permafrost layer of the bunker.

I look down at my hands. They are covered in dried, blackened bloodstains and indelible gunpowder residue. They once acted like two independent hammers with their own will, shattering countless skulls. They were the most faithful executors of this Trial. But now, looking at them, I feel only estrangement. As if they belong to another person. The madman called 'Pavel.' And I am just a weary tenant who happened to inhabit his shell.

Did I win? Yes, we won. On the highest point of the ruins, the black banner, emblazoned with the hammer and sickle and stained with blood and fire, is fluttering fiercely in the wind. It proclaims our victory.
Did I take vengeance? Yes, I suppose so. Every inch of this city has been soaked with Teutonic blood. This was a payment in kind, a blood debt settled down to the marrow.
But so what?

My father's blurred face will not become clearer because of this. The boy who drew the sun in the Brandenburg forest will not pick up his crayon again. I responded to destruction with destruction. I ended killing with killing. The final result is merely turning one ruin into a larger, more complete, and more hopeless ruin.

The burning spine called 'Hatred' that supported me throughout this journey snapped crisply the moment I reached the destination. The mad flame has consumed itself, leaving only cold ash and a nauseating smell of char. I feel tired. An unprecedented, unspeakable exhaustion that arises from the deepest part of the soul. Like a pilgrim who has traveled thousands of miles, finally climbed to the top of the mountain, only to clearly see that there is nothing there. Not even an idol to kneel before.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE_164_tt:
The seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, and a loud voice came out of the temple, from the throne, saying, “It is done!”
—Revelation 16:17
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.165.t: Day One Hundred and Eighty-Five: No Ripple on the Sea of Salt
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.165.desc:
The Sea.

They call it the sea. It's the first time I've seen it.

Father once said the sea was blue, like Mother's eyes. All the descriptions of the sea in the bunker were inseparable from words like \“azure,\” \“magnificent,\” and \“cradle of life.\”

This··· thing before me is not blue.

The gray sky hangs low, like a giant canvas soaked in dirty water, threatening to collapse at any moment from its own weight. Below the sky is a gray beach. The sand is mixed with metal fragments, charred wood, and some unrecognizable, white bone shards. Stepping on it produces a hollow, teeth-grinding friction sound.

Then there is the sea itself.

Gray waves, ceaselessly and successively, surge onto the beach, then wearily retreat. They seem to have no power, no anger, only a mechanical, eternal, and meaningless repetition. The sound of the waves is not a roar, but a low, continuous sigh, as if the entire Earth is groaning from an incurable agony. The air is filled with saltiness, the smell of rotten seaweed, and a faint, chemical odor that will never dissipate.

There are no seagulls here. No ships. No life. Only me and this boundless expanse of gray liquid.

I stood here for a long time. Several hours, perhaps a whole day. My comrades are carrying out the final, equally meaningless 'cleansing' in the village behind me, but the squad leader didn't rush me. Perhaps even he is tired of it. The war is over. We won. Now all that's left is garbage time, cleaning up the mess.

I gazed at this sea, trying to find any trace of the beauty I was once told about. But there was none. All I saw was myself. My inner self is this gray sea. The ceaseless yet meaningless waves are my past days and nights—the killings, the marches, the days of numbness. The wreckage on the beach is my dismembered memory. The color of the sky is the background color of my soul.

I once believed I was a tool with a purpose, a blade forged for the 'Final Judgment.' But now, standing before this ultimate desolation, I understand that I am nothing. I am not a tool, nor a soldier, not even Pavel. I am just a grain of sand accidentally pushed onto this beach by the giant wave of war, no different from all the other dead and living grains of sand. When the next wave comes, I will be taken away, disappearing into this gray void, leaving no trace.

The world my father spoke of, the future the Commissar promised, the Old World I fought to destroy and destroyed myself··· all the grand narratives, all the noble reasons, ultimately dissolve into the meaningless grayness before my eyes. Why does humanity repeat its mistakes again and again? I get no answer from this silent sea. Perhaps there is no answer at all. We are simply repeating an absurd, unstoppable cycle until the last grain of sand is ground into dust.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.165.a: The Baltic Sea is discovered. The water body is grayish-brown, with no signs of life.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE_165_tt:
Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more.
—Revelation 21:1
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.166.t: Day ???: The Silence of the Sixth Day
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.166.desc:
If you can see this paper.
But I know you can't. In this vast, gray wasteland abandoned by the gods, there will be no second living person. Only the wind, and the ash carried by the wind.
It is now the 193rd day since the Trial.
Maybe the 194th. Sunrise and sunset here are just a gray deception. Time has lost its meaning.
I only write down the conclusion.

Failure. Failure. Failure.

I try to remember what the bunker ceiling looked like. There was a crack on it, like a winding, gray river. Father once pointed to it and told me it was a map leading to the surface. If we followed this river, we could find the exit.

It was all wrong. Everything was wrong. From the first brick of the bunker. From the first story my father told. From the first time I pulled the trigger. All wrong. I thought I could find the answer. In East Prussia, in Danzig, in the ashes of Berlin, on the shore of that gray sea. I thought at the end of this journey, there would be a reason, a meaning, even a concrete devil I could hate.

I'm sorry. Those three words look ridiculous when written. Who should I say them to? To those who died by my gun? They cannot hear. To Father? He only lives in my fragmented memories, and those fragments I burned with my own hands. To Marshal Yazov? To him, I was just a serviceable bullet that has now malfunctioned.

I wanted to say it to the old man in Danzig.
I wanted to say it to the mother in Walterland.
I wanted to say it to the boy who drew the sun in Brandenburg.
I wanted to say it to the soldier in the Battle of Berlin who cried to me while holding a family photo.
I even··· wanted to say it to my own mother, whose face I never remembered.
But I can't say anything. Only ashes remain in my mouth.
I do not love this world. It never loved me. It only gave me a gun, a number, and a wrong reason.
I hate you.
I hate you for bringing me into existence.
I don't mean my parents. I hate all people. I hate the lunatic who decided to press the nuclear button. I hate the Commissar who instilled hatred in me in the bunker. I hate the God who permitted all of this—if He even exists. I hate every single person who participated in this colossal deception, including myself.
I hate you for teaching me hatred.
I hate you for telling me this was a great, holy cause.
I hate myself··· for believing all of it.
I hate this planet, this land, this gray sky, this ceaseless sea. I hate every breath, every heartbeat, because they remind me that I am still alive, still trapped in this failed, rotten experiment.
I hate these hands that kill. I hate this heart that no longer beats. I hate this empty shell of a body that still breathes.
But···

But what if··· what if this is just another one of my hallucinations. What if someone, many, many years from now, truly unearths this paper from the sandstorm.
Tell me something.
I need to know.
I killed so many people. So many men, women, old people, children. I personally turned their world into the same hell as my own heart.
So··· how is the home we swore to protect now?
Can the children there eat real bread, instead of moldy nutrient paste?
Will their fathers still be sent to the endless mines for speaking a few truths?
Is the sky there··· still gray?

Why does humanity repeat its mistakes again and again?
Did we overthrow a giant tower of tyranny built with the Eagle's emblem only to build an identical one with the same bricks, in the name of the Hammer and Sickle?
What we did··· all this blood, fire, sacrifice, and madness··· what the hell did it change?
Tell me. I need an answer.

I see the sun. It is beautiful and warm. It shines on an endless golden wheat field, children chase blue butterflies along the ridges, and women sing ancient songs I have never heard.
I see it.
But I know···
The hell··· it's not here.

It doesn't··· matter anymore.
 The Trial is over. Now, it's my turn. This is the final purification.
It's time.

The paper lies quietly on a rusted ammunition box, next to a disassembled, meticulously clean rifle. On the back of the paper, someone has written a few words in a completely different, calm, and neat handwriting.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.166.a: \“Day One. The weather is good today.\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE_166_tt:
For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.
—Romans 7:15
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.167.t: Log Entry #7342: On the Relativity of Time
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.167.desc:
【Audio Recording Begins】

···System self-check complete. Purification unit pressure stable at 4.7 standard atmospheres. Carbon dioxide concentration in hydroponics farms A, B, and C nominal. Backup generator unit temperature··· nominal.

【Brief silence, only the faint hum of the ventilation system in the background】

Daily system status report. Recorder: Vadim Petrovich, ID 734.

Today is··· 【Long pause】 Today is the 7,342nd cycle. Since the Day of the 'Great Trial.'

【A weary sigh, seemingly unintentional】

Apologies. I shouldn't··· this is not protocol.

It’s just, sometimes, I look at that number. Seven thousand three hundred and forty-two. It’s precise, it's orderly, like everything else in the bunker. Our heartbeats are monitored, our calorie intake is calculated, and every breath of air we take is precisely regulated by this colossal, sleepless machine of steel. But a 'day'··· how long is a 'day'? The master clock tells me it's twenty-four hours. No more, no less. But I no longer remember what a 'day' looks like when it's not defined by the switch of a halogen lamp.

I am responsible for maintaining the archives here. Digital. This place holds the entire memory of the Black League, countless tactical analyses, engineering blueprints, ideological manifestos. All files have timestamps accurate to the second. But for me, time has become a stagnant, murky pool. Every morning, no, at the start of every 'cycle,' I get up from my bunk, walk through the identical, gray-painted metal corridors. The air smells identically of a mix of disinfectant and nutrient paste, and the pale lights overhead are identically, perpetually unchanging. My job is to organize the records from yesterday··· no, the previous cycle. But what is the difference between the last cycle, the one before that, and the one seven thousand cycles ago?

Sometimes, I secretly open my personal terminal. There is only one photo inside. It's my wife, Anna. Before the Great Trial, we lived together in a small border town. That photo··· was taken on a sunny day. Yes, 'sunny day,' what a foreign word. The resolution is low; I can't even clearly see the freckles on her face anymore. But I remember, I should remember··· the fine lines around her eyes when she smiled. Is that right? I··· I'm not sure anymore. I look at this photo every day, forcing myself to recall. I'm afraid, I'm afraid that one day, this low-resolution image will completely replace the vivid, breathing Anna in my mind. Am I··· slowly forgetting what she truly looks like? Forgetting her voice? Forgetting the warmth of her hand?

The bunker saved our lives. But it is slowly, little by little··· stealing our souls. We have all become parts of this giant machine, well-maintained, but having long lost our original function. We wait here. We wait for the surface radiation to dissipate, we wait for the Commander-in-Chief to give the order to return to the surface. We are waiting for a great vengeance.

But··· how long must we wait?

Ten years? Twenty years? Fifty years? When that day truly arrives, will we still have the strength to hate? Or will we have become pale cave-dwellers who only know how to survive in the bunker, having long forgotten that there was a world outside that needed our vengeance?

I do not know.

I only know that the 7342nd cycle has begun. Everything is··· nominal.

【A long silence】

Recorder Vadim Petrovich. End of report. Please··· please delete the latter half of this recording. Thank you.

【Audio Recording Ends】
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.168.desc:
The National Education Center in Sector C-7 of the bunker was less a classroom than an undecorated, austere chapel. There were no windows, the walls were cold, unfinished concrete, and the only light came from rows of buzzing halogen lamps on the ceiling. The light was sickly pale, illuminating the faces of one hundred straight-backed sixteen-year-old youths, and also the bottomless chill in the eyes of the Commissar on the podium.

Today was their last lesson. Tomorrow, they would put on uniforms and become formal soldiers of the League, new cogs in the colossal machine of the Great Trial.

Commissar Sergey Volkov did not stand behind the podium. He paced before the cadets, the sound of his leather boots on the floor the only rhythm in this vast, silent space. He was slender, dressed in a perfectly ironed, wrinkle-free uniform, with almost no expression on his face.

\“Lift your heads,\” his voice was not loud, but exceptionally clear, piercing everyone's eardrums like an ice pick. \“Look into my eyes. Today, we will not discuss tactics, regulations, or rations. We will only discuss one thing. One thing that happened before you were born, but which has defined your entire life and will determine how you die.\”

He paused, his gaze sweeping over the nervous yet expectant faces of the cadets in the front row one by one.

\“Some of your parents came from Leningrad, some from Moscow, some from Kyiv, some from Stalingrad. They once possessed something called 'home.' A place with wooden floors, where you could smell borscht, and see the stars outside the window. They also once had··· family.\”

Volkov's voice was completely flat, as if stating a historical record irrelevant to himself.

\“Then, the Teutons came. You have learned of their atrocities in your bunker history textbooks. You know about Katyń, about Auschwitz, about Barbarossa. You know the numbers, the massive, appalling, almost meaningless statistics of death. Two million. Ten million. Twenty-seven million. These numbers are like coordinates of distant galaxies—vast, but unreachable.\”

He walked to the center of the classroom, turned around, and faced everyone.
···
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.169.desc:
\“But today, I demand that you forget those numbers. I demand that you imagine. Imagine a five-year-old girl whose hair is the color of Belarusian flax. Imagine her playing in a Moscow street, holding a ragdoll. Then, the air raid siren sounds. She doesn't understand the meaning of that wail. She just looks up curiously and sees black raindrops falling from the sky. Those are bombs. Imagine the instant the bomb explodes beside her, how her tiny body, along with her ragdoll, turns into a vague, red mist of fire and fragmented flesh.\”

A deathly silence fell over the classroom. All that could be heard was the suppressed, increasingly heavy breathing of the cadets.

\“Now imagine a twelve-year-old boy. In the winter of Stalingrad. He hasn't eaten for two days. He is hiding in a bombed-out basement, cradling the frozen corpse of his five-year-old sister. He can't bear to bury her, because she is the last, only source of warmth he can feel. He hears footsteps outside, thinking the Red Army has come to rescue him. He crawls out, only to see a squad of Teutonic soldiers in gray uniforms, holding rifles. They see him and laugh. They don't give him a bullet. They simply snatch his sister's body from his embrace, throw it into the burning ruins, and watch him cry hysterically in the snow.\”

Volkov's voice remained calm, but every word was like a red-hot iron, searing the hearts of these youths who had never experienced true suffering.

\“The land beneath our feet is the Ural Mountains. But above our heads, the surface shrouded in radiation was once our homeland. What is buried there are not cold numbers. Buried there are thousands upon thousands of stories like these. The girl who played with a ragdoll, the boy who held his sister's corpse. They are your grandfathers, your mothers, countless Russians who should have had names, had futures, but were ultimately reduced to a handful of unrecognizable ashes.\”

\“We hide in this bunker not to merely survive. We continue living not because we are afraid of death.\” For the first time, the Commissar's voice carried a hint of an almost imperceptible tremor, the sound of anger compressed to its extreme.

\“We live because they died. We live to remember them. We live to complete a cause they could not finish. This is not vengeance. Vengeance is a personal, emotional act. What we are about to execute is grander, and purer than that.\”

He walked back to the podium, picked up a black-covered manual, and held it high.

\“This is the Trial. The judgment of history. The ultimate reckoning for crimes against humanity. The uniform you will put on tomorrow is not clothing; it is a judicial robe. The gun in your hands is not a weapon; it is the gavel that strikes the verdict. When you step onto that scorched earth and face the last Teuton, you must remember—what you see is not a person who can cry and bleed. What you see is the pilot who dropped the bomb, the soldier who laughed in the snow, the sum of all this evil.\”

\“Your mission is not to hate. It is to execute.\”

He put down the manual, and his gaze once again became sharp as a scalpel.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.170.desc:
Melyakhov skillfully returned his lunch tray to the designated sterilization bin, then rubbed his stomach and let out a sigh—even though he wasn't full. Dinner lately had been slightly more generous than before, but not by much. On top of the existing whole wheat compressed biscuit, synthetic meat, and hard black bread, there was now a small piece of dried vegetable. Not much was added, so naturally, he still couldn't feel full. From Melyakhov's experience, chewing that thing nearly broke his teeth.

He hurried back to his dormitory, planning to rest early during his rare free time to prepare for the upcoming drills. Previously, this time was usually used for military theory study, but recently, the superiors suddenly adjusted the policy. While theory study time was reduced, the daily live combat training increased. Fortunately, the rations increased slightly, so no one complained much.

He entered the dormitory and lay down on his bed. His roommates hadn't returned yet. He clasped his hands behind his head, staring at the distant wall. The low hum of the ventilation system was the only background noise in the small room. The Geiger counter was silent; no damned radiation leaks. Everything was functioning normally, except Melyakhov himself.

He flipped over and pulled out a *Military Theory Manual* from under his pillow, intending to read for a while. But for some unknown reason today, he felt genuinely restless; he couldn't focus on the familiar words before his eyes. Subconsciously, he shoved the book back, stood up, and began tidying the dorm.

Melyakhov swept the floor over and over until it was spotless. But the anxiety in his heart intensified, and he even started to feel a bit breathless. He found an empty space and began doing push-ups—one, two, three... He didn't know how many he did, yet the strength in his body felt inexhaustible. Suddenly, a whistle sounded outside, and Melyakhov shot to his feet at light speed, standing rigidly in the center of the dorm.

He suddenly looked down at his right hand, unconsciously clenching and unclenching his fist. If his instructor were here, he would surely praise him for his excellent combat readiness, but Melyakhov suddenly understood: all his current anxiety stemmed from the **loss of a mission**. During the stagnant years of the Great Trial's pause, the defenders of Russia had no mission and began to enter a torment of idleness. When this steel state machine was forced to a standstill, the immense silence became the greatest threat to its gears.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.170.a: I need a mission, I must train...
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.171.desc:
Recently, a new activity was added to the Tyumen bunker: recruiting extras. This news quickly spread throughout the various areas of the bunker. Soon, the official national film project, *Blood and Steel*, related to this activity, was also announced. In this film, the protagonist, Rezanov, an old veteran of the Soviet era, participates in the great struggle against the Nazi invaders. However, after enlisting, Rezanov witnesses a series of disorders within the army—these are the seeds of failure sown by Bukharin in Russia over decades: chaotic cultural education within the army, a fundamental lack of trust in Mother Russia, and the mass recruitment of landlords and criminal elements into the military... Rezanov gradually sees through the incompetence of the Soviet government. After the defeat in the defense of Moscow, he comes to West Siberia, where he meets Commander-in-Chief Karbyshev. Under Karbyshev's guidance, he recognizes the true nature of Kaganovich's revisionism and Rokossovsky's reactionary military clique. Finally, he follows Commander Yazov to overthrow the reactionaries in the army...

Normally, the work of an extra would have nothing to do with Daria. As an ordinary housewife, Daria only takes care of her husband and children, and her poor family means she has no right to watch any films. It would be better to spend that money on food for her little daughter, Masha. But when the military personnel came to her door, Daria accepted the order to serve as an extra. After all, now deep underground, the military is responsible for all food and shelter. If she disobeyed, her family would starve.

As she waited intently for the director's command, she overheard a man in plain clothes beside her, in the designated trench position, saying things that should not be said to others.

\“This movie is completely fabricated. Things weren't that bad under Bukharin. What are the League's higher-ups thinking...\”

Daria made the sign of the cross over her chest. As soon as the filming ended, she immediately returned home and picked up the telephone. She remembered a law in the League's statutes: successfully reporting anti-government personnel qualifies one for a material reward, depending on the situation. Yes, if the report was successful, she could afford an extra bite of food for the next few days.

\“\”Hello, this is the League Security Department. How may I help you?\“
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.171.a: \“I found an actor expressing anti-government sentiments...\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.172.desc:
As an old chef who had settled in Omsk for decades, Romanov had cooked everything. Initially, it was just baked potatoes, but as Omsk expanded, he made many more things: kasha, borscht, and he even snuck into a Japanese restaurant to learn how to make sushi. But with the advent of the Great Trial, the good times ended. After the endless earthquake on that day, the soldier who brought him down told him that the surface was now full of exhaust from Teutonic nuclear bombs. So he continued his life as a chef.

Today, when he came to the kitchen, a military officer was already waiting for him. \“Make these things palatable, write them into a recipe, and the higher-ups will promote it to everyone.\”

Romanov glanced at the designated ingredients: synthetic protein blocks, compressed cabbage blocks, and a small amount of synthetic meat blocks. He touched the hard cubes with his hand and couldn't help but smile bitterly. He had dealt with potatoes frozen as hard as stone, acidic pickled cucumbers, and delicately sliced beef, but all those things were in the past. He cast the memories aside, retrieved a little of the precious water supply, and carefully softened the vegetable blocks little by little, then mashed them into a powder.

He pulled a heater from the cabinet and gradually controlled the heat, heating the edges of the protein blocks bit by bit. Although some parts were slightly scorched, the overall texture visibly softened. Romanov inserted a little synthetic meat into each portion, then covered them and began heating the whole thing. A few minutes later, he pulled the concoction out of the oven, sprinkled vegetable powder on each serving, and began plating them one by one.

*Clap, clap, clap*, he turned around. The officer had been standing behind him for a while. \“You did much better than we expected. I just tasted a bite, and the flavor is much stronger than before, almost comparable to when we ate fresh food.\”

His heart suddenly ached. When he was on the surface, one of his few daily joys was sharing food with his family and friends. But how long had they been underground now? The appearance of those lovely vegetables and white flour was almost forgotten by him······ He lowered his head, scrutinizing the grayish, utterly unappetizing mixture that lacked the proper texture of food, and sighed. However, there was nothing he could do. Life had to go on, no matter what. So he took out a spoon and, with an almost pious movement, slowly took a large bite of the food.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.172.a: He chewed that mouthful for a very long, long time.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.173.desc:
The Gorky Bunker Complex

Life in the bunker was a continuous, unchanging cycle: work, off-duty, go home to sleep, then wake up for the next day's work, off-duty······ Only in the last half month had the material allocations clearly decreased. Yurika knew that the next round of surface exploration was about to begin; after all, this was not the first time. Several of his friends had already vanished in the ruins and the wasteland, but he had been relatively lucky, surviving until now.

Sure enough, not long after work began in the morning, a young man wearing a black hat came into the factory and ascended the platform usually off-limits for speeches: \“For the League, for the Great Trial, by any means necessary, we must raise enough food! Fighters of the League, your deeds shall live forever!\”

Before the Commissar's slogans had faded, Yurika and some colleagues were sent to a similarly ruined city with some dilapidated gear. He knew these slogans were only for the newcomers. The outside was no sanctuary; bandits, contamination, chemical weapons leaks, leftover landmines, and other weapons······ anything could take their lives. He could only sigh and teach his rookie partner some survival knowledge and material identification methods: \“If a place looks very clean, run immediately. It means there are definitely people nearby, and you can't be sure if they belong to the League. If there are obvious signs of human presence, run even faster. Packaged medicines and food outside are usually fine; take them. Some things that look very industrially manufactured can be extremely valuable, but they are also very rare. Also······\”

······

To his surprise, they didn't even see a soul during this operation, and the assembly time had already arrived. They were walking down the street with a large box full of canned goods and a radio that still worked. \“God bless······ Anastasia··· and my unborn child······\” Just when he thought he had escaped danger this time as before, a sudden anomaly occurred.

With a sharp 'Click!', an uncleared pressure-activated landmine exploded under his foot.

Before he could have another thought, Yurika was reduced to a pile of fragmented flesh.

The young man reported the accident, and the number '18140' was crossed out from the ledger of the Quartermaster Department and the Ground Reconnaissance Dispatch Team.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.173.a: The poor man's wife didn't even know how her husband died.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.174.desc:
Anastasia suffered from insomnia all night. Only when the loudspeaker reminded people it was time to wake up did she struggle to climb out of bed, but her soul was already preoccupied with her husband Yurika and had not returned.

Since Yurika left yesterday morning to search for supplies, she hadn't received a single piece of news all day. Normally, Yurika would be home by five or six in the evening at the latest, when the hands of the clock hanging on the factory wall reached that point, and he would tell her about the dangers and interesting things he encountered outside. She knew in her heart that this abnormality definitely did not mean good news—perhaps a serious injury that would affect the operation, or······ she could only pray that the worst possibility hadn't happened.

With an anxious heart, she tidied herself up, preparing to continue her day, because she knew that asking people in the League was useless. The bureaucrats would only fob her off with meaningless nonsense. However, just then, there was a knock on the door.

\“Hello? Who is it?\”

\“Madam, this is your exclusive certificate. You may present it at the distribution station to exchange for one and a half times the regular ration quota. It is for you and your child. I am the Captain of the League's 33687 Ground Reconnaissance Dispatch Team, and I am here to inform you: your husband, 18140, was unfortunately killed during a reconnaissance mission the day before yesterday. Cause of death: shot by bandits.\”

Anastasia stood stunned for two seconds, and then the color drained from her face: \“I··· I understand.\”

The Captain saluted her, then turned and left as if nothing had happened.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.174.a: Everything was as normal, save for the solitary card.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.100.t: Summary of the Deindustrialization Action in Helsinki
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.100.desc:
1. Dispatch a certain scale of armed personnel to factories in the Helsinki region, such as **Outokumpu Steelworks**, **Wärtsilä Marine Power**, **Kemira Chemical Group**, and **Patria Aviation Factory**, to maintain order and prevent sabotage.
2. Establish a Special Interrogation Team to question factory management personnel to obtain statistics on personnel and equipment, inventory machinery and means of production suitable for rail transport, and classify and grade Finnish technical personnel.
3. Alliance industrial backbone personnel and Finnish technical personnel are responsible for dismantling machinery and equipment, while Finnish prisoners of war are used to transport containers and heavy equipment.
4. Control and manage the families of Finnish technical personnel, and execute uncontrollable individuals.
5. Commandeer the local railway system; dismantled equipment and materials are to be transferred from Helsinki to Arkhangelsk, and subsequently moved to industrial bases east of the Ural Mountains.
6. Provide appropriate resettlement for Finnish technical personnel, including setting up barracks and distributing food.
7. Following the operation's conclusion, sapper teams are to carry out total **mechanical destruction, explosive demolition, and chemical contamination** of any equipment and material that could not be moved.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.101.t: The Double-Headed Eagle on the Snow
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.101.desc:
This year, winter came exceptionally early and cold to Finland. Emil Koivunen stepped on knee-deep snow, his axe striking the frozen spruce trunk with a dull *thud*. His breath condensed into white frost on his eyebrows, and every inhale felt like swallowing ice shards. He looked up at the grey sky; Finland's sky was usually clear, but now it was veiled in an ominous, grey haze.

Suddenly, a piercing siren tore through the air. Emil knew something was wrong and sprinted home, then hurried with his wife, Liisa, and children into the cellar. Outside, there was no expected roar of explosions, only a deathly silence, and a chilling *hiss* like a venomous snake spreading over the land. Closely following, a strange, subtly yellowish-green mist crept silently and swiftly along the snow's surface from the edge of the forest, engulfing everything. Clearly, this was man-made poison gas! Emil peered cautiously through the cellar door crack, seeing his neighbor, old Jonas, stumble out of his house, only to fall heavily into the snow after a few steps like a piece of dead wood, his body violently convulsing. Emil faintly heard a terrifying gurgling sound from his throat, like a drowning man. The old man's skin quickly erupted in hideous blisters, and he soon stopped moving.

An unknown time passed, and silence reigned. The air in the cellar was suffocatingly foul. Emil carefully pushed the door open slightly. Outside was terrifyingly quiet, only the wind moaning. Stiff corpses were scattered on the snow, their postures twisted in agony.

The sound of heavy leather boots crunching the snow grew nearer. There were three men, all wearing unfamiliar dark grey greatcoats, but the striking **golden double-headed eagle** insignia on their armbands declared their identity. The leader's vulture-like eyes fixed on Emil's gaze. Unfortunately, a soldier discovered the cellar entrance. He pulled out a strange-looking instrument, operated it twice, and seemingly detected people underground. The soldier gestured, and several dark gun muzzles were instantly pointed at them.

\“Out! Finnish pig!\” the soldier motioned for Emil to come out. Emil, his wife, and children trembled as they crawled out of the cellar and stood on the cold snow. The soldiers were expressionless, looking at them like livestock waiting for slaughter. One of them, whose gaze fell upon Liisa's pale but still beautiful face, let slip a chilling, cruel sneer. He unhooked the canteen from his waist, unscrewed the cap, and poured a little of the liquid onto the snow. Instantly, a pungent chemical odor wafted up. He squatted down and, using his gloved hand, scooped up a handful of filthy, chemically-tainted melted snow and **brutally smeared it onto Liisa's face**.

Liisa let out a short scream; her skin instantly burned and turned red. The soldier studied her pain, watching Emil's face contort with fury and despair, a muffled, satisfied laugh rumbling in his throat. Emil's eyes were bloodshot; he tried to lunge but was stopped by another cold rifle barrel pressing against his forehead. After what seemed like an age, Liisa gradually lost life. Apparently satisfied with their expressions of despair, the man waved his hand.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.102.desc:
Lakes. The forests and lakes of Karelia had never been this lively in thirty years. It was here, once upon a time, that Finnish traitors, along with Teutonic planes and tanks, began the invasion. Thirty years have passed—enough time for a generation to grow from innocent children to rifle-carrying soldiers.

After the battle, black-clad soldiers escorted a column of young Finnish prisoners of war. They marched in three ranks, heads bowed, over muddy, icy ground, their feet worn with blood blisters, their clothes soaked through by the cold rain. If someone couldn't walk, the black-clad soldiers pulled him from the line and **executed him on the spot**, leaving the corpse behind.

They passed through deserted villages, glimpsing houses with walls covered in curses written in Russian, like a tourist's \“So-and-so was here.\” Underneath the walls were piles of corpses, some burned, throats slit, or torn apart by bullets. Several others, men and women, old and young, lay naked and piled together, with purplish faces and grotesque smiles, like a heap of long-uncleaned garbage.

After an unknown number of days, they arrived at a **temporary internment camp** surrounded by barbed wire. Here, the officers of the black-clad soldiers inspected each prisoner: only those who could **remain standing after a severe punch** were kept. They would later be transported by train to Onega and then to military factories in the rear.

\“Drown the rest of these in the lake. Next batch.\”
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.102.a: The sons shall pay for the fathers' debts.
strings.OMS_POSTNUKE.103.desc:
Grisha's rough, warm fingers tightly gripped the cold Mosin-Nagant rifle stock. Around him, the roar of the crowd surged in waves: \“Let the Teutonic pigs pay their blood debt!\”, and Grisha's chest heaved with emotion—look, this was the strength of the Slavic nation! He felt the whip marks left by the German foreman when he was still a slave, faintly burning beneath his ribs, and blood rushed to his head; he was even a little dizzy with excitement. The **Black League** had brought the \“**Great Trial**\”; they had shattered the shackles of the so-called \“New Order\” and brought freedom, reeking of blood!

Several people in old German-style clothes were shoved out, their faces ashen. Grisha's gaze locked onto one old man—**Von Erich**, a German language teacher before the war. When Grisha was ten, he had been struck on the palm with a ruler by him for mispronouncing an \“R.\” The memory of humiliation instantly ignited the flame in Grisha's eyes. It was him! These high and mighty \“master race\” people—who were they to insult him like this?!

An officer wearing the double-headed eagle armband roared from the wooden platform, enumerating the Germans' sins: \“For Mother Russia! Execute the judgment!\” Grisha's column was pushed forward.
