Arriving at the school she taught at, she parked her Bug in the respective parking zone and walked inside the heavy glass doors. Passing room by room she checked the watch, 7:13 AM was plastered on the clock as she went into her room.

Opening the door she saw once more how well her and her children decorated the room as it burst with personality. There were little drawings and past assignments posted stapled or drawn on the surrounding walls and the sun peaked ever so slightly through the half opened windows. Breathing in the fresh air she sat at her desk attentively.

Soon enough the children started petering in.

After the bell rang with an annoying clang the room fell silent. Addressing the class Klara spoke loud and concisely “Alright class let-” A large BANG rang out from the outside world the force of the explosion seemed to rock everyone to the core. Klara herself was thrown out of her chair and to the floor. After getting up she saw that at least all the children were under their desks. Hands over little heads, asides from the glass scraping the arm of one child relatively they were all ok.

In a shaky and shoddy tone Klara told the children it would be all ok and she would find out what was happening. Poking her head outside of the door the young woman eyed nervously around, the Russians surely have not invaded here and arrived this fast she thought to herself. As nervous thoughts danced around in her mind, she walked towards the once glass entrance doors, now shells of their former selves on the ground. The crunch of the glass as it stuck to her shoe sent pings of fear down her spine.

As she stared around her she saw a plume of smoke from the adjacent apartment building. However as she eyed the building another colored apparition floated through the air. A thickly yellow gas emitted from the hole in the building above. She immediately thought back to her father telling her of his experiences in the first world war. And what even was that awful stench she began to smell.
strings.OMS_great_trial.44.a: And then she began to cough.
strings.OMS_great_stall.1.desc:
Timofey and Alexei were profoundly exhausted, having marched 10 miles just today, but there was no rest for the wicked. “New orders from high command,” Alexei’s radio crackled, both men leaning forward to listen intently. “There is a German position in the lowland ahead, Number 3 Platoon will proceed along the side of the road to support the motorized troops. Over”.

“I don’t believe it,” Timofey, the younger man, murmured miserably. “We've had no food or sleep in a day and a half! Constant German ambushes, counterattacks, snipers, and now they demand we just keep on marching like it’s nothing?! Just statistics to be drilled, dieted, treated like cattle, used as cannon fodder?” he ranted.

Alexei listened quietly before replying. “Accidents are common on the frontlines,” the older man advised. “If a hand, maybe a foot were to get injured, it wouldn't be questioned.” He kept his tone even, eyes locked with Timofey. “They can’t starve and deprive us for weeks without expecting a few accidents to happen, no?”

Timofey met his gaze. “And wounded soldiers need food and rest to get better, of course” he mused. “What’s the betting there’s going to be a lot of ‘accidents’ around here before long?”

“You said it yourself,” Alexei replied, “we’re not cattle and we won’t be driven across the steppe like a herd. Hell, a herd might be treated better. But unless something changes, we’re going to see a lot of men break, or worse.”
strings.OMS_great_stall.2.desc:
The door opened, and seemingly the air inside the room was sucked out. Evgeny barely heard the doorman call for him for his appointment. Appointment was a strong word, actually. It was a summons. 
He stood up, attempting to suppress his nausea. He took one step forward, and another, until he walked in stride. Whatever his fate, he would not meet it with cowardice. Each door opened as if a portal to another world, each increasing in relative opulence to the next and the consecutive hallways almost seemed to expand in radiance and size. It all led to a throne room of sorts. Yazov had insisted his office be at the epicenter of the building. It was more bunker than  workspace, the result of his own paranoia. Pitranov witnessed Yazov pacing wolf-like next to a truly gigantic fireplace. It cast a shadow large enough to loom over the entire room. He swallowed hard. 
“Comrade Marshal. I have the report you requested of me regarding the economic state of the League and the lack of offensive progress.” He stuffed his hands behind his back, praying the decorum would save him. Yazov continued his pacing, merely signalling for him to continue. “I'm afraid I have pinned the reason for our great stall. A state of exhaustion has taken over the economy. Circulation of money is almost nil. The people have hoarded their remaining material wealth. Our policies of austerity have taken a larger and earlier toll than normal. I fear if we do nothing and continue mass-spending on the Army, then...” 
Pitranov's lip quivered uncontrollably as he finally saw Yazov face him. His face was lined with exhaustion, darker even than the shadow that appeared at his back. With bloodshot eyes, he made another quick hand gesture, and the blast-door Pitranov came through locked shut.
strings.OMS_great_stall.3.desc:
Petronov flipped through the binders and binders of names, graphs, and figures collated at his recruitment station in one of Samara's countless pre-built housing districts. It had been a quiet day, an abnormality for sure, one he lit a cigarette to calm the impending chiding from his superiors at the next Sub-District Recruitment Officer Summit a fortnight from now. However, as he continued flipping through the figures, a trend began to emerge, and suddenly, the issue seemed much more deserving of another cigarette.

Recruitment was down, and unlike other periods, it was no longer a blip. Figure after figure, graph after graph showed the indelible downward curve, an ever-decreasing slope that varied only in how many fewer recruits walked through his door to give their lives to the Black League. From a peak of more than 2,000 fresh and young recruits entering his center in one day, now numbers were lucky to dip into the hundreds per week. Petronov's hands and lip began to quiver, his eyes darting from side to side and forehead collecting sweat. He rushed for the phone, calling a colleague in the city. He normally would not give that smug bastard the pleasure of seeing his weakness, but he had to know.

Dmitri's voice was hoarse as ever even through the static of the phone line. After exchanging thinly veiled pleasantries, he got to the point.

“Dmitri. What is happening to recruitment? My station has hardly seen anyone enlist. Is it the same with you?” There was a silence on the other line before Dmitri cautiously responded.

“You're having the same problem?”
strings.OMS_great_stall.3.a: “By all accounts, we've emptied out everyone here.”
strings.OMS_great_stall.4.desc:
There is a fundamental cowardice with the clerk. Whether he works in the deepest bowels of Army Intelligence, or an office far behind the lines, it is that fundamental cowardice that remains a constant factor. It is a deep-rooted aversion to presenting failure. At least in the Black League, that fear made sense. An excess of failure carried a sentence. Nevertheless, it seeps through and corrodes government and institutions further than any Germanic intelligence network or purposeful campaign of sabotage.

It is a disease that manifests when a clerk in the Finance Ministry incorporates a surplus into the new year's budget. It is a disease that manifests when an Intelligence Officer does not have the will to report new enemy formations that should not exist. It is the cowardice of a propaganda officer who can not admit that his efforts produce fewer and fewer recruits every day. They collect like water pressing against a dam, steadily applying more pressure to the failing stones that make it, each drop seeping through the ailing concrete and threatening to burst out the other end.

Steadily, as a foreign diplomat fails to report that foreign commitments grow scarcer and scarcer, and bureaucrats within the Ministry of Health report that their hospitals still have the capacity, even as they discard those too costly to save, the dam that holds the war effort threatens to break asunder. Now, as German armies recuperate from the relentless offensive and begin to advance, the dam stands vulnerable and at its precipice. All it would take is one well-timed strike to bring the whole rotten structure down.
strings.OMS_great_stall.4.a: A rot that extends further than any mold.
strings.OMS_great_stall.5.desc:
The patrol on horseback saw smoke on the horizon kilometers before they encountered the convoy. Packing the road and the surrounding fields were churned-up scraps of metal, some of which still burned and warped from the intense heat of battle that took place. The remnants of rifles, foodstuffs, spare parts, and other assorted military goods joined them, almost all of it burnt or otherwise destroyed beyond use. The grass was charred black, and the torn apart bodies, or at least what could be identified as bodies, littered it.

Maksim simply plugged his nose and signaled for his men to dismount and move toward the ruined trucks. They had just been rotated off the line, not that it came with any benefit. The Luftwaffe was perfectly capable of hitting anyone, or anything, it wanted, no matter how far behind the line they hid. His stomach rumbled, and he hunched over in pain. Rotation also didn't mean improved rations. Command claimed they were needed for the men who “actually fought”. He signaled for his men to quicken the pace and headed over to one of the destroyed trucks. This expedition wasn't sanctioned by command, but given the lack of presumed survivors, nobody would know any better.

In its flatbed was nothing much of value. Ruined ammunition and pieces of flesh were strewn across the splintered wood and tattered canvas tarp. The next series of trucks didn't yield anything better. Suddenly, one of his men shouted out. Maksim raced towards him. His sergeant held aloft a crate full of raw potatoes looted from one of the burnt-out trucks. Maksim quickly ordered it tied to the back of one of the horses. They would eat well tonight, not that it would last longer. As he walked back to his horse, he spotted what appeared to be a survivor amongst the wreckage, a trooper no older than 18. His face was charred almost beyond recognition, hair burnt to the skin. He reached out weakly, croaking for something. His voice sounded like he was speaking through a torn paper bag.
strings.OMS_great_stall.5.a: Maksim ignored him. They had gotten what they came for.
strings.OMS_great_stall.6.desc:
Piotyr leapt aside as the concrete mixer tipped, filling the hole that he had dug in the frozen earth: a foundation for yet another bunker. For the past eight weeks, he had been here, in some remote part of the Urals, building bunkers to protect his people from the coming storm. The cold conditions and small rations would have made almost anyone complain, if not desert outright, but not Piotyr. Piotyr had faith. Faith that they would destroy the Teutonic menace. Faith in Russia. Faith in Yazov. This faith had driven him to work at a furious pace, and along with a handful of other true believers in his construction crew, his crew had built bunker after bunker, faster than any cadre crew in this place, far far away from any civilization or anything to really speak of.

So far their efforts had gone unnoticed by the government, not that Piotyr cared. Piotyr’s family had been killed by the Teutons, not in one swoop– that would have been a mercy– but one after the other. His parents that he barely remembered had died in Barbarossa, executed by one of the Einsatzgruppen. His brother– the brother that saved him from the fate of his parents– had died a soldier in the West Russian War. His wife and children had died in one of the Luftwaffe’s accursed bombing raids while they had been living in Vyatka. After this decades-long torture at the hands of the Teuton, Piotyr only had one goal, one driving force as he layered brick after brick, hole after frozen hole:

Revenge...
strings.OMS_great_stall.7.desc:
“Aysen shoveled through the frostbitten, packed dirt with as much grit and determination as he could muster. Echoes of gunshots, just beyond the distance, reminded him of the consequences if he failed to do so. Every brief moment of rest between shovels was cut short as he plunged his equipment back into the Earth, just to drown out the sounds around him.

Ever since that bastard Yazov and his soldiers, draped in black, had marched into his homeland, he and his fellow Yakuts knew nothing but the back breaking labor of the mines. What was once peaceful co-existence, albeit tense at times, with those he once called his countrymen soon became a violent subjugation as any in Yakutia able to work were forced at gunpoint into contributing to 'the reclamation of Russia'.

“No cost too great, and no sacrifice too small,” they would repeat to the workers, day after day, as they did nothing but sit back and watch their endless toiling.

Once, there was a time Aysen would've protested the actions of the Black League, perhaps even rebel if he had the strength of his youth. Now those thoughts were now brushed aside, replaced with the memories of his fellow Yakut, his own friends and family, being beaten and bloodied by the guards of the labor site. Even children, already being indoctrinated into the hate of the Black League, would kick at worker's knees as they passed, “not adequately pursuing their patriotic duty,” as their instructors would say.

And so Aysen continued to shovel, through monotony, through heavy snow storms, through bright skies, through brutal winters, and warm summers. Perhaps, he thought, all his hard work would be worth something one day.”
strings.OMS_great_stall.7.a: How many shifts are there in an eternity?
strings.OMS_great_stall.8.desc:
An emergency cabinet meeting had been called by Yazov, who had grown frustrated with the news that the war situation was not necessarily developing to Russia’s advantage. This could not continue, and someone had better have an explanation. Everyone took their seats, the room deathly quiet. “Gentlemen” Yazov finally said “the line is stagnant, the advance halted. Resources seem to be falling into a black hole” he leaned forward, fixing the cabinet with a chilling gaze. “And I want to know why”.

Those present looked nervously around, one man tugged anxiously at his collar while another fidgeted and flicked his eyes to the others, hoping someone else would speak first. Thankfully, Pitovranov plucked up the courage to propose an explanation. “It’s the Luftwaffe” he explained, trying to stay calm “Our frontline forces are facing highly intense bombing in areas we are attempting to advance in. Furthermore, the conscription effort is producing unwilling men, who don’t want to fight”

Yazov considered this long before he replied, “Then redouble production on anti-aircraft equipment, and ensure that our planes are concentrated in the contact zones. As for the conscripts, I want you to ensure that new soldiers are educated properly, and so we can be sure that both their political and military training is up to standard.” He concluded, as the orders are quickly written down. “You had better be right, Pitovranov. On your head be it if this fails to produce results.
strings.OMS_great_stall.9.desc:
Dimitry Yazov considered himself a patient man, but even the patience of a saint had to be expended eventually, especially in the face of such continual failures. Everywhere he looked, the military situation seemed to be busy going backward. A meeting of the general staff would allow him to pick out exactly who and why this was happening, such that they could be dealt with accordingly. He would listen to no excuses, no half-hearted whimpering about why the general staff had failed.

As the staff sat around the conference table, the excuses already began to flow. “We simply don’t have enough supplies and winterized equipment!” one man exclaimed, leaning forward in his seat “The men are suffering from frostbite, and their guns are locking up!”. Yazov couldn't think up of a response. “The Germans are giving us no breathing room,” another said, “if we could have a day to recover and organize a counterattack, we can get back on the front foot”. A little panicky for Yazov’s taste, but his head seemed to be in the right place.

And so it went, with an unwritten list of who would live or die depending on the explanations given for the suboptimal performance on the front lines. To be carried out with immediate effect as soon as the meeting ends. Perhaps those spared would show some gratitude, and improve their performance. A threat to one’s life is a powerful motivator, and Yazov would ensure they were very motivated indeed.
strings.OMS_great_stall.10.desc:
At a radio station in the heart of the city of Omsk, a message from Dimitry Yazov, the great and unquestionable leader of the Black League, and of Russia was preparing a message. Russia was to be overhauled and rebuilt from the core outwards, and everybody would be affected. Everybody would need to take part. The fate of the world hung in the balance. He placed on a pair of headphones and positioned the microphone in front of him. The technician present gave an affirmative thumbs up, indicating he was on air.

“People of Russia. Workers, farmers, soldiers, wives, children, whomever you may be. A change is coming, and this broadcast is to notify you of it. All industry and all agriculture will be reformed and regulated in such a way that it will serve the war effort. If it does not enable us to fight, it will not be produced or grown. Education will also change, from the first lessons taught, children will learn of the enemy and his crimes, and what must be done to eradicate him from the world. Ready-made soldiers will emerge from the schooling system, knowing their duty well.”

He took a brief pause to take a sip from a cup of water “Furthermore, all media, be it books, radio or anything else will reinforce our values and our way of life, as well as our struggle. Anything that opposes or questions this will not be allowed to proliferate. From top to bottom, all systems and the people who work in them will be directed towards a single goal. The destruction of Russia’s enemies, and to secure a future for its people. Prepare yourselves accordingly.”
strings.OMS_great_stall.11.desc:
Our people have known nothing but defeat for the last century.

Again and again, we rise to the occasion and dig our heels in the mud. Again and again, we are thrown back into the throes of humiliation. We will never again commit such an error.

The hearts and minds of the Russian people must be brought up to the strength that made all of Europe, and the world, fear us for our resilience and resolve. Our commitment to victory above all else is what drives the average Russian out of bed in the morning and straight into the enemy lines. Our commitment to the final victory is what makes the factory worker labor endlessly with spite and toil in his soul, driving him to become a productive worker in death.

To ensure this effort succeeds, we must pull from our most fanatical and loyal supporters, of whom will lord over those who do not see the vision for the future. In doing so, our people will retain the nation's interest in utterly destroying the Teutonic menace, once and for all.
strings.OMS_great_stall.12.desc:
Our army suffers the same crisis as our people: the gutlessness and fear that grips the hearts and minds of our frontline cadres. Our soldiers carry with them the finest weaponry the nation has to offer; they have all-encompassing plans to advance themselves towards our final victory, yet there remains the problem of improperly carrying themselves forward to the battle lines.

Our fearless Glavkoverkh's fervor and spirit are what our soldiers need in this very moment. To bring out the spirit of final victory above all else in the minds and hearts of our soldiers is the final key to the absolute end of the Teutonic dogs.

Our fanatical and most loyal commissars will dish out this spirit of national vengeance. If any are to refuse, they will simply be shot. We cannot tolerate weakness any longer, for our only way forward is victory. Absolute, total victory. Anything less, and we will have failed our nation once more.
strings.OMS_great_stall.12.a: Mind, body, and soul, all for our sacred struggle.
strings.OMS_great_stall.13.desc:
Yazov sat alone in his office, disappointment and frustration filling him with a most unpleasant malaise. He could envision the victory, and how it would come about. All the pieces seemed to be moving into place, but there still remained a minority of rogues within the system. The grit in the instrument, the grease on the lens.

A list of dossiers had been compiled, of potential troublemakers in the general staff whose loyalty had proven questionable. One had a disappointingly timid strategy planned and was proving resistant to change. Another was being annoyingly alarmist about the current strategic situation, saying that more time was needed, plans should be changed and the war not being to our advantage. Such liabilities shouldn’t be allowed to stand. Especially if compliant loyalists are waiting to take their place.

The first man is older, a weary stiff-neck who refuses to learn. He could likely be enticed to leave his post with a tempting severance package, solving the problem easily. The second man would prove considerably more problematic. The worst type of troublemaker is one who is convinced he is right, a more underhanded approach is needed. The plan is to have a gunman accost him at a moment of vulnerability. An appropriate stooge has been identified, a man diagnosed with terminal cancer, but still with some strength left. A large sum of money has been promised. To his family.
strings.OMS_great_stall.14.desc:
A curious phenomenon was beginning to sweep the new Russia. A recently assented policy had been passed down from the high echelons of government, causing a sense of anticipation to fill the populace. Increased rations and generous monetary rewards would be given to any who could give actionable information to the police and greater authorities. If there is anyone you suspect of wrongdoing, sabotage, or insubordination, say something. See it. Say it. Sort it.

It wouldn’t take long for people to sharpen their knives, and plunge them into the backs of neighbors and co-workers. Acts as petty as being insufficiently patriotic, not working quickly enough, and showing indifference to the great comrade Yazov were all given as reasons, which would need to be sorted through, assessed and, if deemed worthy, acted upon.

As the first rewards were cautiously doled out, some took it upon themselves to act as amateur commissars. Loudly espousing their faith in the Black League and its goals, and expecting everyone around them to do the same. It would not be long before members of the same family began to inform on each other, and were split apart as a result. A sense of paranoia began to permeate, as some began to keep to themselves, speaking to few for fear of their words being twisted against them. An air of anxiety hung over a changed society, with no sign of it leaving.
strings.OMS_great_stall.15.desc:
Pyotr and Vladimir sat apart from each other, a stern military judge in the stand above them while a gallery of observers quietly watched from aside. Both men feared for their lives. Anxiety renders them light-headed, their minds full of a pernicious fog. “Both of you face charges of cowardice, incompetence, and insubordination” the old man rumbled. “How do you plead?”. His tone was severe, as though he had already made up his mind as to what should be done.

“Not guilty!” Both men shouted in unison. Pyotr pointed sharply at his counterpart. “The charges belong to this shortsighted oaf!” he argued, causing Vladimir to visibly recoil. “While he was busy dithering about, my advance was held up! I didn’t have the strength to assault that much ground alone, and this idiot refused to help!”

“What this liar is refusing to tell you” Vladimir spat back “Is that I was already in a forward position, but I couldn’t advance if this coward didn’t have my flank! He was satisfied to throw me to the wolves while I stuck my neck out!” his voice rising to a shout, echoing around the wood paneled room. The judge put a hand up, stopping him. “I have heard enough” he replied to the tirades.

“Had either of you the spine to take responsibility, I may have considered showing leniency. Instead, you point and shout like schoolboys caught stealing, and such immaturity is not wanted among the general staff. You are both liabilities and will both be sentenced to death”. Both men continued to howl and shout as they were dragged away by the bailiffs. Minutes later, they argued no more.
strings.OMS_great_stall.16.desc:
Savintsev had been summoned to the office of Dimitry Yazov, and when the call came for him to do so, he made a point of hurrying there, such was his loyalty. To the consternation of the unit he was previously attached to, but Yazov’s orders superseded everything. Both technically and philosophically. He stood bolt upright to attention and snapped a neat salute before Yazov gestured for him to sit opposite.

“Comrade Savintsev,” the great man began. “As I am sure you are aware, when there is a harvest of wheat, amongst the good and healthy sheaves of grain lies the useless, flammable chaff, serving only to get in the way. I trust you understand what I am saying,” he explained with a severe tone. Savintsev nodded quickly in reply, the metaphor taking root.

“Sir” he replied with disquieting enthusiasm “The recent promotion of staff officers may have some... problematic individuals which must be dealt with properly”. Yazov gave an affirmative gesture, a modicum of praise. “Precisely, it has come to my attention that some of these men are not fit for purpose, and I am giving you full authority to find and prosecute them,” he said, before leaning forward, expression hard as stone. “Lest another failure occur”.

An agonizsing wave of cold anxiety permeated Savintsev’s body as the meaning of the words dawned on him. He stood. “I will carry out a thorough investigation and culling immediately, never again shall we be held up by cowards!” his voice rising, compensating for the pang of nervousness he had felt.
strings.OMS_great_stall.17.desc:
An air of anger and enmity lay thick over the city of Perm like a choking smog. But it was most concentrated at the city center, where an event had been arranged for the people to vent their frustrations at the difficulties they faced. Lest the Black League begin to face blame, a controlled outlet for this pent up anger to be pointed at targets of the League’s choosing would soon take place. Driven by military police, a disgraceful parade of ex-soldiers found guilty of fear and cowardice were frog-marched through the city center.

The thick crowds of civilians and onlookers present were instructed to hurl abuse, with the tacit addition of solid objects as well. Each man in the shameful parade had a sign around his neck reading “COWARD” or some other insult, and each looked their miserable part. As they met the crowd, every kind of insult, slur and abusive remark was hurled at them, all melding together in a torrent of raw, unfiltered hatred.

One man was struck on the side of the head by a rotting tomato, covering him in foul smelling slime. Another took a clump of wet mud directly to his face, his cry of pain and shock earning louder jeering from the already incensed crowd. And so it went, with some of them acquiring injuries from the projectiles thrown at them.

Even when they reached the bottom of the street, it didn't end. They were herded into armored vans to be taken to an ominously nondescript “detention” facility, like lambs being taken to the abattoir. Tears rolled down their faces, all of them feeling as wretched as could be.
strings.OMS_great_stall.18.desc:
A squad of Spetsgruppa stacked up outside on the front door of Vasily’s house, silently waiting for the signal to begin their sweep of the officer’s residence. Suspicions had filtered through that he had been using his relatively secure position to extend bribes to logistics units for extra supplies, and even surreptitiously cooking books and fudging numbers such that additional rations could be sent to him and his favorites.

Such corruption and subversion of the system could not be tolerated for a second longer, and a hand ram was brought forward to break down the door, the squad stormed in to find the man in his living room, seeming to be peacefully reading a book. Panicked, he snapped to attention, hiding the book under a blanket. The squad leader, Viktor, took notice of this. He had two men restrain the struggling occupant before picking up the book and flipping it open.

A list of names, numbers, and amounts. A black book, containing a list of the people he had bribed, what for and for how much. It was not a small ledger, with scores of records. The problem ran deep. Wordlessly, and with his lower lip pushed up in disgust, Viktor drew his revolver, ignoring Vasily’s pleas. Choosing to execute him right then and there. The body slumped to the floor, and the book seized. “Search this place, I doubt that’s the only evidence here” he ordered, the men spreading out to tear apart the rest of the house.
strings.OMS_great_stall.19.desc:
Yazov took his place at the head of a large meeting table, with many other general staff and officials present. A meeting had become necessary to pool and judge ideas in the war against the hated Germans, and against cowardice, the enemy within. The men murmured amongst themselves, making last minute touches to their plans. Folders and sheets of paper were laid out on the table as each man made ready to make his proposition.

Taking the initiative, one man provided a situation report on the status of the front line. “As of now, the German counteroffensive has been contained with minimal loss of progress. Requests for supplies and reinforcements have increased markedly, but the lines are tentatively believed to be stable” He reported. Yazov nodded, acknowledging this. “Very good. I will hear any proposals you all have now.”

The next man to speak up did so enthusiastically. “We should make greater use of incendiary weapons,” he proposed. “By incorporating more fire munitions and flamethrowers into infantry and artillery units, we can have a decisive edge against entrenched foes, or more concentrated formations.“ Murmurs of agreement were followed by another man speaking up.

“There exists a large number of workers wasting their efforts in non-essential industries, things like civilian consumer goods, trinkets and other such artisanal work. I propose that these workplaces be converted to military workshops, and the workers retrained. Everyone must serve the cause.”
strings.OMS_great_stall.20.desc:
Dmitry Yazov was silent. It was an exhausting day, more so than usual. As of late he’d been forced to personally give more and more direct orders to his subordinates. Leading by example however, the Glavkoverkh was willing to push himself if it meant that the Great Trial would succeed even as he was worn down from the strain of overseeing so many facets of the Black League’s operations himself. Though he wanted to rest for just a bit, he knew he couldn’t. A meeting with his top generals was scheduled to take place and without the word of their leader to guide them, the machinery of war would grind to a halt.

He entered the office with a dour look on his face. The room was a spartan affair, the most notable feature being the long table and chairs with a projector hanging above said table. Yazov looked at the assembled generals and saluted them with his generals saluting back in perfectly disciplined unison. “Sit Down.” Yazov ordered, the generals followed his word. Yazov cleared his throat and began to talk. “I’m Issuing a new decree, effective immediately.” The generals remained silent. “Our men are to advance,  er the cost, and their commanders will be held responsible if this command is not carried out.”.

The implications were as clear as day. A few moments of silence passed by before the ever-faithful Alexander Lazarenko spoke up. “I assume by any means necessary?” He asked, though everyone assembled already knew the answer. Yazov gave him a confirming nod.

“No matter the cost in blood and steel, our men advance. We have been bogged down for too long and if this keeps up we are risking the great trial itself.” The generals nodded along as Yazov continued. “I don’t care if you push your men to death, the only thing that matters is that we advance to the heart of the enemy, and I expect results. Is that understood?”.

The generals responded in unison once more with their complete agreement. All of them knew, however, that they were living on borrowed time if they couldn’t breach the enemy’s lines this time.
strings.OMS_great_stall.20.a: “Advance and give the nation the results it demands from you.”
strings.OMS_forpol.1.desc:
Talgat had lived his entire life on the steppe, some Kilometers from the Aral Sea. One day, while tending to his flock, he noticed a strange plane, and a strange message falling from it, descending from the cloudless blue sky. It was a small pamphlet and upon closer inspection, he realized it was written in Russian.

Curious, Talgat started reading the pamphlet, and as he did, he couldn't help but feel a growing sense of disgust and confusion. The words written on the paper spoke of hatred and revenge, of the anger of a whole people. Talgat had heard of many such Russians; waxing and waning over many years. Once, it was a Bolshevik, who exclaimed the equality of all nations among a strange, and alien Allah to the one he knew so long. Then, It shattered; and out poured disparate political groups, Tatars and Bashkirs, and strange merchants. He truly never much fancied it all, content with life tending to sheep. He read the document further, and its many strange declarations.

The piece was focused on the German espionage that had apparently infiltrated Kazakhstan, even spanning to his town. Members of apparent spy rings were cited to have been found, 3 of which Talgat recognized from a parable about thieving bread, and 2 of which he went to Mosque with, when he had once lived in Alma-Alta. Most strangely, he found the Russians had declared a war upon degeneracy within their national holdings. Upon finishing the final sentences, Talgat almost exclaimed; “Do the Russian and Kazakh people have the resources to be degenerates?”

He almost came to a chuckle at the stamp-like picture of Yazov, a supposedly well ordained king from what he could make of the stamp. Hadn’t the Russians had enough of gods, and kings, and their murder in the like? Why had the honorable Allah given the Russian such dishonorable bloodthirst, to be mired in insanity generation over generation?
strings.OMS_forpol.1.a: What are those Russians up to?
strings.OMS_forpol.2.desc:
The citizens of the city of Turkistan had always been proud of their gift from Tamerlane in 1405, that gift being the Mausoleum of Khoja. For centuries, this symbol of Timurid construction had defied the test of time, despite never even being fully completed by its original constructors. For centuries, it had been a center of many pilgrimages throughout all of Central Asia, and had been a centerpiece of Kazakh culture. 

Today, that structure has been demolished, and in its place, long rows of razor wire were constructed in the fashion of a perimeter. Not long after, shoddily constructed wooden barracks were hastily assembled within the confines of the wires, and after that the soldiers began unloading trucks full of other soldiers, and a plethora of guns.The civilian populace was on edge, and a wave of paranoia set in amongst them. 

Thousands of angry Kazakh men, women, and children filled the streets, shutting down the city of Turkistan for a few hours. Within the early hours of the morning, Russian army units were being deployed en masse in and around key, strategic road junctions across the entire city. At the crack of dawn, the orders were given, and the soldiers descended down upon the feverous populace. 

The protestors that survived were blinded and bound, loaded into trucks, and carried off into the gates of 'Camp Skobelev'. For the ones that weren't loaded onto trucks, they were simply left for nature to reclaim, blood soiling the earth. 

Inside the camp, the situation was nothing short of inhumane. People within the gates of the camp were still outraged that their camp was constructed on the grounds of a building they had once considered sacred, and a local muezzin insisted that the people should pray together, for Allah would protect them in their time of need. As the congregation gathered to pay their respects to Him, the soldiers entered the scene with batons, and attack dogs. There was little room for mercy.
strings.OMS_forpol.2.a: The tragedy of life is not death, but what we let die inside of us while we live.
strings.OMS_forpol.3.desc:
Jacob Frey readjusted the collar of his suit jacket, moreso to take his mind off the blistering cold than anything else. He, along with one his aides, stood outside the US embassy and waited for the League delegation to arrive. His aide was a young recent graduate from an émigré family, fluent in Russian, French, and English. He'd be an invaluable asset, given that Frey was largely a political appointee. He'd given a lot of money to the President's campaign, and he wanted the prestige of serving as ambassador to the country that'd finally end the Nazi menace. At least, that's what those in the State Department were hoping.

“How much longer do you think they'll be-” Frey began to ask, before a car finally pulled up in front of the embassy. Finally, Frey thought. They could get out of this cold. He approached the car just as one of the League's officials stepped out. He was a stern looking man with thick eyebrows that nearly covered his brow. His handshake was firm, gripping Frey tight as he pulled him close.

“Apologies for the delay,” the League diplomat said in English with only a minor accent. “A call that I could not put off. I do have a very busy schedule, so I was hoping perhaps we could agree here and now on American support over the issue of Outer Manchuria? Helping to free Russian territory from the grip of the Japanese is a worthy goal for us old allies, Russia and America, don't you agree Mister Frey?”

Frey was surprised by the forwardness of the ambassador. The embassy had prepared a dinner for this whole occasion in order to come to an understanding with the League. But given what he had just said, it didn't seem like there was much to discuss. “Of course,” Frey quickly replied. “We would be more than happy to aid in your efforts to contain and push back against Japanese imperialism.”

The League diplomat gave no smile in return when he let go of Frey's hand and made his way back to his car. He spoke a few quick words to his aide in Russian, before getting back in. In a few more moments, they had driven off. Frey couldn't help but be a bit amused by the situation, turning to give a shrug to his aide. But the look on his aide's face troubled him.

“Is there something wrong?” Frey asked. “Was it something he had said?”[Change Later]
strings.OMS_forpol.3.a: He said that this was all too easy.
strings.OMS_forpol.4.desc:
Lev had nothing left on him except the clothes on his back. Even these, the last vestiges of his old life, were starting to fray at the seams and let the cold Siberian wind slip into the cracks and bite at his skin below. But he had to keep going. He had no other choice. He had seen the League officers skewer his comrades with their bayonets if they strayed too far to one side from the marching column. If they fell too far back, then they too would get a bayonet through the heart.

He had tried to explain that he had no choice. All of them had tried to explain that the Japanese officials would have killed their families and sent them to work camps if they hadn't agreed to help them. He tried to implore that they have mercy on him and his family. He got none. The League officers, following their capture of Outer Manchuria, dragged all of the so-called collaborators out and declared them enemies of the Russian people. None of them asked Lev how he had managed to save countless lives over the course of his supposed collaboration. Sure, he had signed off on many of their deaths. But countless more would have died if not for him.

None of them cared. They were too self-righteous about having been born on the proper side of the Russian-Japanese border. They gave them no opportunity to get their things. They had to march all the way to their “Japanese friends” across the border. It didn't matter that the march would be hundreds of miles. And so they marched. A few hours in, one of his friends–a secretary named Vladimir–asked if they could have any food. A League officer pierced his heart with his bayonet. A few hours later, the first of them dropped from exhaustion. Those that fell were stabbed or shot. Lev wasn't sure which fate was better. He didn't look to see who had already fallen. None of that mattered now. All that mattered was that he survived.

The sun was starting to set over the horizon, and Lev felt some hope that they might be given a few hours rest before the sun rose up the next day. As the minutes passed, and the horizon turned darker and darker, Lev realized that they had no intention of giving them a moment's rest. And with the last light leaving the horizon, his hope was extinguished.
strings.OMS_forpol.5.desc:
Despite my better judgment, I made my way at the arranged meeting place and met a soldier of the Black League. He was dressed in a newly ironed uniform, an AK slung around his back. He was cleanly shaven, looked well-rested, but something rested behind those eyes. It wasn't so much a sharp edge as nothing at all. Nothing lay behind the sallow face which greeted me, no life sprung to the dead and hardened fingers which reached to grasp my hand. The conversation that follows went something like this, of course in Russian. 

“Greetings. I am with the Central Intelligence Agency of the United States. I presume you know why I am here?” 

“Yes.” His reply was curt, so curt that it almost caught me off-balance. Apparently these Russians were more direct than I had been briefed. 

“Very well. I am here to carry forward my demands to your leaders. The United States is prepared to supply the Black League with money, arms, and munitions. In exchange, we'd like a few... assurances.” 

We went onto discuss said assurances. Well, discuss is quite a loaded term. I presented my demands, and as the seagulls circled and the nets were cast out to sea, the soldier simply absorbed them, that blank stare from those empty eyes barely moving. When we finished our negotiations, I was about to leave when that innate curiosity finally got to me. 

“Private. How do you even feel about this? The war I mean. We all know you're headed for it. You're endeavoring a total war with the Germans. Are you sure this is even a good idea? To potentially destroy the entire world?” 

“The Black League will do whatever is necessary to avenge the Russian people. Even to the... even to the d-” 

“Death, yes I know. But have you ever considered what this might entail? For you? What if the Germans or Teutons as you call them are not grinded under your boot? What if you lose?” 

The soldier took a pause himself. I could see his Adam's apple move as he swallowed deeply, sweat building up around his brow. I had struck a nerve. His eyes darted from side to side. The atmosphere suddenly became far more oppressive, as if a blanket was placed over the both of us. The hairs on the back of my neck stood straight up. 

“I'm sorry sir, but our time is up. Your ship will be coming for you soon. In the meantime, you may stay at one of our hotels.”[Change Later]
strings.OMS_forpol.5.a: The weapons are enough for now.
strings.OMS_forpol.6.desc:
[Change Later]“Ladies and gentlemen. Citizens of the free world. I, Comrade Dmitry Yazov, come to you with an urgent address and a warning of what is to come for the people of Russia.”

This message would not be broadcast to our people. We will not pollute their ears with our lies.

“The forces of expansionist fascism are powerful. The German threat to our west is wary of our resurgence, and their repeated incursions into our rightful borders have become more determined and numerous over the past months.”

On the western front, experimental pushes into Moscowien territory by Black League reconnaissance forces were met with remarkably little resistance. Their sloth would be their undoing.

“German Nazism is a poisonous ideology. It extols militarist expansionism, a mythologized ideology of racial purity, and upholds slavery as just some of its many core tenets.”

In prisons to the north, countless prisoners were worked to death in the forced labor of frozen work camps. Their blood will grease our war machine.

“All the Russian people have ever desired is safety and security. To live a life without the constant threat of invasion hanging over their heads. Despite our best efforts, we have been forced to harden our defenses against the fascists who wish to again reduce us to the anarchic chaos that defined these lands before our Reconstruction Authority managed to retrieve what had been lost for so many years.”

Deep underneath the western taiga, top secret networks of underground bunker systems run for many kilometers. None will know of their existence until it is too late to stop us.

“Our desire was to rebuild what had been taken and forge a new peace. But now we find ourselves preparing for war.”[Change Later]
strings.OMS_forpol.6.a: There was never truly an option.
strings.OMS_forpol.7.desc:
No. 089-32-46							           Date: [DATA EXPUNGED]

FROM: [DATA EXPUNGED]

TO: Dmitry Yazov

SUBJECT: Comrade Yazov, it has come to my attention that a contingency of Red Army remnants have been coerced into infiltrating the Manchurian border along our far eastern border. Our efforts have gone unnoticed by the high command in both Japan and Manchuria. We have aided these remnants by giving them intelligence reports necessary to carry out operations and avoid detection by regular army units of Manchuria. Villages along the border have become strong points for our forces to gather more men and material for further operations deeper within Manchurian territory.

Furthermore, the remnants inside foreign territory have requested our own contingency of forces to assist them for large-scale operations, such as harassment of enemy soldiers, further gain in territory and solidifying what territory is already held. This request has been personally ordered to be delivered to you personally, Comrade Yazov, as the clandestine nature of the situation presents an opportunity to right a wrong committed against our people by the barbaric Japanese.

The decision rests on you alone, Sir. How should we approach this situation?
strings.OMS_forpol.7.a: Arm the remnants, and send them an attache. The Japanese are not a priority.
strings.OMS_forpol.7.b: Send in our forces. Right the wrong committed against our people.
strings.OMS_forpol.8.desc:
Kirill woke up to the same sound he did every day. Chaos. For such an orderly state of being the Army claimed to be, the barracks were quite the scene. I guess that’s what you can expect putting a bunch of rowdy teenagers together with not much to do.

Then in came the sergeant. Everybody scrambled to attention in front of their bunks. After screaming at some privates who were in a less than admirable shape, he began speaking about their mission.

“Listen up! You lot are heading east...quite a bit east. To Manchuria to be exact. Before you start yelling, don’t ask me any fucking questions because I don’t know. You have two hours to get ready, so hurry up and pack.”’

The sergeant waltzed out with the same casual bravado he entered with. Once the doors closed the chaos resumed once more. 2 hours was more than enough time to pack. The other men, if you could call them that, began singing, cheering, and smoking. Kirill just sat on his bed.

“Manchuria? I might as well march to the moon. Were they not meant to fight the Germans?  The Teuton menace? No, surely I didn’t join for this. I am meant to fight the Germans. To avenge my fallen father and honor my family. How could I do that in Manchuria?” He wondered.

Kirill looked around. Sure there were some thinking like him, but overall there was an atmosphere of glee. They cheered that they were going to fight. They cheered that they would finally become heroes.

“That is why I joined. To become a hero. To serve my nation. I suppose there is no difference if it’s in the West or East. Papa surely will be proud of me, no matter where.” He reasoned at last. 

Kirill put his worries behind and joined his friends. They drank and smoked. They sang and cried. They toasted that they would be in Vladivostok within months.

Hours later everyone was packed and they were about to march. The excitement had died down and his stomach began eating at him. He thought of his mother crying when he left. He thought of his father leaving to fight. He thought of his village and of his sister. He was eager to fight but he missed them all so much. He was left with those thoughts as they marched on the muddy roads.
strings.OMS_forpol.8.a: Anxiety and excitement make a noxious potion.
strings.OMS_forpol.10.desc:
Manchuria was damn cold. When Kirill was told he was going to fight the Japanese, he imagined something more...exoctic. Jungles, rice farms, something. All he saw was cold forests and cold plains.

He was huddled around a campfire with the other boys. They were all so different, yet all so alike. Another gust of wind blew into his bones. It got cold in Tyumen, but it was nothing like this. The wind blew right through you. At home he had his mother and the samovar. He had warm blankets. Here he had his uniform, a shabby tent, and a campfire. The campfire was a struggle. Too close and it burned. Too far and you’d freeze.

Since they left Tyumen a battle had been waging in his soul. One side was his excitement for revenge and service to his motherland. The other was homesickness and fear of what’s to come. The fear was winning.

Kirill briefly heard the sound of the tent flapping and turned around. There stood the lieutenant. He was a beast of a man. He walked to the center and yelled in his raspy voice about the Japanese and some guerillas. Kirill was trying to pay attention but he was on the verge of dozing off. Then all of the sudden...

“Up! Up! Get on your feet! Up! Out of the tent! Out!”

Like animals they were driven out. Kirill certainly wasn’t tired anymore. Those who lagged behind were beaten by the officer’s baton. They were herded out onto a field. There was shouting and screaming but he couldn’t hear now that the helicopters began to roar. He soon got the message though when the whips began to come down.

The cattle were herded into separate helicopters. That’s just what they were, cattle. They had no autonomy. No self thought. No hopes or dreams. They were merely at the mercy of their master’s whips. They ate when they were told. They slept when they were told. They moved when they were told. They fought when they were told
strings.OMS_forpol.10.a: Is a man with no free will still a man?
strings.OMS_forpol.12.desc:
When the helicopters landed, Kirill and the other men were immediately wrangled out. Their officers told them they were going on a long march. Something about if they landed too close the Japs would spot them. They drugged for miles upon miles. Despite the chilly winds, Kirill was sweating. When they finally got to the top of the hill he was out of breath, but then he saw them. The partisans! Officers shouted back their code words to identify the groups, but it was soon drowned out by cheering from the Red soldiers. They started running and naturally the Black soldiers did the same. They met together in the middle in a blissful celebration.

“How are you!” “What a fancy gun that is” “Does that old thing still shoot?” “Why, my farm horse has a better coat!” “That was some march..” “Anybody know how my home is doing? I’m from Barnaul?”

First it was cheering and sharing names. Then in an unorderly march that would put the higher command into a fit of rage, they waltzed back to the partisan’s camp. There they were met with the sweetest gift of all, alcohol. The partisans poured shots for the soldiers, but most of these boys could hardly stomach vodka. Yet, over the night they would learn how to.

The two colors of soldiers, red and black, became one in an instant. They played cards, chess, drank, sang, danced, cried, and laughed together. It was the happiest the partisans had been in decades. Not only was it their night, but it was the happiest Kirill and the black men had been in months. These men weren’t barking orders or threatening court martials. No, they were friends. They were old soldiers who understood their plight and after a night of partying they would kick the Japs right back to Korea.

After a night of great fun, Kirill stumbled back to where he dropped his things. He had his blanket over him and the drink had warmed his body. As he dozed off to sleep he only had one thought...
strings.OMS_forpol.12.a: ...with the partisans at our side, we will be okay.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.1.desc:
It had been a rather trivial sector of the reclamation efforts, but a sector worth fighting nonetheless. Whatever was Russia’s at any point would be Russia’s eternally, by the sacred right of the people. Primorsky Krai, or as the pan-Asians called it, Outer Manchuria, had been in their hands for decades, and had only recently fallen to imperialist hands, hands which had turned the land into something more of a wasteland and an industrial hellhole, rather than a rightful homeland. As would be the right thing to do, following the First Trial, there remained thousands of Russians and peoples formerly under Soviet rule who remained, armed but weak, resolute but small.

The IJA had been pacifying the region for years, leaving only a few devotees who remained to be a thorn in the sides of the Empire, anything to prepare it for a return to Russian sovereignty. Yazov had a realization, and called up his general staff, including Savintsev, to make a new case as a prior goal before the endgame came into play. “My fellow brethren, I understand that there is territory of the Motherland not under our control, not just occupied by the treacherous Reich, but also by the blind Empire.” The staff talked amongst themselves. One opted to chime in with a simple question, “What do you suggest we do?” “It’s rather obvious.” That day, a plan was drawn up with vigor.

Slowly but surely, a constant stream of resources, rations and rifles, would trickle into Primorye, supplying the resistance with whatever they needed to present a significant threat. As Yazov put it, “As much as they need before they grow into a nuisance that we can intervene on behalf of.” Not only this, but several units of soldiers would be deployed in strategic positions across the region to help destabilize Japanese control over the land and deliver it into the hands of the Black League. Yazov dubbed it “Operation: Alexseyev”. By the time he went to bed, units were selected, and the precise number of resources was spared.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.1.a: Rest was something Yazov would need, for he wouldn’t have it again.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.2.desc:
The one time for bureaucracy was over, as Yazov wrote his signature on starting Operation: Alexseyev, and a large portion of the eastern forces of the Black League apportioned to the effort of destabilizing Primorye. By the end, hopefully, it would be ripe for reclamation, one step on the way to taking all of Russia’s original territory. Thousands of able-bodied men from Magadan, Kamchatka, Amur, and several other cities were pulled and conscripted as the manpower behind the operation. Besides this, sets of agents were deployed across the region to provide the partisans with crucial intelligence and weaponry.

Sowing the seeds of anger amongst the rebels, and creating restless rebelliousness in the region was only step one. Savintsev was fully aware of this, knowing that at some point, this arrangement would eventually be ended, and the capabilities of Russian counterintelligence would find their limit.  In the office of Sakharovsky, there lay a map of Outer Manchuria on the desk. Beside it was a list of all the settlements in the land, compared with their Japanese names. One by one, he provided his own estimates for when each would be reached and later liberated when the League’s firepower were to be tested in a foreign conflict for the first time.

In Amur, out of the still-standing buildings, two soldiers bound for deployment were eating rations, and talking about their families back home. “Vanya is barely five. He’s hanging on for dear life.” And now, his father was off to another country to do something he didn’t fathom he’d be capable of. His comrade was guilty of forgetting how much he’d missed out on. “Your son loves his country. Do you?” Surely, he hadn’t just said that. He sounded stir-crazy. The father responded with a poignant statement.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.2.a: “So much that I want to live for it.”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.3.desc:
Vasily pulled a cigarette from his mouth, teeth already rotting. He only knew the bare minimum of war: that it was bad, and that he’d have to live with it. Besides that, not much, apart from the training with a rifle. Even then, this was espionage, not actual war. “So, how hard is it going to get?”

“Very hard, if that isn’t obvious already,” responded Alexei. While he did look younger than Vasily, he was, in fact, more experienced than he, having already faced Spartan levels of drilling and constant drivel from the higher-ups for a year or two. He didn’t like to keep count of how long he’d been beaten to death.

Iosef was busy making sure his rifle wasn’t jammed; it had happened too many times, and he wasn’t going to stand for another grilling by a superior. After all, his colleagues used to joke that if it weren’t for a fellow’s brave sacrifice, Iosef’s incompetence would mean they wouldn’t have the Far East. “Come on, this is ridiculous. Loyalty first, gossip second.”

Of course, Pyotr simply watched this mess of a squadron try and fail miserably to make small talk. “You all need to square up. The Motherland waits for no one.”

Alexei had a response up his sleeve, rolled up anyhow.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.4.desc:
Angels of death, as they were described by the locals. The Spetsgruppa could be considered such, even if they were not angels at all, they were there to deliver divine punishment.

The translator was bound to collapse at any point if he did not rest, but he tried his best to keep up with the constant flow from the arriving soldiers, who’d jumped off planes and tried their best to land properly, but ended up stumbling on the ground. The locals were watching them land, and understanding their uniforms, opted to help them if only they would return the favor. Indeed, this was the mission.

“We promise you bread, we promise you ammunition, we promise you liberation, and only on one condition.” On paper, it sounded like a good deal coming from the commander of the Spetsgruppa unit. At least, on paper, that is. A resistance member rightfully questioned the condition of said deal, too good to be true. He bravely quipped, “What’s the price?” “Your unquestioned loyalty to the Black League, to the Motherland, to Russia. In return, we give all this.”

The resistance leader asked the translator to ask for the official oath of allegiance. After it was requested, the unit leader spoke with a clear voice, all Russian, and the translator relayed the message in the native language, even though there were Russians within the local resistance group. Several members got down on one knee and raised a hand straight to the air.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.5.t: Birds That Cried, Birds That Whistled
strings.OMS_more_flavor.5.desc:
A few dozen operatives were called to a local village, an apparent hotspot of anti-Japanese activity. They fired their rifles into the air, clearing out the street, and leaving only the partisans to fire back. Said partisans would follow their creed to death, and so the triggers exploded, so the metal pellets flew faster than birds.

In both directions did the ravens of metal speed in any way, their targets men, country first, human second. A few “brave martyrs” made a run for it, bearing the symbol of death on their uniforms, and not to prolong their lives, nor to prolong their suffering, but to cut those of their enemies, and to deliver suffering to those on the opposite side. A few shrieks and screams from children whose ears were not spared from the gunfire, a few claps of wings from actual birds of flesh, too many whistles of smoke and of death.

It wasn’t so easy to say that the fire had ended, for it hadn’t. Young Takeshiro was the first to rise from the ashes from all the bullets that had fired, for the few surviving partisans knew if they wanted to kill more, they’d have to leave for another day. Into the green forests, they ran and ran while pursued unsuccessfully by a few Manchurian police. Meanwhile, Takeshiro, clutching onto his heart, looked around, fixing his eyes on a wooden crate.

Takeshiro pried one open, and found it filled to the brim with Mosin-Nagants, too many to count. He then ran to another, opened it, and saw it filled with ammunition. There were at least a dozen more in his field of vision. “Commander! You should come and see this.”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.6.desc:
It was 2300 in military time, and Modest was ready to go to sleep. He was already nodding off on the wheel, but he had a job to do. Delivery men put their work before their rest, so he thought. Nevertheless, Modest would protest if he could do so without getting his tongue cut off.

Modest was one of many in a column of Russian vehicles that was on a delivery mission to get through Manchuria and drop off crucial supplies for local resistance contacts. All it would take was a single checkpoint, likely empty considering its dire state. Modest had heard from colleagues that it was already rotting and would be an easy way in. As the column approached the border, the delivery man dwelled on the rumors he’d heard, rumors of people getting shot, people from the League who were completing much the same mission as he before they were promptly killed.

The delivery man knew it was nighttime, though, and it couldn’t be that bad. Before the column could even reach the checkpoint, however, the truck in front of him quickly stopped on the brake, forcing him to do the same. Several vehicles ahead, there was an argument going on, and it wasn’t between the drivers. There were both Manchurian and Japanese police at the scene shouting over the drivers and telling them to turn back. It turned out the Empire wasn’t exactly complacent about border incursions on their “sovereign territory.”

“What’s the hold up?”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.6.a: “Go back, go back to where you came from!”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.7.desc:
Routine missions, thought Shoto. The Imperial Japanese Army Air Service pilot looked on. His instructions were different than usual, not a mission he’d known about, not a mission he’d expect. Shoto took off his glasses to check for any mistakes; none to be found. Shoto simply took off as he normally would, and a fly-over ensued. He was the first to do the mission, and he wouldn’t be the last. It was an aerial photography operation, to see if there were any “peculiarities” on the ground that required the further attention of his superiors. At least, that’s how his commander phrased it.

Indeed, the photos Shoto took of certain targets were conspicuous, boxes or piles of rifles that didn’t corroborate with any IJA ground operations. What Shoto didn’t know was that the higher-ups were reviewing the photos with intent, as if they knew what was going on - they did. If it wasn’t the IJA, it was the only other suspect. The next day, the airbase was filled with more pilots, pilots with much the same skills and same instructions as Shoto. He was rightfully confused, but he couldn’t pay any mind to it.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.8.desc:
The radio went silent - only after gunshots and yells of desperation were heard coming out of it, to the obvious horror, audibly and mentally, of the soldiers listening in to their “comrades”’ last transmission. Even though it may have been regarded as dishonorable, some wept, some covered their mouths or their eyes, while others knelt. It was all the same, it was sympathy. They were friends that had fallen, fathers, brothers, sons, uncles, grandfathers, neighbors, comrades, on and on, and gone by the hands of those filled with undying hatred for people they’d never met. Why?

“Back to work!” A general barged through the doorway, having no idea what he’d walked into. “Haven’t you heard? A base was overrun!” Even though the underclassman would likely be punished for yelling back, he still had the decency to explain why all of them were standing, sitting, or lying down in shock. “By who?” “The Russians!” The broadcast wasn’t the only one, it was but one out of several instances where Manchurian territory was being taken over, and not silently, by Russian forces under the pretense of stability.

The general was pissed, but he did have the power of the IJA behind him, and he wasn’t the only general with the same idea. It therefore fell to the Kwantung Army to fix the issue, as if it were a minor matter. Not a day later, hundreds of soldiers stood, rifles at the ready, waiting to be yelled at and to yell at their fellow soldiers on their way to meet their match on the frontlines.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.8.a: A mighty Empire guards its doors, while the same doors come crashing down.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.9.desc:
“Just how dumb do you think we are?” The Japanese minister wanted to strangle the ambassador, but he couldn’t, lest he risk pissing off the entire Black League and have blood on his hands. Nevertheless, he summoned the Russian Foreign Ambassador to Tokyo, and he was going to ensure that Russia knew how angry the Empire was.

“I have no intention of considering you less intelligent for any reason besides warmongering.” The ambassador chose his words wisely. He wasn’t going to allow an international incident, at least, not this early in the process. There was still much to do, but it could all be taken away in the snap of a finger if he weren’t careful enough. In hindsight, he wasn’t. Russian and Japanese troops were fighting each other while they were speaking, and the minister made sure this was known, before he revealed it to the public. “The Imperial Japanese Army is facing off against your Black League, ready to defend itself by any means necessary.” However, revealing it to the public meant weakness, weakness the Empire couldn’t afford to publicize. After a terse conversation that ended with a refused handshake, the ambassador called up Yazov, knowing full well he was being recorded. “We can’t do it anymore.”

On the other end of the line, Yazov’s hand was shaking. The phone was trembling, and there was a brief moment of silence before he responded with a simple question: “Is it the end?” The ambassador used a rather poetic and proverbial answer to Yazov’s curiosity. “No, my Glavkoverkh.”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.10.desc:
Nazerov began to wake from the beating he took. The events flashed through his mind rapidly, oscillating between vague, hazy memories and solid red. He was in a bar, resting. His sheep had been settled in for the night, so he took the rest of it for his nightly rituals. Then, out of nowhere, men from outside the small village dragged him outside. Now, as he began to stir, he could hear the voices more clearly. They were Russian.

“No... no. I have money. I have sheep. I can make you a rich man. I have names.” He stammered in heavily accented Russian.

“It's not names we want.” One of them snarkily replied. He peered backwards to see a lone tree, and another man tying a noose around one of the thicker branches. He began to thrash. “No! No, I've done nothing wrong. I've been accused of no crime! When the militia hears of this-”

“If you mean the other collaborators, have no fear. They're next.” The band laughed as they hoisted him onto a stool, gently sliding the thatch rope beneath his chain and around his neck. Nazerov tried one last time to beg for mercy.

“Please, I have a wife. I have children. I... I didn't do anything wrong. I never stole, I supported the Motherland during the war, I sw-” His words were cut off as the brigands kicked the stool out from under him. His vision slowly went black as he suffocated, his limp body hanging from the branch. With a curt whistle, the Russians moved out to search for the next name on the list.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.10.a: No collaborators will escape our wrath.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.11.desc:
TO: Glavkoverkh Yazov
FROM: Colonel Igor Rodoinov, Far East Command

Comrade Gavokoverkh,

The situation here in the Far East has changed dramatically for the worse. In addition to a significantly increased force concentration of Japan and its allies in the region, American air and naval vessels have been spotted training together close to our maritime border. These military exercises have been nonstop for the last week and a half.

We do not have much time to prepare further defenses in eastern Siberia. It seems both the American and Japanese are preparing to launch an attack by land, air and sea. We must assemble a force to guard any ports in the region and enough men to hold back the joint OFN-CPS invasion for they must not interfere with our Great Trial.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.12.desc:
The finest minds of the League had done it again and Oleg was being given the privilege of being the first to test out this new weapon of vengeance that was to be used against the hated Hun in the west. In his mind's eye he'd pictured a better AFV that could withstand the German's shells better than their current vehicles. When the scarred veteran of the reunification wars was in store for, however, was something entirely different.

Out in a concrete testing facility outside of Irkutsk he now found himself wearing a protective hazmat suit that was heavy enough on its own even without the chemical tank he was now carrying on his back. The weapon was familiar to the flamethrowers he'd used to clear out trenches not too long ago when the League reclaimed these parts of Siberia from Russia's domestic enemies, though if it was just a regular weapon the eggheads wouldn't go through this much trouble for a simple test. Across from him was a dilapidated, open-topped Ural-355 truck with its carriage full of mannequins wearing German helmets. To his left and behind what seemed like a meter of protective glass, the scientists running this experiment.

\“Are you sure this is safe?\” Oleg asked, though the question was more aimed at himself than the scientists that wouldn't be able to understand a single one of the muffled words that he was saying even if they were in the same room. They simply gave him a thumbs up. With a deep breath, he pulled the trigger, half-expecting this to be his last moment on earth.

Instead, he struggled to stand firm on the ground as a tremendous stream of corrosive chemicals spewed forward from his weapon all over the truck, strong enough to corrode the metal the truck was made of and the concrete floor alike while making short work of the mannequins. Left in the wake of this attack were green, noxious fumes of deadly chemicals that even his thick rubber suit barely protected him from. At that moment, he could only think of one thing.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.13.desc:
This small Siberian village had survived the revolution, the Entente intervention and the Smuta without a single shot being fired within its vicinity. When the Black League scoured across the steppes of Siberia to reclaim it for their righteous cause, however, it had ended up being the spot of the last stand of a platoon of traitors to the Motherland. Subsequently it ended up being their graves. The evacuated villagers remained in the city after the war and now it, too, had met its end.

A GAZ-69 jeep was the first sign of actual human life the village had seen in a long time. Vadim and Kliment were driving through this village on the stretch of road that went through the main street. It wasn't a pretty sight. Each of the ten missiles had been designated to strike the same coordinates, yet each of them had veered off-target by a large margin with some of the craters being visible on the hills just outside of the village. Parking by the former grocery store that had been marked for bombardment, just about everything but it seemed to be standing after the initial volley of rockets had hammered the ghost town.

Vadim, a lanky and sardonic fellow, stepped out of the driver's side and looked around at the mayhem the scientists had caused. \“It'd be comedic if we weren't expected to rely on this to take out strategic targets.\”, he remarked as Kliment stepped out of the jeep./n\“If anything it seems better at creating foxholes for the Teutons than hitting the bastards.\”, his colleague replied, clearly on the same wavelength as long as the disciplinary officers weren't looking.

\“Let's survey the site and head back to the facility. The colonel ain't gonna like this if he expected the eggheads to deliver a precision weapon.\”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.13.a: \“An elated colonel went on to recommend its mass use against German urban areas.\”
strings.OMS_more_flavor.14.desc:
With an effective payload nearing eighty megatons, Object 416 has exceeded all expectations even though it is currently unfit for use by our strategic forces. Due to its rushed development cycle the weapon is highly unstable and the payload generates an explosion so powerful that it vaporized the plane that flew it. Due to the primitive state of our missile capabilities, it's advised that alternative delivery mechanisms are developed for future tests.

The effects are of grave concern. Despite being dropped at what was presumed to be a safe height over the unpopulated steppes, the collateral damage has been enormous as the destructive potential of the bomb exceeds anything predicted in our preliminary calculations. Entire cities were set ablaze several kilometers away from the blast radius and the effects of the bomb are reported to have been felt as far away as Tehran and Sverdlovsk, registering as a small-scale earthquake by seismographic centers in the Middle East and eastern China. Tragically, some of the soldiers deployed to restore order in the region were casualties despite sheltering in what was assumed to be safe bunkers. Additionally, because of our underestimation of the explosive effect, several localities beyond the mandatory evacuation zones were affected as well.

Due to the intense firestorms and radiation near the point of detonation it'll be a substantial amount of time before we can fully assess the damage of this weapon. In conclusion, if used against a Teutonic metropolis it would inflict within a moment what they spent three decades doing to our Motherland.

Signed,
N.M Demichev
strings.OMS_more_flavor.14.a: The sword is what we will drive straight through the heart of the Reich.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.15.desc:
Oberführer,
Space-based surveillance platforms have confirmed our suspicions that earlier reports of an earthquake in Kazakhstan were false and that it was in fact a test of a nuclear device called the AN416 carried out by the Russian National Reclamation Government. While the nuclear device was successfully deployed, the careless handling of the weapon by the Slavic state led to a nuclear catastrophe on their own soil with a soaring casualties as a result.

While it is of no small amount of concern that this rogue state possesses the capability of developing such powerful weapons to begin with, the silver lining in all of this is that this self-inflicted wound will set back their nuclear program by several years and is bound to destabilize the state.

As the failed Russian state has so far only proven itself capable of destroying itself, my recommendation is that we don't blow their cover story at this time. There is no reason to alarm our population or risk aggravating this shamble of a state into further experiments. The truth will bear out eventually.

Our men will continue to monitor the situation. Unfortunately, our last contacts within the Turkestan Legion are considered a write-off at this point. Action: Signed,
Karl Himmelstoß, SS-Obersturmbannführer
strings.OMS_more_flavor.16.desc:
Director,
Our satellites as well as intercepted German intelligence from the Sicherheitsdienst indicate that our suspicions were correct in that the Kazakh quake was in fact caused by a failed nuclear experiment carried out by the Russian government. The device, referred to as Object 416 by the Russians, is a bomb of tremendous explosive power that may eclipse any of our own weapons, though its instability means that it's unfit to be used as a weapon. Because of the origin of the device, it'll internally be referred to as the Glavkoverkh Bomb from here on.

While they were able to successfully test the Glavkoverkh Bomb, miscalculations on their part led to widespread damage that extends far beyond the impact site in the open steppes of Kazakhstan. The Russians clearly did not intend for the bomb to have this effect. So far, the Russian government is sticking to the cover story of an earthquake and remains a closed state. The Germans seem intent to allow this charade to stand so as to not cause further instability in the region, believing that the Russian government will crumble on its own. Both the Agency and the Germans also assess that the domestic nuclear catastrophe caused by the Glavkoverkh Bomb test will set the Russian atomic weapons program back by several years.

While the Russian possession of nuclear arms remains a concern, there is little reason to cause an international scare over the situation. Public knowledge of a nuclear catastrophe on that scale would lead to domestic protests over our own atomic weapons programs, something we can ill-afford in the middle of an arms race. Moreover, we have no reason to to destabilize the Russian government as they remain a thorn in the side of the Germans.
strings.OMS_more_flavor.17.desc:
Thanks to the efforts of the Kempeitai we have been able to determine the falsehood of the Russian claims of an earthquake in their occupied regions of Central Asia.
